input_chunk: It's nice to be with people but it's nice to be alone. And you never had that, something that was your own. And in the 06:60 Aussenkommando we had to cut bushes down on the Vistula River which was the main river of Poland. It was pretty chilly by then, it was the end of September and October, it's very cold there, the climate is horrible there. There's malaria there, it's a bad climate. And one of the guards, he was a Hungarian that was taken in, he took pity on me and gave me his food, and I asked him why, if your doing it he could be killed by that, and he said, 'I don't want to be here, really, I didn't wanna be here. Where I lived there was some Jewish family who were very good to my family and I want to pay it back.' And things like that gave you extra strength, that you saw that the world didn't go completely cuckoo, you know, that there are some humans even here who are decent. That sort of gave you courage, and the other thing was that my father kept in touch with me through human messages, telling me where he was. He worked very hard, he had to carry toilets and got a doublesided hernia because he didn't know how to carry. He had to shine trumpets, polish instruments for the musicians. He had to put up hard shoe polish, I understand. But then at the end, some of the people from my home town who had been old prisoners, because the old prisoners, you know, it was . . . there were 07:02 people at higher ranks and some old prisoners had higher ranks. The Germans trusted them and gave them jobs to do. And some of them were able to get my father to become a doctor in the camp taking care of the prisoners. So his life had improved a great deal, he didn't have to stand Zell Appell. We got better food. Some of the prisoners who got cigarettes they would give to him and because he didn't smoke, he was able to exchange it for food. And he would send me a tomato sometimes, which was a gift unthinkable. And, those things kept you going. And then I heard there was woman, her position was 'Schreiber' or Writer [secretary?], and that was the highest position a Jew could have. She spoke several languages, she was very smart. And her position was to be in charge of all the accountings, of all the Zell Appells and responsible for it. That the numbers jived and are correct. Now that was a very responsible position. And she found out that under this number who is the name, and one day she came to us, she wants to help. She called the number and I was terrified that the number was called. And I said, 'Why do you want to help?,' you know, even from Jews you become suspicious. And she told me that her sister, and I knew who she was talking about, her name was 'Goldstein,' lived in our home town and she resembled her a little bit. She said, they were I remember big Zionist, her sister and brother in-law and the two children, and my father saved the sister's life and the child in childbirth. 24 And even they don't live anymore, but she wants to help us through it. So, you know, I always say you never know in your life when you help someone who benefits from that help. It might be someone totally unrelated or, you know. I was now standing on the roof, cold and trembling, my stockings and my coat were torn and try as I might I could not climb back in. Then I heard the key in the door and the official appeared to fetch me for the interrogation. I will never forget his sneering words when he saw the empty room. “You thought you could escape. But that does not happen with the Gestapo.” He refused to open the door and pulled me by my hands through the small window back into the room. Then I was taken to the interrogation. The address on my identity card was still the one of my former lodgings in West Amsterdam and so I insisted that I lived there and that my name was Jo Bosch. He called me a damned Jewish liar and told me that he knew my name already and that my initials were B.L. That was a slap in the face for me, for I realised that I had been betrayed. My bag was searched, I had 80 fl with me which were at once taken away. These officials were Dutch N.S.B[14]. Their hatred was almost even worse than that of the Germans. In the evening I was handed over to the central prison in Marnix Street. where I stayed in a cell until the morning. - 8 - It consisted of a plank bed, a chair, a wash bowl and a toilet. A woman came in to search me. She took my scarf and gloves away and my shoes were put outside to prevent me from trying to commit suicide. The walls of the cell were covered with names, threats, and farewell letters, which were evidence of how many had been incarcerated before me. After some time I was handed a bowl of food through a glass window. Until late at night I heard the banging of doors, because, as I learned later, the same evening a big round-up had taken place. At 7.00am I was woken, I was given a small piece of wartime soap, a towel and an iron comb, and the official came in with water for the wash bowl. Then I got a jar of coffee and four slices of bread, which was the ration for the whole day. The police officer was nice to me so that I dared to ask him whether I could help him with his work in some way, thinking of a chance to escape. He informed me that I would soon be taken back to the Gestapo. In the assembly room were about 12 Jewish people and we were transported together on a lorry. I was among the first ones who were called from the cellar for their interrogation. They repeated all the questions of the day before and moreover they wanted to know who had provided me with ration cards. I told them that a man called Piet had brought them and that I did not know anything about him. After being threatened and insulted I was led back to the cellar and at noon all of us were taken to the German prison at Weterinsschans. After a second search – I had nevertheless succeeded in smuggling 20 aspirins – we were taken into a large room with 15 plank beds and about the same number of palliasses. All the women there were sisters in faith, most of them of course Dutch, who had been arrested during the past days. Q: Was there Œ from what you remember as opposed to what you know from history Œ do you remember a tension between Zionists and non-Zionists, because clearly the Zionists wanted people to say they wanted to go to Palestine. A: There was a lot of tension. There was a lot of tension between the non-Zionists and the Zionists. Some people were almost forced to go to Palestine. I know I would give people letters to say they were registered with me for the United States so that they could not be forced onto a transport to Palestine. Remember also, at this time, there was a lot of illegal immigration into Palestine and these people didn™t want to go. They™d suffered enough 53 from their point of view. They had not been Zionists because if their parents had been Zionists, they would have left Poland before the war and gone to Palestine. When one thinks of it, very few Jews really were going to Palestine from Poland, where there was tremendous poverty, tremendous anti-Semitism, long before the Hitler regime, and they didn™t go. It was a very difficult time for a lot of people, but it was a political situation and they were pushing these people to go. I was never in favor of it, I must say. Q: Do you remember Ben-Gurion visiting the DP camps? A: He came. Yes, he came up into the British zone. input_chunk: to leave Munich immediately. The woman thought, though, that this was an illegal recommendation and that it was just a ruse with something else behind it. She had heard this when speaking to Hess the day before. The matter had been mentioned. Following her advice, Mrs. Maison put herself to bed as if she were ill, and her old mother sat beside her. And so they waited for the Nazis. And indeed the three men they were expecting came, entering forcefully. One said mockingly: “Wherever one goes, the Jews are ill,” laughing nastily as he spoke. They soon backed down, however. After that, Miss. Negelsbach came more often and laid foodstuffs outside the door, but never rang so as to avoid thanks. This was at the time when Jews were not allowed to go into shops in Munich. As Mrs. Maison had heard nothing from her husband, she went to the Gestapo to enquire where he was. Straight away, someone shouted at her to ask what she wanted. Her question was answered with the words: “You’ll hear about it soon enough.” When her husband had been gone for 14 days, Mrs. Maison received an obviously dictated letter from him from Dachau with the message that he was well. On 14th July 1939 the Maisons emigrated to France on a direct flight to Paris. Initially they lived in the city with their daughter and her husband, Mr. and Mrs. Kochricht, but then drove – just for the weekend for recreation – to their simple little house in the countryside[4] near the Belgian border. However, the Maisons stayed there for six months while the Kochrichts returned to Paris. The Maisons then returned to the Kochrichts’ home later. When, in the early summer of 1940, German troops were outside Paris, their son-in-law decided that they must all be ready to travel within the hour. And they set off in their own car. Mrs. Maison reports that she and her husband took everything in good humour and had probably not really grasped the seriousness of the situation. On the journey, in astonishing optisimism, they wanted to have a look at the castles which interested them and send picture postcards along the way. Mr. Kochricht forbade this quickly and forcefully. They stopped on the way in various small towns and it must be emphasised that town committees were obliged to provide refugees with accommodation and straw sacks. Later the travellers learned that the way they had chosen to go was the most frequently bombarded route to the south of France and that many cars had been destroyed and many people had been killed on it. They didn’t make the link with the number of ambulances that crossed their path. They drove to Arcachon in the south of France because their granddaughter was in a children’s sanitorium recovering from a protracted illness there. This area near the Spanish border started off as unoccupied territory, but when the Maisons and the child’s parents had been there for two days, German soldiers appeared. And so they travelled onwards, leaving the child behind at the remote sanitorium in the woods at the doctor’s request. They went by car and stopped only in small places. In a village made up of only a few houses (Léglésand) the only inhabitants were old people who were not capable of real work. Every couple of days, they had to empty the pots which hung on every tree in the nearby woods and pour the resin which had collected there into large barrels. All those able to work had left the place. The Maisons and Kochrichts stayed there for a while in a little house on their own and could only walk little in the woods, because as a rule, they wanted to keep themselves hidden as much as possible. Our intended destination was Mauthausen in Austria. As we were going through Czechoslavakia, the Czechs spontaneously threw sandwiches, cigarettes etc. from railway bridges. Our train was longer than 70 trucks. - 7 - We could feel the sympathy the Czechs had for us. Some of my friends wanted to die. I talked to them, to give them encouragement and hope. I had managed to get hold of water, and also of a newspaper in which I read the military report. That raised my morale. One stop before Mauthausen – at any rate, it was after Linz – the train came to a halt. Here we were not accepted[9]. So we had to go all the way back to Nordhausen in the Harz mountains. Presumably the man in charge of the transport had misheard (!) things over the telephone. But what did it matter? It only cost a few thousand deaths. So we continued our round trip all the way to our final destination. Four thousand prisoners lost their lives during this transport that must be unique in history. Approximately 6,000 arrived in Nordhausen. There the same performance began all over again - bathing, shaving, disinfection etc. While bathing, I used the opportunity to pump myself full with water. But no matter how much I drank, for several days I was unable to quench my thirst. After a few days, 400 prisoners were selected to be sent to a smaller camp near Blankenburg am Harz. I was one of them. The train took two days for a distance of 50km. Having arrived, it took some time until the kitchen and everything else had been improvised. Then we were introduced to our new work. Whereas in Nordhausen the subterranean tunnels where weapons production took place had already been dug, in Blankenburg we had to start with hollowing them out from scratch. I thought to myself: do the Nazis still want to use that for this war? They would have needed a magic wand to complete the work for this war. Our masters knew this as well as I did. However, that did not stop them from shouting at us and hurrying us along while we were working. They were Germans who had been recruited as mining specialists. They found it impossible to deny their German mentality, in spite of the desperate military situation. Most of them came from the Ruhr Valley. When they heard how tricky things were getting there, many left their work and travelled without permission to their homeland, to see their families once more. They were all discontented, because of the hopelessness of the war and also because of the lack of food. And they had almost no cigarettes left to smoke. People were expecting the end within the next few weeks. Everyone was aware of the situation. Propaganda was now useless. Nevertheless, they were afraid to offer resistance . - 8 - Our food was getting very scarce. There were days when we were doing the heavy work in the coal mine on just one piece of dry bread [per day]. Our SS-chef, who was responsible for the catering for the prisoners, was an unscrupulous thug. Frequently it was too much of a bother for him to go and shop. This guy, Franz Kirchgassner, came from Hungary, where he used to work as a hairdresser in Vienna. Whenever he needed something for the SS-kitchen, he simply stole it from the prisoners’ store. I can therefore not remember having ever been given sweetened coffee in Fürstengrube, even though, according to our ration card, we were entitled to a certain quantity of sugar and it was recorded as having been handed out to us. Then we dined in complete calmness - 8 - I immediately went to my flat where I met my girlfriend and several comrades. We had a rather critical discussion. They all said to me: “you mustn’t lose time, you must go abroad immediately. Freedom for you will only be of short duration. In such a situation you are not going to be able to keep up playing a double role.” I was taken as quickly as possible across the green border into Czechoslovakia. From there I wrote a letter to my lawyer in which I terribly regretted to have abused his trust. I also wrote to the commissar saying that I had had a complete nervous break-down and would not have been able to help him in this situation. The commissar really did write me a letter to Czechoslovakia, in which he asked me to come back immediately given the troubles I had created for him through my flight. The trial against the group with which I had been arrested was held later, and high sentences were announced. From February 1934 to the end of 1937 I was in Czechoslovakia and Austria, from 1938 to 1940 I was in France, and from December 1940 to 1950 I was in the United States. The outside contact from the emigrated comrades to the inside [of Germany] from 1933 until the start of the war was never stopped. Illegal material always came in[to Germany] from abroad, and one was well informed about daily life in Germany. One of the crucial issues, however, was our help activities. Thus in honour of Ernst Eckstein who had been murdered in 1933 in Breslau, a fund had been created named after him which supported the next of kin of detainees, and which paid for their lawyers. There were inescapable difficulties during the emigration, it was not a selection but a mixture, highly qualified people and very primitive people came together. In France, for example, the work prohibition was almost demoralising especially for the artisans among us. We tried to hold together. The collective was very important when it was time to immunise individuals against all sorts of offers. Hence everything was done to ensure that no one became a victim of foreign secret services. Spy work was not our thing. Big political differences occurred among us, the attitude to Russia was always the cardinal question and created internal schisms. Until the time of the popular front in France we lived very isolated as a political group. But there had been points of contact with the SPD. When we then had to flee from the Germans, we first came to Motauban where German and Austrian socialist were living. We were - 9 - supported in the framework of the solidarity actions of the AFL and the Jewish Labour Committee, and from there got our danger-visa to the States. The benefit of the political emigration was that this type of immigrant was not yet known. One was not alone, one found one’s way together. Europe at that time was at still the feet of the Nazis, the perspectives for the future were dark. Our main activity which was similar to a full time job, was to try to secure affidavits, that we did everything to save friends in danger. We obtained the most obscure visas for Mexico, Cuba etc.. Slowly we calmed down again and got together to analyse the situation. The US agencies were suspicious of us, they did not yet know this new type of immigrant. To get a base for the creation of our own circle, we had joined a circle of workers which had been founded years ago by east-Jewish workers, whose social institutions we could use. Within this organisation we rebuilt our political work. However, little by little one depended on oneself in terms of one’s existence. For a short while Alma lived together with her father, but then doing nothing became too much for her as she wanted to earn money and fled to Holland. She was also a great musician and had made a name for herself as a violinist. - 2 – In Holland Alma had a very difficult time, she lived hidden away and was then sent to France in 1942 by the Dutch underground movement, who then sent groups of up to 5 or 6 people. These groups generally received addresses of trustworthy people, who took them in and then sent them onto other friends. But Alma had no luck. When she came to Dijon with her small group the Nazis located this movement. She was stopped[2] and sent to Auschwitz. From this place there are different versions, but I can’t guarantee which one is correct. People said that she was used and chosen as a victim for experiments and was mistreated in the hospital camp. Then I heard that the camp commander, who really loved music, allowed her to keep a violin and form a small orchestra in the camp. He was so impressed by her music that he ordered the small band to play each time a new group of victims were led to the gas chambers. Alma died in Auschwitz in 1943. A Dutch nurse brought her violin to her father and told him that she saw Alma in Auschwitz. She was treated with great respect by all of the Nazis. She was laid out after her death, candles were lit and all of the camp inmates paid their last respects. Another friend, Professor Gottwald Schwarz, a well-known radio specialist in Vienna, responded to my card and asked me – between the lines – to get in contact with the Committee for Protection of Science and Learning, which dealt with helping German and Austrian scientists with emigration. After a lot of effort, I managed to get the institution to promise help, if it would mean that Professor Schwarz and his wife could successfully come here. She promised to pay 5 pounds[3] per week for him and his wife. But how could this good message be sent to Vienna? This is where the “English Friends”, Quakers helped out. A man, who was not allowed to take anything in writing with him had to keep the address and all of the details in his memory and drive to Vienna especially to take the message to Professor Schwarz. That worked and on the same day Professor Schwarz and his wife left Austria to head to England they had relatives who took them in. They were both physically and mentally completely broken when they arrived here. They told us how - 3 - they had suffered in Vienna. input_chunk: I could feel (translator’s note: the words ‘the attitude of the teachers and’ are here crossed out) my fellow-pupils turning against me. I was verbally abused, and my ‘Aryan’ female friends were increasingly distancing themselves from me. In our mixed school in 1934 we had to write a declaration in our exercise books stating that we were of ‘Aryan origin’. My father thought it appropriate to instead give this required declaration in a letter. As a result, I was shouted at by the class teacher with the words: “I thought as much!” Whenever I wanted to give an answer, or indeed say something about whatever was being taught, the automatic response was: “Insufficient. Sit down. Number four……” One day I clearly gave the teacher my opinion: that he should not treat my achievements with such antipathy. Whereupon he replied: “It’s certainly not a matter of antipathy, it’s just that I don’t appreciate the type of person that you are…..” These events had the consequence that I become conscious that I was a Jewess. I was proud to be ‘different’. In 1935 I was able to complete my Abitur, and in order to gain time I went to female higher school in Silesia which was run by nuns – School Sisters. I had tried to go to the Art Academy in Berlin to study enamel painting, stained glass window painting and drawing. I had passed the entrance exam, but I was not admitted as I wasn’t allowed to become a member of the Reich Cultural Association. Then I wanted to study the art of the goldsmith, but I encountered the same difficulties, as I wasn’t allowed to join the relevant art organisation. I also tried to study in the fields of medicine and chemical technology ….. no luck again. In the meantime in 1934 my father had lost his job. He was doing private work, sometimes as a journalist, sometimes as a book-keeper. I wanted to earn money as fast as possible, and so I entered a home for expectant mothers and their new-born babies – the ‘Dahlem House’, run by nuns. Here I learned the job of being an infant nurse and passed the home’s examination with distinction. However the Medical Council of the City of Berlin did not allow me this qualification ….. but I was ‘permitted’ to do the night shift for four weeks while the other girls took their exams. But they found me unsatisfactory in this role. I stayed for one year, from 1936 to 1937. Then I decided to try everything I could to learn the craft of a goldsmith, and because that was not possible for me in Germany I wanted to try in Denmark where the skills of the goldsmith are very popular. But I had counted on the fact that my father was not able to deposit enough money into a Danish bank and there was nothing left for me than to go to a Danish family and give up my idea of study. Unfortunately, I was particularly unlucky there, as the family comprised a Norwegian and his wife, who was a born German. She was very antisemitic and had made a point of having young Jewish girls come to her as ‘house daughters’ so she could then completely exploit them. When I realised that it was completely impossible for me to pay for an education, I went back to Berlin for some months. I tried to study medicine, but had to break off my studies after two months. I was then encouraged to study chemistry as there was a shortage of chemists. I had passed the matriculation examinations, but in common with other Jewish students, I had to sit on special seating with a Jewish textbook that bore a yellow stripe. My attempts to become a medical assistant also came to nothing. This educational path was blocked for Jews and half-Jews of the first grade. input_chunk: wire fence. A corridor, also lined with barbed wire, led directly from the camp into the IG-Farben complex. The workers had to pass through here, so that even on the way to work they could not escape being hemmed in on all sides by barbed wire. Later on, the blocks were better equipped and divided up into “sleeping areas” and a “common room”. However, the latter was soon taken over by “special prisoners” and the rest of the inmates were forced to occupy the cramped sleeping area, with no choice but to eat, sleep and spend their ‘leisure-time’ crammed into three-storey wooden bunks. The blocks were primitive, with no washing or toilet facilities, and it was a long walk to the latrine and washroom. Next to the prison camp was a separate camp for English prisoners-of-war, of which there were around 500. This camp was well-equipped and had spacious sleeping areas with decent-sized beds; the prisoners were given excellent food, and they had easier jobs with shorter working hours; they could also cook for themselves, and were allowed to receive parcels. There were also camps for civilian workers, recruited as part of Hitler’s “total war” strategy; these were organised according to nationality, with separate camps for French, Czechs and Poles. In addition to these, there was a much better-equipped camp for German workers - also civilians - and - 2 - another special camp reserved for skilled workers. All these camps were surrounded by a wire fence, but unguarded – with the exception of the prison camp, which was surrounded by SS guards. Location and organisation of the camp The IG-Farben complex at Buna was the chemical company’s new central plant, constructed for the Nazis as a site for the production of a range of synthetic products, principally fuel. The location was ideal, as the complex was sited close to the rich resources of the Upper Silesian Coal basin. By 1944, the plant was producing up to four wagons of fuel every day, as well as carbide and medicines. By 1944, the company’s entire research operation was centred on Auschwitz-Monowitz, and in the summer of that year there were around 63 chemical laboratories carrying out research and experiments using drugs of various kinds. These laboratories were concentrated in Buna mainly because a human experimentation station was situated just 6 km away. IG-Farben used to buy (mainly female) ‘recruits‘ from the camp, so that SS doctors, who were in the company’s pay, could use them to test the various medicines and drugs that were being produced in the 63 laboratories. You could get an idea of the sheer size and scope of the laboratory operation by the many thousands of special thermometers, pharmacy scales and test tubes that were kept in the stores, not to mention the wagonloads of laboratory glassware that were ordered. All of this equipment was used in the research laboratories at the Buna-Werke plant, where thousands of men and women became victims of the experiments carried out in the laboratories at Auschwitz by the likes of Clauberg, Göbel, Schuhmann, Dering and Wirts, among others, to discover the effects of the chemicals that IG were producing. Whenever representatives from IG‘s headquarters in Frankfurt visited, they made no secret of their intention – once the Nazis had “secured victory“ – of building a huge “slave city” around Buna, which would guarantee the SS a vast income and provide shareholders in the Buna plant with cheap labour for decades to come. Prisoners working in the offices recorded how the SS were paid 4-6 Reichsmarks per labourer per day, despite the amount of money spent on each prisoner amounting to just 60 pfennigs. It was, you know, he was in charge of the whole city, of the Catholic community. Mr. Richter was his name, Rev. Richter. I have even a picture of him because he taught us in the gymnasium and he taught us Latin. And he, when there was a nun, when he taught the Catholic religion, we were permitted to leave, you know, the classes. But, you know, we could choose to stay, but my father was his doctor and his mother's doctor, he chose him to be. And I know later on that my father was not permitted to practice anymore as a Jew. He personally, and I have his letter, wrote to the Papal Nuncio to allow this Jewish doctor to practice because as he wrote, he brought so many Catholic children into the world and cared so much about the poor. And my father used to give lectures because they were very primitive, some of the population, and they believed in all kind of nonsense, like a cat runs across the street, you know, this and that, and they practice this kind of medicine sometimes. And he used to go to schools and show how they should 05:29 wash their hands, how important that is, and taught them some simple health, you know, gave them health education. And he was written up in the Catholic newspaper, I still have some of the newspapers, even though they are almost in shreds. But, he made a name for himself as a very caring doctor who didn't choose, if it's someone Jewish or non-Jewish and many people were that way. I didn't see such a terrible distinction between Jews and nonJews, until the laws came against the Jews. After about four weeks, on 2nd October 1942, a group of four people was formed. These people, along with a group leader, would have to travel overnight from Chamonix over the Col de Balme at the expense of the IRRC. The leader would be able to take them 100m from the border before leaving them in the hands of fate. After several hours walking, the group found themselves on Swiss soil. They were stopped by a Swiss guard in Trento and taken for questioning. Switzerland did not want to accept them as political refugees, so they were sent back over the border to France. My wife managed to make a telephone call at a hotel and got in touch with Ms Kägi-Fuchsmann from the Swiss Workers Relief Agency in Zürich. (Refugees were strictly forbidden to make telephone calls). Ms Kägi was granted permission from Bern within half an hour, and the group was allowed to stay in Switzerland. They were sent to a reception camp. After my wife left the hospital, I still had a fracture that required an operation and due to a hematoma, I had to stay in hospital until the beginning of March 1943. During this time, Ms Kägi-Fuschmann pushed various members of the socialist party in Basel-Stadt (where the social democrats held the majority) to grant asylum to 12 German refugees. I was one of those 12. But because I could not get the departure visa from France, I had to make my way to Switzerland illegally. I was taken from Chamonix to Châtelard by a two trade union civil servants, both their sons and, due to my illness, two leaders. As we entered Switzerland, we were stopped by two border officers. After checking our papers, the officer informed the military authorities that the papers were in reference to five refugees who were all in possession of Swiss entry visas. The radiation was directed at their ovaries. She told me that men underwent this procedure too, with their reproductive organs being exposed to radiation. She did not name Dr. Schumann. She believed that this work was being carried out by Dr. Clauberg. She told me that Dr. Wirths studied the early detection of cancer. She also told me she assumed Clauberg was studying artificial insemination. Dr. Samuel later told me himself that he was working on examinations with the colposcope. Apparently, he dyed the cells at the cervix using the colposcope. When he observed changes, he cut out part of the cervix. These samples were collected and sent to a laboratory. A few days later, I began my work as a doctor without any special instruction. The occasion for this was the arrival of a transport from Holland. I determined that a few women were suffering from scabies, some had scarlet fever and three or four of them were pregnant. As I knew that sick prisoners were gassed, I did not report the scarlet fever cases. I later also carried out abortions for the pregnant women. I did not perform abortions - 5 - only on the Dutch women. I had Dr. Wirths’ permission for this. About three weeks later, I talked with Dr. Wirths in Block X. He summoned me to the room which is marked as the operating theatre on Photo 42. He was there with Dr. Samuel. Dr. Wirths told me that I was to continue Dr. Samuel’s work. I told him that I had already examined the newly arrived women. He asked “All of them?” and added that I had no business with Prof. Clauberg’s women. When I replied that I had screened them for scabies and other illnesses, he said that that was all right. As he left, he said in the corridor – so that the block elder and the female SS overseers could hear him – that I was now to be in charge of the medical direction of Block X. As was already the case before, I took over the general medical care of the inmates in Block X, from that point onwards on Dr. Wirths’ behalf. Dr. Wirths also mentioned that – apart from Prof. Clauberg and Dr. Muench – no SS doctor or SS officer was allowed to enter Block X without explicit permission from Dr. Wirths. I knew Dr. Dehring from my time at university. I talked with him in Block X a few days after my arrival there. He was the camp elder for the sickbay. Dr. Dehring told me that he had performed 17,000 operations in Auschwitz over the past year. He spoke mostly of stomach operations. He also told me that he had removed testicles and operated on the ovaries of the girls who had undergone irradiation. As far as I can remember, he told me that he carried out the latter of these operations with or for Schumann. Later, I saw for myself that Dr. Dehring performed oophorectomies. input_chunk: SS man finally said, ‘Now we’ll cut off his balls.’ I was taken into the medical room where I had to take off my trousers and had to stand to attention with my face turned to the wall for ten minutes. Then I was allowed to put my trousers on again but had to take off my shirt and stand to attention, stripped to the waist for quite some time. At last also this performance came to an end and eventually I was taken into a dirty cell where I had to put my suit and underwear on the floor and lie on a straw mattress, wearing only my shirt. The door was slammed shut. Ten minutes later an SS man appeared and threw a dirty blanket, reeking of sweat, to me. But there was still no undisturbed sleep for me. About an hour later the door to my cell was pulled open noisily by an SS man who made a speech full of threats to the ‘Scheißjuden’ who would be treated with a ‘Kellermasche’ . When this pest had disappeared there was at last peace for me for three to four hours. - 4 - On Monday 12 March, soon after the order ‘Get up’, the SS guard on duty appeared in my cell and constantly threatening me with punches and pointing his revolver at me he forced me to repeat the following sentence, ‘I am a bloody Jew and a Jewish rider in the desert.’ Then I had a wash in the communal washroom together with other concentration (camp) prisoners when suddenly two people, ordered by the SS man on duty, held on to me and forced my head and my body down to the waist under the water tap. After this procedure I had to sweep my cell and the corridor while being insulted and threatened all the time, and afterwards I had to do so-called morning exercises which mainly consisted of press-ups on the dirty floor. This cruel treatment came to an end when a policeman came to take me back to the Geheime Staatspolizei. All that Monday I waited in the police cell of the Geheime Staatspolizei for an interrogation but in vain. In the evening I was taken back together with other prisoners in a police transport car to the Columbia Haus. During the following days I was treated extremely strictly and severely in the concentration prison but there were no more atrocities like those on the first night. An extreme hardship of the arrest in the concentration house is that the prisoners can relieve themselves only at certain times. It once happened that I could not go to the toilet for twenty-six hours. On Monday 12 March I was allowed to go to the toilet at five pm in the Prinz Albrechtstrasse (Gestafsa) where I had been taken for an interrogation which did not take place after all. Soon afterwards I was taken back to the Columbia cells in a police car. On Tuesday morning I requested to be allowed to go to the toilet. The SS guard whom I asked while standing to attention refused permission and pointed out that I could go to the toilet at noon. As I had not heard the order ‘Washing up of food dishes’ because of the permanent noise of commands in the corridors unfortunately I also missed the chance of going to the lavatory at noon. In the late afternoon when I already felt very miserable I tried again to be allowed to go to the toilet by putting the flag out of the cell. About an hour later the stick of the flag had been pushed back again into my cell. In despair I put the flag out again a little later. After about half an hour an SS guard opened the door to my cell but did not let me out because I was not standing to attention - 5 - satisfactorily. Only after another fifteen minutes did he come back and at last, after twenty-six hours, he allowed me to go to the toilet. In vain had I been waiting all the time to be questioned.

input_chunk: was a criminal who hit, blackmailed and bullied us. The luck in misfortune for me was that one day I was no longer in the condition to carry the so-called kerbstones. The barrow fell on my feet and the kerbstone cut through my right shoe and injured my toes. Despite my injury, the foreman would not allow me to go to the sick-bay, but my friends took me there in the evening and I was immediately admitted. The tip of one of my toes was amputated the next day and a Jewish prisoner, who had a good position in the sick-bay, ‘Jumbo’ Jellinek from Vienna made it possible for me to have two weeks there. After this accident, the foremen behaved a bit better and an acquaintance spoke to him, so that he did not bully me as much as before. In the spring of 1942, apprentice brick-layers were sought whether they were Jewish prisoners or not. I also reported to this command on the advice of a prisoner from Brünn, Robert Platscheks, who did the same and perhaps had good information. At the beginning, I had to carry water or bricks. Even here though, especially at the beginning, there were beatings and abuse. I was injured on the right leg by a brick which an SS man threw at me. In comparison to the other commands for Jews, for example, hauling carts, the camp streets or breaking stones, the building command was a relief. Then there was a very radical decision taken by the SS: one morning at the early assembly only the Jews in the building command were marched out. The others had to stay. At the same time, the Kapo, a prisoner called Robert Siewart, tried to send some prisoners, for example myself, to the camp, in order ‘to exchange’ them for prominent prisoners, as we later found out. I never followed the order and went walking with a water bucket and by the afternoon all of the ‘exchange’ was over. For example, I remember that the next day Carlebach fell in dressed as a bricklayer, that is, in the special work overalls of the building command. August Kohn also found a similar pretext. Some important people simply lay in the sick-bay as ‘sick’. Anyone who was not a builder or important was taken to some special block which were under the strict guard of the camp leadership. All of these Jewish prisoners were deported to Auschwitz from where some returned again to Buchenwald in 1944. At that time, only around 250 Jewish bricklayers remained in Buchenwald. The number increased again in the following months and years. After many months of apparent peace, apart from an air attack on the Gustloffwerk in 1943, approximately in the winter of 1943/44, a new action occurred and the first Jewish bricklayers were put on a report at work, that is, they received a notice as a result of allegedly bad work. The first cases went relatively well: withdrawal of food and later 3 days in the bunker accompanied by mistreatment by the SS. One day, some young bricklayers, actually from Vienna, were reported and we prepared in our community to give them bread and food. Instead, they were ordered at the morning assembly to gate 1 which was very suspicious. Gate 1 meant actually release and that was only for the Germans or other non-Jewish prisoners and never up till now for Jews. Of course, the Jewish bricklayers were not released, but taken to the sick-bay. Two days later they were murdered by an injection. Now panic spread amongst we Jews again. Nobody knew anymore how many days he had to live. Q: When did you realize the full extent of the genocide? A: When I -- when I finally got into Auschwitz, that™s when I first saw what was happening with the piles of bodies laying around there and the stench and the Interview with Henry Greenbaum December 20, 1999 71burning. And then we saw what happened. And then of course I -- I was always thinking about my mother and the other sisters that were taken away and I didn™t know where they were taken away and I still was hoping someday that maybe they™re alive, but -- but it™s not so. They perished somewhere. Q: You said you were in DP camp, but were you living with the other prisoners, or were you staying with the Americans? In fact, there was a building in there that we stayed with. We had our own beds and we stayed with them. We even wore the uniforms. Q: Did people help each other or did the whole morality change? A: Some helped. Now, it was all . . . I tell you, it was who you were. You didn't change that much while you were there, to tell the truth. If you were nasty, you got nastier. If you were mean, you got meaner, you know. Of course, circumstances could make you that way too. For instances, I was offered a job of the Stubendienst, and sometimes the Stubeindienst had to hit because if someone wasn't 'schnell' enough, you hit them to make them 'schnell,' some couldn't, they couldn't move. And I thanked them very much, I really didn't ask for such a job. But, it's a . . . Q: There were a lot of people though, that just..I mean, had to survive themselves, and . . . A: I have to talk about this. I had a cousin, who came with us. She died not long ago in Switzerland. Now, I have never met anyone like her because she came with us with the old lady and when we were first taken into the sauna she helped her to soap, not enough that she had to 'schnell! schnell!.' She took care of this old lady, and if someone was hungry she was able to give her food to that person, and you know, no one did that because the hunger was to such a degree, I mean, it's unbelievable to be able to be so hungry that you just didn't give what you had, you know, so she was able to be so good, and so, there were such people. There was a job called "stubendienst", "Stube" means "room," "Dienst" means "service," so it's room service. In this place, they took great care to paint the tiles red, or whatever. They broke bricks to make the color with water. And I offered to help and I had an advantage with that, that they let my mother lie up after the bunks were fixed and she could lie there and rest, so that was my advantage. And we worked hard, and one time, we had to work outside, it was called "Aussenkommando" , meaning "working outside." So after we stood we'd file out there and got our ration, there were an orchestra playing for us. There was an orchestra at the gate of the camp that led outside with the vicious dogs on the other side playing a march for us to march out. And I remember seeing a rotten apple as I walked and I was dying to have that rotten apple and one of the guards just kicked it away before I could get it. And as 23 we walked, I saw a little hut, I guess some of the guards lived, seeing some steam coming out and shade, by biggest dream was to live in such a hut, to be away from everyone because you were never alone, you couldn't wash by yourself there are millions of things in the wash room. You couldn't run the toilet alone, there were latrines that you sat back to back with people. It's nice to be with people but it's nice to be alone. And you never had that, something that was your own. And in the 06:60 Aussenkommando we had to cut bushes down on the Vistula River which was the main river of Poland. It was pretty chilly by then, it was the end of September and October, it's very cold there, the climate is horrible there. There's malaria there, it's a bad climate. And one of the guards, he was a Hungarian that was taken in, he took pity on me and gave me his food, and I asked him why, if your doing it he could be killed by that, and he said, "I don't want to be here, really, I didn't wanna be here. Where I lived there was some Jewish family who were very good to my family and I want to pay it back." And things like that gave you extra strength, that you saw that the world didn't go completely cuckoo, you know, that there are some humans even here who are decent. That sort of gave you courage, and the other thing was that my father kept in touch with me through human messages, telling me where he was. input_chunk: The swearing in was made possible by the approval of the Chamber of Commerce in Muenster and also the Chamber of Crafts there. This led the way for my technical accountancy examination, which was spread across a time period of 2.5 years. I was never a member of a political party. Likewise I have never been politically active. Well, I always actively worked for the interests of the Jewish community in Stadtlohn (Westphalia), my home town. Of course I am German. My family has played a role in the history of my home town for approximately forty years. Due to the so-called Aryan Law, my professional accreditation was withdrawn in writing on 3 May 1933 by the President of the Inland Revenue in Muenster. However, it was earlier, on 4 March 1933, that I was forbidden entry to all state and municipal administrative buildings. On 4 March 1933 I was arrested. The reason: I had allegedly been in close contact with the German Communist Party, smuggled weapons over the Dutch-German border and worked to provocate Hitler's government. Despite suspiscion, proof could not be obtained from the S.D.A.P (Socialist Workers' Party), on whose instigation I was arrested, so I was released in the evening of 7 March 1933 at around 7pm, although only to be exposed to an enormous smear campaign. I was no longer allowed to dare to enter the street. Constant surveillance by day and night was supposed to prevent me from making an escape to Holland, because it had been planned, as was said openly in public, to send me to prison by hook or by crook. Additionally to my occupation as an accountancy and taxation expert, - 2 - I was the representative of the old, pre-Hitler local authority, as well as of the savings bank in Stadtlohn under the previous director, who has since died. Because of my work, I always carried a gun and gun licence. My gun licence, as well as my gun and even my passport and accreditation certificate were taken from me on my arrest and the documents were immediately destroyed. I enclose the following reports: My dismissal due to the Aryan Law Statement of grounds for arrest (4 March 1933) Statement of grounds for dismissal (7 March 1933) Written refusal of passport from the consulate of Amsterdam (dated 15th June) everything in faithful copy. On 12.4.1993, I succeded, with the help of a smuggler I was acquainted with, to cross the Dutch border near to Winterswijk without a passport. From 12.4 to 5.5.1933, I stayed with friends in the community of Denekamp/Holland, to allow my nerves time to steady themselves because I'd experienced all sorts of things in the past few weeks. Regular encounters with the Storm Troopers, continuous harrassment, shootings in the middle of the street, the Storm Troopers shooting at our house in the night of 21 March 1933, when dozens of bullets were fired at our house out of rage because I wasn't at home and therefore could not be reached by the attackers. My escape was a flight to save my life. I want to spare myself by not describing minuatiae. When they said goodbye Herr Perschke told them he would help them if they stayed in Theresienstadt. Frau Perschke, being married to a Christian, was allowed to stay in Prague with him; because of her husband she was safe from being deported.Herr Perschke very soon fulfilled his promise, namely to help his relatives. Despite the risks he was facing he went to Theresienstadt and as a Christian succeeded in meeting the commandant of the camp. He explained to Inspector Wüstehoff, who was at that time in charge of the management, that it was almost impossible for him to run his business in Prague any longer since his managing director and several employees had been deported; on the other hand, it would be useful to give the Jews who were in the camp something to do. This last argument was well accepted as they wanted to give the Jews interned in the camp something to do. - 3 - Herr Perschke developed his plan to make the people produce craft objects and the talented ones, among whom there were also well-known artists, draw and paint pictures. He would deliver the material if there were rooms at his disposal for his workshop and office. At first they agreed to give it a try. When Herr Perschke, however, arrived one day at the camp with a removal van full of machines, all kinds of material and furniture he chose suitable rooms and established workshops and also offices. And that was the beginning of real business activities under the company name ‘Lautsch’. Herr Perschke had been clever enough during his time in Prague to secure his firm for himself, using this assumed name mentioned above. Actually the camp commandant and also the business manager had only given permission for a small business, but they very kindly turned a blind eye when they saw the size of the firm that had been set up within one day. Presents for the commandant and probably also for other people were very helpful in this case, and Herr Perschke definitely invested a lot of money in this relief action for his wife’s family and for imprisoned friends and strangers. True, it was easy to sell the goods produced there like lamp shades, all kinds of gifts, book binding articles and many other things, but above all the many first-class paintings, etchings and drawings which were made by international professional artists because such articles were not available because of the war – and yet their sale hardly covered the expenses because the authorities in charge of the pricing fixed very low prices. Still, the beneficial aim was achieved. - 4 - For the various jobs ‘Lautsch’ had to pay piecework rates to the camp management. As far as I remember the Jewish workers were not paid at all for their work. Herr Schlesinger had been engaged by Herr Perschke, his brother-in-law, as business manager. When visiting the place for the first time at Herr Perschke’s request he informed him about the opening of the firm without anybody learning that the two were relatives because Herr Schlesinger immediately understood everything and acted accordingly. When it now came to providing the firm with the necessary equipment – as I have mentioned before – Herr Perschke first of all requested some women to do the cleaning and he succeeded in arranging for his mother-in-law, his sister-in-law and also other relatives to be in this group. As one prisoner missing at the roll call had not been found after a search, the rest of the prisoners had to stand shivering in the cold - which many succumbed to - for one hour, until the missing prisoner who had hidden himself was found and murdered on the roll call ground through blows from a club and kicks. Already in the autumn of 1942 - October or November? - the prisoners had to stand for a whole night. A prisoner had disappeared and 50 Russian prisoners-of-war had been sent to look for him. They were part of a large group of Russian prisoners-of-war who stayed in a special block. Those Russians were preferred for search operations. One that occasion, 13 of the 50 men sent on the search tried to escape, upon which SS officers set out with dogs to capture them. Christmas Day 1942 was a terrible day for the prisoners: They had to carry gravel and were constantly beaten by the SS guards, the foremen, the kapos and the Stubendienst. - 5 - Bleich was able to hide on that day; he is convinced that he would not have survived that day. At the time, he had a good block elder whom the prisoners called Jupp. In early 1943, Bleich became a potato peeler, which was a fairly coveted job. Because he was so hungry, he ate potato peel, constantly had diarrhoea and became increasingly weaker. When he also developed scabies, he was thrown out of the kitchen and deployed to the outdoor jobs again to dig pits and build barracks. With his body covered in scabs, he became weaker with each passing day. Shortly after this, all the prisoners in the Birkenau concentration camp had to march 4 km to Auschwitz and back three times to fetch pallets for a new camp. On the way back from Auschwitz, Bleich collapsed and was dragged back to Birkenau by comrades who grabbed him under the arms. When he arrived there and was put on the ground by a block elder, a nearby SS officer asked, “What’s wrong with him?” When the block elder answered, “He’s worn out!” the SS officer reached for his revolver to shoot Bleich, but the block elder dissuaded him by remarking, “Forget it, save the bullet!” Bleich was so exhausted that he did not react at all to the danger of being shot. In the evening, he dragged himself back to his block and tried to go back to the outdoor work the next morning, but his comrades had to drag him there and back. One day - in March 1943, as far as Bleich can remember - there was such a dense fog one morning that the work crews had to wait for the fog to lift before they could set out. By coincidence, two Jewish prisoners who belonged to the so-called Aufräumungskommando or order commando passed by. This work crew was considered to be very advantageous and was called “Canada” in the camp lingo, as the conditions there were apparently so good it was like living in Canada. One of the two Jewish prisoners passing by noticed Bleich and realised that Bleich had come from the same transit camp Poprad, and that only few from the group that Bleich had been in had survived. One of the prisoners, whose name was Meyer Mittelmann, asked Bleich to come to his block, No. 16 - the accommodation of “Canada” - in the evening to give him food. Bleich accepted this invitation, went to Block 16 in the evening, received food from Mittelmann and was once again asked to come back to get food the next evening. I reproduce such a menu in the attachment, recreated from memory. - 3 - One sees all that we were to receive per person and per day. But that was only nominal; for us at any rate. In the two months we were there, we never received bread spread, never margarine or any other of the mentioned “supplements”, never sugar or salt. Instead of the 250 g of bread per day due to be given to us, we were at first (i.e. for almost a month) given a loaf of bread of about 1200 g for 11 men daily. Later, 14 men had to make do with one such loaf per day. The soup we received cannot possibly have contained the amounts of potatoes and turnips in the 1-1½ litres per person that the menu had stated as an instruction for the kitchen. When our health worsened alarmingly, the HANOMAG had a total of 1400 kg of meat and 2000 kg of flour delivered to us in several consignments. I entered all this in the books and had to deduct 100 g of flour daily and 50 g of meat every other day per person, following the orders of the SS chef. In reality, we obtained absolutely nothing from the HANOMAG offering. Despite all my experience in camp life, I was thoughtless enough to show the camp senior the menus and kitchen records to impel him to speak with Quakernack and push for an improvement of the food, as was his right and duty. The result was that the Imperial German prisoners received special food. That was all. Our doctor was a Jewish prisoner from Vienna who came from the Ablem camp, which belonged to the Stöcken district. There, prisoners worked in underground lead mines. The man was either completely shattered by the gruelling work there or he was not a doctor at all. The resources at his disposal were indeed completely inadequate, but even a trained medic would have been of greater use to us. When, finally, 4-5 death cases per day became too many even for Quakernack, our “doctor” was sent back to Ablem, and we got a “proper” doctor from the infirmary in Neuengamme. That was a Jewish doctor from Budapest, an energetic man who immediately pushed through the delivery of medication and put our infirmary fairly in order. But the damage had already been done. Lung infections, hunger oedema and exhaustion carried off our men. After everything that already been suffered before, this camp – with the state of our nutrition, the twice-daily 2½ km-long journeys to and from the workplace and the severe maltreatment – shattered the resilience of even the most determined people. As the main camp Neuengamme and its crematorium were too far away and the incineration facility of the city of Hanover were damaged by bombings, our dead had to be “properly” buried in the municipal cemetery, the Neuer Lindener burial ground. But the cemetery regulations were more coercive than the violence of the SS. The bodies had to be sewn into cloth or, later, into packing paper, and delivered with a medical death certificate indicating the name, place of birth and date of birth. A Polish doctor in the neighbouring foreigner camp (Ausländerlager) was probably readily prepared to sign and stamp the death certificates without performing a post-mortem examination. They indicated “circulatory insufficiency” as the cause of death. But in - 4 - the cemetery records, one will be able to determine the names and graves of our dead, who were brought in during the period from 6th February to 6th April 1945 with the place of death indicated as “Hanover-Mühlberg”. input_chunk: Given: Hungary, we received land near the Jordanian border by a town called Afula and started our own settlement. So, I was really working the, as a farmer, kibbutz. Q: Did you play any role in the War of Independence? A: Very little, almost none. I got there very late, remember, so I do not claim any, any real major role at all. No. Q: And then you decided to come back in 1950? A: In 1950, then, it was part of a homesickness for my parents and part of stupidity on my part, that I believed that things are the way Communist papers describe it in Hungary. I decided to return, perhaps temporarily, perhaps not. And when I arrived in Hungary, I realized that it was a fatal mistake. Q: Had you found any of that sense of home that you were looking for when . . . A: No. Q: when you went to Israel? A: No, no. I found my parents, but other than that, it was, it was a terrible period for any human being, especially people who came from the West. It was the worst for those, because you were considered unreliable and especially coming from Israel, even more so. The reason was, that by that time, Stalin was very paranoid and Zionism was one of his main targets. So, it, it, this is, this is something that is not much to do with the Holocaust anymore. It was just very hard for anybody to live under Communist rule at that time, but especially for Jews. Well, I don’t know if you know that in 1953 when he was dying, he looked up and he saw some Jewish doctors around his deathbed and he said, ‘They are poisoning me, they’re against me.’ And he said, ‘Arrest them.’ And practically hours before he died, they arrested Jewish doctors and I was just at the University in Hungary, studying and that was my state, the time of my state examination. And Hungary had to follow everything that the Soviet Union did so they were looking for anybody who had anything to do with Zionism. And they found me at the university and I was let go, weeks before my state exam. So, it, it was difficult but of course that has nothing to do with the Holocaust anymore. Q: When you had been in Israel, had you, do you feel, did you feel that you had found some of what you were looking for there? Was your intention to go? 33 A: Yes and no. Yes and no. I had some very deep feelings about the country as such and then again, I was still a young man, eighteen, and I was also influenced by a great deal of these revolutionary Marxist ideas. And there were many things that were not to my liking, that I would have loved to see differently. And so when I left Israel, I did not just leave it with nostalgia. I left it because I thought that finally, somehow, in Hungary, I’m going to find, find that utopistic state, that, that is, is justice and equality for everyone. And, I was just a little bit too stupid, to, to think that way, but I did. So it a was a, a double reason to return. A, a totally unfounded idealism and homesickness. Q: What did you do for work when you returned home? A: I couldn’t work for awhile because I was unreliable, anybody who came from the West, especially from Israel. Finally, with some great connections, I was hired to sweep and clean a garage, a state-owned garage. And that would have been my future

We were then taken to Prinz Albrecht Strasse and then to Columbia Haus. I had barely arrived there when I was dragged to the cellar. I had to undress completely; was strapped to a trestle and had a towel wrapped around my head. I was then beaten with a bullwhip by several SA men until I lost consciousness. After a bucket of water was thrown all over my body, I regained consciousness. The procedure was then repeated from the beginning. I do not know how oft this was repeated. Finally, I was dragged off and thrown into a cell where even the folding bed was taken away. I lay on the bare cement floor. When I gradually sensed life in me again, I felt that my entire back and my legs were bursting. I was completely blood-soaked and blood-stained. The scars which remain still hurt me often today. When the guards saw that I moved, they looked into the cell and said: “If he is already so far, then it must be his turn again.” They said that several times but only to scare me. Now we got SS guards. There was one who looked like a well-groomed son from a middle-class family. When he came into my cell, I was immediately beaten by him. I had to clean his shoes in my awful circumstance. I knelt to do it then he hit me continually with a bunch of keys round the head. This went on for days. We had prison hats as a headcover. I had to put it on in such a way that it sat skewed over my face and covered one eye every time. If I threw the hat angrily into the corner after an SS man had left the cell, he rushed to me again, beat me from the right and the left, and I had to go through with the theatre again. I got nothing to eat. I was also too anxious in the first days to feel any hunger. Then two other prisoners were put in the cell to whom food was given. Now, of course, a terrible hunger-craving started. The two, who would have liked to have helped me, did not dare to give me anything from their bowls because we were constantly observed from outside. It was all very tortuous. Some days later, a somewhat older SS man could no longer look at the situation and gave me a full bowl of soup which consisted of hot water with 3 bits of potatoes and 4 leaves of white cabbage, which to me at that time tasted better - 4 - than every roasted goose that I have eaten later. After a while, we were taken to Oranienburg. Then, from September 1933 came the interrogations in the Polizeipräsidium on Alexanderplatz. There, a Gestapo official greeted me with: “Now, tell us a little young man”. To my answer: “and if I tell you nothing”, I got a blow on the head with a truncheon from an official who was standing behind me upon which I immediately rolled under a table. Then I was led to an adjoining room to two young officials to record a statement. I worked feverishly because I knew that I would not be able to endure a second spell in the concentration camp. I also knew that “only” five weeks could not easily be brushed aside. Any longer could not be endured either physically or morally. However, the German finance authorities and the foreign office work slowly. The entry permit for England for a temporary stopover without the permission to work arrived late. The currency office, which had to give permission for the export of a few old suits, kept me waiting, and as a result, the Gestapo, the only authority in the whole of Germany that worked on its own authority, reported again and decreed that I appear punctually day after day at 1 PM at its police precinct like a released felon or a prostitute. They wanted me out of Germany, but they hindered me through these measures, as well as all of the required courses and ways. Nazi methods! However, at first it only appeared to be petty harassment. Yet I knew that I could not move outside of the city and that I could be seized at any time. I was like a dog on a lead. I finally left the country, a place that no wanderer ever returned to, on the 12th of April, even though I was not furnished with a “Jewish passport”, and travelled at first to friends in Denmark who received me hospitably, and from there, I travelled to England on the 24th of April where again I had to live on money from others: “You are to know the bitter taste of others’ bread, how salty it is, and know how hard a path it is for one who goes descending and ascending others’ stairs.” (Dante, Paradies, XVII. 58/60) The suitcases were sent afterwards. They arrived with soap, razor and hand crème stolen. Of that our remaining wealth, we had to pay a third to a half in tax, and of what was left only 6% was transferred. Captain Foley took over responsibility. What impelled him was the noblesse of background, disposition and upbringing, who let a man in such a position feel that he has been given power, to help the powerless: noblesse oblige. People who don’t know Captain Foley or only know him fleetingly might think that I’m exaggerating or that I created a torchlit procession for him for whatever reasons. Far from it. The number of Jews that were rescued from Germany would have been smaller by the tens of thousands – yes: tens of thousands – if an "industrious official" had sat in Captain Foley’s position. There are no words of Jewish gratitude that could be exaggerated with respect to this man. After the 1938 November pogrom and the mass arrests there was a savage onslaught of all foreign agencies. Everyone hoped for a miracle and a visa. The B.P.C.O. was so overwhelmed for two days that the work became impossible. Then Captain Foley established order. He wasn’t just a man who – like all of his personal employees – worked a lot and worked thoroughly. (The English would say about his justification: - 8 - “Oh, don't mind that. And we arrived to Budapest many hours later, it's a short train ride normally, but you know some of the tracks were torn or ruined so they had to always had to get out and correct them and continue. And, when we arrived to Budapest at the train station, the Jewish community was waiting at the train. You know, what's sad was no body else but the Jewish community was waiting, there was no one else, you know, the whole city should have been waiting or, you know, some other people but no, it was always the Jewish community who set up the food kitchens and who did everything. It was a Joint Distribution committee who did all that. The people were waiting with makeshift transportation to bring some people who arrived with the train had no legs, had no way of walking, they were in a horrible shape, much worse than my mother and I, and so they were waiting for them to transport them to the hospital. And they had a food kitchen already set up too. And some had big posters with blown up pictures of 08:07 their lost children or husbands or wives. The fears asking, "Have you seen this person? So, we made our way, walking, to my father's address and the landlady hardly wanted to let us in the way we looked, you know, she couldn't believe who we were. But then I knocked on my father's door, but typical of him, he said, "Just a minute, I have a patient I have to take care of right now." So he did. Q: He knew it was you? A: Sure! And he then came out and, of course, we were together, which was incredible after all that time. His first job was to delouse me with all kinds of mixtures, then we went to eat. input_chunk: aeroplanes arrived with almost scheduled punctuality and we were chased down the stairs to the air-raid shelters. We then often spent several hours there. However, there was not a lot of work to do during the rest of the night either since we were either lacking essential materials and heating material or due to the machines standing still and, moreover, everything generally already being very chaotic; a major part of the factory grounds had been bombed flat. In order for us not to spend our time idly, we were chased from here to there by the SS supervisors, often had to unload the cargo stream boats and rafts that were landed along the river during the night, and other tasks of that kind. That way March went by. On 31 March a big, British-American air raid took place. This time, all the detainees had been taken to a concrete bunker near the train tracks next to the river and we all survived the raid without any losses. When we emerged from the bunker three hours later we saw that all the factory buildings, that had still been there, were now bombed flat, including the one I had worked in. The bunker of the SS had suffered a direct bomb hit and 70 SS soldiers had been killed. - 7 - Still on the same day, all the detainees and forced labourers in Siemensstadt were divided into groups and placed in various adjoining camps where we were then put in emergency barracks. Very early in the morning on April 3rd, we were transported to Oranienburg via train and from there had to march to Sachsenhausen. The DAW (Deutsche Ausruestungswerke) had a factory there and we were told that that was where we should work from now on; however, everybody was in absolute panic and all we did was clear away some of the debris. On 13 April, we were gathered again and, on the back of lorries, brought back to Siemensstadt. There, everything was lying in ruins. The engineers and some of the labourers that had stayed behind were engaged in loading all the machinery they had managed to save from the rubble onto waggons. Eventually, we were also loaded onto waggons and the train started moving. We were told that everything, the machines and all of us, were to be brought to Bavaria. Since the whole railway traffic was already in a complete chaos it was only possible to do so taking various detours. We arrived in Bodenbach but could not continue from there onwards. The train was standing still for a day, then tried to take a different route but without success. That is how we spent several days. We were under the impression that both, the SS soldiers as well as the civilian personnel accompanying us, were aware of the fact that it was impossible for the train to reach its designated destination but that they had still taken on the challenge in order to evade serving at the front; because everywhere we now went we saw boys and old men wandering around wearing uniforms or brassards. The rumble of gunfire was clinking all around us. All the regions we crossed and all the stations we entered depicted an image of pure chaos. After eight days of senseless driving to and fro, we returned to Siemensstadt on 20 April. Upon arrival, the carriages with all the machinery were left in the rain on the track whilst all of us were ordered by the SS to march back to Sachsenhausen. Even the roads were now all completely blocked; we had to wait for hours along the way and only reached Sachsenhausen after 24 hours. There, everybody was all over the place; detainees, forced labourers and refugees. After three of four days, all of us detainees were once again gathered and ordered to march in the direction of Mecklenburg. input_chunk: became an eyewitness to horror scenes which I had never seen before. Among the numerous Jewish forced labourers being driven in one line across the bridge there were several who, old and sick, were so exhausted with the strain that they were not able to keep up the pace and were staggering at the back of the procession. At least five or six of them who collapsed were shot on the spot by the barbarous Pfeilkreuzlers and their bodies were thrown over the railing of the bridge into the Donau. That happened in front of all of us in broad daylight. Afterwards we were driven the length and breadth of Budapest and its suburbs; we came to Albertfalva, to Kispest, to Rakoskeresztur. Everywhere we were told that we should build fortifications against the advancing Russians; in some places ditches were dug, indeed, and fortifications were put up, but there was so much confusion and chaos that we never stayed in one place but were given orders and counter orders about where to go. We got the impression that the Pfeilkreuzlers guarding us did not know themselves what they wanted and what they should do. But they were all agreed on making life for us as unbearable as possible; they maltreated us, pushed us and chased us until we collapsed. We got food only very irregularly, had to sleep mostly outdoors in these cold October nights and had no chance to change our clothes. More and more people collapsed, sick and exhausted, more and more totally exhausted ones were murdered by the Pfeilkreuzlers. But also the number of those who tried to flee during that general chaos was increasing every day. In November when the situation became more and more intolerable I also decided to take refuge in flight. Together with two comrades we hid one afternoon in a toilet and waited for nightfall. We actually succeeded in escaping and protected by the darkness reached the centre of the town through the blacked-out streets. But we soon learnt that it had been easier to escape than to find a place to stay. Of course our homes had been confiscated long ago and occupied by other people, mostly refugees from the East, and our relatives had disappeared in all directions. My wife and my mother-in-law had just been dragged from the ‘Judenhaus’ and at first been taken to the brickworks in Alt-Ofen where they had to spend several nights on the bare floor under indescribable conditions together with innumerable other women and children. Later they had been taken to the newly established ghetto. My daughter by my first marriage, a very young girl, still lived with my former wife in a ‘Judenhaus’, from where she was deported, however, soon afterwards, never to return. My sister had a Swiss Schutzpass[9] and was living in a so-called ‘Schutzhaus’[10]. It was a long and laborious job to find the traces of these family members. Besides the Ghetto, the ‘Judenhäuser’ and the ‘Schutzhäuser’ there were all sorts of hideouts where numerous brothers in faith stayed, either hidden by Christian friends or in deserted rooms, attics, cellars etc. I, too, hid myself for several weeks and spent the nights in turn with various relatives. Also non-Jews helped me during my ‘underground’ life. In particular one policeman whom I had already known in former times was ready to help in exchange for money and friendly words. At Christmas 1944 Budapest was surrounded by Russian troops and instead of the liberation we had hoped for daily the town was now besieged for many weeks, with incessant bitter fights for each quarter of the town. The search started once more, and again it was my mother who was tireless and did everything to get me into safety. She received the address of a woman who had a caretaker job in the American church in Motzstrasse near Mollendorfplatz. This church had a Swiss minister to look after it who spent most of his time in Switzerland. This women provided me with a tower room in this church after the usual hush money. I was safe inside the church because I was on American soil. But I had to get some air from time to time and I did this usually in the evening, in order not to be seen. It happened, that one evening when I came back from a walk, the church door was bolted from the inside and a light was on in the living quarters. The minister had returned from Switzerland and I was on the street. First of all, I called my aunt in order to get a night’s accommodation, and the next day, I took up the search again. It was now even more difficult because young men who were on the streets for long periods were stopped by the military patrols. Then my friend Karlchen helped me. I must say something more about it, in order to explain who my friend Karlchen was. - 3 - Karlchen was one of my friends who hated the war and did everything in order to boycott the Nazi regime. Because he was healthy, he had to be a soldier. He came up with the idea of going into the orderly room and looking after his future. This idea manifested itself firstly in stealing a Wehrmacht stamp, and in addition, a large quantity of blank leave permits and some blank service books. I had my photograph taken in his military uniform. He was a corporal in the Luftwaffe. Karlchen then made out for me a service book in my right name with this photograph. He also supplied and a leave permit that needed to be renewed every three weeks with permission to wear civilian clothes so I did not have to wear a uniform. I had borrowed his just for the photograph. The boundaries of our effrontery were so wide that we organised a ski course for the Wehrmacht on the Bodenschneidhütte at the Schliersee. For that, an old uniform was organised for me because for this course I had to go in uniform. For this purpose, I went with a false leave permit to Rheda in Westfalen, where at this time, Karlchen lived with his girlfriend Pummelchen. I have forgotten to mention that Karlchen when he had stolen enough stationery, deserted. For the ski course, he promoted himself to lieutenant with the help of the papers, stamp and false signatures which he had organised before he deserted. In Breda, I learned on the floor of the house where Karlchen and Pummelchen lived how to conduct oneself in uniform. Then I had to learn off-by-heart all of the ranks of the Wehrmacht, so that, in an emergency, I was able to speak correctly to my superior and above all to greet him correctly.
