input_chunk: He is the most uncalculating of men. Leo Baeck was born at Lissa, Posen (then part of Eastern Germany), in 1873. He was the son of Rabbi Samuel Baeck, who was himself a distinguished Jewish scholar and historian. Lissa, though it contained an ancient and distinguished Jewish community, was principally a Calvinist colony in Lutheran territory. One of the three Calvinist parsonages was rented to the rabbi, and it is a token of the good relations between the two communities that the rent remained unchanged even when other rents in Lissa had more than doubled. Baeck's childhood was mercifully unembittered by anti-Semitism, and this fact must have helped him greatly to achieve and maintain his own total lack of racial bitterness. He had no early ambition to follow in his father's footsteps, and it was only after he had studied at Breslau and Berlin that “the spiritual condition of German Jewry” persuaded him that he had a role to play. It was a time of great confusion for European Jews, in which the die-hard and orthodox conservatives were fighting a losing battle against a progressivism which was leading, more and more, to a total lack of faith. What was needed, it seemed to the young Leo Baeck, was a passionate restatement of the fundamental and unitary theme of Judaism - not, certainly, a return to narrow orthodoxy, but an insistence that the poetry of the ancient Jewish religion is not inconsistent with a proper participation in the contemporary world. “Among us,” he says, “there is always a conflict between the millenia and the years”; and by this he means that the antique message of Israel is in perpetual conflict with the chances and changes of history. He wanted, not to resolve this conflict, but to fructify it. In his great work, “The Essence of Judaism,” which was first published in 1905, he was one of the earliest modern thinkers to recognise that fundamental human conflicts are not “soluble”; they are what is given and they are what we must use. “Judaism,” he wrote, “arouses a feeling of tension in the human heart. It is filled with anxiety because of the remoteness of God and of a longing for his proximity.” So although Rabbi Baeck has been the president of the World Union for Progressive Judaism since 1938, he represents the conservative wing of that body. Because he perceives, and rejoices in, spiritual conflict, he can never be one of those progressive churchmen who progressively surrender everything valuable in their religion. Baeck was first of all a rabbi in Silesia, and then in Düsseldorf, so that he was able to study in his youth the widely different worlds of East German and West. German Jewry. In 1912 he was transferred to a synagogue in Berlin, which he describes as “colonial territory,” a new city and a melting-pot for Jews and Gentiles alike. He served as an army chaplain during the first world war and then returned to Berlin again. By now succeeding translations of Das Wesen des Judentums had given him a worldwide reputation among scholars. (At the moment a Japanese translation is being prepared.) For example the so-called criminal prisoners never made an inappropriate request whenever they, secretly and under cover of darkness, snuck into the barracks of the so-called political prisoners, with whom they were forbidden to take up contact, in order to ask for a bit of bread or a little money. An unusual scene in the drama of camp existence has inextinguishably branded itself onto Mr Zimmermann’s memory. During the march on a Sunday morning the camp commander called, through scornful laughter, to a Catholic priest: “Old fellow, would you like to pray to your God?” The tall, white haired Father, his countenance marked by lines of suffering, quietly replied: “Yes, with pleasure!” The commander, clearly disappointed that the Protestants, Jews, and Communists, who were represented in great numbers amongst the other prisoners, did not appear to give any signs of displeasure, now ordered in an excited tone: “Alright then, show us your dark art!” Still the prisoners showed no displeasure; on the contrary- a wave of warm-hearted sympathy appeared to meet the courageous priest, who addressed the inmates with head held high : “I speak to you not as a cleric but as a comrade and fellow sufferer. I stand before you to strongly urge you not to let your spirits sink in the face of the grave situation in which you find yourselves. It will not remain so forever. The day will come, upon which each of you will return to your families and your homes, the day upon which Germany will be free once more. Now might everyone who longs for this join me in a prayer to our Father in Heaven.” While the inmates repeated the words of the white-haired priest with one voice, the shine of their eyes and the sound of their voices expressed new courage and hope. The camp commander was speechless; his face dyed dark red out of anger, and as he laboriously hid his temper, he spluttered out the words: “Now, would you like to continue with your dark art every Sunday?” The priest responded quietly: “If it were granted me, I would always remain at this post.” The commander roared: “To the devil with you, you pig,” but from now on he refrained from challenging the cleric in this manner. Later, in the relative privacy of the barracks, every inmate was delighted with the priest whose brave conduct had raised their sunken morale once more (morale in the military sense: that is, spiritual power of resistance). Mr Zimmermann was released from Esterwegen concentration camp on the 27th March 1936. His elderly mother, then still living- and in Germany at that- had worked most eagerly to force through his release. On this day he was ordered into the commandant’s office, where, without introduction, he was told: “You are no longer an inmate. You have not been here as a punishment, but rather you have been held here in custody for so long, until the charges laid against you could be investigated. I warn you against telling anyone anything about your stay here. You can rely on the fact that, wherever you go in the world, it will also be known to our agents. Should you ever express a word about your stay here, the day of reckoning will soon come for you.” After his release from the concentration camp the Nazi government rescinded Mr Zimmermann’s citizenship and deported him. input_chunk: the National Socialists. They understood anti-Semitism as a negative spin-off of the general anti-intellectual attitude of the Nazis. H. cannot remember concrete relationships to Jews at that time. Leaflets were prepared by and distributed by the group amongst which was a poster by H., a parody on “who wears this sign is an enemy of the people” only that here, the swastika instead of the star of David was affixed. H. was arrested on 19 April 1943, accused of high treason and set free again. After the Scholl brother and sister were executed, he was arrested once again with 16 others, “tried” within 2 months and sentenced to 5 years in jail. His youth and blonde appearance had softened the yelling though shrewd Freisler a bit: “a blond young man” such as H., whose parents were “good Germans” could perhaps be useful to the German people. H. spent his imprisonment mainly in Heilbronn where he worked as a librarian and (he of all people) was tasked with clearing - 4 – all anti-fascist books from the library. He thoroughly read some of them there. H. states that after his imprisonment, he often felt like he was playing in a “comedy with a false-bottom”. He speaks about the fact that the trial which was conducted against him had been a show process because the guilt had already been anticipated and they had already executed the brother and sister Scholl. Justice could not have been given in that court of law. Those who had the real “guilt” were often treated with less severity than others against whom there was hardly any proof submitted. He himself had also played in this comedy with his conscience, because he had minimised his resistance activity and disposition before the court because he wanted “to stay alive”. He had moved the main part of the “guilt” to the Scholls who were already dead, as did his comrades who were likewise accused. H. still speaks with some resentment against the Scholls. At the same time, he admires their selfless and total sacrifice, but then reproaches them for having put the lives of other people on the line. However, H. appears to not only moan about their final fate, but also to envy it. At present, a certain intellectual and emotional tiredness is noticeable with H. He appears today not to reflect too deeply about the political situation. The most important Nazis have been mostly punished. The situation of the world does not shock him very much.

And voluntary agencies were allowed to give these out because ostensibly, the voluntary agencies in the United States were going into communities and asking them, and they were very good for all displaced persons, Jewish and non-Jewish, to give job and housing assurances which they did. If you were eligible, we could get a job Œ we would contact the States and we would get Œ this is under normal circumstances Œ a job and housing assurance for Ivan Schwartz to go to Seattle to be a tailor, which he had been before, and on the basis of that, providing he passed his medical with the consulate, providing he passed his security with the CIC, the Counter Intelligence Corp, he would get a visa. Those were the only people who were eligible. So, what I did, since I had job and housing assurances already for people, I just had to sign a name to them. In a sense, I did it without authority. Our foreman had what was for us a dangerous idea of going into the Buchenwald woods under the pretext of emptying the contents of the latrines there. There were two waggons. In the meantime, we had to cut down trees, break them up and sneak them into the empty latrines. In doing this, we were always nervous in case a check was made at the gates of the camp by the SS and the deception emerged, and then we were punished as thieves. The foreman carried out such a booming trade with the wood. Occasionally, the SS had the idea to make us load stones and rubble into the empty waggons, in order to make the work more difficult, and then we had to work for half a day or a day only on the camp streets. In the spring of 1942, a part of the prisoners were dismissed by the foremen. He said to us that he needed stronger people. I had to drop out and I learned later that the foreman only had very prominent people around him, in order to cover the prisoners’ performance, whilst the ‘normal’ prisoners had to give him a variety of ‘presents’ or bread, cigarettes etc. Apart from the fact that I did not know that, I did not have the means because in the interim, my family in Brünn were also without resources and were later sent to Theresienstadt. It was only later that I, along with many other impecunious Jews, received a steady stream of money from an Austrian Jewish organisation, which sent money to all Jews who turned to them. The money was sent formally by a woman whose names escapes me. I was put in a bad command, the camp roads command, which had to improve them by the breaking of stones accompanied by danger and drudgery. The foreman, a Jew from Berlin, who was murdered by the prison leadership around 1944, was a criminal who hit, blackmailed and bullied us. The luck in misfortune for me was that one day I was no longer in the condition to carry the so-called kerbstones. The barrow fell on my feet and the kerbstone cut through my right shoe and injured my toes. Despite my injury, the foreman would not allow me to go to the sick-bay, but my friends took me there in the evening and I was immediately admitted. The tip of one of my toes was amputated the next day and a Jewish prisoner, who had a good position in the sick-bay, ‘Jumbo’ Jellinek from Vienna made it possible for me to have two weeks there. After this accident, the foremen behaved a bit better and an acquaintance spoke to him, so that he did not bully me as much as before. In the spring of 1942, apprentice brick-layers were sought whether they were Jewish prisoners or not. I also reported to this command on the advice of a prisoner from Brünn, Robert Platscheks, who did the same and perhaps had good information. At the beginning, I had to carry water or bricks. Even here though, especially at the beginning, there were beatings and abuse. I was injured on the right leg by a brick which an SS man threw at me. In comparison to the other commands for Jews, for example, hauling carts, the camp streets or breaking stones, the building command was a relief. Then there was a very radical decision taken by the SS: one morning at the early assembly only the Jews in the building command were marched out. The others had to stay. At the same time, the Kapo, a prisoner called Robert Siewart, tried to send some prisoners, for example myself, to the camp, in order ‘to exchange’ them for prominent prisoners, as we later found out. input_chunk: be safer not to spend the night in the camp and hid myself in a block in one of the empty adjacent camps and slept there. In the morning, I went back to the camp and tended to my patients, as in previous days, organising food for them and people to care for the other blocks. 24 January, 2pm: On the camp street, 2 covered figures trudge through the snow, dragging a machine gun on a sled behind them. They stop in front of the camp gate. Curious, we creep closer. We recognise the Red Star of Soviet troops on their fur caps. A cry of joy peals through the camp: “The Russians are here!” Whoever is able to crawl crawls out of the beds and comes outside. Our joy knows no bounds! We kiss the bearded figures, we make tea, we bring out cigarettes which had previously been kept as holy relics, and do not know how to show our gratitude to these two liberators with our poor means. We laugh and we cry and cannot comprehend our luck at being liberated. We still harbour the fear that the SS might return. In the evening, however, things start to become lively. Hundreds upon hundreds of panje carts of Russian soldiers arrive and are billeted in our camp and the neighbouring one. A jeep drives up and a senior Russian officer steps out. He speaks to us in Yiddish and when I explain to him that it is mainly Jewish prisoners who are accommodated in my block and ask him to say a few words to them, many of whom cannot leave their beds, he comes to our block. He opens his coat, shows his decorated chest and tells us that we no longer need fear for our lives. He says that the Soviet Army is driving the Germans out like rabbits. He tells us how happy he is that it was possible to save some more people from the barbarians. He will do all he can, he says, to ensure we are accommodated and catered for in a dignified way and the patients will from now on receive proper treatment so that they can recuperate. He kept his word, the very next day we were given decent meat soup, pieces of meat that we knew only as a distant memory, and cake. But the dead were seen to as well. - 6 - A team of pathologists came, each corpse was opened and a precise record was made of the cause of death. Former Nazis from the surrounding area were taken to the camp to be put to work, the barracks were cleaned and the dead were solemnly buried.

input_chunk: background, disposition and upbringing, who let a man in such a position feel that he has been given power, to help the powerless: noblesse oblige. People who don’t know Captain Foley or only know him fleetingly might think that I’m exaggerating or that I created a torchlit procession for him for whatever reasons. Far from it. The number of Jews that were rescued from Germany would have been smaller by the tens of thousands – yes: tens of thousands – if an "industrious official" had sat in Captain Foley’s position. There are no words of Jewish gratitude that could be exaggerated with respect to this man. After the 1938 November pogrom and the mass arrests there was a savage onslaught of all foreign agencies. Everyone hoped for a miracle and a visa. The B.P.C.O. was so overwhelmed for two days that the work became impossible. Then Captain Foley established order. He wasn’t just a man who – like all of his personal employees – worked a lot and worked thoroughly. (The English would say about his justification: - 8 - “Oh, don't mind that. He was educated in France”.) The three night watchmen from the embassy building in Wilhelmstraße were transferred to Tiergartenstraße. They arranged the visitors in rows of four which stretched from the street through the front garden and the stairwell through into the waiting room. They didn’t understand any German, were very polite (but also energetic), wore uniform, (Livree) with lots of medal ribbons (from the previous war) and – were “Gojim”(gentiles). As a result an exemplary level of organisation prevailed even though the November and December weather was terrible and the visitors were very nervous. Captain Foley wrote personal Laisser passers for people who didn’t have any time to stand and wait. In this way, we as representatives of the Jewish Organisations were able to move freely and quickly. Until the pogroms Captain Foley had two permanent employees (Assistant Passport Control Officers), Mr Insall and Mr Newman. After the pogroms three young men and a woman also joined his team. The office personnel were reinforced accordingly. We have to be clear here about what it means to expand a single department of an embassy in this way during peacetime and in a country with strict parliamentary budget controls. It wasn’t even the man who will go down in history as the author of “The Failure of a Mission” who had carried out this increase in staff. It was Captain Foley. As different Jewish and non-Jewish organisations in collaboration with the Reichsvertretung discussed the question with the British government, whether it was possible to make the immigration and crossing through the United Kingdom easier, the London central authorities obviously also asked the “man on the spot” for his opinion. I don’t know to what extent Captain Foley had an influence over the details of the “Refugee Scheme”; I just know that he mentioned this. The “Refugee Scheme” is on record. It represents a liberal breaking down of the barriers of the slow English immigration policing law for certain categories from mainly, but not exclusively, Jewish refugees from Germany. The manner in which the British passport office collaborated with his smooth handling is best characterised by the passport office distributing free printed leaflets, which described all of the details of the process precisely and contained all of the important committee addresses. The nature in which the Reichsvertretung collaborated with his smooth handling is best characterised by the fact that the Hilfsverein - 9 - official formally responsible for handling the process in relation to the English and German authorities, namely myself, was notified of the scheme by the British Passport Office, but not by the Reichsvertretung. Despite his contacts at the convent, the couple had the greatest difficult being accepted and their discussions went back and forth for weeks. I had no idea what would become of me and my child and it was very bad, as Frau Wieth had, initially, to pack her things. At the time, I just thought constantly how lucky it was that we had the zyankali. Then, a miracle happened! The couple had finally succeeded in persuading the Metropolite to take us in. And, exactly 24 hours before they had to leave our house, a nun in the convent, where the woman was to be taken in, agreed to take in my daughter and me. Of course, she insisted that we would have to move into the convent within 24 hours. This was difficult for me, as I had promised Frau Wieth I would remain with her until her departure and help her. There was, thus, no option for me other than to take my child to the convent for 11 o’clock the next day. Once there, I explained to the nun why I had to return to Frau Wieth and then returned to her apartment. I helped her pack and took her to the train; then I went to the convent as well. I could, of course, not speak Ukrainian, yet they were very good to us. My daughter went into an orphanage annexed to the convent. And, again, I was lucky that I could sew. I was immediately given a sewing machine and a pile of sewing. It was in this way that I sewed for the orphans until the end of the war. We were fed well and amply and actually began to recover somewhat physically. A fairly long while passed until I began to notice that the nun was becoming rather a little less frien - 15 - dly with me than at the beginning. Finally, one day, a Jewish woman said to me, who was also hiding in the convent, rather as if in passing, “the nun no longer wants you here, because you won’t be baptised!” I was absolutely horrified, as I had not given it any thought at all. It was then explained to me that those supervising the convent always expected such things without having to speak of it. Although I was anything but that which could be described as a pious Jew, I stuck to my beliefs and the thought of baptism to me was horrifying. At that time, I could not sleep for many nights until I decided to have my daughter and myself baptised. But, the nun’s stance became ever more unpleasant and so I went to her one day and explained that I would like to have my daughter and I baptised. The nun immediately became filled with interest - 14 - and changed her stance in an instant. A priest was assigned the task of instructing my daughter and I. My daughter was immensely pleased. She found everything great and was completely happy and content. And, with that, I had no way out, if I wanted to save my life and my child’s life. One night, I dreamt of my father. In my dream, I asked him what I should do. He replied very calmly “Just do it! It is the right thing to do! There is, of course, only one God!” Afterwards, it was much easier for me. input_chunk: 5th March towards 4 o’clock of the morning I suddenly noticed that the door of my cell was open. I could not believe that I was not suffering from hallucinations: when I stepped forwards into the pitch-dark labyrinth I observed that simultaneously three other hostages, 2 Americans, and 1 Englishman were also stepping out. The doors of their cells had also been opened. We were now haunted by the fearful suspicion that we were to be the guinea-pigs in another story of “shot while trying to escape”. Suddenly we were blinded by the glaring light of a torch and one of guards hurried to meet us and spellt out the magic words: “Resistance Nationale, vous êtes libre, messieurs!” But the 16 other miserable victims did not dodge their fate as we did, but were defintely shot on the 6th March. The guard showed us the way among a labyrinth of subterranean pathways and water-canals underneath the harbour and finally we emerged again on the surface nearby a dilapidated shed. The guard was in possession of a (stearin) candle and even that kind of candle was a precious rarity already at that time in Marseilles) which he lit and fastened to a table which was standing in the shed. Then he produced four yellow envelopes from his pocket which he handed out to each of us while he recited his final instructions: “Lises, messieurs, bonne chance and suives nos orderes, et cela trés strictement. Moi, il faut disparaître par la voie que je suis venue. Dieu vous benisse, messieurs!” And then hevanished. We thenread the contents of the messages by the light of the candle. We had been liberated for special services in the resistance movement. Our guardians had been bribed 40 000 francs per head (!!!) to allow us to escape. It was a fact that each of us had discharged important functions in the resistance movement. Myself, for instance, I had employed my skill and knowledge of chemistry to forge innumerable quantities of passports and to supply endangered politicians and jews with forged certificates of birth. This then was the reason for the present gratitude of the resistance movement. All four of us were instructed to come to a “rendez-vous” at 4 entirely different places where we were to receive further instructions for our flight. In each of the envelopes we also found 10 000 francs to help usin our escape. I was to appear at a column of the “kiosque” of the Marseilles Main railway station (St. Charles) at 7 p.m. I was in possession of cleverly forged papers and a certificate of birth and of baptism, from the Alsatian village of - 7 - Heidingen. This was one of the masterpieces of the resistance movement, as Heidingen was a hamlet consisting of 10 houses only, that had already been so completely destroyed in World War I that it had been struck off from the French official register of towns and villages. The Nazis could thus never have checked up on the authenticity of these papers. They had been branded with dampstains through a chemical method, thus made a genuinely ancient and dilapidated impression. When I made my appearance at the place that had been convened upon in the letter, near the railway kiosk, on the 6th March at seven p.m., I found an uncannily old, ugly, hump-backed nun with a big hood as it is worn my some catholic orders, standing there waiting for me. Her face was hidden by a black veil. She supplied me with the instructions for travelling to Switzerland, with some provisions and a few hundred francs for any expenses on the train. input_chunk: and where consultations took place. Then came the dining room 1, called the refectory. This contained tables and the cupboards of some of the inmates. From there one could access the men’s sleeping quarters which contained initially two-storey, later three-storey wooden bunk beds. A badly fitting door led to the outside. On this side one had a view of the narrow square which abutted on the workshop (hut 9) and the bunker. On the opposite side one could look across a thick fence, obscured with layers of - 2 - straw, into the KL, the concentration camp where prisoners of all nationalities who were recovering (or dying) from illnesses were kept. After the men’s sleeping quarters came two small rooms, the sick bay, for sick men and women. Adjoining it was the washroom for men and women alike, where men and women could not only wash at specified times, but also use the single, originally open WC, later furnished with a wooden door, and the urinal. The washbasins were also used for washing the dishes while the sinks for washing the feet were used for washing clothes and for emptying the night soil containers. The washroom led into the women’s sleeping quarters. After that came the second dining room, and then a separated room where the pharmacy was situated and which served as a lounge for the families of the former and current camp elders. In the space behind the hut were two toilet huts, one with a row of toilets, separate for men and women, (frozen in winter), the other a latrine with holes that could be covered and with a well-used standpipe. The whole terrain was surrounded with thick barbed wire. In one corner a white skull on black ground grinned at us to warn us of the danger zone. From the watchtowers, every move of the camp inmates was observed. The gate leading to the street was permanently locked and could only be opened by the corporals (Scharfuehrer). In January 1945 the Neutral Nation Camp acquired a new hut. It lay on the other side of the main street, but set well back from it, and could be accessed via the bath house. It was a rust-red hut (No. 202) which was situated within the women’s concentration camp. On both sides of a corridor were rooms containing the three-storey metal beds. Washrooms for men and women were in this hut, also the permanently blocked toilet. The corridor had become even narrower through the erection of cupboards on either side of it. The whole hut was characterised by the lack of space. There were too few beds, although all the beds had been pushed so tightly together that one could barely move. In this dark corridor, people had to squeeze past each other with difficulty. There was no room for recreation or food distribution so that the meals had to be given out in the passage whilst food rations were brought into the rooms. The inmates became even more nervous. Some of those who, because of the shortage of beds and alleged infestation with lice, had been made to sleep in the passage died quickly. Because of a complaint or in consideration of the changing character of the Bergen-Belsen camp, yet another move occurred after only 2 weeks. The new – and for us last – camp terrain was situated immediately next to the bath house, opposite the kitchen - 3 - of the prisoner-of-war camp which was unused when we arrived and only later-on resumed service. This camp consisted of one large hut which was allocated to the Spaniards, with a separate room for the camp elder and the camp administration, as well as two special rooms for a group of privileged Dutch Jews, furthermore a smaller hut which was given over to the Turks, then a hospital hut, and a hut for a privileged French and one Hungarian family which was located a little further away. It was all very beautiful, and when I told Mrs. Godem, because she would come back and forth, she said, ﬁHe can do watch covers. My brother would be very pleased to see him.ﬂ And this man said to me, ﬁWhich one do you like the best?ﬂ Well, I knew he was saying to me, ﬁI will give you that one.ﬂ I said, ﬁThey™re all beautiful.ﬂ I wouldn™t admire any, and the only gift I ever have or had from a survivor or from a refugee was a dish he sent to me. He knew I wouldn™t take it. We allowed them to bring flowers to the office, and sometimes it looked like a mortuary, there were so many flowers, but gifts were fo rbidden because gifts lead to bribes. But I have at home still this lovely tray he gave me. It™s a dish about six inches in diameter, St. George and the Dragon. I think he must have made it for me. And, they did very well in the States. We had some wonderful people, we really did, who immigrated to the States, and America is richer for them. It really is. The operation in Germany went quite successfully, I would say, because we got all the offices to work in the same fashion. We set up some of the filing systems. And I sent Mickey through Germany to the States. Now you can imagine how I felt seeing my mother in this place, and probably she also felt seeing me, but I have to tell you that as soon as we got there, she was not my mother anymore in a practical way. She became the child and I was the mother. She just couldn't function in this place. And, so my allotment of clothes was a black dress with short sleeves, and no underclothes at all. The shoes were the most dire thing because they usually didn't fit, no one measured you, and if they were very bad, if the fitting was totally out, you were doomed because most of the time you were on your feet. There were no places where you could sit or anything. And many people died on account just not having the right shoes. Your feet swell or were so hurt that they couldn't continue, but my shoes were acceptable. And they were both the same size, both the same heel because it didn't have to be. You could have had the right foot in the wrong, you know, different size than the left foot, or different heel. So, then "Schnel! Schnel!" they painted a red stripe on our backs because they without this you could maybe escape, which was ridiculous. I don't know how they imagined that. Then they gave us, over our left chest, describing us, what kind of prisoners we are. And then there were stations . . . 21 Q: What did yours say? A: Jew, you know. Q: Was it a special designation for political prisoner, or? A: Not here. Not here. But then there were stations, you know, where you went through like, when you go to a subway or something you have to go through, and there were girls tattooing people because, you know, you lost your name the minute you arrived at Auschwitz, now, I had already two names that weren't mine. First my cousin's, when I came to Galanta they gave me my cousin's name to really legalize, then I became 'Anna Voyachickola' and I lost my name altogether because everybody was called out by number, and my number was one number higher than my mother's. The irony of it is, my mother was such an esthetic person that she checked each girl that did the best job in tattooing and she found that this one who did me did the most beautiful job, and I really never saw a nicer tattoo, if you can call it nice. [Shows tattoo] And then I got this triangle which meant 'political prisoner'. Now the girls told me "Your lucky," the ones that tattooed me, "you have a living number." I said, "What do you mean by that?" And she said, "Well, if you don't have an 'A' or a 'B', that means that this number is as many people as there were now in camp and your the first one with this number." I rather think that he was in prison because he behaved worse than the proper career criminals with the green badges. Some weeks later, when I, as a result of sickness ill-treatment and hunger, I almost could no longer continue, I was so weak that I was carried that evening by friends to the assembly place, Theo called me to him and hit me with a wooden slat. I remained lying half dead, but the next day my friends helped me to leave the barrack, and as I later heard, Theo was reprimanded for his behaviour towards me and other victims and he gave us peace for some time. For me, the time in Sachsenhausen was the worst that I experienced in concentration camps. They appear to me to have been worse than the punishment company in Dachau or the life in Buchenwald. It was also the worst camp that I was in and I never knew how I was supposed to behave in different situations. I was in a block where there were not even enough sleeping places and we sometimes lay on top of one another and so on. The labour at the brick works, the carrying of the clay for the bricks and with the brick moulds at the double was only a way in which to exhaust the prisoners and leave them in the so-called standing command until they died. This was a command for those prisoners deemed unfit for work. In place of work, the prisoners stood in rank and file at the barracks for all of the work hours. Most of them got water in the feet and died soon. I was also in the standing command for a time. The camp was cleaned at a stroke at the beginning of September 1940 and the sick prisoners were all summoned to the sick bay and separated from the other prisoners. I was also sick because I had injured both feet; phlegmon. We were crowded into some empty barracks, from where, after a few days, we were again released and accommodated in the old barracks. It had all occurred in the following manner: a commission of the International Red Cross had come to Sachsenhausen, in order to visit the camp. I could see the International Commission myself, but they could not see us because along the barracks where we the sick lay crowded together there was a label attached: Attention, Danger of Infection etc. It was then clear to us what the point was supposed to be of the temporary separation of the sick from the healthy: the International Commission saw only the healthy prisoners and had no access to us because we presented a ‘danger of infection’. Shortly after that, around the middle of September, I was transported to Dachau with most of the other sick. The transport was carried out as usual in railway cattle wagons. In Dachau, we were loaded into lorries in front of the station and taken to the camp. The transfer was better, that is, more orderly than in Sachsenhausen, and in comparison to Sachsenhausen where the greens, the career criminals, had the upper hand in the leadership of the camp, here it was better led by the reds, the political prisoners. After our admission, that is our transfer, we were all put in separate entry units, in order to be led to the sick bay for the first 3 weeks so that we could recover. After a short period of time, we were all, that is the Jewish prisoners, whether sick or not, taken to punishment block number 15. input_chunk: mines. They worked in these mines to be protected from air raids. It was unspeakably hard there for the prisoners. During the day they worked in these mines and by night they had to build the camp. The food was bad and so was the treatment. The smallest transgression resulted in 25 lashes with a rubber tube which was filled with sand. It was winter and terribly cold. During the six weeks that they worked there, they never saw daylight. It was still dark when they descended down the pit and dark when they returned in the evenings to the camp. From there Kenneth was taken to Flossenburg in Bavaria, to an immense camp for 20,000 prisoners, which lies high up in the mountains, near Nürnberg. Long before the war Hitler had this camp built for dangerous criminals who were forced to serve their sentences there. The camp consisted of 24 barracks. 800 men were housed in each barrack. Four bunks were stacked one above the other and every bunk had to have space for four people. One piece of bread, black coffee, some soup and occasionally another soup in the evening! That was all the nutrition. For those doing hard labour there was an additional piece of bread at 10 a.m. Kenneth remained there for four weeks in quarantine, received a striped prison uniform and was taken 25 km from Nürnberg to a camp where he had to work terribly hard. The workers had to haul heavy iron poles or dig deep pits. The water contained copper and people dropped like flies. However, Kenneth Roman and the other mechanics were called back to Flossenburg to disassemble the Messerschmitt airplanes. A quarry, a penal colony, was nearby. Many who were forced to work there never returned. They were slayed by the stones. The camp in Flossenburg was very clean. There was a weekly hot shower, every week they went to be deloused and everyone’s hair was shaved off. There was a hospital and a crematorium. In the hospital the sick received water injections which entered the blood and the victims died in a constant stream. The washroom doubled up as a concert hall with a piano and an orchestra; music making was permitted on Sunday afternoons and different groups could take turns listening. The parade ground, too, became a sports area on Sunday afternoons. They could play ball games there. The supervisors were dangerous criminals who had been released from penitentiary; they and the most senior people in the blocks had a room to themselves and everyone had a bed. They were terribly cruel. They were allowed to torment and to murder whom they wished. They had installed a brothel in the barrack where they entertained women from the prisons. They had everything they wanted, just no freedom. Nor were they permitted to leave the camp. The camp was first surrounded by barbed wire, then by an electric wire. Towers were set twenty meters apart and a watch was stationed on the towers. Many desperate people committed suicide on these wires. The food was distributed by the most senior people in the block. They divided up the rations as it suited them, according to their mood: one received less, the other a bit more. The smallest transgression was punished with 75 lashes. Things were a bit better for Kenneth Roman because he was permitted to do the washing for the most senior people in the block, and, unnoticed, he would wash his own shirt at the same time. He received warm clothing to wear and sometimes a second bowl of soup; he was the youngest in the camp. He had met a distant relative there with whom he shared everything he received; it is only thanks to this circumstance that this relative survived. In Flossenburg there was a barrack for the very young. They had slightly easier working conditions. They had a bit more to eat and were not hit as terribly. But the others! – Many of them suffered from swollen legs and feet and died in their hundreds.

input_chunk: who she was. She answered: “Don’t ask. I am Polish and I call myself Kathrin.” “What are you doing in this house?” She answered again: “Don’t ask.” Frau Kathrin spoke perfect Russian. I asked her to give me Russian lessons. Then her sad eyes lit up, and she said: “You are the first person here who has responded to me as a fellow human being and has appealed to my intellectual gifts.” I became her student. She refused to take any money for these lessons. But when I saw that she was probably living in a decent room in the house, but was barely given anything to eat and she owned very few clothes, I knew how I could show her my appreciation. It wasn’t easy to find out how things were really going for Frau Kathrin. She was a Polish Jewess, from Warschau (Warsaw) where she managed the Vasenol-Werke for years off the interest of her own assets. Dr. Köpp, a member and representative of the National Socialist Party - 4 - – information that Frau Kathrin apparently first learned of in Berlin, was her debtor. He took this woman, when the systematic persecution of Jews began, to the Villa Kutschera which now belonged to him, acted like her savior, but never failed to humiliate this Jewess who “had gone into hiding.” She went hungry, she had to do the work of a cleaning woman and she was constantly afraid of the “rescuer” who exploited her and could inform against her if he wanted. How did that man, who claimed to want to save Frau Kathrin, dare to assign her such a lowly position so that she went around like a criminal; it could only be attributed to a strange stroke of luck that nobody betrayed her! – I remember how this woman, whose character was attacked and who was in very poor health, fell and hurt herself at work (I think she broke one of her hands in the process), but was ruthlessly driven to work in a manner similar to the Russian deportees who had to do forced labor on the Kutschera properties. Gradually the secret got out: other housemates learned of the presence of a Jewess without a Jewish Star. Frau Kathrin suffered very badly from this. She was also, painfully, without news about her children and her close relatives. We became very close on a human level in our lessons. After the capture of Berlin, Russian troops also came to Hottengrund and officers moved into the quarters of Villa Kutschera. If I was allowed to show Mrs. Kathrin some love in her need, she repaid me a thousand-fold for everything she had ever received from me, if one is even allowed to speak of repayment among friends. The knowledge of the Russian language that I gained from her was a great help to me, but this was even more important: when a Russian officer pointed a revolver at me in a contentious situation, Frau Kathrin stopped him, cleared up the facts of the matter and apparently saved my life, since I was totally paralyzed by fear. After the war, Frau Kathrin went to Sweden via Poland, where she found her children again. Her relatives in Poland had all perished. Mrs. Kathrin lives in Stockholm today. She tried to file a suit against her “savior” in Hottengrun. We still correspond by letter and by now I know that her name is Mrs. Esther Warsztacka. At that time, Herr Zoegall (Mr. Zoegall), who emigrated to California, had allowed the birth of his daughter Yolantha to be registered in the Jewish Kultusgemeinde (Religious Community) in Berlin. input_chunk: 6,000 people were deported to Belzec. A further 3,000 people were sent to Belzec on 12th May. The majority of those who were sent there, belonged to the B and C categories. Those, who were in category A, wore that letter on their armbands and it was also in their work permits. On 23rd August 1942 they carried out a Strafaktion. An incident had occurred earlier, whereby a Jew had injured an Ukrainian policeman, and as a punishment they carried out a Strafaktion. The Gestapo gave Kapitän Sztreger full authority. He was the head of the Schupo. The Aktion lasted two days and an additional 6,000 people were arrested. Moreover Sztreger gave the order that thirty Jewish policemen [illegible word] were to be hanged from the lanterns in Belvedere Street. They later sold admission tickets for two Zloty and an enormous number of Poles came to look at the hanged Jews. There is a mass grave on Belvedere Street; it contains those people, who were murdered during that Aktion. They had all been stripped naked before being buried. Stapel allowed a further Aktion to be carried out on 12th September, whereby 5,000 people were transferred to Belzec. There was a similar Aktion each week. The number of streets in the ghetto gradually became fewer. One street after another was cleansed of Jews and its inhabitants were sent to Belzec. Each week, around one to two thousand. The so-called Rudolfmühle (Rudolf Mill) became a slaughterhouse, in which a group of mainly older Jews, who came from the countryside, were killed. The Germans forced the adult sons and daughters to die along with their parents {fespeifer} The ghetto was dissolved on 23rd February 1943 and only 500 Jews were left behind in the camp. This was then liquidated on 23rd July 1943. - 3 - The liquidation of the Stanislawow ghetto was carried out by people from the Gestapo Krieger, Brand, Möller, Szot, Willi Astmant, Willi Maurer with his brother and Spiro. Hass, a Gestapo man, raped and killed girls and young women. His victims were Bergmann and Racerowna. I also remember Wachtmeister Szgrrer, a Schupo, who was a hangman by profession. He had to see blood flow on a daily basis, he also shot my brother dead. Röhn, a Gestapo man, was always accompanied by his dog, which tore apart, every day, at least one person from the large group of those who worked in the ghetto. Another Gestapo man, by the name of Zajdel, ran about the ghetto all day long, as if it were his home, whilst murdering, raping and shooting. Before they killed the rabbi from Bursztyn, they tore out his tongue and pulled out his eyes. About a hundred people went into hiding in Stanislawow. 31 people sheltered in the house of a certain Stasik Jackos in Kazimierowsky Street. Mrs Janka Ciszewski sheltered myself, as well as my wife and a further nine people. We just sat in her room and Maciek Ciszewski, her seven year old son, was our most important protector and helper. He warned us all whenever Germans were approaching, so that we could quickly go quiet. During one raid, the Gestapo searched in the attic and in the cellar, however it never occurred to them to look in the other rooms, especially not after Maciek had stated; 'there are no Jews in our house'.

input_chunk: movies didn't change that often but as kids we had always Sunday afternoon cartoons or stuff like that and we had ice skating rinks. And there was a little hut where you put them on or off and they served their hot chocolate or something and it was just fun. The same thing changed in summer to the tennis court, and so we played tennis, I don't say I was ever great in that. And then there was a lumberman, who was very nice, and so he gave some lumber and at the river he made like a little beach area, there were a few very primitive, wooden sort of thing that you could change your clothes and there was a place where the local pastry shop owner in summer brought out there some yogurt and food and you could buy something and he would bring some corn, or you brought your own food. It was quite a distance, you walk through fields, but we were use to walking and we didn't mind that, and so there's summers and winters were spent that way except of course for going to school. And unfortunately, close to 1938 all this pleasantry disappeared. It happened quite, it didn't happen suddenly, but it came suddenly into our house, I would say. My mother loved music and she played very well the piano herself, and she spent her afternoons listening to music that was coming from Vienna, certain times in the afternoon. Once she listened to the music, expected to hear music, there came an angry voice through the radio. A man yelling and especially against the Jews. Of course, we then became to know that this was Hitler. And this was our first time that we heard his voice and what is behind that voice. And then, as he entered Austria, there were some refugees coming to us and they told us about how they had to disrupt their lives and run and come to us, they were guests many times at our house. But, even Vienna was only few hours from where we lived. It was distant, because it didn't happen to us. And then, they came into Poland. And then we started to feel that it's getting closer and closer, and in fact my father went to the American Consulate in Prague, that was in 1938, to get some visa because he had distant relatives in Chicago who supplied affidavits for us to come out. And he was told that there's just no way he could come. I recall very well he came back with a globe. He said "Now we can point our finger to where America is." And, we still weren't terrified. I use to go with my father to Gentile patients and next door to us was where the local Priest lived, he lived with his mother. It was, you know, he was in charge of the whole city, of the Catholic community. Mr. Richter was his name, Rev. Richter. I have even a picture of him because he taught us in the gymnasium and he taught us Latin. And he, when there was a nun, when he taught the Catholic religion, we were permitted to leave, you know, the classes. But, you know, we could choose to stay, but my father was his doctor and his mother's doctor, he chose him to be. And I know later on that my father was not permitted to practice anymore as a Jew. He personally, and I have his letter, wrote to the Papal Nuncio to allow this Jewish doctor to practice because as he wrote, he brought so many Catholic children into the world and cared so much about the poor. And my father used to give lectures because they were very primitive, some of the population, and they believed in all kind of nonsense, like a cat runs across the street, you know, this and that, and they practice this kind of medicine sometimes. And he used to go to schools and show how they should 05:29 wash their hands, how important that is, and taught them some simple health, you know, gave them health education. And he was written up in the Catholic newspaper, I still have some of the newspapers, even though they are almost in shreds. But, he made a name for himself as a very caring doctor who didn't choose, if it's someone Jewish or non-Jewish and many people were that way. I didn't see such a terrible distinction between Jews and nonJews, until the laws came against the Jews. They were mostly things of luxury or, you know, like recreational things. You had to even give up your fur collar, from your coat. And they gave you, for each of these items, a receipt. input_chunk: After being entered in the register that I kept, they were sent to be exterminated in the gas chambers. Clauberg’s block could hold a few hundred people. I know that a few of the women went straight to him from the transport without even being tattooed in the concentration camp first. To register them, I just received their identification number for the women’s camp with a note that these women would be placed in Clauberg’s block. I estimate the total number of women who returned and were struck off from Clauberg’s list – as they either were sent straight to the gas chamber or were gassed a few days after their - 4 - return – to be around a thousand. In my opinion, only a few survived – maybe ten in total. This means that around one thousand women died or were killed as a result of Clauberg’s actions. I also know that there were cases where only the identification numbers of women who did not return to the camp were struck off – these were deaths that occurred in the block itself. At the time, I read in the newspaper that Clauberg had allegedly stated that not one single woman had died in his block. I can confirm that this is not true. As I already mentioned, I know this because there were cases in which numbers from Clauberg’s block were struck off – this signified fatalities in the block. I also still remember well that when Clauberg started selecting women, he would ask if they were still untouched /”maidens”/. I am also aware of cases where women got pregnant in Clauberg’s block. The rumour spread, but these women never came back to the camp. They were some of the women whose numbers were struck off straight away, in other words they were sent straight to the gas chamber or died in the block. I am certain that it must be very distressing for those involved to talk about this matter – whether they were employed as carers in the block or perhaps even women who had been subjected to the trials and survived. I can understand if some of them could not bring themselves to undergo questioning. This is a situation that I am more than reluctant to look back on, even under questioning. I would like to correct the preceding statement: Clauberg’s block could hold around three to five hundred women. Read, approved and signed. [1] There is a spelling mistake in the original scan. input_chunk: attributed to Dr Martin's intervention or to the simultaneous action of influential English circles. m) In the conversation following my release from the prison and in a large number of discussions in the months from December 1938 to the middle of April 1939, Dr Martin vigorously expressed his indignation at the pogrom and at the incidents that had taken place in its wake. The situation in Nürnberg around the middle and end of November 1938 was dominated by a special operation by the Gauleitung [regional administration]. Jews were summoned or taken to the house of the Arbeitsfront [Labor Front] at Frauentorgraben 37 and, there, by means of threats against them and their relatives, and often also by means of the roughest physical abuse, forced to transfer property, mortgages and businesses to named people - usually, the representative Gauleiter [regional party leader] Karl Holz - or to issue powers of attorney[14] which authorised transfers. Notaries stood by on the premises of Frauentorgraben 37 in order to receive appropriate documents. The equivalent values 'agreed upon' were fractions of the actual values and, moreover, were regularly not paid. Holz, for his part, passed on the extorted assets to party favourites. When discussing this situation, Dr Martin initially explained to me that he was powerless; it was a campaign by the Gauleiter. His police officers could not even enter the premises of Frauentorgraben 37. I was given the particular impression that Dr Martin was not in control of the situation. This gradually seemed to change. Dr Martin explained to me later that he wanted to act, but, for that, he required help from higher places. In addition, he needed a range of information which he could not gather. This particularly pertained to details of the proceedings at Frauentorgraben 37 and to the transferred assets. Martin told me that many of my fellow believers were so intimidated that they did not dare give information to the police officers for fear of reprisals on the part of the Gauleitung and the Arbeitsfront, which, in this campaign, were practically identical. This corresponded to my own impression. Dr Martin requested me to procure him the information. After consulting a few colleagues and with their help, I complied therewith. Martin's request further extended to summary listings of the losses caused by Streicher's campaign from a general economic, fiscal, foreign trade and foreign exchange point of view. About this as well, I compiled - with support from my friends - the material for Dr Martin. It was and is evident to me that Dr Martin wanted to set in motion a large-scale action against Streicher. Of the action itself and its course, I have no personal knowledge. n) The preparation of this listing and the handing-over to Dr Martin took place on both sides with the greatest precautionary measures against detection or malpractice, during discussion of the details. This corresponded to the impression, which I had already increasingly been given before, that Dr Martin viewed himself as under surveillance and spied upon. He had become more and more cautious during telephone conversations. He asked for my visits over lunchtime or late in the evening when the administrative building was relatively empty. I too also used appropriate caution; I often had myself announced, for example, not to him but rather in some routine affair to Regierungsrat Dr Kiessel. Despite these difficulties, I recollect no case from the years between 1933 and the middle of April 1939 in which I was not received by Dr Martin upon demand within the shortest period. Not uncommonly, he also requested my visits himself. In my opinion, the significance of Dr Martin's conduct can only be judged with respect to the entire backdrop of conditions in Gau[15] Frankonia. input_chunk: People died in the cars, you know. It's tragic for me to explain, you know. People died, you actually sat on them because there's no room. And some them, they did take off in Auschwitz. And some they didn't; they sent to Mauthausen. Q: And were you all men on these boxcars? A: Yes, yes. Q: And were you able to say goodbye to your mother and sisters? 37 A: No, they were taken away one day or one night in the middle -- or early morning. They didn't show up. All the women were gone. They didn't have an inkling, nothing. Q: So you and Maurice are in this cattle car? A: Yes. I even had a blade to cut, like a little saw that can cut steel. And I kept it, you know, under my pants, under my shoes. And I told my brother when I said, "Maybe we'll have a way of cutting out the window, the steel, or the floor when the train stops." We never used it, we didn't use it because there was no room. Plus I had an SS man on each side where the door was. Q: Outside the door? A: Outside. Maybe where the -- I don't know it they stayed there all the time or when the train slowed down and they came to a halt. You always had SS men, you heard them giving commands, you know. Q: Do you remember the smells and the noise? A: The smell, noise? No. People were not scr eaming or yelling or crying. No, I don't remember. Maybe when we were first taken to Plaszów, the women and children, yes, but later on they dulled our life. They took everything out of us, you know. We just were like sheep in a way. We had nothing to fight with. They starved out, tired out. We knew if we rebelled, we had no arms. They had machine guns. Just whatever somebody did, some people, say, one of these SS men 05:07:30 would kick you or hit you, you would curse them back. They pulled you out and shot you right on the spot. We saw that, so everybody kept quiet. Q: Did you throw away your . . . A: My blade? Q: Yeah. A: I have to think. I must have, yes. Because when we came to Mauthausen, we came there at night. They undressed us completely, we had to undress. Nude. Not only that, we had to go on a chair or table and they looked all over your body and in your rectum. In your mouth, to see if we had any -- would have anything hidden, you know. Because they would find some gold, and maybe somebody may have had a diamond or a coin. They didn't give us any clothes for about two days. We had no barracks either; we are outdoors. Then they gave us some of these striped uniforms, you know. 38 Q: Was it cold, or this was in . . . input_chunk: 4Dr. Hercy Gonzaga Gama Angelo. 17 where I began to get really exercised about this case and seeing what I could do to to to take it a little bit further, so together with my assistant uh Vice Consul by the name of Fred Kaplan, we began to to...well, first of all, uh pour over the diary. His hand-writing wasn't all that good, but I was trying to get more information out of there and at the same time trying to find out if there were other Dr. Gama's in the area, and then we had the, really the top question was what does Sama stand for. He said he went to see Dr. Gama in Sama, but there is no town called Sama in the area of Sao Paulo and uh there was abundant evidence to prove that Mengele didn't wander very far away from his hideout, so he wouldn't have traveled two hundred miles to see a root canal specialist. He would have had it done somewhere close to where he lived, so we uh went to all of the different dental associations and uh so on and uh with the help of a dentist uh friend of mine in Sao Paulo, we put together the most comprehensive list possible of Dr. Gama's in the state of Sao Paulo. The city of Sao Paulo has a population of about sixteen, seventeen million people, and the state of Sao Paulo has about thirty-two million people. We are talking about a big area. So we put together this list and we came up with about eighteen dentists by the name of Gama, of whom one, of course, was the one I'd interviewed and already ruled out, but of the remaining Gama's , most of them had graduated from dental school after 1979, at least a majority of them had. Uh one had died. One had moved away from Sao Paulo immediately upon graduation. Uh to make a long story short, there was no Gama left who could remotely fit the situation that uh we were trying to to clarify. 02:20:58 So at the same time I was pouring over this diary and saying now what could Sama stand for. What could Sama stand for? It's obviously not the name of a town. There is no town by the name of Sama. And by reading the diary over and over again, I realized that when it came to names, Mengele was using a bit of a code. When he didn't want a possible reader of his diary to know who he was referring to, he would use an abbreviation of using initials. The first initial of the first name, and the first one or two letters of the second name. And so I noticed that there was a repetition of this pattern throughout the diary, and then I started to think of Sama in terms of how I could interpret that word as a possible abbreviation. And it finally came to me in a in a flash that Sama could very possibly stand for Santo Amaro, the name of a suburb of Sao Paulo where I was living, and where he was known to have lived with the Brosserts and the Stammers. input_chunk: barracks of which this small garrison had plenty, there were old, partly dilapidated blocks of houses in the area assigned to the Jews, with crooked, dark steps and hardly inviting rooms to which most of the new arrivals were not allocated, instead to the attics where they initially had to bed down in the dirt, without mattresses or blankets. We were lucky and were given a room on the first floor after only 5 days, but there were many who had to stay up there for a long time. And winter was coming. In our room which was about 20sqm we were 14 women. There were bunk beds, i.e. planks without mattresses or blankets unless one had brought some in one’s hand luggage. In my experience it was better to live in a “flat” on the first floor because one was able to arrange one’s life apart from one’s fellow occupants who were moving to and fro in the narrow corridor in front of the beds. Now it was important to adjust: the bed was at the same time sleeping-living-eating- and storage space. The most necessary hygiene facilities were missing. Only one wash bowl existed, and one had to be on good terms with its lucky owner to be lent it in the morning. Thus the first days since our arrival were spent in the task of acquiring the most necessary objects for a rather primitive life and to achieve a bearable relationship with one’s roommates. New observations Immediately during our first days I had one of the most unpleasant impressions of my entire stay in Theresienstadt : on the street, endless processions of frail old people walked haltingly towards the Bauschewitz station – a transport to the East! Fortunately, we did not know until the end of the war what these transports signified, but one guessed that they did not bode well and certainly meant something worse than Theresienstadt. In any case, this sight was harrowing. One could tell that these people were completely resigned to their fate, no longer capable of showing any emotion. This sight will be unforgettable for me. In addition, there was the fear of when will it be my turn? – This fear did not leave you right until the end and was probably the worst aspect of the entire stay in Th., worse than the hunger from which we would suffer horribly. - 4 - The second thing initially was the treatment of the sick and the “interment” of the dead. Both institutions became properly regulated later on, so that one might call the medical attention and the hospitals exemplary, considering that we were in a concentration camp. The sick lay in a so-called “Marodenstube” (infirmary), mostly close to each other, and often not even the most necessary procedures could be carried out. It was quite impossible to do so as time was short and new transports arrived daily. Because these were mainly elderly, physically and emotionally weakened people, mortality was naturally high. Most prevalent was diarrhoea which, under normal circumstances, would be cured, but here quickly led to death. The one good thing was that because the patients were so weak they passed away without great suffering. Dreadful was the transportation of the deceased. They were put into some kind of shed initially, barely covered, and then driven off on a cart- several at a time – in front of the eyes of the people in the street. As I mentioned, all this improved greatly later on. Another thing came to my attention and amazed me: vehicles were rarely drawn by horses let alone cars. It was often human beings who had to pull or push the vehicles which were laden with heavy loads. Old hearses, no longer in use, were the means of these transports. At times, something comical occurred: some young people who were manipulating these vehicles accompanied this by singing the funeral march by Chopin. input_chunk: sold the house, so we could now take everything with us. We first lived with ‘Aryan’ acquaintances, who were becoming increasingly worried as time went by. So we were pleased when shortly after the start of the War the wife of my doctor offered us a small flat in one of her houses. We paid the required rent, but the wife of the housemaster was so hateful that we just could not stay here for long. My Jewish looks were making the situation too dangerous. The father of a fellow-pupil finally managed – through the head of the Steglitz community - to get us a small and very modest two-room flat, but we never had a moment’s peace again. My mother and I were ordered at regular intervals to go to the police station on Alexanderplatz and we were interrogated there for hours: Why was my father in England? Examples of his handwriting were presented to us, and he was under suspicion of being a spy. They asked me whether General Sherman, after whom the American tanks were named, was a relative. I said he was, albeit a distant one. They also asked me about the activities of my Catholic youth group, which had actually significantly declined in numbers. With all the increasing complications, everything was becoming more and more difficult. We received anonymous letters. One of these stated: ‘The Jewish pig is being killed’. Whenever I would come back late from the practice, my mother would always pick me up from the station. I would always telephone before leaving, and in all weathers, my mother would always come for me and we went home together…… she was just too worried about me coming home alone. A female friend who worked in a private bank always warned us in advance whenever a raid was about to take place. This bank had many SS-customers who were grateful for good tips and showed appreciation for these, whilst warning my friend whenever they were planning drastic measures, as the wife of the bank owner was allegedly also ‘not entirely Aryan’. After receiving the warning, my mother and I fled Berlin. My mother went to friends in Hirschberg while I went to my good “Poor School Sisters’ who hid me. This happened seven times between 1941 and 1943. We were of course in a constant state of nervous tension. Whenever there was a knock on the door, we thought it was the ‘Gestapo’, as they never rang the bell. At that time I was still working for the doctor. At the start of 1943, I developed scarlet fever and had to stop working for a while. And at this same time, the practice ceased to function for a while as it was hit in a plane attack. Whenever the planes attacked, Jews and highest-level mixed-race people were not allowed to seek the protection of the cellars; but the people in our building were anti-Nazis, so if we did not come quickly to the shelters, they went to fetch us. I was not able to continue my job at the doctor’s practice as the Chamber of Doctors explained that he no longer needed an assistant, and in addition as a high-level mixed-race person, I would no longer be allowed to work with the public. On 31 March 1943, I went with my mother to relatives in Freiburg. I tried to find a post there, but it was impossible …… it was too late. What was I supposed to do? My last hope was a friend of my father in Berlin, to whom I turned in my hour of need. We did have some money, but it was still very important to work because without a job there was always the danger of compulsory service such as factory work. My father’s friend was the only one of many who was able to help. He was the general director of a large company, and he took me on as a private secretary and told the head of personnel to employ me without an application form to complete. This was in July 1943. input_chunk: this highly interesting spectacle we witnessed, we saw fully laden lorries and private cars rushing down the streets: the Nazis who, just before the arrival of the enemy, were making their escape and taking whatever they could. Thus the 8th May 1945 arrived – the Russians moved in, the day of liberation was finally upon us. The days that followed, in the knowledge that we had survived the time of terror, will remain unforgettable for all concerned. The iron gates were opened, the road to Leitmeritz was clear, the Russian soldiers moved in as victors and distributed chocolate, tea, cigarettes etc. to the Jews standing along their path. The Czechs hastily removed the German street signs, on the main square music was playing and there was dancing. The Russian horses grazed on the well-tended lawn of this square so that it soon became unrecognisable again. There were other matters that we did not like about the Russians, in particular the younger women had to protect themselves from them, but all in all it did not even resemble the conditions in the German cities and did not interfere with the general joy and the feeling of gratitude for our liberators. In the following days, cars arrived from every part of Germany. Laboriously they had to find a way through the destroyed streets which were crowded with soldiers and refugees. But they came: Americans, couriers who took our mail to our relatives, and as far as possible, the families and friends of the Jews. It was not very long before German cities sent buses to bring home their Jewish citizens. The return journey of the Danish and Dutch Jews was especially warm-hearted, their departure was accompanied by music. Often it was not easy to take leave of the fellow-sufferers of the past years, and despite the great joy there were also some tears. The most problematic was the transport to Berlin; the railway only covered short distances, there were of course no connections, the roads in an appalling condition, and so the journey to Berlin in the early times took 8 to 10 days, the speed of a mail coach without its comfort. Nevertheless, the journey was undertaken by many intrepid individuals. Because of this, Berlin could only begin the transport of its Jews belatedly. - 12 - Those who intended to emigrate or had not yet made a firm decision were taken to the camp at Deggendorf in Lower Bavaria. From there they were sent to the destination of their choice over the course of 4 years, until 1949. Signed : KAETHE BRESLAUER - 13 - Report on Interview with Frau Studienrätin Käthe Breslauer, Heerstr. 36, Berlin-Charlottenburg, on 15.1.56. On 31st March 1933, Frau Breslauer, then a school-teacher in Berlin, was warned by a colleague, who was a Nazi but well-disposed, that she would do better not to come to school the following morning, and when the morning came, the headmaster telephoned to her not to come. Since she had served as a teacher for more than ten years, she was pensioned, but younger Jewish teachers, being turned out of their jobs, had to find work of another kind, unless they had fought in the war. Teachers who had done that held their posts until 1935. In 1934, Frau Breslauer started to teach at one of the special Jewish schools which had been founded in the previous year. With support from the Jewish community, these were kept open until 1939, when it became impossible for Jewish children to receive any public education. Until 1939 there was also the Jewish Kulturbund which organised plays, concerts and so on under supervision. In 1938 travel restrictions on the Jews had become severe, and it was only by getting special permission from the authorities that Frau Breslauer was allowed to travel on holiday to Palestine. input_chunk: the ground was frozen. One day, a commission was due to arrive, and Seck ordered the digging of a mass grave by blasting the ground. If the commission had not been expected, the corpses would probably have been there until the summer of 1942. On 26 March 1942, everybody had to line up on the parade ground for roll call, and about 1400 people, among them children and the elderly, were chosen. They were told they would be brought to a new camp in Duenamuende. We never heard about the transport having arrived. The Latvian locals told me that Latvian guard squads had already dug a mass grave in the high forest four days before the transport set off, which had been intended for this transport. In this context, I would like to mention that a young girl called Marianne Klemann, whom Seck apparently wanted to spare, had been sent to the sewing workshop by him. The young girl wanted to go to Duenamuende with her family. When some people were still missing for the transport and this young girl came forward yet again, Seck said the following to her: “Go, you stupid girl, you will regret it today.” I had concluded from this that Seck understood this transport as a death transport. The terrible conditions in the camp Jungfernhof lasted roughly until the end of 1942. Then, most people were brought from Jungfernhof to the ghetto, including me. Only a few - 3 - remained at Jungfernhof, who worked the farm and transformed it into a model farm. According to reports we received in the ghetto, the situation of the people at Jungfernhof had been quite tolerable since then. The people had to work hard, but they were no longer ill-treated with regard to food and otherwise. I remember the frightening torturers from the ghetto period in Riga, who have so many lives on their conscience: SS-Obersturmfuehrer Dr. Lange, Major Sauer, Krause, Gymnich. (signed) Lucie Levy. Witnesses: Dr. H.G. Van Dam

The long ends of a white scarf hung down over his breast. He replied to my greeting in a soft, melodious voice. I trusted him on the spot, but before I could start a conversation, he stood up hastily and quickly disappeared into the darkness. Then I met him a couple of times, but it never seemed to happen that he wanted to justify himself to me. However, one day it occurred that he lost some papers whilst standing up which he was carrying under his arm. Whilst I was bending to pick them up, a dedication caught my eye, which was written at an angle over the first page. “My dear friends, Jakob and Franziska Bender” Josef Joachim. “Joachim, not the famous violinist?” I called out in surprise. The face of the old man was infused with a mixture of pride and intimacy. “You knew him, sir?”, he asked in a friendly manner. I said, "yes." It was the year 1945, and how the face of the world had changed since those days when I heard Josef Joachim play for the first time in Goettingen. The old man sat down once again. "If you have heard him, then you will understand that you cannot forget him”, he said intently. “You would like to know how I received this dedication? Well, that cannot be explained in a few words. I grew up here in Berlin, in a humble, small, three-windowed house in the Bruedergasse, near the river Spree. My father ran a glass business there. I was supposed to take it over one day, but I did not want to. I was still only a mere child when I chased after every stringed instrument as if I were possessed. This did not change as the years passed and finally my father allowed me to remain a musician. And so, it happened at a small spa in Meiningen that I, as the leader of a small orchestra, became acquainted with Josef Joachim. Shortly after that, I returned again to Berlin and I married a few days before Whitsun in 1880. I was so happy that all of the difficulties which had been placed in the way of my marriage had finally been overcome. The protest of my in-laws, who did not want their daughter to marry a musician, and the objections of my mother, who was deeply religious, and wanted a child from a Jewish house for me.” I looked at the old man and realised that he had forgotten that a stranger was sitting at his side. He explained the past as if it had happened yesterday. - 3 – "I remember this feast of Whitsun well”, he said. “The air was saturated by the warm wind of May, and I decided to travel out to Charlottenburg with my young wife.
