input_chunk: the management committee of the Jewish parish registered our arrival with the Gestapo in Gdańsk. Our fears that this could result in difficulties for us turned out to be unfounded. In October 1939, I travelled from Gdańsk to Berlin to my old parents, with whom I could live until 1943. We had two aunts staying with us, and after their deaths, two fellow Jews moved in with us. I had to do a lot of physical work. In addition, we lived in constant anxiety. There was no end to the alarming news about new measures discriminating against Jews, evictions and the like. We also continuously had visits from Aryan people looking for accommodation. Once, we had to leave our five-room flat within a week. I sought out the Jewish organisation that was responsible for evictions and managed to have the eviction order reversed with great difficulty. One day, my 74-year-old mother broke her femoral neck. We thereupon had to bring her to the Jewish hospital. However, I brought her back home after 6 days as I was able to take better care of her there. I myself never slept without sleeping pills and constantly had problems with my gall bladder. At that time, I lost 28 pounds. I thought a lot about my future without making a firm decision. In 1942, my parents and I received permission to enter Sweden at the instigation of my younger brother. However, the Nazis denied us the exit permit. The Gestapo told my father that we could perhaps leave in two years, but that we would be long dead by then. The time came for my parents to be taken away. My mother was at that time not fit to travel. When the Gestapo came to get her, we did not yet have the medical report on her condition. Instead of my parents, I was brought to the retirement home on the Rosenstraße because of how I was walking and standing. There, I immediately looked for the doctor, intending to talk to him, but could not find him; so I left behind the papers that our doctor had prepared for the Gestapo. Soon after, a gentleman came to - 5 - my room and asked for me, as he had noticed my name. It turned out that he was a former classmate of my late husband. He promised to do everything in his power to help me. The next day, my papers were examined and as everything was in order, I was free to go. On the morning of 8 January 1943, Gestapo officers came to our flat without prior notification to take my parents away for good. My mother still could not walk on her own. I prepared everything for the departure, packed their luggage and food for the journey, and cooked lunch. While the Gestapo officers and their Jewish attendants sat down to eat, I escaped from the flat. I had agreed with my mother that I would do this, as we would have had to part ways soon. It is hard to imagine how we all felt in our hearts then. I was lucky in my escape. First, I found accommodation with a devout Catholic woman, then with my Catholic brother-in-law. Thereafter, I was constantly moving. I often did not know in the morning where I was going to spend the night. On the advice of a Protestant matron who also hid me for some time, I decided to change my name. I thereafter I asked a landlady whom I knew if I could have a small room only at night for 14 days, as I would be staying with a friend whose husband was on a business trip during the day. I secured the room. The first morning, I found a woman whom I knew in the kitchen of my landlady’s flat. I was very frightened, but she promised me that she would not betray me. The compass was, however, absolutely no good to us in the woods as our torches no longer worked and we had no matches with us. Now, we were happy to have a clear night sky above us and we found our way once more by the ‘Great Bear’ and the ‘Southern Cross’. It was bitterly cold, but as we were running quickly and out of fear, we did not notice the cold as much. We had been running for 5 hours already and it was around 12 midnight, when we heard the barking of dogs behind us. We ran into a young part of the forest and hid, but it served no purpose. The dogs picked-up our scent and the Border Guards soon found us. We had to go back until we got to a large building in the woods. There, our personal details were written down, we were asked many times whether we had any money. Very wisely for us, we had none and we said so. It was of no use…, we had to take our shirts off and were searched. Even our rucksacks were rummaged through. In the lower section, I had my shaving brush, a 5 Mark piece, but they did not find them. At the interrogation, we told the truth that we were Jews wanting to get to Holland, but we were still not believed, because we were really without money. I gave them the address of the Dutch man in Amsterdam. They then went in and asked Berlin first of all whether we had anything outstanding. Around 3 o’clock, they took us by the shortest route to the border and said “be aware, that if you both come back or get sent back, you’ll both go to a concentration camp! For sure! Now run!” And how we ran! As they short at us! We ran until we could do so no more, then we threw ourselves in the snow and crawled on until we got to a haystack, where we took a breather for around 5 minutes, in order to them go further. To give in to tiredness and to rest would have meant certain death. We then came upon a small path in the field and were in a small village after 2 hours. In a cow byre, where milking was in progress, we asked the farmer’s wife whether we could rest awhile in the warm byre. As we told her everything, she took us into the cabin and gave us hot milk and something to eat. She even gave us some money, so that we could get across the river and described the way exactly, that we had to take. But, we should be aware of the police! The Queen had ordered that all refugees should be sent back. The flow of refugees had become too great. We got to the river successfully and had avoided going through villages. We even successfully avoided the police, as they rode on bikes. Around midday, we went round a large village and had to go past a small farmstead, in order to get to the path. Just at that moment, a policeman saw us, who was on business there. He arrested us and took us to the Mayor. He questioned us! Then, he gave us a good lunch, but told us immediately that we would have to return. No amount of crying and wailing helped. The work in the camps with coal mines was exceptionally hard. That was the worst thing my eyes ever saw. The work was divided into three eight-hour shifts. In some of the mines it was very wet. The prisoners’ shoes were worn to pieces, leaving many with permanently wet feet, which inevitably resulted in severe diseases. Many tunnels were only 70cm high, so that the work had to be done LYING ON ONE’S STOMACH OR KNEELING. Eight hours in this position, almost without any breaks and subject to beatings, that takes its toll. We were slaves! A coal shovel was at least four times the size of a normal shovel. Many prisoners in these mines met their death in collapsing tunnels, their skulls smashed by lumps of coal or by stones. Needless to say, since we returned from the tunnels - 5 - completely blackened, we had to bathe every day. That was no great pleasure either as one had to undress in the open air and wait one’s turn, even in the most severe cold. Hardly anyone possessed a towel. So the prisoners ran back to their barracks naked and dripping wet. It is interesting that the SS loved music very much and that our artistic performances, which were really very good, constituted their only entertainment in those villages. That way, the performing artists had the good fortune to be able to practice their profession and were, by order of the commandant, treated better than other prisoners. IV. The most dreadful things I saw occurred during the evacuation of Auschwitz in January 1945, when the Russians were approaching. I will attempt to describe it. All those able to walk [any distance] set off for Gleiwitz. Some camps were 75km away. On the first day we walked 45km, covering the remaining distance on the second day. It does not take much to imagine that after long imprisonment, beatings, hunger, disease and back-breaking work not all prisoners had the strength to walk this enormous distance[7], and almost without a break at that. Those unable to walk on were simply gunned down and left by the roadside. This began to occur so frequently that a SS officer had to give the order to not leave the dead simply lying by the roadside, but to carry the bodies away to the forest nearby. Mengele stood outside by the truck with nurse Hanka, and then Mengele grabbed me by the shoulders, the nurse had to take my feet and they threw me, like you would throw a sack, into the truck. There were already so many women on the truck that I landed almost at the back of the truck. Mengele then used his feet to push me with great force further into the truck to make room for more women after me. More women then arrived and they were all thrown on top of those who were already in the truck. In this way layer upon layer piled up. When it looked as if the women lying at the back of the truck would slide out, the rear flap of the truck was closed and then they threw more women on top so that there were 3 and 4 layers on top of one another. While the sick were being loaded up, Nurse Hanka wept at Mengele's unbelievably sadistic behaviour. Mengele saw this, grabbed the woman's hand and turned this hand around so that the top of her fingers touched her arm. Then he sent the nurse back into the block, fetched the block elder and with her the loading ended. 2 fellow-sufferers lay on top of me and they threw a third on top. It was only because I lay to the side and had my head free that I did not die from suffocation. - 4 - We were dressed only in a shirt. This dreadful transport resulted in 2 dead on arrival at E-Camp. Their death was caused by suffocation, during the night another 7 women died and then a lot more later on. The next day Mengele appeared in our block and asked how many deaths there had been. When he was told only about the two who had suffocated, he exclaimed: "Only two and later?" They gave him the same answer. Hearing this Mengele said: "Impossible, only two". During my time at Birkenau I saw Mengele a number of times, but I never saw him as unhappy as he was on the day where he was told that only two had died. As a result of this brutal incident, because I was at the bottom of the truck with three other women thrown on top of me, I suffered heavy bruising on my sides and shoulders. input_chunk: and be with my friends and relatives in 1946. I sorted out business matters from there. I then had to return to Denmark, and there was no other option but to move back in with my husband. The living conditions there were so tough that I had no other choice but to persevere. It was a bitter time for me, which brought back plenty of dismal memories. I was 70 years old at the time. I was finally able to return to Germany in 1953, as the Wiedergutmachungsgesetze (Reparation Laws) had come into force and I counted on being able to support myself using these funds. By chance, I was given a small apartment in Dahlem with my two sisters, who had also lived through extremely tough conditions abroad. Once life had generally calmed down again, the tensions of wartime and post-war life were slowly forgotten. My husband and I were now living apart, and my relationship with him became more reasonable. We somehow ended up with a good amicable arrangement, as we had planned when we first entered into this fictitious marriage. I am now deeply grateful to him, as he ultimately saved my life. He visits me every now and again in Berlin, of course as my guest. My sisters, my friends and I, we all do whatever we can to make life easy for him. After all, he is now an old man (he has just turned 70), and it is not particularly easy for him in Denmark as a single man. He even visited on my 80th birthday. - 7 - I was happy to be close to my two sisters again. Almost all of my old friends had emigrated, were killed or died; I am almost a stranger in my old home country, where it was initially very difficult to get an immigration permit. In 1932, I owned 500,000 marks in assets. I was able to help countless poor friends to emigrate with a large amount of this money. When I returned in 1953, I had to fight tooth and nail to receive a modest livelihood from the reparations. Today, I am once again living in a nice, small apartment with my sisters. I once went back to Denmark to visit my friends – I am thankful to this beautiful country and its amazing people, who saved me and so many Jews with their genuine philanthropy and their sense of justice, and who themselves suffered through unspeakably tough times during the German Nazi occupation. [1] Believed to be a former street name in the outskirts of Berlin. [2] For British emigrants, later those of other nationalities, one’s “lift” was the box or container taken on the voyage and representing everything that could be brought from home.

input_chunk: this was the Viennese office, which I worked in as well as administrating. Then I administered the office in Salzburg, the one in Linz, which was the other side of the Russian zone, and the one in the French zone in Innsbruck, and then we had representatives in all the displaced persons camps because we would go out to them to save people having to travel to Vienna, which they couldn™t do unless they had permits to go through the Russian zone, and that, nobody was keen to do at this time. We would go into the camps, and tell them things which were necessary for them to know, or collect papers, or bring them papers for signature. It was a bit of an awkward program, although it worked very well. Or they could go into Salzburg, where there papers were held. It was not an easy situation actually because we were always worried that there might be Russians around trying to pick up people because sometimes we had Russian army officers who were Jewish. For example, a woman came to me one day dressed almost in rags with dyed hair looking very ugly, and she said her husband and daughter were in Palestine. She was a doctor in the Russian army, and there was a certificate for Palestine for her at the British consulate, could we help her? Well, the first thing you think is, ﬁA ha! She™s a spy. She wants to see what we™re doing.ﬂ And I took all her particulars and I went across to the British consulate, and sure enough there was a certificate, but that wasn™t enough as far as I was concerned. I contacted friends who were working with the Jewish agency for Palestine, told them the story, and asked them to check in Palestine that she did indeed have a husband and a daughter there, because one never knew how honest these people were. There were many ways by which you could trick somebody, and the answer eventually came back that yes, her husband and daughter were there and they confirmed her story. Now, how was I to get her out? She had to come at times when very few people were around. I had to try and do everything so that she wouldn™t be seen, and eventually I got her certificate, and how to send her to the airport which was in the Russian zone? And the only way to do it was to take her myself, and don™t think I wasn™t scared. I™m not so brave, but she sat in the car with me and we handed in her papers, and my propesk, my permit to go into the Russian zone, and we put her on a plane. And there were others. I had a young woman who was working at the Polish consulate, who had a brother in Canada. My goodness, my memory™s going back, and she said she had a visa to go to Canada, and again, I was suspicious, and checked her out in the same way. I checked through the consulate and then I checked with the agency, the Jewish agency working in Montreal, and they confirmed her story, and she told the Poles at that time she was going on vacation, and off she went to Canada. It was tricky doing this because you were always suspicious that perhaps these people were not genuine, and that you might be picked up yourself on the street because people were being picked up, particularly by the Russians. People would be walking along and suddenly a car would stop, and like a 41 gangster film, people would be whisked off and not seen again. It never happened to any of us. I™m just adding drama to the story, I guess. Q: Who were they picking up? Who were they looking for? A: I have no idea. Q: You don™t know? To initially leave the 'stories' to one side, I should inform you that from the entire Engel and Lewin families, the following people are still alive. Hanna Marcus in Palestine. Walter Jacobi is with his wife and child in Ecuador. And that, my dears, is the rest of the whole family. Of the Engel family from Düsseldorf, you certainly know that they were transported to Minsk and lost their lives there. How is it looking in the Meyer family? Who is alive? In 1936, I spoke in Karlsbad for the last time to Arthur and Ida. The son had just married in Palestine and how so very unhappy you were about this marriage. Now to a few details that you should know about my own experiences, which were very sad. You still know that I went in October 33 with Gerda and my mother to Prague, where I opened several businesses in accordance with my great love of magic. The businesses went so well, that it was no longer possible for me to manage it alone, and I let Hettie from Berlin take over parts of the business. I inducted her into the whole matter and she managed the winter business in Teplitz and the summer business in Aussig. Hettie married Rudi Freund, with whom I had Bar Mitzvah and even he worked for me. We did well, Gerda and I had - 2 - a delightful boy, who was my entire bliss and made us both so happy. Our dear mother doted on the child like she did her own children. She slept with my little Peter in a bed and, as he grew, he did not leave her side. In September 1938, on the basis of an entitlement to an inheritance from the Freund family, Hettie had the chance to emigrate from the Czech Republic to America under the 'capital quota' without a Dollar in her pocket. We had, unfortunately, to remain behind, ever hoping, that Hettie would succeed at the eleventh hour in still bringing us over. Admittedly, the affidavits were lying with the consul in Prague, but the quota had already hit its limit, so that the thugs caught up to us in Prague. It was always clear to me what threatened us, but I was powerless, as our little mother was already almost 70 and our little child too small to jump onto a coal train, as thousands of people had done, in order to get to the port of Gdingen via Poland and, from there, via Sweden to England to save themselves. Even as Hitler entered Prague, it would still have been easy for individuals to intentionally jump onto the slow moving coal trains from the Czech coal region. We had to run towards disaster with our eyes open. At any rate, we had 5 good years until his entry into Prague in 1938. And I offered to help and I had an advantage with that, that they let my mother lie up after the bunks were fixed and she could lie there and rest, so that was my advantage. And we worked hard, and one time, we had to work outside, it was called "Aussenkommando" , meaning "working outside." So after we stood we'd file out there and got our ration, there were an orchestra playing for us. There was an orchestra at the gate of the camp that led outside with the vicious dogs on the other side playing a march for us to march out. And I remember seeing a rotten apple as I walked and I was dying to have that rotten apple and one of the guards just kicked it away before I could get it. And as 23 we walked, I saw a little hut, I guess some of the guards lived, seeing some steam coming out and shade, by biggest dream was to live in such a hut, to be away from everyone because you were never alone, you couldn't wash by yourself there are millions of things in the wash room. I think they were able to cross the Suez into Palestine. Q: And was the same true in Italy? A: No, in Italy, it was different. Firstly, there were the displaced people. They were Yugoslav Jews. There was a Jewish orphanage in Rome, for example, which had been taken over by the Catholics. The Catholics had taken the Jewish children from the orphanage and had hidden them in their orphanage out of town, and then they™d hidden them again, and when the Catholic orphanage was bombed, the one that was out of town, the American Joint Distribution Committee rebuilt it for them as a thank you for having saved the Jewish children, and then our units Œ because we had volunteers Œ the Joint had administrators who, we had volunteers who set up the orphanages again. They had experience in working in orphanages. It was quite an exciting time in a way to do positive things Œ to see children smiling, children who hadn™t been incarcerated, because we™d seen firstly the Yugoslav children who had been starving, and we began to get pictures of what was happening in Germany. We used to occasionally get shown German film that had been captured of the Nazis throwing children over the balcony, you know, it was ghastly, ghastly. 16 Q: Did you travel around Italy or did you stay primarily in Rome? A: No, I traveled around. I traveled around Italy. Q: So, what was your job, then, in terms of traveling around? What was your task? A: Right, for example, if I went down, let™s sa y to Santa Maria di Bari, I would go there, first you™d see how the camp was running. It was amazing how, without any experience, one became an expert. I did have something kind of social administration training, and I think I was instinctively an administrator. I would see what was needed in that camp. For example, we had one of our unit members in charge of a search bureau which we set up immediately because the important thing was to try to reunite families. We had no baby clothes because once people Œ the camps were liberated and people began to lead normal lives, women began to menstruate again. They hadn™t menstruated all through the war, and being normal human beings they began to get pregnant and have babies. We needed sanitary napkins for the women. We needed baby clothing. We needed special food for pregnant women. There were some older people who survived. We needed special food for them. We needed doctors. We needed more social workers. And one could assess this, and gradually these people came in to work in the camps. It was exciting in the sense that you felt you could do something positive, and then the most important thing, I think, at that time was the search bureaus that we set up. input_chunk: USHMM Archives RG-50.549.02*0057 71A: This letter I™ll -- I™ll read an excerpt from, is from a girl from a -- Kosovo. Dear Nana, I™m writing this letter to thank yo u for coming to Duke on Wednesday. I -- although I was unable to attend your formal talk, I enjoyed hearing your stories from an intimate perspective. They™re extremely vivid accounts of your experiences in the concentration camp, and encouraged me to think more about the situation in regards to my relatives in Kosovo. I am sure that those who have heard you speak will agree that you have made a tremendous impact on their lives. I will never forget being moved to tears by your words and emotion. I find it extremely fortunate that I was able to hear your experiences. Again, I thank you so much for coming. Until then, to your health and happiness. Melina.ﬂ And th is is from my granddaughter. ﬁDear Nana, thank you for doing something for me that forever will be part of my memories at Duke. Your speech was wonderful and inspirational as us -- always. The presence that you have while speaking to o -- strange rs, bearing your soul and revealing some of your most painful experiences, astounds me. As I have said before, your family can rest in peace knowing that you told and continue to tell their story. You are -- you have touched many lives with your testim ony, but you have touched me because of the person you ca -- became -- become after the war. Your generosity, love and strength are your greatest as sets and you have taught me well, as I now enter my senior year of Duke and begin to look for the road I will travel next, I will keep all that you have told me in my heart. Thank you again for coming to Duke and for sharing yourself so unselfishly. I love you. Always, Alexis.ﬂ USHMM Archives RG-50.549.02*0057 72Q: How does that make you feel when you read that? A: Wonderful. Wonderful. Th-There™s so many of them here, it™s -- well, but Joan has it. Q: Yeah. So you -- our listeners who would like to read more of those can find it at the Holocaust Museum. A: Yes, the booklet is -- I -- the teacher was thoughtful enough to send me two copies, one for me and one for the museum specifically, and I forwarded it to Dr. ronga -- Ringelheim. Q: Well, since we are with the museum, let me follow up with a question about the museum. How do you -- how do you see the ro le of the Holocaust Museum in -- in Washington, D.C.? How do you fe el about what -- what they are doing, or what they have done already? A: Well, I express myself, I feel very eloquently about it on my video. I -- I was absolutely delighted with the creation of this museum, because it is a tremendous tool, not only of showing people what ha s happened, but as a tool for educating people for the future, how to learn to get along. How to -- how to see things from the perspective of different human beings, pe ople who went through it, people who did help, people who taught about it. The museum has testimonies of so many survivors, and they range from people who can hardly express themselves to people who are very articulate and who can just bare their soul, and try to teach the listeners, and open their eyes and ears and teach them the lessons. And he went around the room and each individual stood up and said "Dr. Tuma, based on the examination that I've performed and the data that I have seen, I believe that these are the remains of Josef Mengele." And each one in turn stood up and said that in front of all the others, in front of Dr. Tuma, including the American specialists from the Simon Weisenthal Center and the specialists from the U.S. Department of Justice. And I was sitting next to Menachan Russek again who was taking notes uh but was there as strictly an observer, and uh I didn't know what was going through his mind and I don't want to speak for what may have been going through his mind, but I did ask him, "How do you feel now at this moment, Mr. Ruseck, in light of what you said to me before," and he said with that wonderful Jewish sense of humor, he looked at me and he said "Well, better I should stand on his grave than he on mine." input_chunk: to find this a strange letter. I think, perhaps, you will not understand why I write such a letter - until after you have read it. I have written my parents a similar story. Now I write you - for a little different reason. You'll see what I mean some pages from here. The Seventh Army has authorised us to write - has allowed us to say - that we're in Munich. I'm there now. Munich - Hitler's cradle-city. It's damaged and quiet. We're near Berchtesgarten, but I haven't been there. We're also near Dachau - remember Dachau? It's Jan Valtin's Dachau - Jan Valtin of “Out of the Night”. Remember? Dachau - an early mystery place of Nazism. But there remains no aura of mystery today. No, it's all clear - so very clear. I met a Polish Jew the other day. He had been liberated from Dachau. He was twenty-four years old - and looked fifty. His face looked fifty - his body was about as healthy looking as a normal patient at Harrisburg, Pa. He had no teeth - but they hadn't fallen out. Hitler's S.S. were the dentists. He was just one of the lucky ones. There were other unfortunates. I haven't seen Dachau - but all I say is true - I swear it on my own life. Disbelieve me - call me a liar - if you dare! There were found some fifty, fully-loaded boxcars - loaded with bodies. I saw a picture of one - it was overflowing. We buried - with bulldozers - some 4,000. They were from the railroad cars and from rooms in the camp where they were stacked like cordwood covered with lime. We spoke to a Pole who had been forced to throw his parents into the incinerator. And how would you like to hear about these incinerators - it makes for nauseous reading. There was a plaque in front of each one saying something about “ashes to ashes” being better than "dust to dust”. Some compensation for the victims, eh! And they were run in a very businesslike fashion. It was necessary to burn 250 bodies each day to keep the furnaces in good working order. How was the quota met? Easy. They always had at least 150 on a list. But the rest were gotten like this. - 2 - These prisoners were divided into groups of sixteen. These sixteen slept on four shelves, approximately six by six, with six inches clearance between shelves. Any infraction by one of the sixteen resulted in the death of all of them. And infractions were easy. Under the S.S. - the trained beasts - the quota was always met. And how were they Killed? No outright death for them - oh, no! They walked or were pushed, through a door when they fell through a four by four hole in the floor to the cement floor some fifteen feet below. There a noose was thrown about their throats and they were hung on hooks on the wall to meet their God. If any still lived after a reasonable length of time - a “man” with a heavy mallet crushed their skulls. The room - hooks on the wall - accommodated fifteen. Then the furnaces. The heat generated was not wasted, by the way. It was piped to the S.S. barracks for warmth - the barracks, where the S.S. troopers celebrated their 10,000th killing by drinking toasts from the scoured skulls of their victims. input_chunk: I was a spy. Then I spent a few months at Steffy’s maternal friend Frieda Sachisthal’s place in Charlottenburg, who had already housed Steffy for a few months. It goes without saying that we compensated our hosts fairly with money for their love and bravery for taking us in – basically it was all too little and felt like we had paid nothing at all. Frieda lived in Charlottenburg, in a four storey building, where everyone lived on top of one another and knew everyone’s business. We had to be careful there. I would carefully scurry down the stairs in the morning and come back up again in the evening. My worries about finding accommodation for Steffy and Susi were resolved in one fell swoop on 1 May 1943. I got to know the Mucha couple, Uncle Fritz and Aunt Erna through distant relatives. We only found out after a few months that Aunt Erna was a committed Jew. She looked after our child for four months. One of our charwomen, Ms Nimz, had a small apartment in Emserstraße in Neukölln and Steffy found a home there for 9 months until the move to Horst. As Frau Nimz only came home after 5, she could cook for both of us. We no longer needed to meet in restaurants, where we were always scared of the Gestapokontrolle. - 4 - Meanwhile, I had built up a nice little existence for myself thanks to friends and acquaintances. I taught for five hours a day, which I was properly paid for so that I earnt 3,400 Mark per month, which was a comfortable allowance for us. In Tempelhof in particular I had a small group of pupils thanks to our dear Meta’s recommendation. Meta was a previous maid of ours, and stayed with us for four years – it was like having a child at home. I repaid her for her care with lessons, which I gave her boy 3 days a week, and then I stayed there for lunch. Meta’s husband was a Stabsfeldwebel at the ministry of aviation. Despite his position she allowed me to stay in her apartment for weeks when she was away. There was always worry. We existed without being registered. The following event shows how hunted and exasperated we were – we had spent another weekend in Teltow again. Early on Monday morning I heard the words "How funny that you are getting up so early already". I immediately assumed that someone was watching me and planning to ambush us so I hastily left the little house with Steffy without saying goodbye. We hurriedly walked a long way on a different route, out of breath and imagining that the Gestapo were behind us. Only later did it occur to us that Mrs Fischer may have said these words to her husband and that really had been the case as we later found out. Another experience could easily have turned out a lot worse. I had promised dear Aunt Erna (Mucha) to teach her Latin and we had finally decided on a day to start. I wanted to go straight into the house. There, in front of the door a strange woman asked me "Are you Mr Ludwig?" and handed me a note from Mrs Nimz, who worked for Erna, on the note it said "the Gestapo are here, scarper immediately, and get out of my apartment too" I went straight to Steffy and we cleared out the comfortable room. Fortunately we were able to go to Oranienburg, where I had rented a room from the beginning of September 1943 from proper Nazis, supposedly as a refuge from bombings. And this time my wife came with me, who up until now had been with the child somewhere in the region, that’s what I said. By now the dear Muchas were in a state of painful distress. The whole of the SS in Buchenwald were open to bribes and that saved our lives in part, because the crew would smuggle food into the camp against payment of extortionate over-inflated prices. Even alcohol; and over the New Year period of 1939, a section of the prisoners, the so-called professional criminals, who were blatant murderers and burglars, became dead drunk. The prisoners in Buchenwald were walking corpses, countless instances of death were the order of the day. A taunt, the slogan on the camp gate: “Right or wrong, my country”. In contrast to Dachau, all the jobs here were filled by professional criminals. Death by beating occurred on a daily basis. The first person who was beaten to death was Dr. Ziffer from Vienna. The SS and professional criminals bludgeoned him to death with wooden truncheons at 12 midday on Buchenwald’s main street, our 5th Avenue. The camp doctor, as much an animal as the rest of them, refused to help and Ziffer died gasping for breath. Jäger, the camp foreman, battered a prisoner to death, who had bitten him in the hand in agony. He had to have his hand amputated because of blood poisoning. Jäger continued to batter people with his left hand after his recovery. Prisoner Richter, the hangman of the camp, was no better. It is astonishing that the morale of the other prisoners - 9 - didn’t falter under the impact of these events. I am thinking here of our revered Raoul Auernheimer in particular, the world-famous author. I was aggrieved for this highly cultured man, who was far too old to be addressed informally; I had spent so many pleasant and uplifting hours reading his carefully drawn studies and novels in my spare time. I am also thinking of the Protestant bishop, who was held in excruciating darkness in solitary confinement for many years, and yet who still had the physical strength to break open his darkened window and to shout out, through the gap, words of comfort time and time again. Although every one of his sermons always ended with him being violently beaten, he never missed an opportunity to practice his vocation, to comfort us spiritually and physically with his humble words. In the name of all our comrades I would like to thank him, he led many of us back to God. I was given the job of foreman for the reconstruction of the prison huts. In this role, I was commissioned, at the end of September, to erect five wooden huts with space for 2,000 people. Two latrines were approved for the 10,000 prisoners who were expected. The whole premises was enclosed separately by barbed wire. It was not until Rath’s death in November that we knew who it had really been built for. How it was that the Gestapo, as far back as September, could have anticipated Rath’s murder remains unclear. Could it be that the murder was instigated by them in order to eliminate someone who had become undesirable and who was acting as a conduit to the confiscation of Jewish property? Who knows what goes on in the ‘noble’ mind of a German? On 11th November around 16,000 Jews were beaten and led into the camp. input_chunk: in solitary confinement for 3 months, and lost 6 kg during this time. P. was then transferred to Untermassfeld prison (Germany), where conditions were very bad. P. continued to lose weight. On 10 December 1943, he had his first haemorrhage next to the cardboard packaging machine. The Hauptwachmeister just said: “Here is a washbasin, spit into it as long as you can!” P. pulled himself together. He overcame his weakness and made cold compresses for himself with a towel, 15 minutes later, the blood stopped to flow. The next haemorrhage happened half a year later. This time, P. was in a very bad state. He did not believe himself that he would survive. On 17 July 1944, he was brought to Hohenasperg for three weeks. Here in Hohenasperg, you were practically just waiting to die. He was admitted at the station[1], but was given practically no help. 2 spoons of cod liver oil every week, that was all. The prisoners dropped like flies. Young ones as well. Only 2 survived in the room P. had been admitted to. A young lad wanted to see his parents once more. He asked the minister whether he could arrange that. The parents came. They were not allowed to see their son. They brought honey and - 2 - white bread for their sick son. He did not receive it. A few days later, he closed his eyes for good. Herr P. says there is nothing much to say. This is how it was, as was usual in Hitler’s prisons. All nations were dying here. P. was released on 20 January 1945. Before that, he had to sign that he would keep all his experiences to himself. The carriage that took him home was full of SS officers. The feelings this would evoke can only be appreciated by someone who was once under the control of the SS. During the farewell, P. tells us that he feels he will need to very much pull himself together again. He coughs as he says this. It is the cough of someone with a very weak lung. He could still be a healthy person, if he had not been arrested in Hitler’s Reich for listening to foreign radio stations in January 1941. [1] It is unclear what “Revier” means here. Hohenasperg was a prison at the time, so it could possibly refer to an internal ward for the sick.

input_chunk: women and demand large sums of “hush money”. “Jüdische Spitzel” - Jewish informants In this case it was a lawyer. Jewish informants came predominantly from the integrated intelligentsia, mostly under pressure from the Gestapo. Among them were lawyers, students, teachers, journalists, and office workers. This was also the group from which the Jewish police were later recruited. Naturally, the underworld also contributed to their number. In comparison the strictly orthodox, the socialists such as the radical Zionists, seemed with few exceptions to have retained their integrity. They would even stand side by side with their fellow sufferers and expose themselves to the greatest danger when they tried to help them on the day of the killing. The majority of Jewish informants were apparently driven by family feeling and family interests; deep down they were caring, even tender, husbands and fathers who would stop at nothing in order to protect their loved ones from every danger. At the same time they were driven by ambition to reveal their special kind of reliability and efficiency. A lack of success in their professional life and resultant inability to care for their nearest and dearest and to achieve a “good life” for them often drove the unhappy people to violence, a lack of scruples and brutality towards their own race. On the other hand others were naturally mean and malicious; during the miasma of the Hitler period these latent qualities became glaringly apparent; yes, they competed with each other and did not want to come second in bravado and gruesome cynicism. Knowledge of the German language made it easier for many a rogue to win the favour of the Gestapo - 6 - in this way, in order to be drawn in and pressed into service as an informant at a later date. “Convoy” Various attempts were made to get Jews out of Lemberg. People thought that better conditions existed for them in Hungary. The route there led through Czechoslovakia, which was not far away. Girls especially crossed through the newly occupied areas, disguised and entrusted with important tasks by the Zionist “Hechalutz” , in order to get help to escape and to gather information. Many escaped successfully; some even managed to get across Romania to reach the shores of the Promised Land. These were the altruistic members of the “convoys” driven by ideals. In comparison with these there were paid “convoys” - a non-Jewish undertaking, in which Poles, Ukrainians, ethnic Germans, yes, even members of the German occupying forces, took part. The latter were “in the know” and were correspondingly rewarded. With sacred oaths and in return for generous payments the young girl, Irene, was entrusted to just such a convoy in order to get across Slovakia to Granye in Hungary. Some went via Skole, Dolina and the Dukla Pass, others took the train as far as Stanislawow or Nadworna, in order to be smuggled into the border town of Jasina. The refugees repeatedly suffered much “bad luck”, and their rescue would become a “flight into hatred”, when as soon as they arrived in Slovakia a bestial “operation” would get underway. They were rounded up, captured and annihilated. “Zuständige Stelle” – Authoritative agency The Christian identity papers were from an authoritative agency, ie completed in accordance with regulations. Certainly documents for someone who was already dead or missing were sometimes used, but in other cases documents were used relating to people who were still alive, but with a different photograph inserted, and the people in question would have no idea that in a far distant region of Poland their “Doppelgänger” was walking around. “Die vertrauenswürdigen polnischen Frauen” - The trustworthy Polish women. They had been killed off. But they soon learned. These women had mother™s instinct. They were so thrilled to have babies, to start again. The men who were their husbands, because there was no license there, there weren™t women who weren™t married having babies. These were young women who were married and having children, starting a life again, starting a family again. They were very careful. I think they all cared. Some of them probably were better than others, but even in our society, we have women who are better than others in rearing children. But it was wonderful for us when they first started to get pregnant, because while they were incarcerated or in hiding, most women didn™t even menstruate. They only started to menstruate again when they were free. It™s an interesting phenomenon how nature takes care of itself. input_chunk: baptised. My mother asked him for advice, and he admitted he knew about what had transpired, but unfortunately could do no more. It was intended that I go to Buchenwald; to gain some time he had sent me away. He had himself gone to the military command in Liegnitz and had managed to have me transferred to be a worker at Askania. But the plan fell through: as enquiries were being conducted, he was given spiteful information by an office deputy wearing gold Party insignia. The technical manager had equally tried to act for me, but everything was in vain. After I heard this - when I came home in the evening – I went to the Party and local area council. But it was made clear to me that they had nothing to do with the matter. I had to go to the Gestapo and tell them that the local council had sent me. In the meantime my mother suffered a nervous breakdown and was given morphium. It was nine o’clock in the evening and already quite dark. Yet I went to the Gestapo. The house was closed. I rang. A voice asked who was there. I said I came from the local council and wanted to speak with Mr X (I no longer remember his name). Someone came down, opened up, let me in, and then locked up again behind me. I was far too excited to give the matter the importance which it merited. I was made to wait. I was told the head of the Gestapo was not yet at home. He arrived at around 10 o’clock in civilian clothes, a very good-looking man. He greeted me with a hand-shake – I had indeed come from the local council. I told him about my summons to work, about my sick mother, and asked him to exempt me from this. At first he did not understand – and wanted to exempt me from the work – but of course …… naturally ……. I was now delighted. But when he saw my card – I then saw how he completely changed into a different person in just a few seconds - he raged and shouted, his hands banging on the table – I pulled mother’s ‘Proof of Aryan Race’ out of my bag and said that this definitely proved that I was an ‘Aryan’. He was now shouting even more, raging, and yelling again and again: “In England a Jew lives like a lord and you are his spy!” He gradually calmed down and explained that he will make sure that I will have to do one of the harshest types of forced labour, but that I’d be allowed to stay in Hirschberg and would not be deported. He moved away from me in a fairly normal manner and shut the door behind me. Only when I heard the key turning in the lock did I realise into what danger I had put myself – but this had not been completely in vain. By this time it was almost midnight. I rushed home. Darkness, no lights ….. and always the feeling that the Gestapo was right behind me. My aunt was already sewing in names into the things that I was to take with me. It was inconceivable that I could stay in Hirschberg. On 2nd November I was called to the work office. Until that time I carried on going to Askania every day. I did not wish to draw attention to myself in any way. In the work office the following was made clear to me: “This disgraceful person – a particular assistant work metal fitter apprentice – Heine and Seifert …. start date 7 November. input_chunk: SS-men had picked out several men from every room just as it pleased them. The doors between the corridors and the schoolrooms had partly been taken out, the Jews lying in the rooms were ordered to turn round, so that they could not look out. But some nevertheless lay in a way that they could watch proceedings with their eyes half open. Men were dragged about between the school desks upside down, held by their feet, their heads being banged against the seats and the walls. Others were thrown down the stone stairs. The guards amused themselves vy tearing open the noses and faces of the Jews with the sharp oints of their helmets. Generally these people were killed afterwards to avoid these cruelties getting known. Jews were ordered the next morning to wash up the blood from the floors, walls and school desks, they were told that there had been small accidents. There was a big place, formerly a riding school where about 2.000 Jews caught in the streets and other places were brought into On the first day they did not get anything to eat nor drink. The next day water was given in the mornings and evenings, a piece of bread in the middle of the day. For all the wooo people only two glasses had been supplied so that it took a long time before one could drink a little. The water was taken from a tub generally used for cleaning the floor. The water was clean, however, but in view of the many applicants every man tried to snatch the glass from the man in front of him while he was drinking. One glass was emptied by three men as a rule. All the people drinking from the same f[illegible] glass without the possibility of cleaning it, it follows that infection might easily have spread. One epileptic man broke down and died, another suddenly became mad, rose at night, crying ‘mother, mother’ about fifty times without interruption; his piercing shrieks were long heard while he was carried away. At one place the following scene occurred: about forty men were lying in one room. At 2 o'c in the morning a uniformed SS-man appeared and called out: ‘You stinking Jews, think of your bad deeds! All of you will be shot within half an hour’. Of course, every idea of sleep had vanished, time passed but nothing happened. At 5 o'c in the morning again a SS-man, about 22 years old, came in asking: ‘Is there any lawyer in this room?’ One man came forward and said he was a barrister. He was about 56 years of age. The SS-man placing himself in front of him asked: ‘So you are a barrister?’ - ‘Yes’. The answer was a mighty box in the ear and again the man asked: ‘What are you?’ - ‘A barrister!’ - again a box in the ear, this time on the other check which swell considerably and was bleeding. ‘You are a barrister? A pig - 6 - you are. What are you?’ - ‘I am a pig!’ - ‘Did you serve in the army?’ - ‘Yes’ - ‘During the war?’ - ‘Yes’ - ‘Where?’ - ‘In Poland, in France, in Italy. I have many decorations, amongst them the Iron Cross’. - ‘Down you go!’ The barrister had to lie down flat on the floor. ‘Up you go!’ He rose again. ‘Down!’. This was repeated about twenty times in always quicker succesion the barrister getting quite exhausted. The SS-trooper drew his pistol asking ‘Whom did you leave at home waiting for you?’ - ‘My wife’ - ‘Anybody ‘else?’ - ‘My mother and my child’ - ‘Do you want to die?’ - ‘Yes please’. input_chunk: about 35° below zero. He was soon dead. We had no shoes, no underclothing - not even any rags. Many people tried to commit suicide but had not enough sense to do the job properly. We had the Leibstandarte Adolf Hitler Tank Destroyer Division as guards for a couple of months. The guards always consisted of S.S. Tank Destroyer Divisions who, after being victorious and distinguishing themselves in France, Italy and the Balkans, were sent here to pull guard duty on the unfortunate prisoners. The living conditions for the troops in that village were appalling and they tried continuously to get their own back on the prisoners. I used to beg the guards to shoot me, but they said that I was not worth the bullet, and told me to hang myself. Unfortunately I was so much out of touch with reality that I had not the strength or the sense to do so. Kurt Warner used to see us assemble at morning and at night - sometimes we had to stand for hours in the winter without shoes or caps. Those who were too weak to stand died, and when they were dead they were - 4 - placed in front of us so that nobody was missing. Groeschel was always drunk, and used to do many things on his own initiative. Once as I was coming back from working in the forest, I saw him arguing with a German civilian - as it happened that civilian was no other than the commanding S.S. Officer of that district in civilian clothes - and Groeschel was reprimanded and sent back to Kaiserwald. The next commander of the camp was a man who could, with one punch, kill a prisoner. His name was SORGE and he had already acquired fame in Sachsenhausen and was known throughout the world as “Eiserner Gustav” - the Iron Gustav. He was tried and convicted to hard labour at the Sachsenhausen Concentration Camp trial. As the medical Supervisor of the Dondangen extermination camp, Warner was responsible for the well-being of theprisoners, i.e. for seeing that the prisoners were fit enough for slave labour. Unfortunately he did not even do that for the prisoners. It may be that he will blame Sturmbannfuehrer Krebsbach, or the directive from the Reich S.S. Security H.Q. in Berlin - or hemay even blame Hitler - for carrying out the extermination of hundreds of human beings. It is lucky for him, having done a good job, that there is only one person alive to testify against him - maybe he even regrets that! The food at Dondangen was worse than at any other camp andthere were even days when we did not get anything at all. I shall never forget one particular day when I went out with the working detail called “Bauhof”, Our job was to unload trains which had brought sections of barracks, to sort out these sections and to stack them up. The guards that day were especially rough and furious, right from the first moment that we left the gates of the camp. We had with us a Czech Doctor (unfortunately I cannot at the moment recall his name). He was a very intellectual and well educated man and spoke English well. He asked the guards if he could be excused, went to a small tree nearby and hanged himself with his scarf. Goreschel and Warner were immediately summoned from the camp and they brought with them several other witnesses (german officers from the armed organisation Todt, builders of bridges and roads). I had been chosen to carry the Doctor back to the camp, and was standing about 10 yards away from the party. They even brought a Doctor from one of the units to take part in this sarcastic pantomime of concern over one dead body. Four of us were chosen to carry the unfortunate victim back to the camp. input_chunk: all day and on weekdays you are glad when it rains, so how is the Lord God supposed to please us? 3.6.42 Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday flew by. The weather is lovely, Koloheisl in a good mood, not much work and just a good mood because we will pack the day after tomorrow and leave on Saturday. We will carry on working until midday tomorrow, in the afternoon we will go for a walk with our hainy, he calls it an excursion. We have just been told that budiček is to be at 3am on Saturday. That's too bad when I so like to sleep! But we are going to Terezin and that is worth the sacrifice. We have been given Friday off so we can pack, so tomorrow is the very last day in the forest; that does make us very sad, the area here is a paradise, our Karlicek is now Sroigim nach Sukkous {fruit after Sukkoth}* being very nice to us and we are already used to the work. We will enjoy recollecting and pine for the forests. Now in the evening it is absolute mayhem here in the room – a madhouse. On Saturday I am to see my mother and my husband again, I can't imagine it at all. 5th June, our last day in the hut was spent packing and clearing out, so we did not think of yesterday, and that is good. Our Herr Kolo distinguished himself by way of farewell – he hounded us and was dreadfully vulgar, so that we went home tired and despairing, weeping bitter tears, he is the worst person here and deserved it when we ignored him and did not even say goodbye. Yesterday evening Trude Popper gave a thank you speech to everyone on behalf of all of us and said exactly what we all felt. Cilly has been at the station all afternoon with 6 other girls loading the luggage of 1000 women onto the wagons, she will get back dog-tired and at 3 in the morning an 18km walk to the station awaits us. So the 8 weeks have indeed come to an end and we are setting out on the long journey back to the barracks with very mixed feelings. 8 weeks – which mean a small piece of our lives, are over. Full of *{When someone tries to be good at the end, when it is too late anyway.} - 18 - many good and bad experiences – happiness and joy, despair and fear, friendship and disappointment, often hunger and tiredness. And nevertheless for the large part we are taking good memories with us. The good people, the glorious region, the air and the forest, we will not forget all that. We have recovered, we are all tanned and pumped up with good air. We do not want to think of what awaits us, until the last moment we will collect all the lovely days in our thoughts and be deeply grateful for 8 weeks of mental and physical recovery. May God protect you Bušohrad {Pürglitz} and all the good people who belong to you. [signature: Valerie Fink] Translator note [1] Puszta = Hungarian steppe [2] Budiček = wake-up call, reveille. [3] nástup = muster. [4] hajnis = foresters. [5] Czech. military song: 'What kind of soldier'. [6] Dresdner Kaserne = Dresden Barracks. [7] “truant from school” (Czech úlevárna = relief). [8] hoes (translator's note: grub hoes). [9] ňam ňam = (mhm) (translator's note: yummy). [10] God's help. [11] Erna I am your real (big)mouth}”.

input_chunk: we were sorted immediately, right next to the unloading ramp. I could see that one of the detained persons, who had some kind of position with a duty squad, kept saying under his breath to people newly arrived: “You’re young and fit! - You’re young and fit - You’re young and fit.” We didn’t realise at first what he meant. We soon did. Anyone who was old or sick went straight from the ramp to the gas chamber. All the children, all the mothers with children, all the pregnant women went from the ramp to the gas. It was at this point that I lost my own friend. My friend – her name was Susi Weiss – lived in Vienna, like me. We made the journey to Theresienstadt together, and we also travelled to Auschwitz together. She had taken under her wing a 6-year-old boy whose mother had died. At the ramp, that sealed her fate. She and the little boy, whom she loved dearly, went into the gas together. There were many who refused to be wrenched apart from their loved ones and went with them into the gas. First of all, we were all shaved down to the scalp. All body hair was also removed. The clothes they gave us were rags. We made our way through a number of barracks. We slept, five of us side by side, on a plank bed, we had a torn piece of cloth, between the five, to cover us, and we ate in a group of five – without cutlery, scooping with our hands out of a shallow bowl. One day we had to strip naked. The SS herded us into a neighbouring barrack. We had to remain standing there all day. Young SS men came and enjoyed their japes. - 3 - So far I had not deteriorated physically all that much, could pass myself off as younger than my true age, and so was selected after a few weeks at Auschwitz, in November 1944, along with c. 1,000 other women, to join a transport to Germany. We were taken to an aircraft factory at Freiberg in Saxony, near Dresden. It was night-time when we arrived. We were pushed into a barrack recently occupied by Italians. We could still feel the warmth from them. One of us had scarlet fever, so we were kept in quarantine for 10 days. Each of us received 10 decagrams of bread per day. We cut it into small pieces, so that we could put something in our mouths reasonably often. Along with the bread we were given very dilute coffee water and stew. Relatively speaking, the work was not particularly arduous, but the hours were very long – 14 hours every day. Very often we were physically ill-treated. A female SS company leader Scha[illegible]ührerin was a specialist in this. For instance, she would stand on a work-bench at a point where we had to file past, take off her leather belt and use it to belabour every passing woman indiscriminately, wherever on her body the blows happened to land. For picking up 1 piece of stale bread a workman had dropped on the ground, a Czech woman was soundly thrashed by this „SS-Maid“. In January we were moved from the factory to the barracks assigned for our use. We had to walk there through knee-high snow, barefoot. We requested clogs. And I said, "Why do you want to help?," you know, even from Jews you become suspicious. And she told me that her sister, and I knew who she was talking about, her name was "Goldstein," lived in our home town and she resembled her a little bit. She said, they were I remember big Zionist, her sister and brother in-law and the two children, and my father saved the sister's life and the child in childbirth. 24 And even they don't live anymore, but she wants to help us through it. So, you know, I always say you never know in your life when you help someone who benefits from that help. It might be someone totally unrelated or, you know. And so, she wanted . . . her help was to give us job in the latrine, that was a big job! Because if you worked there, you got double portions but I said "I really appreciate the job, but it's one job I just can't do," you know because, they were just holes and you take a stick and clean it with a stick and no matter how hungry I was, that was something I just couldn't bear to do. So I thanked her a lot and had to give up. But then one day I heard that about forty-two girls that came in '42 with the original transport that I escaped, you know, when I went to Hungary, are being taken out to a camp, which was called I think "Auschwitz II" but I heard later it was called the Statsgebaeude, which means "a state building." It was just an hour or less walk from Birkenau, but the circumstances were compared like from Hell to Heaven, you know, compared to the situation. So I again was pretty courageous, you know, they had alarms, block alarm. Block alarm meant between each A-B-C-D there were electric gates. And then transports came, they locked these gates so that you shouldn't see wants going on, or shouldn't tell those people where they are being taken because if two, three hundred people come and they find out and they started to fight, you couldn't do the killing job properly and, well. I was taken to Le Vernet concentration camp (South Pyrenees) which was an extremely inaccessible facility with leaky wooden huts with straw floors, unhygienic conditions, no medical care, poor nutrition and until February 1940, no heating. It was a malicious way to keep control of us. The Lieutenant – we called him “Himmel stoss” – left the grief inside the camp to simmer below the surface so that he could keep things running as normal. An infirmary was eventually built but it didn’t have any medication available. As the Fifth Column moved through Paris, socialists, Christians, communists and many others slowly withered away. There were some Russian and German doctors in the camp who tried to leave to get to their homes for medicine. They were arrested because they weren’t allowed to leave. Some people in the camp had also received the Legion of Honour…and their hair was cut short like everyone else. After being detained we were called to the commissioner one by one, where we were told of our deportation to France. Those who wouldn’t go to France had to stay in Le Vernet. They were hungry and began to slaughter dogs to eat. The guard treated the inmates horribly, with only a few exceptions. Some executions were even carried out. The only help the inmates received was the broadcasts from the Quakers, the United Service and the Swiss Workers Relief Agency. I became ill some time after being detained. The days following the defeat were the worst, because this meant that Hitler was on his way to the South of France and we had to destroy our papers. After Italy declared war, many Italians were brought to Le Vernet. Because space was limited, they were housed underground. The Kunz Commission – an official German commission - came to Le Vernet immediately after the defeat. Their agreement with the ceasefire commission allowed them to visit the French camps and free as many inmates as possible to send them back to Germany. It seemed like they had been following orders from Sauckel from the very start. But Captain Kunz was the leader of this commission. We also discovered that the Kunz Commission visited other countries with the same objective and that when they left France, they headed for Belgium. After a while, some of the German inmates were called for – at this point their nationality was irrelevant. The Polish engineer, Finkiel – nephew of Polish historian Prof. Finkiel, a non-Aryan – who cooperated with Parisian engineers was also called for. I don’t know what happened to him after that. The leaders of the camp left the inmates to march in front of the commission as they prepared for the departure of the non-Jewish Germans and Russians. As soon as the camp had emptied, it filled up again as the International Brigade was detained. In the meantime, I was summoned to the American Consulate in Marseille - the International Rescue Committee in New York had applied for an entry visa on my behalf. After some time I was taken to the barracks for elderly people. Even this part of the camp didn’t have medication; people were still starving while others froze. The only difference was that instead of 300-400 people, there were approx. 50 people, all aging or sick and hoping that a doctor would come a visit them. A month after receiving the summons, I, along with 40 other inmates, was taken to Les Milles concentration camp near Marseille. As Nina Gurfinkei wrote in her book, all Le Vernet inmates were moved further east between 1942 and 1943. The Les Milles concentration camp gave inmates much more freedom. The French doctor from the barrack hospital granted holidays to Marseille. The food was still insufficient, but if you had money, you could buy something els. On the windows of many shops there were fixed printed placards with the inscription ‘Judah is conjointly responsible’. Later I went to an ‘arian’ friend. He said: ‘Why did you go into this Nazi hotel? Why not coming to me and stay here as long as this spell of terror has not gone?’ So after having spent 2 days in the Hotel Bellevue I moved to my friend. Here I thought to be in hiding but it turned out to be worse than in the hotel or even in my Berlin home. This friend was in financial difficulties and his wife, a person of dubious character, as I later had occasion to state, persuaded her husband to be treacherous. I was there one night, the next day was what the Protestants call ‘Penitentiary Day’. My friend and I made a walk to the ‘Grosser Garten’ and when we arrived home - he came and told me that 2 Gestapomen, one a relative of his wife, had come to take me to the Gestapo because I had fled from Berlin to evade possible arrest. My friend told me the improbable fib that one of these men had seen me and at once realized that I was a Jew. The tale about me was probably betrayed and inspired by the wife of my friend, and being in straits he had and his wife thought they could get a lot of money from me in case I would be spared the arrest. So my friend fell into line. It was an outspoken conspiracy. I did not fall into this trap to pay for my liberation. This was the greatest diappointment I had in my life. ‘Deutsche Treue!’ The Gestapo-men took me to the Headquarters where a young man - SS, of course - abused me and at last sent me to the Mathilden prison. On the way I had a talk with the Nazi who escorted me. I asked him what I was arrested for? In civilized countries there is a law protecting all people not accused of a crime from arbitrary arrest. The Nazi shrugged his shoulders and said nothing. In the prison, I was assigned to a ‘Justizoberwachtmeister’, a former N.C.O. who was very harsh as he felt it his duty with prisoners but au fond he had a little bit of sympathy with people who were no criminals. At first I should have solitary confinement but when I told him I would get mad there he put me in a cell with 2 other Jews of Dresden. One was a Jewish butcher and 6 or 7 years my senior. We were lead into a dark, unheated wooden barrack had to strip - 4 - all of our clothes and wait like this until dawn. Still in the dark, we reported in front of the barrack and heard the marching steps of, as it seemed to me, numerous people who were moving towards the muster ground. Suddenly I heard a familiar voice, I called the name of a comrade, who at first did not react, I called again and now he stood beside me. A short understanding, he would help me to get in a block with my old friends. When I came to the writing room, where inmates were employed as well, he had already pre-announced me, so I was sent to Block 39 [to the comrades][8], who helped me where ever they could. In the block we had a table at which only former operatives sat, I was one of the youngest. Gradually I could help many of the older ones with all kinds of matters when they did not get further. The reason was probably that I never for a moment lost faith in the cause, I was never internally downcast. I knew that none of my friends had told on me, despite all the agony that they had to endure, I knew that it succeeded to let the chain break after my arrest because out of my own group, no one had been arrested since. During the interrogations by the Gestapo I could always notice that I was politically superior to them, that they always fumbled unsurely and I had the feel of triumph inside of me, that despite of the gruesome beating methods in those 70 interrogations they got nothing out of me, that they did not achieve it. All that helped to endure these times, of which the duration was not foreseeable. But also our good solidarity and our intensive political discussion work gave some internal strength. We not only had the chance to talk in our barrack rooms about politics, we could also read the daily newspaper[s] from our home towns which, although all of them had been redacted more or less from on high, still presented the news with slightly different nuances, especially then in war. A bad problem for us was the behaviour of the communists. They initially tried to spark friction, captious discussions with all groups. Through the terror they exerted, they became exactly as dangerous as the SS-guard troops, with whom they worked together on many occasions. There were some [communists][9], who have 80 prisoners on their conscience. It was especially bad in the time after the German-Russian pact. The informer system was incredibly well organized. We therefore had to cover from both sides. For me it was also very important to know, that my parents, who prior to my arrest had no idea about my illegal activities and were financially badly off, were still faithfully at my side. - 5 - It was also important that I was immediately launched by a friend into a gang[10]. A workshop of the camp looked for pipe layers and, although I am a machinist, [I][11] went there immediately. That was important insofar, as in the workshop the supervised SS-people, who were by large trained specialized craftsmen, could decide over us and not the rough SS-camp guard units. There were of course conflicts of responsibilities with the SS block leader and our workshop SS-people. When I became foreman and responsible for the work performance of my gang, I also had two severe conflicts with the SS-guard troops, which entailed for me to have to be whipped twice with 25 whips each on the whipping bench[12]. My gang was, among other things, used for the maintenance of the sewers in the so-called stable. In this stable, the shooting of the inmates took place. input_chunk: – Transport’ and were given preferential treatment from then on. On the platform in Birkenau we were received by SS men and women, who immediately separated the men from the women. Those in each group were asked individually about their age. The older ones, from about forty upwards, were loaded into waiting cars, and so were the mothers with their children, the weak and the sick who were not able to walk, and pregnant women. One man with an artificial limb did not want to part with the younger comrades and wanted to walk the whole way. The SS people persuaded him in a nice and friendly way to be driven as the march was difficult. He would of course meet his comrades again afterwards. Another man had to do several complete knee bends in order to check his pulse. Later he, too, was sent to the car. Later we learnt that all the passengers in the cars had been driven to the crematorium. We had to line up, in rows of five, and were led by SS women to the gate. On either side of the gate there were guards with dogs and also SS men and women. We were led into a barracks where we had to hand over all our valuables. We were told that anyone holding something back would be shot. We had to leave our luggage at the station where they promised to send it on by car. We had to take off our clothes. We were registered in alphabetical order, and got a piece of paper with a number on it. Then the number was tattooed (onto our skin). We were led into the entrance hall of the bath house where we had to take off the rest of our underwear, in the presence of several SS men, our bodies were shaved completely and a disinfectant rubbed in. In the bath house we were given a shower. We got male underwear, a jacket and a Russian military uniform, all of it torn, and shoes and stockings. Being the privileged ones we later received sweaters, which were so infested by lice that we threw them away. - 2 - Usually we slept on the bare stone of the sleeping quarters, which were about the size of two normal beds, but in which eight of us were accommodated. Every morning there was the roll call, lasting between two and three hours, which everybody had to attend except those who were really sick. During the first three months there were no selections as these had been carried out before our arrival. So out of a group of 64 girls whom I had known and who had arrived one month before us only two were still alive. They all had been big and strong and well suited for work outdoors. According to what the two survivors and other eye witnesses told us the selection had been done in the following way: on Sundays they had to put their coats on back to front and had to hold the skirts of the coats up with their hands. The coats were then filled with sand and the girls had to walk in this way along the camp street which was lined with SS men and Kapos. Any girl who could no longer walk steadily or whom the SS people did not like had to step to one side and was gassed later. Another girl of this group was shot by an SS guard because she refused to give him her wellington boots. This was arranged in the following way: the female supervisor sent the girl with some task in front of the line of sentries so that the guard had to shoot at once. Incidentally, the guard got some days off as extra holidays as a bonus for having delivered a certain amount of dead people. The female head of the warders in Birkenau was the SS senior supervisor Mandl, the Arbeitsdienstführer was SS Oberscharführer (?) Moll, the doctor in charge was the SS doctor Rohde. Later transports had losses amounting to 12 men, and on one occasion the SS, who were quite literally drunk, started shooting with such wild abandon that they even shot their own Hauptmann (SS-Hauptsturmführer), either deliberately or by accident. He was a much hated man and the prisoners and the SS watched with unbridled joy, as the black flag of the SS was lowered to half-mast. Our arrival, we were the first Austrians there, and moreover the so-called elite, was a joyous occasion for Dachau. All those who had rank and distinction in Bavaria’s SS, were present. We were bombarded with the most blatant and vile insults imaginable. Then each of us was asked what crime we had committed. I must stress that Bürgermeister Schmitz in particular, my immediate superior in the Patriotic Front, and Major Stillfried, the former camp commandant of Wöllersdorf, were beaten for the duration of 12 hours, that is to say, all the way from Vienna to Dachau. Schmitz received a double dose when in response to the question: “And why are you here you scum?” He replied proudly: “Because I have kept my allegiance.” Dachau itself is not far from Munich. The food was not the best, but the provisions were ample and you could buy almost anything, albeit at prices that were twice as high as they would be outside. Yet there were only a very few who had remittances, it was forbidden for Jehovah’s Witnesses and communists, who were in the camp for a second time, to make any sort of purchase at all. These poor people weren’t even allowed to write or receive any post, and many of them had no news of their relatives for several years, and they didn’t even know if they were still alive. Such things, and the uncertainty about how long one would be imprisoned for, are a terrible burden and only help to make things worse. - 6 - The Dachau camp was almost up and running and there was nothing to complain about from a sanitary point of view. On the contrary, great value was put on the very cleanliness of the prisoners and the accommodation huts. On the second day of our attendance we were divided into work parties. These work parties were supervised by fellow prisoners, mostly communists, who had been in the camp for many years. Barring a few exceptions they were sympathetic comrades, likewise those who supervised the accommodation barracks. We were made to sing whenever we marched out of the camp to work, so that any civilians we encountered on the way would believe that we were happy with our lot. The songs were pre-written for us. I myself was working with both sons of Franz Ferdinand, the former successor to the throne. We had to ensure that the ducts were cleaned. A not particularly appetising, but nonetheless not especially physical type of work. It was astonishing how bravely both sons put up with all the work and I really grew to admire them. Whenever you saw an SS-man in the distance, you moved out of his way. Because they never passed us by without lashing out at us in the most rough manner. A favourite hoax was to send newcomers into a zone close to the barbed wire, which they were forbidden to enter. If the poor wretches followed such an order, they would be mowed down by the nearest machine gun post without warning. You can imagine how embittered we were by such occurrences. It was soon our turn too, as Austrians, to mourn our first death. It happened to Kotanyi, the well-known wholesaler in spices, who cut his wrists and hanged himself.
