I should get out at the station before.” So this is what I did - 8 - and went on foot to Bernstein, however in my agitation on the journey had the bad luck to have one of the lenses fall out of my spectacles. Because of this I then looked for an optician and had the lens put back in. When I asked how much it cost, he only said, “Just get out of here as fast as you can.” I took his advice and set off for the nearby stream marking the border, having first had to ask some schoolchildren for directions. There were some signs by the stream at the border, which said that crossing it was a punishable offence. However I managed to get across the stream away from the customs road without attracting the attention of the border patrols. Now I was happily in Czechoslovakia. It was November 1935. First of all I went to Weipert, the nearest Czech town, and tried from there to get to Prague. I could not take the bus that went there, as the route went over German territory. Therefore I walked to the first railway station and there climbed aboard the train for Prague. On arrival at my destination I found lodgings with an aunt for the time being. In the days that followed I tried first of all to find myself a job. An uncle, who was head of a government department in Prague and whom I asked for advice, turned me away, as he apparently considered me to be a criminal. He obviously could not imagine what conditions were like in Germany. However I soon succeeded in contributing articles on industrial law to various legal journals. Moreover I became the permanent correspondent of the German newspaper “Bohemia” in Prague, which published one of my articles each week. In this way I had a constant source of income and supported myself quite well. In the end I was also invited to give lectures at the University of Prague and worked on my postdoctoral thesis. Meanwhile in October 1938 the Germans had occupied the Sudetenland. Then came 15th March 1939. At this time I was living in a big block, in which a man known to me, Herr Jaeger, and the well-known Otto Strasser, leader of the Black Front, had apartments. I had spoken to Jaeger and Strasser from time to time. They had tried to recruit me into the Black Front, which did not reject Jews who seemed acceptable because of their nationality and the length of time they had been in Germany. However I could not forget that as the former editor of the Saxon edition of the “Voelkischer Beobachter”, Strasser had published articles against me in that newspaper. - 9 - On the morning of 15th March 1939 I woke early with a feeling of deep foreboding. I looked out of the window and caught sight of my neighbour, Jaeger, running with his wife and his baggage across Wenceslas Square. At the same time it seemed to me as if I could hear German military music. I turned on the radio and heard an announcement, that every student who had received special orders from the Gestapo should carry these out. This made it clear to me that the Germans had marched into Prague. One hour later, the Gestapo were already in our building looking for Otto Strasser and Herr Jaeger. During the search they also rang my door and asked about Strasser, but did not trouble me further. Our Czech caretaker behaved extraordinarily well. He said if the Gestapo were to return, he would lean with his back against the bellboard and thus ring all the bells of the individual apartments. It usually lasted half an hour, during which one heard the terrible howls of the bombs, the air pressure of which made our barracks shake, causing some damage. Later, isolated planes came, apparently to ascertain the damage that had been done. It was, as we saw later, very severe. In any case, there was heavy traffic on our road in the nights following the bombings. The injured and the dead were taken away then. The air raid siren almost every night always involved only aircraft flying over our area. We knew then that Hamburg or Berlin would form the targets. Very often, all sorts of flyers were dropped during the day. The Hitler Youth then swarmed around everywhere to collect them. But we often still managed to also get hold of something, risking our lives in doing so. What was read in secret was passed on from mouth to mouth and was our greatest source of new strength in our distress and despair. We also managed to get hold of a newspaper from time to time. We knew then that the front was rapidly approaching. Again, the apprehensive question of what was going to happen to us arose. We feared that the SS would disappear one night and that our camp would be finished off with a couple of bombs. Because of this, we secretly organised night watches to monitor the SS accommodation and guard posts. In early April, the units were alerted on two consecutive nights; they had to get into formation ready to march. But after a few hours, they went back to their quarters. On 5th April, the work in the factory was shut down, and on the following day, the order was given to make the camp ready to march. Where to, nobody knew. - 6 - A large wagon and 2 handcarts were requisitioned in the city. They were loaded with the luggage of the approximately 70 guards and the SS, as well as the kitchen supplies and equipment. All the office supplies as well as the books belonging to the infirmary and the block senior were burned under the supervision of the SS. Otherwise, each person was to bring along only his 2 blankets. On the morning of 7th April, the whole camp fell into formation. It was explained that we had to walk a long distance and that anybody who did not feel capable of doing so was to stay behind with the invalids. An Unterscharführer and a few SS officers were to wait with them for the arrival of lorries, which would catch up with everybody else. As this assurance rang hollow and everybody assumed that the SS squad would shoot the people after our decampment, many joined those who were able to march although they were in reality unable to hold out any longer. Anybody who did not go along was herded into the infirmary. The others each received a loaf of bread and a quarter pound of margarine. During the to-ing and fro-ing of the people who were undecided about whether to go along or not, as well as during the distribution of provisions, there was of course a lot of chaos and noise. Herr Quakernack then personally shot a few men dead with his revolver; the Rottenführer achieved the same result in their own way, and the line could be formed. The wagons and carts, which had to be pushed and pulled by us, led the way. The whole thing was encircled by the guard units with guns under their arms, ready to shoot. We marched through outer districts of Hanover, where we saw the immense destruction. Then we continued never-endingly through woods and fields. input_chunk: midnight. I was working at a machine consisting of a long table with a rolling production line transporting the bullets. At the table sat 6 women in a line who had to examine the appearing bullets as to their usability. At the upper end stood a woman who poured the bullets into a funnel from which they emerged singly onto the table. Our task was to pick out bullets which, in our opinion, were unusable and to remove them from the table. My own task was the most responsible at the table, I had to check that the projectile had the correct hole at the back. For this purpose, I had a mirror with an electric light in front of me which the projectile passed so that I had to examine in the mirror whether it was so-called “blind”. The projectiles rolled past all 6 women in boxes marked with the number of the table. If it turned out that a projectile was blind or bad, all the women of that table were punished not because of neglect of their work but because of deliberate sabotage. This punishment consisted of whipping, minimum punishment 25 strokes of the whip, administered by men selected especially for their strength. The whipping was carried out in specifically adapted rooms where water dripped on the bodies to prevent them from fainting during the execution. An additional intensification of the punishment was the timing of the whipping before the start of work so that we had to sit on our wounds for 12 hours without being able to treat them. During this period I was whipped at least 20 – 25 times; the scars are still visible. Every day, mistakes were discovered as we were exhausted by starvation, and 12 hours of this monotonous work - talking was forbidden – was like the torture of Tantalus. How easily one’s eyes could shut, even just for a moment, and a blind bullet would pass unnoticed. Also, work could not be abandoned because of any physical need. The notice that mistakes had been discovered was given out at the end of the shift without any indication of the table so that each woman feared constantly that she might be whipped the following day. Naturally, this contributed substantially to the shredding of one’s nerves. In addition, we were slapped almost daily by the foreman or =woman without any cause, just out of sadism. A foreman once knocked out two of my front teeth, another beat me on the head with an iron bar, again without cause, just from sadism. I have the scar to this day.During the air attacks, there was no protection for us whilst our tormentors crept into the shelters. When the factory was hit during an air attack, we were not permitted to leave the room and watched as the flames got closer and closer.When in January 1945 the Russians approached, all camp inmates were to be sent to Germany which happened in fact; as I learnt later on, none of them is alive today. I myself hid and was liberated by the Russians on 18th January 1945, together with a few others who had also gone into hiding.A witness to my time in Lodz and departure for Czenstochau is Mrs. Elly Kafka, wife of the late chairman of the Religious Community in Prague who is also one of the 120 survivors (out of 5000) of Lodz. Her address is: 34 Langbourne Mansions, Holly Lodge Estate, Parliament Hill, Highgate, London N.6.I myself fled from the communists in Prague in 1948 and am here as a political refugee. On 18th February (1949) I applied for British nationality, had my interview 14 days ago and hope to receive it within a short time.I work as a housekeeper and carer to an old gentleman and am completely without means and of poor health so that I can only do light work.My son who also lives in London cannot support me as he is still an apprentice, receiving just pocket money.

input_chunk: fremdvölkischen Arbeitseinsatz in Ost-Oberschlesien[2] Waffen-SS General Schmellt[3]. LINDNER, SS Sturmbannführer[4], roughly 50 years old, medium height, fat, red face, looked like a butcher. He was an active element in tracking down Jews who had no papers for labour deployment. Anyone without an identity card was conveyed by him in a taxi to the transit camp. From there they were sent to the labour camp. He inspected labour camps. He always arrived suddenly. If someone was not working, he hit him, shot him dead or set his dog on him. He did not acknowledge sickness on principle. He sent many to Auschwitz. - 2 - He played an active part in the main deportation in SOSNOWITZ, in which approximately 15,000 Jews were deported. This deportation was organised by Lindner and HAUPTMANN DREIER[5] of the Gestapo, tall, fat, around 40 years old. Both sat at a table – we had to go the table in family groups. Together they allocated each person to a category: 1. Released (in possession of 'good' work cards (for the Army etc)). 2. Labour deployment (those in possession of a card, young workers). 3. Deportation to Auschwitz, held back for the time being. 4. Immediate deportation to Auschwitz. We knew that Auschwitz meant gassing. Families were separated. When people tried to move across from one group to another, chaos ensued. Dreier[6] decreed that groups 3 and 4 be sent together for deportation immediately and gave the order to shoot. The Gestapo and the police shot into the crowd. The square was strewn with dead bodies. Children and babies were stamped on by the police. This situation lasted for two days and a night, when I was then sent to the transit camp (I was on the square during this from 12th August until about 7pm on 13th August 1942). Then Group 2 was taken away. Groups 3 and 4 stayed for another night and a day, until they were taken to the collection camps, put in the waggons and taken to Auschwitz. It was raining and the people were without food. Because then, I gradually built a picture of who in case of emergency was reliable and who not. Also, I had the choice between the units of two corporals: one which was led by a humane, relatively sensible Schwaben, but who took everything to do with military service very punctiliously, and the other by a humane, engaging young NCO from Berlin who was a bit lax from a military point of view. I thought to myself take the lousy one because when it gets to the point the outcome will be better with him. Meanwhile, we get an 18-year-old lieutenant as the troop leader who ruffled us up frightfully and bullied us in unimaginable ways, although we were much older and had previous convictions. At the heart of it was, he had an inferiority complex. He knew how humanly out of sync he was. When we were flown to Africa for duty, he revealed that when he said to us on the plane: “I know that hated officers are often shot from behind at the front. - 9 - But I will show you how it is going to be.“ Right after the landing, he took us terribly close to the front, and then had himself on the same day transferred to another unit. In Africa, everything was already in full retreat. We were supposed to cover the elite troops. Up until then, we only had carbines. Now we were provided with pistols in some cases. I felt somehow securer when I possessed a pistol, you could say my spirits were lifted. You could defend yourself better against your own people. We were for a short time in action. During that, 7 men in the neighbouring company were arrested and suspected of running away. 5 were shot. An order was issued: if again anyone runs away, the 10th man in every company will be shot. Now it meant being particularly attentive. Before such a punishment action was started, the warning signal for us was the order: “to hand in all weapons.” That would be for us a sign to abscond, come what may. I looked around for suitable comrades for the case of an escape together and learnt that the former proven comrades whose political toughness had formerly stood the test for many years, had meanwhile become soft. I considered after careful observation to let 2 comrades into my plans, who were aesthetically-minded throughout not only in discussions about political questions, but also about special literary problems. When we noticed that the circumstances at the front were heading towards a resolution as the Americans advanced closer and closer, we remained towards the back of our company which was now dropped. There was hopeless confusion. Despite that, most of the old comrades remained with the unit. And the few, who remained in our area, were scared and also unreliable. Finally, it seemed to reach the point that some attempted to move us to go in the direction of our troops. Then I bluffed them by shouting out that they were striking out in the wrong direction and delivering us to the Americans. They got into complete confusion and we simply pushed off. Everything now sounds so simple, all the same we were deployed in a desert type area with great hardships, heat beyond all measure, a lack of water, dust and a land without any paths. Thank God we soon bumped into an American tank unit and were taken prisoner. Already in the African prison camp, but it especially later in the USA, there were fierce brawls between us and the Nazis, and not only that, but also the coarsest disputes between the Stalinists and we socialists. - 10 - In the prisoner of war camp, we now formed and anti-fascist action front, and immediately took up political work. input_chunk: Perschke’s flat and said he was not ill. Now he reported to the camp to start work, and they kept him there for a fortnight without suspecting anything. When they started to transport people he rang his wife to inform her. She assumed he had been moved to a labour camp, but he was taken to the prison in Pankraz, after that to the fortress in Theresienstadt and finally to the death camp Flossenbürg in Bavaria, from where - 7 - he took part in the infamous death march only shortly before the war was over. This lasted for a week before they were liberated by the First American Tank Army. Only six thousand out of fifteen thousand prisoners survived this march and arrived in the area of Cham in Bavaria. Meanwhile Frau Perschke was above all busy sending parcels to relatives and also to friends in Auschwitz and other camps. One day the door-bell rang and opening the door she faced two Gestapo men who had got orders to take her with them without giving any reason. But first they searched the house without, however, finding anything suspicious. The food which she had got ready for the parcels made them grumble. ‘How much money have you got here in your house?’ she was asked. She happened to have a considerable sum at home but she managed to push some of the bank notes under the cupboard in the kitchen. But this was totally in vain, for when they left the house she had to hand her keys over and the flat was locked and sealed. Frau Perschke felt that she would not see her flat again. Indeed, the flat and everything in it was confiscated by the German Gestapo, and whatever was not nailed or screwed down was carried off to Germany. She was allowed to take a few of the things that were absolutely necessary with her, just what was permitted in a cell, and then the two men accompanied her to the Gestapo head office by tram, which is worth mentioning because Jews were not allowed to go by tram. Incidentally, being married to a Christian she did not have to wear the Star of David and so she was occasionally able to go by tram without being noticed, and she did not have to obey so very carefully the rules which had been made especially for the Jews. At the Gestapo office she was questioned very thoroughly, also about her social contacts. She said that she had had her own Jewish circle while her husband had often met his Christian colleagues. The officer asked her, ‘Do you know that I have got your husband here?’ And he showed her the photo of her husband. Then she - 8 - was sent into the neighbouring room where she had to wait, with her face to the wall, until she was taken into the courtyard where many men and women stood waiting. Then they were taken in a police car, which was divided into small compartments, to the prison in Pankraz. They were driven into the building like cattle, one behind the other. Again they were lined up in a room, with their faces turned to the wall and for even the slightest movement they were shouted at or even beaten. The men in particular were terribly maltreated. In this position they spent two hours, full of fear about what would happen to them. During that time Frau Perschke remembered that she had in her handbag, which she was still carrying with her, some document which might cause trouble if she was perhaps searched. When nobody was watching she whispered about this to her neighbour, who, ready to help her, very cautiously took the paper and – swallowed it. When the two hours were over and it was almost evening, they were called individually into the office where they had to hand over everything they had got with them, including money and jewellery. My mother realized that she was no longer alive, so my father on ly took stuff for...clothing for me, shoes and something for the little girl for his sister and he came. He came in here. Get dressed. Where's your sister? She died. He was so rry too. He started crying. He said well, maybe I could have taken her. input_chunk: her way to Naarden, Miss Gompertz had been stopped by 2 members of the Security Service and asked to identify herself. She showed her forged papers which said that she was Half-Jewish; the officers did not believe her and telephoned the municipalities of Naarden and Amsterdam in order to verify her information. Both municipalities said that she was Half-Jewish. The officers, both Dutch, said: “What a pity that you are not a Jewess – we get 50 guilders for every Jew we turn in.” They did not cease their investigations and also enquired in The Hague. At first, they received the same answer from there: “Half-Jewish”; then The Hague discovered the mistake and corrected her statement as “Jewess”. Rita and her sister were taken handcuffed to the police. She did manage, however, to first give her friend “illegal” papers whose creation she had taken over for the underground movement. Back then, Rita was 24 and her sister was 19 years old. At an interrogation the next day, they stated they had only been on a one-day visit to Naarden, but they were unable to produce any papers or other goods because they had been burgled in Amsterdam. In the process, they had to stick with saying they were Half-Jewish because every Jewess who was found on the street without a yellow badge would have been sent immediately to the penal hut in Westerbork and from there, you would get to Auschwitz without further ado. Her mother was on the “transport list” before because she had been baptized after 1940; the Church quickly forged a baptism certificate with an earlier date. That saved her life – she could stay in the barrack at Westerbork. Rita and her sister were sent from Naarden to Amsterdam, to the Central Office of the Gestapo. There, they testified again that they were only Half-Jewish and that their lawyer was still busy with supplying the evidence. The two girls had another, older sister who had gone into hiding - 5 - somewhere else. Again and again, they tried to find out from them where the sister was hiding. They persistently denied any knowledge of the place. Now, they were taken to the “Schouwburg”. It was an old theatre that had been set up to be a collection point for Jews. The Schouwburg was so overcrowded that they had to lie on the floor. 12 different people from the underground movement tried to get them out of the Schouwburg. Opposite, there was a Jewish nursery where Jewish children had been placed who were also intended for “transports”. There was a Jewish O.D. – Order Service – who had to help the Germans with the transports. Among them were people who, at the same time, helped to make prisoners disappear. An Aryan waiter, “Theo” Woortman, made hundreds of children disappear. The O.D. was eternally grateful to this Woortman for his deeds. Now, Woortman made a demand on them to save the two Gompertz girls. The O.D. demanded permission from the SS porter to let Rita, accompanied by her sister, go to the neighbouring nursery because Rita had to breastfeed her little baby there. The porter let them go, their names were made to disappear from the list in the Schouwburg; they were able to stay hidden in the nursery for 14 days. After those 14 days, Aus der Fünten had all the prisoners from the Schouwburg taken to Westerbork in a confined transport. The same afternoon, Rita received a message saying she should flee with her sister and go to the stated address of “Theo”. They arrived at Theo’s house safely and undetected. Specia lly by when we were marching later on. But then the -- why we -- when we came, we sort of kept with one another too. I had this one young man, he was my bunkmate. That happened in Buna. And in Buna we used to get air raids. And the air raids would come also to the -- to the I.G. Farben company, too. And while we were in I.G. Farben company, the Germans had a German kitchen there for themselves, or maybe for the non-Jews, too, I don™t know. But all I know is whenever the air raid came and that young man would find out where the kitc hen was, he was running to the kitchen to see what they threw out. input_chunk: block. They were explicitly told that they would be executed as soon as they disclosed any information. As the women were kind of indifferent towards their fate, they still told the others about the experiments that they had been subjected to. As it was also apparent that they died, or were sent to the gas chambers, shortly after their return, none of the women now wanted to be transferred to Clauberg. They were so terrified of him that Clauberg sent other doctors or people in his place for a time. Later, Lagerkommandantin Mandl selected the women and gave fake reasons, e.g. they were being transferred to do laundry or to clean the SS offices, when in reality they were being sent to Clauberg. I knew about all of this because I recorded information on the women who transferred to Clauberg’s block. When Clauberg appeared on visits to select the women for his block, it terrified them. I know that even rumours of Clauberg coming – sometimes completely untrue – would make the women panic and fear so much that you would find several of them on the electric fence as they preferred suicide over the prospect of being selected for Clauberg’s block. From the stories of the women who came back from Clauberg’s block, I know that some kind of injections were administered to their reproductive organs, and they received radiation treatment. They also said they had allegedly undergone operations, whereby they described the worst experience as having to lie fully motionless for five days after the operations, which some simply could not bear. Some also said they were allegedly placed in a net for a certain amount of time after the operations. Back then, I could not begin to imagine what they meant by these nets and why women would even be placed in them. The women, who, to my knowledge, had been in these nets, were destined to be sent straight to the gas chambers and were not transferred to any other block. After being entered in the register that I kept, they were sent to be exterminated in the gas chambers. Clauberg’s block could hold a few hundred people. I know that a few of the women went straight to him from the transport without even being tattooed in the concentration camp first. To register them, I just received their identification number for the women’s camp with a note that these women would be placed in Clauberg’s block. I estimate the total number of women who returned and were struck off from Clauberg’s list – as they either were sent straight to the gas chamber or were gassed a few days after their - 4 - return – to be around a thousand. In my opinion, only a few survived – maybe ten in total. This means that around one thousand women died or were killed as a result of Clauberg’s actions. I also know that there were cases where only the identification numbers of women who did not return to the camp were struck off – these were deaths that occurred in the block itself. At the time, I read in the newspaper that Clauberg had allegedly stated that not one single woman had died in his block. I can confirm that this is not true. As I already mentioned, I know this because there were cases in which numbers from Clauberg’s block were struck off – this signified fatalities in the block. I also still remember well that when Clauberg started selecting women, he would ask if they were still untouched /”maidens”/. I am also aware of cases where women got pregnant in Clauberg’s block. The rumour spread, but these women never came back to the camp. They were some of the women whose numbers were struck off straight away, in other words they were sent straight to the gas chamber or died in the block. input_chunk: With this intermezzo the danger of selection for a transport was not at all over. The fear remained until the departure of the Nazis and hounded us day and night. In fact, it was a charming custom that the brutes who brought the news to those selected for transport did so mostly at night. This fear was worse than the biting hunger which tortured us. If one was not selected for transport oneself, then it almost always included good friends, and there were constant good-byes as the transports continued without end. Therefore, we were always feeling - 7 - distressed. Sometimes we heard that the transports were cancelled for the next few months; one breathed more freely in the hope – the Jewish optimism did not diminish even in Th.- that in the meantime the war would have turned unfavourable for the Nazis. What rumours were circulating: the Nazis are finished, it can only be a matter of weeks, no: days etc. – but things did not happen so quickly, and the transports began again. Whereas in the winter of 1942/43 the Nazis managed to deport 50,000 to 60,000, they were supposed to bring down the number to 30,000. What this signified I need hardly elaborate. I would like to note that, according to the Brockhaus encyclopaedia, Th. had 6000 to 7000 inhabitants in normal times so you can imagine how much living space was available to the Jews. Theresienstadt, situated on the river Eger, not far from where it flows into the Elbe near Leitmeritz, is in a beautiful position. Unfortunately, we were unable to enjoy the landscape as we were prisoners behind walls and fortifications. However, we were largely able to move about freely within, unless, which happened occasionally because of some minimal misdemeanour, a curfew was imposed. In a few places one was allowed to access the walls, e.g. the so-called Bastei. From there one looked longingly into the distance – the Bohemian mountains, the valley of the Elbe etc. In the summer months this was a ray of light for us. But most of the time even this place of recuperation was forbidden. – In the Spring, in order to improve our vitamin intake, we searched on the lawns for herbs such as dandelion, sorrel, yarrow and others; but at times a statement was issued that it was a punishable offence to pull up even the tiniest blade of grass. The Jewish policemen had to keep strict watch over it, even though these were not well-kept lawns nor meadows. The winter of 1943/44 brought about an experience that nobody who was there could forget. The Centre of Command issued an order that on 11th November a census was to be taken. Apart from the bed-ridden patients, all Jews, small and tall, old and young, even babies in prams had to set off, at the crack of dawn, on a one-hour march to the Bauschewitzer Meadows, the field allocated to this purpose. It was a dull, foggy November day, and totally unsuitable for an “excursion”. Approximately 35,000 people were on the move, and the field was surrounded by soldiers. We were divided into groups, and the primitive method of counting took until dusk. Of course, this counting could have been accomplished much more simply, but then it would not have been torture for the Jews, and that was the whole purpose of the exercise! – When we were already frozen through and through, we were suddenly told that we would have to stay there all night; - 8 - We started considering how we could create a place of rest for the night when, out of the blue, came the order for the return. We had I suppose ten thousand soldiers in Denmark and well, they put ten times as much through Denmark to - his main uh goal was to conquer Norway and they did that too you know. Q: What happened to you? The year is 1940. You're a 14 year old boy. What did you do after the - what was your life like? A: Well, there was not a big change. The only thing happening which was really, you you saw it at the same time, was the black-out. From one day to another, you had to blackout. Denmark was totally blacked-out. And maybe you'll understand how it was later to stand in the blacked-out beach in Denmark and look three miles over the straits, the water demarking Denmark from Sweden, where the lights were just like pearls on a string. It was so fantastic uh but the first thing there was the black-out. And then of course there were lack of goods and uh there was no connection with England anymore, and our biggest trade partner and uh - but in the beginning the Germans tried to act just like 3 human beings. There was what, we should be the model. We were the vikings, and we should be - I don't know what he wanted us to be - but there was not, you was not disturbed much by the Germans in the day-to-day, in the beginning. A: When did that change for you? Q: Well, for me, you see we were shocked to lost our freedom and every resistance movement first part - I was only 15 when I started - it was to be a messenger boy. Deliver ____ for papers. Illegal papers of course. Because the first thing you really noticed is that all the news are censored. You only hear what the Germans, the Germans wanted you to hear. And therefore it was important to keep the real messages, to give the real news and that was to be duplicated and brought out by boys like me and it is of elder people but that was the way we started and it was the beginning to the resistance movement in Denmark, before the _________, before anything else. Q: How did you get recruited? A: Well, one of our teachers was uh became rather a famous figure in the resistance movement and uh as I went to school in Copenhagen, lived forty kilometers from there, I was a very good guy to have to put from one place to another. And then later on it was, we couldn't have all the papers with us on the train, then we duplicated our own papers and brought around. Q: Who was your teacher? A: ____________. Heard about him. Q: So this was going on then for a while? A: For a couple, for one year, two years. Q: When did it start to change? A: Well, some of my friends, they went in to the more heavy uh stuff in the resistance movement. Started the sabotage. Started - and that annoyed the Germans very much because because of course small thing that we could do but the Germans wanted to stop the sabotage and uh they demanded that the Danish government who had cooperated very much with the Germans to uh make uh death penalty for sabotage. That wouldn't, the Danish government accept and they signed and the Germans took over and that was the really beginning to what's happening later.

input_chunk: a former Social Democrat, who took large bribes, but in return alerted Frau Mecklenburg, deleted her name from a list which would have brought disaster and gave her his secret telephone number with the Gestapo, in order to take her call for help should the situation arise. Through a mutual friend, Frau Mecklenburg also got to know an influential Italian female, Andrina Torre, who worked for the Fascio-Organisation in Berlin and was supposedly sympathetic towards Jews. On 5.5.1942 the matron of the Jewish Hospital in Leipzig, Frieda Silberberg, gave Frau Heidenheim to understand that she should be ready to be deported to Lublin with the remark, “Eva it’s your turn!” Under threat, she wrote a farewell letter - 4 - to the matron and acquired a suspiciously large quantity of barbiturates to fake a suicide attempt, while actually telephoning the Torre female for help; this woman arrived promptly in Leipzig, and at the Hotel Astoria in the city handed her cook’s passport to Frau Heidenheim, to whose facial features the passport photograph bore only a very faint resemblance. La Torre, who lacked for nothing in her splendid Berlin apartment on Lietzenburgufer, was initially very kind to Frau Heidenheim, provided her with food etc, however was clearly very pleased that both sisters, Frau Heidenheim and Frau Mecklenburg, left many very valuable things in her custody. Through her sister, Bock had Frau Heidenheim brought to the milliner, Marga Levy in Heilbronner Strasse, a divorced woman who belonged to his circle of protégées. From May to November 1942 Frau Heidenheim lived in hiding with different people; during this period, she worked as a nursing auxiliary. She found that during this period roughly 2,000 Jews were living in hiding in Berlin and were provided, after a fashion, with food by “Aryans”. She heard later about a Dr Kaufmann, an earlier member of Max Naumann’s “Verband nationaldeutscher Juden”, who, married to an “Aryan” (strictly anti-Nazi), helped very many Jews by giving away free food ration cards etc, however perished himself later on as well. On 27.11.1942 Frau Mecklenburg was taken away by the Customs Investigation Department because of an alleged breach of exchange control regulations and later perished. In Frau Heidenheim’s opinion she was betrayed by the Torre woman. The Torre woman warned Frau Heidenheim and advised her to leave Berlin. As her brother-in-law, Hans Heidenheim, who was married to an “Aryan”, lived in Düsseldorf in the same building as a married couple, Hohlweck an engineer and his wife, who were both ardent anti-Nazi “Aryans”, and as Hohlweck, when he discovered - 5 - Frau Eva Heidenheim’s situation through Hans Heidenheim, announced that he was immediately ready to take her in himself, Hans Heidenheim set off promptly to Berlin to fetch his sister-in-law, and there handed her a current passport in the name of Frau Hohlweck. The Hohlwecks, who also helped other Jews, kept Frau Heidenheim, who arrived in Düsseldorf on 1.12.1942, with them until the end of the war. Frau Heidenheim had made the journey to Düsseldorf at night in a very overcrowded train, where an SA man made room for her to sit on his luggage in the corridor and protectively put his arm around her, which triggered the thought in Frau Heidenheim’s mind that she could not be in any safer place than this. This not-knowing, the menacing sense of uncertainty, were hard to bear. On Saturday, 23 September, the order came: 5,000 people who are fully fit to work, for a work transport, allegedly going to the Reich [i.e. Germany]. 2,500 will leave tomorrow and the same number on the following day (Yom Kippur). Much sorrow and sadness as families are being torn apart – the 16- to 18-year-olds who have to leave their parents. The hardest thing about the deportations is when people who belong together are being separated. (All of this is illustrative of the fact that almost no one in Theresienstadt, apart from perhaps those in charge, had any idea where these transports were going to or what happened to the people at their destination.) 2/11/1944 The transports have been going on this entire time, until 28 October! Of around 45,000 people, 10,000 are still left here. The families have been sent to follow their family members (deported on the so-called work transports last September). Where to, we do not know. The only people left here are almost all over 65 years of age. Of the younger ones, only those who are indispensable for the hard work required in certain operations, such as water, electricity, the sewers, agriculture, the kitchens and funeral services are left, and also the prominent figures. – In my department, which was tasked with police work and consisted of 99 people before the last transports took place, only nine (women) are left! Very much against my objections and my wishes, I was put in charge of the department, although fortunately now with a different remit. We only have to undertake investigations, not criminal prosecutions, nor surveillance or patrols. We have to work a lot and, besides working during the day, are also busy nearly every night. It is almost too much. At the moment the re-organisation has to bed in. – Almost all good acquaintances and close friends are gone: Ilse Cohn, Paul Epstein and his wife, Zucker, Werner Simon and his family, the Elkeles, Camille Hoffmann and his wife, Gerhard Cohn and many others. 21 Novermber 1944 Haven’t written for a long time. The last transports were dreadful. Everything has now quietened down. We have been absorbed into the Legal Department as a separate unit tasked with investigative work – although it seems this will not be the case for long. The director [of the investigations unit] is an intelligent, well-educated elderly gentleman, Hofrat[4] Klang, formerly a judge in Austria, who is excellent to work with. Someone who speaks the same language as I, which means we understand one another immediately, even though he is quite a curmudgeon. Some of my female colleagues[5] are difficult people. input_chunk: this was like going from the frying-pan into the fire. The accommodation was in a terrible state and it took us a long time to make it habitable. Vermin were everywhere; we were tormented by thousands of fleas. The commandant was a malicious character who bullied us continually. One of the punishments he had dreamt up, and used all the time, was to make us run up a nearby steep hill and wave from the summit. If you came back out of breath, you were made to climb up again. And so it went on until you collapsed with exhaustion - much to the amusement of the commandant.Things were made slightly more tolerable by some of the staff’s corrupt practices. It was possible to gain all kinds of concessions, but everything came at a price. The cost of having a letter smuggled out to the postbox was a mere one pengő, whereas getting a day’s “leave” cost several hundred pengős. Food smuggled out of the local village came at a premium. Everyone - the company staff, farmers and middle-men - all of them were out to make money out of the Jews. Wherever a Jewish labour corps company were sent to work, food prices would double or treble in price.We tried among ourselves to make sure that it was not only those who still had money who were able to benefit from any concessions, but also those who were worse off. We set up a company “fund” into which everyone paid, each according to his means, and this money was used to cover any outlay for our poorer comrades.As conditions for the company worsened, money started to run out, and the prospect of an imminent end to the war drew ever closer, the number of deserters increased. Everyone wanted to head to Budapest to witness the arrival of the Russians, which was widely expected to happen any day. But staying with the company meant running the risk of being transported westwards ahead of the approaching Russian troops, and maybe having to wait many more months to be liberated. As it turned out, we were right. Later on, most labour corps workers who stayed with their company lost their lives one way or another. In the end, the companies were either taken to concentration camps or - 6 - massacred along the way. On the other hand, those who deserted were also in great danger and many of them died, especially as the Russians arrived much later than had been expected.I too decided to desert at the start of September. The main difficulty was getting hold of false identity papers, without which I would have no hope of reaching Budapest and going underground there. I spent my last thousand pengő bribing the Feldwebel to leave me alone for a few minutes in the clerk’s office. I found what I was looking for: identity papers with Christian-sounding names on. I grabbed several of them to pass on to my friends and relatives.I arrived in Budapest on 6 September. I lived there for a while at various addresses, but after Horthy’s ill-fated attempt at bringing about a truce with the Russians on 15 October, it became too dangerous to stay in the city. Jews living “underground” were being picked up every day and either taken off to the ghetto or to houses owned by Pfeilkreuzler (Hungarian fascists), where they were tortured; many were later murdered and their bodies thrown into the Danube. For a while, I took the name Franz Kiss and hid out in the suburb of Zugló with other deserters and Jewish refugees. On 23 December, with the number of raids increasing at an alarming rate, I headed to Buda on the other side of the river. input_chunk: meantime the resistance movement had achieved firm forward strides in the Sureté Nationale. Then I was to experience my 33th arrest, which I survived only by an act of Providence. In the meantime, the Marseilles maquis had perpetrated their acts of sabotage in ever increasing number. They placed their bombs in the cinemas, the brothels, and the restaurants which had been requisitioned by the Nazis. They stabbed an uncanny number of German sentries in derelict dim hideouts etc. But there occurred an absolutely fantastic case: In Marseilles there were also Italians among the occupation authorities, many of whom could not bear the sight of the Nazis; the whole affair was a flagrant case of “Axis-rift”. Now the Nazis and the Italians both had to frequent the slaughter houses in order to collect the meat supplied for their troups. However, it behoved the Nazis in their truculence to save the most inferior kind of meat, often in a putrid state, for their Axis colleagues. One day, a choleric Sicilian non-commissioned officer shot down the German non-commissioned officer in charge of the stores like a dog. As the Nazis did not want the population to have an inkling of the facts, that the man had perished at the hands of an Axis comrade, they circulated the fictitious rumour that the jewish canaille and the enemy aliens had penetrated this murder. 20 hostages were picked out from the most prominent of the intellectuals. I was selected as the 19th hostage. I was woken up at 3 a.m. and loaded on a truck. These hostages included Englishmen Americans, Norwegians, Serbs, Szechs, Greeks, Frenchmen, Jews and non-Jews. We were dragged to the Sureté Nationale, an dit all began with our receiving fearful blows from Laval’s gangsters, “sur commande des Allemands”. I was dealt out horrible blows in the face, and one blow was punched so close to my eyes that I was saved from blindness only by a miracle. Then we were pent up in the notorious “upright coffins” which the Gestapo had had erected in the cellars of the Sureté and in the vicinity of the draining system in the harbour. These “standing coffins” present themselves as enlarged (proportionally enlarged) cigar boxes, which would be tilted on the barrow base. The only way to stretch your limbs in one of these contractions is to form a “diagon” with the “coffin”, i.e. to rest your feet against the “door” and your head against the natural lid of the “coffin”. There was no thinkable way to lie down in one of these “standingcoffins”, and these miracles of sadistic appliances derived their names from this circumstance. Everyone of the 20 hostages was pent up in such a “coffin”, and the boxes were aligned in a row. We were supplied daily with twenty - 6 - grams of mouldy bread and a coffee cup of muddy water. input_chunk: Jews), an organisation which had been established at the Germans’ command and which had to carry out all the orders of the Germans unquestioningly. This form, which was simply a piece of paper, said briefly, ‘Mr Josef Rosta, resident in Erzsebet Koerut 34, is hereby summoned to appear tomorrow, 24 April, at 6.45 am unconditionally in the Mercedes-Benz factory in order to work for the German occupation forces. Failure to appear may have very serious consequences. Bring provisions with you for one day.’ The male Jews in Budapest received plenty of such summonses in those days. The workplaces they were sent to differed a great deal. Those who did not get these orders were called up to the military Labour Service companies later in May and June. On the stated day I arrived punctually at the stated time at my new workplace. Besides me only one other fellow sufferer had come, thus obeying the summons received. The factory was a Budapest branch of the German Mercedes-Benz works and at that time was engaged almost exclusively in overhauling and repairing motor vehicles of the German Wehrmacht[2]. A foreman met us and allocated us to our work. Though we were not used to this work it was not too hard, at least for the time being. We had to help complete an air raid shelter. It was my special job to transport mortar and building materials to and fro in small wheelbarrows. We had to work ten hours a day. We got a little money, had to buy food ourselves and were allowed to sleep at night at home. We had to take no notice of the antisemitic remarks of the German staff. When we thought how much more difficult the working conditions were for many of our brothers in faith in other places, especially in the Labour Service companies, and how many others were deported, in particular from the communities in the provinces, we were really able to consider ourselves lucky. But that did not last long. In the night of 19 to 20 May there was a heavy air raid on Budapest and among others the Mercedes-Benz works were completely destroyed by bombs. When I arrived there in the morning I saw only the smoke of the ruins. The explosions of the aircraft bombs had been so violent that some lorries which had been in the courtyard had been hurled in pieces into the nearby streets. Also our beautiful air raid shelter that we had built so industriously was now in ruins. On the very same day I was sent to another workplace, and this time the work was much harder. Up there on the Schwabenberg (in the meantime its name has been changed to ‘Freiheitsberg’[3]) I had to help, together with a whole group of Jewish forced labourers, to build a tunnel. Instructed by skilled workers we were pushed to work between eight and twelve hours a day. A deep tunnel was driven into the mountain, debris and heavy boulders had to be transported away. To this day none of us has ever learnt what was to be the purpose of this tunnel which has never been completed. Perhaps it was planned as a safe shelter to protect the German and Hungarian despots from the bombs. For on that very spot, on the Schwabenberg, in the noble villas, which they had stolen from their former Jewish owners, was the exact place where some of the notorious German and Hungarian fascists had established their headquarters. In the hotel ‘Majestic’, once the meeting place of the upper classes of Budapest, now Peter Hain, the chief of the police, lived with his gang; he was Hungarian but an ethnic German, who had made close friends with the German occupation authorities. input_chunk: I wanted to earn money as fast as possible, and so I entered a home for expectant mothers and their new-born babies – the ‘Dahlem House’, run by nuns. Here I learned the job of being an infant nurse and passed the home’s examination with distinction. However the Medical Council of the City of Berlin did not allow me this qualification ….. but I was ‘permitted’ to do the night shift for four weeks while the other girls took their exams. But they found me unsatisfactory in this role. I stayed for one year, from 1936 to 1937. Then I decided to try everything I could to learn the craft of a goldsmith, and because that was not possible for me in Germany I wanted to try in Denmark where the skills of the goldsmith are very popular. But I had counted on the fact that my father was not able to deposit enough money into a Danish bank and there was nothing left for me than to go to a Danish family and give up my idea of study. Unfortunately, I was particularly unlucky there, as the family comprised a Norwegian and his wife, who was a born German. She was very antisemitic and had made a point of having young Jewish girls come to her as ‘house daughters’ so she could then completely exploit them. When I realised that it was completely impossible for me to pay for an education, I went back to Berlin for some months. I tried to study medicine, but had to break off my studies after two months. I was then encouraged to study chemistry as there was a shortage of chemists. I had passed the matriculation examinations, but in common with other Jewish students, I had to sit on special seating with a Jewish textbook that bore a yellow stripe. My attempts to become a medical assistant also came to nothing. This educational path was blocked for Jews and half-Jews of the first grade. I later took courses in the business school during my study of medicine. I learned shorthand, typing, and all relevant secretarial skills. I passed my final examinations in 1938 and started looking for jobs. It was already becoming almost impossible to find anything, and one of the questions on the application forms asked whether I was of ‘the same kind of blood’. Those who already had jobs could retain their positions because either they were protected by their employers or because these application forms only had to be filled when applying for new jobs. By chance, I then found a job with a publishing director of the Deutsche Allgemeine Zeitung (German General Newspaper). The overall situation was becoming increasingly difficult, and as we had relatives in America we were preparing to emigrate there. My father’s 87-year-old mother had suffered a lot under the Nazis. She was living in Freiburg. The Gestapo were constantly making searches of this old lady’s home – they came mostly at 4am and were looking for ‘weapons’ and jewellery. We tried to enable her departure to Poland where she had relatives. We could not just leave her behind alone, and America would have been too far for her to travel. When we finally received her visa after many attempts, she died exactly two days before the planned date. We had a very high quota number for the American visa, and as we were fearing a long wait, my father decided to emigrate to England, for the time being by himself. We had maintained good relationships within Jesuit circles, and these had helped him to get a permit very quickly, enabling him to travel to England in 1939. My mother spent her entire free time distributing ‘Love Gift Packets’ from the Catholic Caritas Association, which was based in Freiburg and led by Fräulein Dr Lukner, giving them to Jewish families. Karl-August was utterly shocked when he had to hear on his journey back from Italy that I was sick in bed and not able to travel. When he learned the whole story his hair stood on end with horror. His hatred of the Nazis grew to gigantic proportions and he showed it so openly that I was in constant fear for him. A rest-cure in Gastein put me back on my feet during the summer. We counted the days until the regime came to an end. The terrible air raids shredded our nerves and we lived only for the radio from London, which strengthened our hope and our will to resist. We became acquainted with resistance circles and I trembled for Karl-August even more. That’s how it was until the summer of 1944. Shortly before our holiday trip again to Gastein our great friend here in Berlin, whose husband was already in a concentration camp, was arrested. Our efforts to help her came to absolutely nothing. On July 16th we arrived in Gastein and on the 20th we heard about the deliberate assassination attempt on Hitler. We were overjoyed! Something had happened at last! It had not succeeded, but it was the start. More would follow. About noon on July 22nd, just after we had settled down for a rest, the door opened, two men walked in, identified themselves as secret police and told us we were under arrest! Here it was, the spectre I had been waiting for all these years. Half an hour later our cases were packed and we were travelling back to Berlin in a police van accompanied by the Gestapo. We were put in prison in Potsdam and the tragedy began. Terrible interrogations! A Communist who had been arrested had given them my husband’s name as a fierce opponent of the Nazis and they were glad to have got something on him at last. He was taken before the People’s Court accused of preparing high treason along with many other people most of whom were condemned to death. His own sentence, of 3 years’ imprisonment for not denouncing a Communist, he owed to his own skilful defence. I, as a Jewess, was plainly not going to be put before the Court. I spent six more weeks in jail at Alexanderplatz and was then transported to the concentration camp at Auschwitz! That meant extermination! I heard nothing about Karl-August’s fate and he heard nothing about mine. This was the greatest torture! You already know what it was like in Auschwitz from other accounts. The ovens burned day and night, the sky glowed red and was darkened by smoke. The atrocities that you were exposed to every day were indescribable. How good that Erna did not have to go through it all. For the first time I was happy she was dead. As the Russians were getting steadily closer the camp, which was like a huge town, was suddenly broken up. The ‘Aryans’ were moved first, and we Jews thought they would just kill us all from the air and claim that the enemy had done it. But suddenly we were put into transports as well, in our ragged summer clothing, without any covering, in December, 70 or 80 people at a time in cattle trucks with SS guards, and we set off to the concentration camp at Ravensbruck. Things would be the same as before, just the oven was missing (they said). input_chunk: Archives RG-50.549.02*0057 73Q: I™ve heard some survivors be quite critical, though, of the fact that this is not a museum solely dedicated to Jewish survivors. Ho-How do you feel about that? A: No, I disagree strongly. I disagree beca use then it would defeat the purpose. If it would be only to perpetuate the Jewish Holocaust, it would be very parochial. I think that the museum is a warning and teaching experience for people of all persuasions all around the world, of all the people who can have the access to the museum. It is a morally and ethically marvelous tool, becaus e it exposes people to -- not only to the evil, but also to the goodness. It exposes people to the teaching of the survivors like myself, what did they learn, and what did they want to tell the future generations? Because we as survivors are getting old, and we are dying out, and we will be the last ones who will be heard from. Q: Do you think there can ever be too much education ab out the Holocaust? Because some people are also a little fearful that too much quote, fixation on the Holocaust takes away from more -- fr-from othe r aspects of Jewish culture. A: I don™t think so. I disagree. This is my point of view. You can never take away from the culture by teaching people how to ge t along with other people. It is this -- my individual understanding, and I hope by -- that people who will listen to me will agree with me, that the museum, it was created for the purpose of teaching people to avoid in the future, genocides not only of Jewish people, but all the people everywhere on this earth. Unfortunately, we have the bad examples occurring now throughout the world. And this museum t eaches people how to -- how to understand USHMM Archives RG-50.549.02*0057 74this, and how to avoid. How can the museum be a -- a -- o-only preaching about the Jewish genocide? There™s genocide now going on. Q: And how do you feel about sort of popular films and -- and sort of popular culture to -- representing the Holocaust? There was an opposition to the fascist government, a unique one because it was one of the unique times in history that Western support partisans by the Western ally and Communist support partisans by the Soviet Union cooperated, essentially cooperated and created an uprising against the fascist governme nt. As you look at the map of Slovakia, if Slovakia is taken away from the German self -influence, it shuts the capability from the south to get into Germany. They invaded . T he force was mainly Waffen SS, which was the fighting unit of the SS. And they had both German and Ukrainian part of the German Army, of the Waffen SS. Ukrainian SS members. And they inva ded. Obviously it was very clear that this is the end of any protection, end of everything. The Germans are here. And the Ukrainians are here, which were far more cruel than the German s ever were, at least from my perspective as a child. I'm not a hist orian. These are my perspectives. >> Bill Benson: So the Germans invade. >> Gideon Frieder: The Germans invaded. It was very clear that we are done. My father was very well -known. It was clear that the Germans really didn't know what the Miranda rights are. They would see him, shoot him, and that's it. So he decided that he cannot stay with us because if he is found , by association he will be killed. So he sent us, us meaning my mother, my sister and me, from the city. But the city was already under siege. Nove Mesto was the city. So he puts us in an ambulance and sent the ambulance toward the German lines. Nobody would suspect an ambulance towards the German lines would have any Jews in it. Once the ambulance was out of the city, obviously we turned around. We fled. The ambulance broke down. A long story. Eventually we had to move on foot. We move on foot for a period that's unknown to me.

The whole, the Zionists did a, a fantastic job in catching the spirit of young people and really giving us what we wanted to have. We had a relatively free life, we had, we had a picture of a heroic future for us, whether we are going to be still serving in the army in Israel or just working in a kibbutz as farmers, almost everything about it had a kind of a super human touch that I'm going to be better than all these people around here who are r unning around like ants on the cities of Budapest, I'm going to lead a very healthy life, and fi nally I' m going to have a countr y, I have a home, I will have a fatherland and it was, it was a marvelous feeling. And also, th e whole, the whole setup, the whole organization, you know, until then, until 1946 or so, most of the picture that we saw of Jewish people is, is like sheep going into Auschwitz. And all of a sudde n these people come from Israel, they are beautiful looking people. And not only that, they had courage, the way they carried themselves and they were teaching us a lot of things, you know, Israel sent a lot of, they called them Schliahs , people that, those who are sent, I think, literally. input_chunk: was not pregnant, but the veterinarian, who I had sent for, and who had by now visited the stall, was able to confirm that the animal was eating voraciously, was indeed pregnant, and that it showed no evidence of gastroenteritis. Both veterinarians were in agreement that the stated age was correct, and that the animal had not rasped at its horns. 15th August was the first day of the hearing. The veterinarian, who I had commissioned, was not permitted in the courtroom, the veterinarian - 2 - from the opposing bench did not appear in court, because allegedly, or it may even have been true, he had fallen off his motorcycle. Irrespective of my solicitor’s objection to the process being continued without the veterinarian, the court convicted me to three months in prison; in so doing they had not overridden the evaluation of the Veterinary University in Hanover;, but, relying rather solely on the statement of the local farmers’ leader, whose details, in so far as they represented the actual natural world and could therefore be verified, had anyway been disproved by the concurrent utterances of both veterinarians. That very same day I was tried for a second case. I had purchased a cow from Ritter, a farmer in Altenstaedt near Hamburg; R., subject to the proviso that he did not have the consent of his son, did not hand over the cow, because it was too cheap, as he reasoned with me in the form of a reminder over the telephone. In spite of this he sold the cow a few days later for a lower price that wasof 25RM lower and accused me of fraud. During the hearing the judge suggested to R., that the reason he had sold the animal for a lower price, was because he was afraid that I wouldn’t pay him in full; whereupon the judge sentenced me to three months in prison, because I had damaged the property of the farmer to the value of this 25.- RM. My appeal to these sentences was heard on 26th October. The presiding judge at the Land court in Kassel immediately ordered a repeal of the second verdict, which took immediate effect, whilst the first verdict was upheld. The relatively favourable appraisal of my character and my behaviour towards my solicitor and the veterinarian were reproached with the [illegible] of these gentlemen. Because it was absolutely impossible for me to continue living as I had before these incidents, and serving my sentence would only delay changing my way of life and by implication thus endanger my health, I decided to flee from these arrangements. The Welfare Department of the Jewish community in Kassel, in the Glassbergerstrasse, is able to confirm the veracity of the details I have given above, as well to give any information required about all aspects of my reputation.

input_chunk: south, in Italy whose unfathomable culture drew me into its spell. The student years were past. It was difficult to find employment. They were the years of the stabilisation of the currency and of unemployment. I did a few months of unpaid voluntary work in a banking business and then obtained a very low position in industry. However, as soon as I got there, it was disclosed to me that also here that I would not be able to receive any salary because they were in the throes of downsizing. After a few weeks though, I received a few pennies, which I could not live on if I had to. In addition, I had to spend 2.5 hours daily in the streets and on the underground. My superior was a former subaltern, a representative of that military administrator type who did not even possess the narrow educational knowledge of a Prussian officer and had only learnt the spitefulness of a career officer. However, there was nothing that could be done. I could not find a better position and so I had to remain until the day that the factory with its 4000 employees was closed. Unemployed, but not starving because the situation at home was such that I could spend some time without earning. Then one day, the telephone rang. It was one of my former teachers at university, a privy councillor: “Herr I, - 5 - what are you doing?” “Do you want to take a job in the … government office?” I happily seized the chance and I was there the next day. The councillor who met me asked: “Are you a Jew?” “Yes!” “You will have a very difficult position here!” “By the way, your doctorate makes me want to vomit!” (It was categorised as “valde laudabile / very praiseworthy” by the Berlin faculty. I had to take it on the chin, but I was employed … 1926! It was immensely interesting work that was performed here. You had the feeling that you were standing at the heart of economic life. All of the economic journals were consolidated here and all of them were available. You learnt to comprehend contemporary economic occurrences and you could choose one day to stay here for ever or if not … to take step which also meant ending this activity. A colleague, apparently well-sponsored, asked for clarification on a certain topic which I had worked on. There were some mathematical things included and they could not be grappled with in an hour. I had a small manuscript lying in my drawer and I handed it to him confidentially. After 2 weeks I received it back. After a few more weeks, it appeared printed under his name. I had to report it because otherwise it would arise that I had actually done nothing over the course of the last few months. What would you require if the thing was “unofficially” arranged the state councillor asked me? “I would require that either the name of the authority or my name as the drafter appears in the article in the same position. I do not mind which of the two”. “You always want to hit your head against a brick wall.” “Look what is here in the introduction to this publication, and (he pointed to another publication), published by the president and signed with his name. It is not his idea, but mine. That is always the case here. ” It was implied that my salary could be improved only if I sorted the issue out. Also, they would give me an official service pass instead of instead of my usual travel pass. However, I declined and left. And 14 days before my departure after I had resigned, the well-connected plagiariser also had to leave not because of his offence, but only so that I, who had quit the service and was no longer bound by service confidentiality, could not say that the president had approved of the behaviour of the gentleman. input_chunk: Hungarian government ha s always been in the hands of the aristocracy, Hungarian aristocr acy, and the Hungarian aristocracy had no taste for Jews but also had no taste for killing or murderin g Jews. They were above this, an d so therefore when the dictator of Hungary, Admiral Horthy, had to appoint a government, most of the time that government would not eventually do everything that the Germans want ed them to do. So we really, up until 1944, we had a great deal of antiSemitism, we had a great deal of persecution of Jews but we were not in fear of our lives. input_chunk: couldn't believe our eyes – for 4 months we had forgotten that the world is so lovely, we felt like people on holiday. We were told that we would be at our destination at 7 o'clock and so we marched off briskly. You feel wonderful when you have so much joy in your heart. My God it was lovely, but our legs were of course locked in as well and not used to going out any more, we were already feeling that quite clearly after 2 hours. The pure unaccustomed air and the strong wind tired us all the more, as we had of course been on our feet since four in the morning and had not eaten properly the whole day. But the beautiful region helped us to march. 7 o'clock slowly drew near but there was no sign of our destination. Erna was wearing small shoes and could already hardly walk. A few had a space on the transport vehicle, some were feeling unwell, things began to be a bit miserable. Our escorts were fantastic – so the people in this region are splendid as well. Slowly it gets to 8 o'clock, our hearts are sinking and our feet are becoming leaden. My God, it is already getting dark and still only forest and no cabin to be seen. The darkness increases by the minute, we are becoming - 3 - scared, our thoughts are beginning to operate independently, they prey on our hearts – what is to become of us, it is pitch black, only the will to keep going drives us on, our feet are starting to burn, they carry us completely automatically, like soldiers whose duty is to march – where to is all the same to us, the world is becoming more miserable than before, our arrival, our 2 hours of happiness are becoming a mirage, we are in despair, weary of life, and quite apathetic. Our poor menfolk believe us already in our beds, and we poor women believe we will have to sleep in the forest. We lose each other, each of us walks alone. Our bags are deadweights in our hands. In my fear I began to seek God, where is He? Why does He watch as poor little women are tormented and hounded arbitrarily? Defenceless, alone, lonely and suffering and so in my despair I began to pray, thought of my poor father, who has been asleep in his grave in the lonely forest for ten years, thought that the stars – the same stars are also shining on my mother and siblings – and grew more confident again – there is a tomorrow after all and the road must also come to an end, my Cilhinka can also hardly go any further – good God, there is a light and so at 10 o'clock we have the 18km behind us at last. The large wooden hut is occupied in a moment, there are wooden bunks in two tiers with straw mattresses prepared for us, Cilli and I crawl up and are refreshed by a good hot soup and proper home-baked bread. My goodness! The bread tastes like Linzertorte – we have already forgotten that there is not only four week-old army bread. It tastes wonderful. We do not have any light, however, but Cilhinka, my tall strong Cilly, has already crept into her blanket like a little child and goes to sleep, thank heavens. I waited up for our luggage, until 12.30 we were still unloading motors, and then at last I too crawled into my bed and went to sleep thinking of my Leo. Worn out, with no volition, indifferent and exhausted we slept until 8 in the morning. A Saturday morning with sunshine, light and glorious air restored our morale. The world is beautiful after all, we are allowed to exist, there are still people – genuine good well-meaning people who see us as people too and give us sweet milky coffee for breakfast. A further policeman had also been stationed in front of the house. That is why my brother tried to persuade me to come out and give myself up. However, I knew better the fate that lay in store for me. I then decided to escape through the back door of the house. The rear courtyard of our building was separated from an adjoining farm by a high wall. I went into the yard without being seen, climbed the wall with some difficulty and then reached the neighbouring piece of land. There a farm labourer, whose attention had been caught by the noise, took me at first for a thief in the darkness that was now falling. I reassured him, and in return for drinking money of 5 Deutschmarks he opened a door leading onto a quiet side street for me. From here I made my way, without anyone seeing me, to the neighbouring village of Loesnitz, and rang the bell of my cousin’s home. He refused to do anything for me at first, until his wife came up and suggested something to me. If I went down the country road, she would fetch their car and drive past me. I should then jump into the car, in which she would take me to Chemnitz. This seemed to me to be a good plan, and I managed to get to Chemnitz as intended. There I went first of all to the waiting room at the station. I only managed to escape the attention of a police checkpoint because of the title of lawyer of the District Court in my passport, but this made it seem to me not sufficiently safe to stay here. For that reason, I retired to a hotel where I stayed the night, and at 5 o’clock the next morning climbed aboard the local train to Bernstein, the last place in Saxony before the Czech border. On the train the ticket collector looked at my profile and advised, “Now look here, it’s a bit too late in the year for trips to Bernstein. I should get out at the station before.” So this is what I did - 8 - and went on foot to Bernstein, however in my agitation on the journey had the bad luck to have one of the lenses fall out of my spectacles. Because of this I then looked for an optician and had the lens put back in. When I asked how much it cost, he only said, “Just get out of here as fast as you can.” I took his advice and set off for the nearby stream marking the border, having first had to ask some schoolchildren for directions. There were some signs by the stream at the border, which said that crossing it was a punishable offence. However I managed to get across the stream away from the customs road without attracting the attention of the border patrols. Now I was happily in Czechoslovakia. It was November 1935. First of all I went to Weipert, the nearest Czech town, and tried from there to get to Prague. I could not take the bus that went there, as the route went over German territory. Therefore I walked to the first railway station and there climbed aboard the train for Prague. On arrival at my destination I found lodgings with an aunt for the time being. An uncle, who was head of a government department in Prague and whom I asked for advice, turned me away, as he apparently considered me to be a criminal. With a visa valid for eight days, I travelled to London, where I instantly realised the impossibility of staying there. Thinking the farther the better, I bought sea tickets to Java in the Dutch East Indies via Genoa. The Jewish community of Java was quite affluent and consisted of around 3,000 Baghdad Jews and 800-1,000 Dutch Jews who were mainly dealing in trade in the capital. At the time, in March 1938, I was the only refugee from Germany, the other six came from Austria. The board members of the two Jewish communities, who were separated according to their origins, helped me in any way they could. In a special decree, Dutch Governor General Jonkherr Starkhenburg-Stachauer, whose wife was said to be Jewish, gave me life-long permission to stay and to work. The police force of the Dutch - 2 - East Indian state (now Indonesia) was riddled into the highest ranks with German civil servants who had settled there after World War I and who were now doing everything in their power to prevent me from obtaining a residence permit. Using trivial excuses, the German consul general attempted several times to get hold of my passport in order to stamp the “J” onto it, which would have had the result that according to the existing legislation, I would have been barred from obtaining a permanent residence permit. Although I had never corresponded with the German consulate about the endorsement of my passport, the consul demanded its submission claiming that it needed to be endorsed for a journey to Switzerland and even threatened me with jail if I didn’t follow his orders. The director of the immigration office in Surabaya (the second biggest city on Java after the capital Batavia) intervened on my behalf and explained to the German consul general that he would notify his superior authority of these actions if they didn’t stop at once, seeing that the German consul was not remotely authorised to threaten jail or any other repressive measures. Soon I became the director of a Dutch-owned import company and found it a very enjoyable position which left me comfortably off. However, when the Germans invaded Netherlands on 10th May 1940, the Dutch Queen ordered the immediate internment of all German nationals. Having barely had time to pay my servants, I was arrested in my home, forced to leave all my belongings behind, and, along with around 2,500 Germans, was sent to prison on an island of 1km square. The Dutch then hurriedly called in all their as of yet undeployed regiments, which consisted mainly of natives, who were put in charge of guarding the internees and ordered to shoot in the event of even the tiniest transgression, which indeed happened very often. For weeks we slept under the open sky, were given the same rations of rice and fish as prisoners, and I reckon we were treated no better than the inmates in German concentration camps. Soon there were outbreaks of diseases such as dysentery, typhoid, malaria and people started dying. It was only slowly, after the intervention of the Geneva Red Cross, that conditions in the camp improved a little. I became leader of a unit of around 80 prisoners, mostly seamen, who had been pulled off their ships and who behaved calmly at first. When the first reports of major German victories started to arrive, however, their behaviour changed and there were antisemitic attacks. - 3 - We only stayed in this camp for a few weeks. We were then returned to Batavia, where the Dutch kept us like cattle in the vicinity of the port until we were moved on to Sumatra, where we arrived after three days at sea, on small ships in rooms on the lowest decks.
