input_chunk: because at that time the last barrier fell. All men under 65 at that time had to go past the camp commander in single file and were graded into those that were noted and those that were not. No one knew under which schema these notes occurred. Very many war wounded were noted, but others in the same boat were not. - 11 - No one knew what this was for, and also, no one knew if it was good to be noted or not. You only knew that nothing good was imminent. Then, some days later the bomb struck. All those who had not been noted were sent to Poland. Since then we learned that all of these unfortunates had been carried off to Auschwitz, where, apart from a few exceptions, they were all murdered. In total it concerned 18,000 people who suffered this sad fate in the autumn of 1944. The rations were consistently inadequate and exacted a large number of victims. On 5 days of the week, at midday there was ½ pound of potatoes with an unidentifiable, nauseating sauce. On the other 2 days, there were cold yeast dumplings made from flower, water and yeast. In the evenings on 3 days of the week, there was a miserable coffee mix, and on the other 4 days of the week a thin barley or potato soup. In addition, we received 1 kg. of bread for 4 days, plus 60gr. margarine and 70 gr. sugar per week. There was almost never meat, though now and again, we received a piece of bad sausage or something called hash, but in reality, it was a thin sauce with a tiny piece of meat which smelt bad and tasted even worse. There was never fruit and vegetables and also no milk or eggs. With this inadequate nourishment, we were constantly hungry and lost more and more weight, until finally only skin and bones remained. The people died by slipping away. They became weaker and weaker, usually suffered from diarrhoea or lung infections, and died quickly. First it was the old who died, and then the younger ones also followed. It became a bit better from the summer of 1944 onwards after the arrival of the Red Cross Commission from Geneva. There was a few more potatoes, and now and again a few vegetables as well as barley or millet gruel from time to time. By the end of 1944, the number of dead amounted to around 40,000, most of whom died from hunger. On the orders of the camp commander, the urns were loaded onto lorries in the autumn of 1944 and sunk in the Eger. At the same time, all the files which referred to those who had died were burnt. This excuse is implausible. Look at it like this: individual shootings were voluntary ‘extra’ tasks. The shooting of the Stern brothers did not happen at one of these general operations. Such a command given by Wyppert, if it even had been given, would surely not be followed. The defendant, Pöll, says in the hearing on 19 July that he had not heard a command of this kind come from Wyppert’s mouth, and Mitas had not told him anything about a command… This statement, made by Pöll, weighs badly on Mitas. Eyewitnesses have also proved that there were further individual shootings. A witness, Wachtl, stated in the hearing held on 18 July that he had seen Mitas shoot Milek Felsen, an 18-year-old boy with an amputated leg. Q: I know you™re going to move the next site, but let me ask you, when you saw these folks from Yugoslavia, what was your first impression? Were they telling the stories of what had happened? A: They didn™t have to tell stories. You looked at them. You looked at the babies with big stomachs and big heads, and some women were breastfeeding children of two and children of four. She was feeding two babies, because they had had no real food for so long. In our units, by the way, there were many doctors who volunteered, women, and they immediately set up a hospital, but we got a measles epidemic, and in eight weeks, I think, we buried Œ no, six weeks, we buried over a hundred children, and that was dreadful because we lived within the hospital compound, and they crying of these women was absolutely dreadful, dreadful. To lose a child, no parent should bury a child. It was awful for them. Q: So, you were in that camp for how long? A: Ten months. Q: Ten months? A: Yes. Q: So, did you consider yourself now a seasoned relief worker at the end of the ten months? A: I never even thought of it that way. We had a job to do. We did our job. The Yugoslavs, as they got well, entertained us. They had beautiful singing voices, and they would sing in four, five parts. There were some others who were musicians, and they were very nice people, very nice. They were very clean people. A lot of them, I would say for the most part, were peasant people, but, you know, they were human beings. Q: And so then, why did you Œ why were you sent away from that situation to another situation? 10 A: Oh, because southern Italy was liberated, and the allies were getting ready for the liberation of Yugoslavia, which we had been trained to enter. Trained in the sense that we learned the language, we knew where we were going, we knew the kinds of jobs we would do, and because of the work we had done in Egypt, we were trained to take care of Yugoslavs who had gone through hell in this war. When we got to Italy, I happened to have been in the first unit of ten people who were sent over to Italy in preparation for going into Yugoslavia, and Teeter was approached by the British American armies. I™m not quite sure of the chain of command. He said, ﬁWe™ll do the job ourselves. Send us the goods.ﬂ And they did. They did a very good job. So, here we were, the rest of the unit had come into Italy, we were sitting there. The Italians were very pleased to see us. The Italians were very nice actually. They were living under appalling conditions, having suffered German occupation and British occupation, and they would have liked us to have stayed, but we really had no job to do in Italy. And then we heard one organization working in southern Italy called the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee. If he wasn't home, he was in the Synagogue and they felt he was right there. You know, that he cared about the religion. And the community was a caring community, they supported a very good public school, I went to that Jewish Public School, and an old-age home, and there were very few poor Jews really, and if they were the community supported them. And . . . 4 Q: But, in general, did the Jewish Community and the non-Jewish community mix, was there any sense of Anti-Semitism before the war? A: I can only tell you what I remember from our home. I use to go with my father to Gentile patients and next door to us was where the local Priest lived, he lived with his mother. It was, you know, he was in charge of the whole city, of the Catholic community. Mr. Richter was his name, Rev. Richter. I have even a picture of him because he taught us in the gymnasium and he taught us Latin. And he, when there was a nun, when he taught the Catholic religion, we were permitted to leave, you know, the classes. But, you know, we could choose to stay, but my father was his doctor and his mother's doctor, he chose him to be. And I know later on that my father was not permitted to practice anymore as a Jew. He personally, and I have his letter, wrote to the Papal Nuncio to allow this Jewish doctor to practice because as he wrote, he brought so many Catholic children into the world and cared so much about the poor. And my father used to give lectures because they were very primitive, some of the population, and they believed in all kind of nonsense, like a cat runs across the street, you know, this and that, and they practice this kind of medicine sometimes. And he used to go to schools and show how they should 05:29 wash their hands, how important that is, and taught them some simple health, you know, gave them health education. And he was written up in the Catholic newspaper, I still have some of the newspapers, even though they are almost in shreds. But, he made a name for himself as a very caring doctor who didn't choose, if it's someone Jewish or non-Jewish and many people were that way. I didn't see such a terrible distinction between Jews and nonJews, until the laws came against the Jews. Q: So, the beginning of the war for you was when . . . was it about the time this teacher came into your classroom? A: Yes, I would say it was in about 1938. At first the rules were very mild, we gave up our radio, we had to give up our skates, even though they were simple sakes, tennis rackets. They were mostly things of luxury or, you know, like recreational things. You had to even give up your fur collar, from your coat. And they gave you, for each of these items, a receipt. But the biggest blow was to our family when some people, not even from town, some detectives from Bratislava, which was a central, the capital of Slovakia and where all the law started, from the Slovak government and they sent those people out and they stole all my father's medical equipment. But I was to stay another eleven long, hard months, virtually put into cold storage. I had expected the affairs of a former KZ prisoner to be given priority treatment, but I was mistaken; there was no conference at all. The Czechs had overdone it by arresting hundreds of thousands indiscriminately. They were simply not able to cope with these ‘cases’. In the meantime I had been put back into section BIII and so I was starving again. So I tried to obtain the Czech rations I was entitled to. I asked to see the director, but the guard took me to the head warder instead. This man listened to me … nothing happened! Section IIIB was run particularly badly, the guard was the mere tool of the trusty, he did not care about anything. We even had to collect drinking water from the toilet; I can well imagine that this was why we all suffered from diarrhoea. In April 1946 I saw the director for the first time on his rounds. I presented my request to him, he promised to examine my case, but nothing happened! When at last I had had enough I tried in vain to file a petition. This was not allowed but had the effect nevertheless that my situation was considered, and that I was transferred to Leitmeritz because the people in Prague did not dare to decide anything. Well, I continued to starve until the wife of a fellow prisoner felt sorry for me and sent me a parcel. This was not allowed either, but for a week I had something to eat. On 26 June 1946 I was transferred to Leitmeritz. Leitmeritz was better organised than Prague. Immediately and urgently I demanded Czech food, which the guard simply denied me, since I had not spoken to him in Czech. When I demanded to be taken to the director, he refused this too. The following week, however, I requested permission to write letters. When I asked the director to allow me to write to the English ambassador, to the Red Cross and to my son, he at once granted permission. Getting bolder, I asked for Czech food, which I received the same day. Now at last I had contact with the outside world, although it took a long time until I received an answer. On the day after my committal to Leitmeritz I was presented to the prison doctor who realised how weakened I was, and promised at once that I would be put into the prison hospital as soon as there was a bed available. But before my admission I had a serious bout of enteritis. At last, on 9 August, I was admitted and stayed in this ward until my release on 9 January 1947. In Leitmeritz for the first time I came across guards who had stayed humane. Prohaska and Faltin, two young guards who had suffered themselves under the Germans and therefore knew how a prisoner felt. But there were also others: the worst ones were probably Adamczyk and Pfeifer. The latter ‘treated’ an Austrian called Seifert on his arrival by forcing him to lie in a bath filled with cold water. He was made to put his feet out, and Pfeifer tortured them so badly that Seifert passed out. Seifert never recovered from this maltreatment, and died in the autumn of 1946. Although as an Austrian he was entitled to Czech food, he did not get it, nor was he taken to the director as he had requested. Adamczyk shattered a boy’s eardrum. The SS guard accompanying us was very mild mannered. He was not a real SS man, but had been transferred to the SS [from the army] and kitted out accordingly. He had been foreseeing the end for a long time and even talked with us about it. But he was also fearful, since he knew that the SS took no prisoners[11]. On one occasion we played music in the village. Immediately the entire population arrived and marvelled at us. The local police made detailed enquiries and presented us with cigarettes. That evening a small food parcel from some of the village beauties was sent to our barn in recognition of our performance. But we did not stay for long here either. Though this time things took a turn for the better – except that we did not yet know of it. One night, at 1am, we had to set off in a great hurry. Yet again, the Allied front was approaching. This time I seriously considered escaping. But then I said to myself that Germany’s hours were numbered – and that we would not be able to walk much further as we were almost at the Baltic Sea. At this point, it was a question of `either – or’. One had to reckon with the SS shooting us at the very last moment. I decided to go with them. Where to was impossible to ascertain. Suddenly the Lagerältester called me away from the column and explained to me that we were going to be handed over, at a port, to the Swedish Red Cross. At that point our suffering would be over. I could hardly believe it. Was the Lagerältester, who had often lied to us, just telling us another tall story? But when I thought about it: the situation was too serious. At that moment I heard two gunshots. Yet again a comrade had died … and that at the 11th hour. I delivered the sensational news to my comrades while we were walking. None of them could fully believe it. I, however, felt as I had always felt, that I would come out of this alive – and that there was some truth in the matter. That re-energised my feet. Finally, we arrived at a barn in Süsel[12]. It was raining heavily. We threw ourselves on the straw and chewed red turnips, waiting to see what would happen. Then – all of a sudden – the Swedish Red Cross car appeared. I did not yet quite want to trust my eyes. - 10 - The chauffeur conferred with the camp elder, and then those from France, Belgium and Holland were called. A few of the others smuggled themselves into the crowd. But what did it matter? What happened to those who stayed behind, I do not know. We were collected by a lorry of the International Red Cross, whose chauffeur was a Canadian. He immediately distributed a few American cigarettes, which raised our spirits considerably. We were driven to Lübeck, where a Swedish ship was already expecting us. On board were food parcels from the American Red Cross for each of us. After years of great deprivation, we could once again eat our fill – the kind of food that by now had become just a memory for us and about which we had been reminiscing many an evening, with our eyes closed. That was lovely! V. Even better was the reception we got from the Swedes. It exceeded our wildest dreams. The love, attention and kindness offered to us went beyond all our expectations. The result of this is 50% TB. Even the least amount of investment to benefit the concentration camp was too much for him. Shop steward Nieviet, spinning foreman Krause and supervisors Brauer and Fieke harassed us the most. They put us starving and exhausted workers on the heaviest machinery that no German woman could or would want to work on; but most of all, they expected maximum output from us, otherwise we would be deprived of food. The supervisor Josef Peter from the factory’s mixing department assigned us the heaviest manual labour. If we could not do it, he became truly sadistic and would beat us until we fainted. - 2 - The German workers Seidler, Hase, Kluger, Opitz, Wenzel, Klause, Hawlitzek, Zdarski, Pohl, Wiesner, Sagber, Schubert, Springer, Dietrich, Flegel, Borowka, Müller, Riko, Schroll, Passler, Dietrich, Rudloff, Steidler, Stranzky, Schmidt, Bohacz, Breuer, Seher, Kaschka, Borwka, Wilhelm subjected us to extreme harassment in the room where we added detail to the cloth; they stole offcuts from us in the spinning room, which then counted towards their work and went against us. It is impossible for us to describe all the dreadful suffering inflicted on us here, mainly by the 44 named above. Hauptsturmführer Ritterbusch was a puppet in the hands of Unscha Rudolf Brun, who was a downright sadist. He had a full cabinet of clothing that the regulations stated he should use to supply us with clothes and shoes. However, when somebody dared to ask for the least little thing from him, they would be kicked and abused. This resulted in frozen limbs that required amputation in a number of cases. Lagerführer (camp leader) Hawlik, Else and her representative, Kirchschläger, Berta, conned us out of our share, as they were quite clearly lining their own pockets. The Lagerführer would punish us by sending us to the dark room, confiscating food and cutting off our hair for the slightest offence. Kirchschlager broke whole truncheons on our backs and tore full clumps of hair out of our heads; she was fury in female form. Our biggest misfortune were the 44 supervisors Erbsch, Grete; Blaschke, Hermine; Wosnek, Gertrude; Heinze, Ida; Spelda, Erika; Rzehak, Hedwig; Taube, Erna; Janouch, Elvira; Hrdy, Anna; Albrecht, Wally; Bodi, Hermine; Bönsch, Elisabeth; Schöps, Anna; Nittner, Filomena; Just, Rosa; Fichtner, Anna; Rosniczek, Isolde; Schreiber, Marta; Döring, Irma. The underlined names were the heads of department. - 3 - As a result of the extremely substandard food, most of us suffered from diarrhoea, so it was their absolute pleasure to forbid us from leaving, which caused indescribable suffering. We were only ever referred to as pigs, sluts and bitches. The sanitary facilities were beyond description. Our sick bay, which was always full to the maximum of 100 beds, had no dressings and the bare minimum in terms of medication. The statements made above are only the most essential information and are based on the whole truth. Copy Sosnowiec, 18/6/1945

My -- my mother and father couldn™t vacation toge ther because he ran the store, but my father would go off, I remember, to -- to Italy and to France and one time to the United States. On Sundays we™d go to -- there was a small like a z oo, with the cafés an -- and there was a synagogue also in the s -- in the suburb there, which is where we went. And my m -- we were -- my mother kept kosher. We were Orthodox and we had an excellent life. Q: What was your father™s name? A: My father™s name was Siegfried Mandle, and my mother™s name was Rita Mandle. Q: Has your father ever served in the military? A: My father was a volunteer in the first World War, and I believe he worked in a barn shoveling manure. He was 17 years old. Q: What work did your mother do? A: My mother -- in those days there were two servants and my mother -- my mother did the cooking. The German hausfrau prided herself on her cooking. And took care of me and I -- and I guess she was in the store once in awhile. But I was an only child. And she had a sister in town an d a lot of friends, you know, and lived a very nice life. Interview with Brigitte Freidin March 12, 2001 4Q: And her name? A: Was Rita. Q: You mentioned that your family was Or thodox, can you tell me specifically what religious traditions your family observed? A: Orthodox in the sense that all the holidays were kept, but the store was open on Saturdays because it had to be. But -- and strictly kosher and my mo -- and we always had Friday night services, you know, at home a nd went to synagogue on -- on Saturdays, at least my mother and I did. And I don™t remember if my father did or not, but Orthodox in the sense that that™s all that was known. Q: Did you have a favorite holiday? A: Oh, I guess -- I guess -- I guess it was Passover, Pesach, because we always had Seders, you know, the whole, long Seders . And this was always kept up, the traditions in -- when we wa -- when we came to the United States too, and whenever possible. I was brought up in -- in a very Jewish feeling home. I started -- I started out that there was a -- a teacher in that small synagogue there in the suburb. And then I started going downtown to the big synagogue, very, very famous art deco synagogue that -- and Interview with Brigitte Freidin March 12, 2001 5that™s where I went with the other Jewish children. And I was only -- what was it? Well, I was born in 1930, so I -- I was -- Kristallnacht I was eight years old. But -- but from the time I started school I -- I couldn™t go. We would go into the camps, and tell them things which were necessary for them to know, or collect papers, or bring them papers for signature. It was a bit of an awkward program, although it worked very well. Or they could go into Salzburg, where there papers were held. It was not an easy situation actually because we were always worried that there might be Russians around trying to pick up people because sometimes we had Russian army officers who were Jewish. For example, a woman came to me one day dressed almost in rags with dyed hair looking very ugly, and she said her husband and daughter were in Palestine. She was a doctor in the Russian army, and there was a certificate for Palestine for her at the British consulate, could we help her? Well, the first thing you think is, ﬁA ha! She™s a spy. She wants to see what we™re doing.ﬂ And I took all her particulars and I went across to the British consulate, and sure enough there was a certificate, but that wasn™t enough as far as I was concerned. I contacted friends who were working with the Jewish agency for Palestine, told them the story, and asked them to check in Palestine that she did indeed have a husband and a daughter there, because one never knew how honest these people were. There were many ways by which you could trick somebody, and the answer eventually came back that yes, her husband and daughter were there and they confirmed her story. Now, how was I to get her out? She had to come at times when very few people were around. I had to try and do everything so that she wouldn™t be seen, and eventually I got her certificate, and how to send her to the airport which was in the Russian zone? And the only way to do it was to take her myself, and don™t think I wasn™t scared. I™m not so brave, but she sat in the car with me and we handed in her papers, and my propesk, my permit to go into the Russian zone, and we put her on a plane. And there were others. I had a young woman who was working at the Polish consulate, who had a brother in Canada. My goodness, my memory™s going back, and she said she had a visa to go to Canada, and again, I was suspicious, and checked her out in the same way. I checked through the consulate and then I checked with the agency, the Jewish agency working in Montreal, and they confirmed her story, and she told the Poles at that time she was going on vacation, and off she went to Canada. It was tricky doing this because you were always suspicious that perhaps these people were not genuine, and that you might be picked up yourself on the street because people were being picked up, particularly by the Russians. input_chunk: German law prohibited them from attending school. Very early on in, I think, 1933, the first law came in which limited the number of Jewish children who could attend school. And so, a number of them came to England to school, and they were taken in by families. There was an organization called B™nai B™rith, which still exists, and they helped a lot of these children, particularly the Orthodox Jewish children. Q: So, at what point do you think Œ was it after the war, or in 1939 that you became very conscious of what was happening? What drew you in 1943 to join the relief effort? A: Well, firstly the war came in ™39. I remember we had the bombing in London, and 90 days of bombing constantly is not very pleasant. Q: What was that like? A: That was pretty awful. Very often, I would be scared and I™d sit under a table, or I would like people to think that I was brave and so I took tea to the shelters wearing my tin hat until I was going out one day with a young friend, and a piece of shrapnel went through his tin hat, and he was no longer. It was frightening and yet, you didn™t like to appear a coward. We did things that we would neve r do. We went into the streets and put out incendiary bombs because, since the government, I suppose, wanted to know how many incendiaries had been dropped, they would pay us a half a crown which was about half a dollar in those days, to bring in the ends of incendiary bombs. So, we™d go out and we™d pick these things up once the bomb had gone off. And, yet, we used to sit on the doorstep occasionally in an air raid, and say, ﬁWhat will we tell our children of the war?ﬂ And, you know, we were eating peanuts and we™d say, ﬁWell, we™ll tell them that we sat on the doorstep eating peanuts.ﬂ But, it was an interesting period because we never saw a fruit. If anybody brought in an orange, if an American soldier gave somebody an orange or a banana, we raffled it to the Red Cross. We didn™t go hungry. We were never short of the most awful bread you can ever imagine, and the American powdered egg, which we even thought made good cakes, you know, we had forgotten what a good cake tasted like. But, as I say, we were never hungry, and interestingly, we always knew we were going to win the war. Don™t ask me why, perhaps this was a moral booster, perhaps this was Churchill™s speeches, but we never thought the Germans would overrun us. Of course, we always suspected that we would be invaded, and this influenced, of course, the British attitude toward the refugees. We suspected everybody with a German accent of being a spy. It was a very difficult period for them, much more so than for us. Q: So, then, 90 days of bombing straight? A: Ninety days of bombing on London. Q: Was your house ever hit? 5 A: Oh, yeah. Q: It was? A: Yeah, but my mother was okay, you know, the heck with the house. Q: So, where did you go? Did you stay in the house? A: I met recently a woman, she called me as a result of my book. She called me and she said, ﬁDo you remember, after the air raids when you™d done all your rounds, you used to come into our house and sleep on a bed or a mat or anywhere?ﬂ No, I went to stay with friends, and after the house was hit, we got my mother to leave London and go into the country. I wouldn™t go.

Als nach einigen Wochen OT-Leute als Bewachung abgezogen worden waren, erhielten Kriminelle unseres Lagers Bewaffnung und wurden als Wachen eingesetzt. Anscheinend war damit auch eine Besoldung verbunden, denn diese Leute kamen oft voellig betrunken ins Lager und misshandelten dabei - auch in unserem Schlafsaal - Personen, ohne dafuer zur Rechenschaft gezogen zu werden. Eine Revolte in unserem Schlafsaal, die mit der Verpruegelung des Wachhabenden (Haeftlings) endete, hatte allerdings auch keine schweren Folgen. input_chunk: So I went to work in a factory, Pionki. It was a big complex in the forest. I knew it was there, but they build it before the war. A big, tremendous factory. They make powder for bullets. And I went there to work. How did I go there? When the Germans came to pick up young people in the ghetto, I volunteered. But every time I volunteered, they didn't want to take me because I didn't have no suitcases. I didn't have nothing to carry. I just had the clothes that I was wearing. They pushed me away. One day, a few truc ks, Germans, German soldiers, came and asked for volunteers. So there was a couple of elderly people, which they didn't want to take old people. Only young people. Came over to me. They knew me. They knew my parents. They said, ﬁDave, here, two bundl es.ﬂ They give it to me. When I walked over to the truck with the two bundles, the Germans took me. And I went to work at the factory. What happened when I came to the factory? They took away my bundles. That's why they wanted bundles. Every Jew had money, gold, things like this. So they robbed me. I never knew what was inside anyhow. So then I worked in the factory. I became an expert in making powder. The Germans taught me how to make powder for bullets. ROUGH DRAFT TRANSCRIPT NOT A VERBATIM RECORD 12 For two years I was an expert. There was sabotage over there, explosions, fire. There were things that we did that was unbelievable stories. But I don't ha ve much time to talk about it, but I will tell you about one story. There was one guy who was a smoker. For cigarettes, would give away his rations, breads, everything for a cigarette. And one night, the night shift, his job was to take the cotton, which we produced the powder, put on a conveyor , and the conveyor was coming to my department , which I mixed in with chemicals. He was smoking the cigarette , fell out of his mouth , and there was a fire. Why did it fall out? Because he was so tired. He worked 12 hours a day for himself and for somebody else who give him cigarettes. Bread or som ething. He gave away his ration for a cigarette. The fire went to my building. We stopped working. The Germans came in. They're going to kill us. That's what they do. They killed you right away for anything you do wrong. There were two Germans. I have to mention their names. One was Dr. Vit ta, and one was another doctor. Two German civilians charged in my factory. They persuaded the Gestapo not to kill us because we are experts. We know what we are doing. If they kill us, they have to train other people , and the factory would not start working. So they saved our lives. In the meantime, they -- they beat us bloody. The next day they said , ﬁG o back to work. ﬂ So that's what happened in the Pionki. >> Bill Benson: David, two things. First, the work that you did was very dangerous in the munitions factory. But tell us, also, what your life was like. How did you eat? What were the ROUGH DRAFT TRANSCRIPT NOT A VERBATIM RECORD 13 conditions like there? >> David Bayer: Ok. We worked with civilians, Polish people , who were coming to work in the factory and then would go home. We worked together next to them. The Polish people brought their lunch, their food. input_chunk: “You must leave some things in the flat, food, linen!” At the end my mother gets an extra suitcase ready with things for my father. They assure her he will get the things.... our last meal in a warm kitchen. I have one last warm wash. I always think of the last hours as a death sentence. Slowly we go to Sokolhaus with numbers on our clothes, dressed for the cold and they watch us go. They we have been warned that we must be there for nine o’clock. Everyone knows why but the official summons does not explain this. We wait by the big door. We are “housed” in the big hall in the Sokolhaus. The room is extremely warm, we sweat because of course we are all wearing two sets of underwear - 2 - and other heavy clothing. Everyone has two mattresses (having brought three with him.) The old people are comforted by the fact that they can lie down on their own mattress. Lie down? There is no space. The days pass in an indescribably tense and nervous atmosphere. There is nothing to do. Now and then they call out for people- to eat, to have their hair cut- they look for men who can speak German and Czech. I volunteer, mainly to put an end to the torture of the enforced idleness. I am made a supervisor, collect linen, try to establish some order. An old lady asks urgently for a thermos flask. I manage to get one for her illegally from outside. She thanks me profusely. There is continual uncertainty as to whether we are going to Poland or to Theresienstadt. During the night I keep guard by the main entrance which is locked. A poor old lady comes and asks if I can open the door. I try to explain to her that this is impossible. The answer: “But they said that I should go home....” It turns out that a supervisor wanted her to go back to her place in the hall. Finally we have to go to a hut and hand in all our documents and valuables. I get back my identity back with a stamp saying “Ghettoisiert.” (sent to the ghetto.) Remarkably it is at this moment that we get our greatest shock. In a temperature of minus 20C we are lined up in rows of five and marched through the empty streets. I look around me. My feeling is: you are seeing all this for the last time. The streets are almost deserted. At the railway yard we get into an old passenger coach. The Schupo (policeman) is strict and shouts. The seats are numbered. There are two supervisors to each carriage. I am supposed to ensure that everyone stays in his place. It is difficult, people in the same family want to swap seats so as to be together. I allow this in one case. A policeman checks the numbers, they are not correct. In the corridor he hits me so that my glasses fall to the floor and shouts, “You damn filthy Jews (Saujuden) outside our brothers are fighting in the snow and the ice. I’ll teach you. You watch out or it’ll end badly for you.” I don’t say a word and get out my spare pair of glasses. This incident has taught me a lesson for my whole time in the camp. Don’t stick out. The train travels throughout the night. At the station in Prague I hear technical instructions for the special train over the loud-speaker. We still don’t know where we are going. No one dares to leave their seat. Finally the train stops. At the tiny station in Bohusovice I see the first prisoners with strange home-made armbands of leather straps and the Ghetto police. input_chunk: by an SS-court for embezzlement and probably killed. The cases grew more and more where inmates were disposed. That happened the most in the quarries, which was cordoned off by a chain of posts made up of SS-people. If one therefore wanted to get rid of a prisoner, one took of his cap and threw it between the SS-posts who had the order to shoot at anyone who approached them to the point of so and so many meters with live ammunition. The prisoner then was ordered to get the cap back and naturally the posts immediately shot, and they always hit. We had it the worse after escape attempts. Once we had to, in the middle of winter at a freezing temperature, stand on one spot on the assembly square for 23 hours. 245 died over this. The behaviour of the population towards us was, as with the wives of the camp leaders and guard troops, very diverse. I once experienced, as we drove with the car to Weimar to an iron wholesale, that people on the street threw stones at us, another time some slipped us some bread. There was a wife of one camp leader who, when we had to do repairs in her house, left the guard troops at front of the door, locked us in a cellar and supplied us with plenty of tea and open-faced sandwiches. An SS-man too, who supervised a pump-station and had his accommodation there, took our gang as often as we had to work for him up to his room and shared all the provisions he had with us. The clear majority of SS-people in Buchenwald were brutal and sadistic. ---- But we also helped each other, I had to repair the water pipes in the storage room of the camp management[13], I did it like this, that every four week some faucet or something else was broken and I took the opportunity to steal whatever there was, tobacco or lard. Yes, I even managed once to smuggle 50 rations of food meant for the guard troops into the workshop, those were eaten within five minutes. How dangerous all these proceedings were, I arguably do not have to describe. After the war broke out, naturally discussion broke out, whether one should volunteer or not. Prospects, we naturally had none. But we would not have volunteered. We justified it back then like this: Here, within the KZ we are hopelessly outgunned by the Nazis and for death and ruin[14] at their mercy. But if were trained ourselves, - 7 - get guns in our hands, then we could maybe once protect our own life. We had to get by somehow in the KZ, which was hardly bordering the possibility of adaptability, and we had to be on our own guard not to lose ourselves anything internally and not lose the goal of the socialist cause. Finally, one only made it through the biggest harassers when he could not find a weakness to exploit. It was most certainly a very contradictory and gruesome situation. At first in the first years of the war everything remained in its old ways. I have with great eagerness worked myself into my new duties and learned not only through work but also obtained technical literature, so that I soon was relocated to the building bureau as a technician and used alongside of technical preparations (constructional drawings and so forth) for the realization of all construction work within the camp and then also for the police in West Germany. These activities acted as a strengthened protection against arbitrary abuse by the SS-guard troops for me and all inmates employed there, as they became more dangerous through the course of the war. I worked twice as hard because I wanted to survive and for the sake of my political convictions. It was possible from time to time, within the smallest boundaries, to get comrades into such working spaces, so they were retained or rather safeguarded. input_chunk: Jacqueline Mendels Birn: That's a very, very long story. My parents' friends where we lived, which was near the zoo -- and I loved the zoo but we were not allowed to go to the zoo anymore. I loved the monkeys. 6 >> Bill Benson: That was part of the restrictions. Jews were not -- >> Jacqueline Mendels Birn: We were not allowed anything. We were not allowed to go to the libra ry, not allowed to take books out. My father lost his business. My sister was learning to swim. She was not allowed to go to the swimming pool. Everything was forbidden for the Jews. We were not allowed to go to the little parks. It was forbidden -- how does it go? It was forbidden for blacks, for darks, and for Jews , in that order. We were learning to ride our bikes and we were not allowed to go to that little park. But, yeah, my parents' friends said you can't stay in Paris. It was too dangerous. They were arresting people starting in 1940, 1941. They said you have to leave and my father, through the Dutch club where he was a member, found two, what he hoped, were reliable passeurs, which means smugglers, and for a fee -- and I don't know where he got the money because he didn't have a job anymore -- offered to get usually to the demarcation line. In the meantime, in July 16 and 17, 1942, was that infamous [Speaking Non -English Language], what's it called? I'm missing that word. Anyway when they rounded up [Speaking Non -English Language], where they rounded up 13,000 Jews, mostly from an area in Paris where there was a higher concentration. We didn't live in a Jewish neighborhood. There were Jews, of course, but not a high percentage. What I should say, also, is that my father wanted to obey the law. And when it was declared that the Jews had to register at the City Hall, he said, well, we'll do what they want and they will leave us alone. Well, fat chance. So we were registered. There were some good policemen. Because that was the French police that rounded up the Jews. They were supposed to round up 27,000 Jews in Paris. But fortunately, and thanks to some good police, people were told don't sleep in your apartment tonight because they are coming to round you up the next morning at 5:00 a.m. So people changed or moved to some nice Catholic neighbors. France is a Catholic country, as you know, I'm sure. So that's why 13,000 Jews instead of 27,000. But there were 4,000 children living in terrible conditio ns. There is a documentary that was made, the roundup about that story. Some people managed to escape. They were rounded up in buses. Some people threw themselves out of the window and died because they knew something horrible was happening. And there we were, they forgot to ring our bell that day. They forgot to ring our bell. They rang our bell one week after we escaped. So that was the -- the roundup was 16, 17th of July 1942 which was very late in the war. The Germans were all over. You hear me use the word German. For me the word Nazi didn't exist. It was [Speaking Non -English Language]. In French it's like that. And I heard it way after the war. So anyway, those wonderful friends of my parents, they come and spend the last night with us. The man of the house -- they lived near the Metro. General cultural needs were served by discussions which took place in summer in the evening or afternoon, either outside or in the dining room. (In the cold season, hunger, cold, illness and lack of space overshadowed life in the camp to the extent that there was no room for such things.) There were discussions on questions of interest to the Greek, Turkish, Italian and Dutch Jews. A presentation on the situation of Palestine in the Near East led to lively and extensive debates. Some young people talked on topics covering science, philosophy and history of music. Businessmen expanded on their sphere of work. French was the most common language, but a Spanish dialect, Italian and Greek were also used. The moving power behind this cultural work was Professor Jos. Nehama from Salonika, a teacher (connected to French cultural circles ) of the Alliance Israelite Universelle who had at his command extensive, encyclopaedic knowledge and the art of presentation. There was only a limited number of books in the camp which were exchanged amongst the inmates. At times, it was possible to obtain books from the general camp. Thus, one was forced to read anything in a jumble, just as one could lay one’s hands on it. Several, especially young, people were studying languages and suffered from the lack of teaching material. Here and there, someone took an interest in children of school age, but there can be no question of serious efforts to teach them. So much concerning the cultural life of the camp. 2. The Spirit of Communal Life - 12 - The spirit of communal life was determined by hunger and the hope of freedom. Inmates were increasingly scared of starvation and dreamt of a future life of liberty. Besides, the cold, illnesses and lack of space had a strong impact on the psyche. This is why a great change in the mental state of the inmates and their treatment of each other evolved. Whereas in normal life steady work for one’s livelihood provides fulfilment, regulates the need for nourishment and converts into social values, in the camp the minds of the inmates were focused primarily on obtaining the food which they had not worked for but were allocated. This concentration of mind and will escalated in the same measure as the distributed rations diverged from the minimum needed for life and the state of health of each individual deteriorated. The members of each family were occupied with queuing for the allocated provisions, considering and discussing how one could use them in the most rational manner and how one could increase their quantity. Food formed in every way the most important subject of discussions and disagreements. Memories of life in the past and dreams for the future circled largely around delicacies or special dishes. In this small social format of a community by coercion in the camp, the relationship between impulse and character revealed itself in its social significance. Large numbers of people who, in normal life, had been throughout useful members of society, increasingly lost the restraints on their character here and became antisocial elements. In this category one should count those who were involved in the distribution of provisions and who, to the detriment of the others, gleaned certain advantages for their clan, as well as those who, by shady means, achieved double and triple portions. Worse still was the theft of bread which was rare in the Neutrals camp, (however rife in the general camp), and also clothes and everyday objects disappeared regularly. There were fights for a cup of “diet” – a soup of better quality available in limited amounts mainly for the sick and for children – and the displacement of values was evident in the fact that even the utterly worthless coffee which, in any case, was readily available occasioned fierce arguments. P., who knew nothing of Jewish rites and the Jewish religion in general, mentioned this to the examining official, at which the Gestapo official hit him in the face with his fist. "You pig, you thought you could deceive us with your blond hair. I think you were supposed to spy on behalf of your Chief Rabbi about when we are going to wring his and his kith and kin's necks? But nobody can deceive us, least of all you Jews." Then the 2 officials who had arrested P. took part in the trial: "Who encouraged you to join the S.A.?" They still used the "Sie" (the respectful form of 'you') in order to maintain the appearance of proper legal proceedings. P. replied: "I joined the S.A. freely and without any influence". "Didn't you know that you were of Jewish lineage?" "No" P. answered, "I didn't know until a few weeks ago, when my mother told me. Whereupon I immediately left the S.A." "You are lying, you Pig!" they all shouted in chorus, "You were ordered by international Judaism to spy amongst the rank and file of us upright Germans!" After these words they all attacked P. and worked on him with their fists and leather straps. Even the typist, a young girl, got up from her machine and stepped on P's face with her high heels. P. was totally battered and was led out of the room by the two officials. There were cells in the cellar. But he was ordered to stand erect in the corridor, facing the wall. A full 6 hours elapsed, during which he stood without a bite to eat or a drop of water, until they came to fetch him back to the trial the following morning. They took him back to the room, to Stuelpnagel, almost fainting, "Well, have you thought about it? And are you going to name the people who gave you your instructions? We have other methods to make you confess. Rather tell us immediately, then we may perhaps let you go!" - 3 - Again and again Petzall insisted on his innocence, but nothing helped. The Gestapo were convinced that he was acting as an agent on behalf of an anti-state or a Jewish organisation. They continued to beat him and now took him to a cell. The bed was occupied, so only a thin palliasse served him for a bed. After the cell had been locked, a weak voice came from the bed: "Who are you?" Petzall gave his name, "I am Hans Litten and I've already been in the power of the Gestapo for more than a year." The Gestapo had shaved a 5 cm wide strip through the long hair of Dr. Hans Litten, the defender of the K.P.D. (German Communist Party). I learned that the whole street had been searched until at last they came to her and took her with them to the Gestapo. She stated that she had been absolutely convinced that I was a Dutch Aryan, and with her daughter’s help she was released after some hours. The German punished me, ordering me to follow him into the cellar. There he opened a tiny ice-cold dark room which was filled with an awful stench. “We’ll cure you of lying and after 24 hours here you won’t be able to work for Germans any more!” I thought I was nearing my end. Trembling with fear and despair I implored him to spare me the torture and asked him to shoot me. I said to him that my only crime was that I had been born as a Jewess. I asked him whether he had a mother or a sister and perhaps that aroused some pity and humane feeling in him. He explained that the Führer had not ordered nor entitled him to shoot me and after a long time of begging he decided to let me go back. Back in our room I collapsed. The women tried to calm me and laid the little Jan in my arms. They admonished me since I had been so brave all the time I should not give up but gather strength for my child. Probably our talks had been overheard for soon after I was called again. This time he wanted to know why I had concealed the child and where his father was hidden. I swore that I had only taken care of the child because there was no living soul with him and he had to be looked after. That night I could not sleep. I decided to take all the aspirin tablets to get so ill that another interrogation would be impossible. The result were loud noises in my ears and in the early morning I was terribly sick. The warden was informed and soon a doctor appeared together with a monk. He allowed me to stay in bed for a day, and thus I was at least left alone. On the Wednesday evening we were told that early on Thursday morning the transport to Westerbork would take place and that one of the women should stay behind to look after the patients and the children. Everybody voted for me but the officer refused to accept me saying that I was an offender. - 10 - At 9.30 on the Thursday morning we got our marching orders. In the courtyard we were stood with four to a row, constantly counted and watched by armed SS men. It rained nonstop and the atmosphere was most depressing. We were about 40 women and the same number of men came into the courtyard because a transport usually consisted of 60-100 persons. Outside the prison there were two trams ready to transport us to the station, to which we were led under guard. I was given a seat because I was carrying Jan in my arms. I thought of Amsterdam, the beautiful city, which I would never see again and I seemed to be left without any hope. At the station we were counted again and led to the train. Special compartments had been reserved for us and each compartment was watched by four armed SS men. They were young and tried to talk to us. Some girls told them where they had gone underground and in which way they had been betrayed. They offered to post our postcards if we should want to ask friends or relatives for something. At each station there were extra guards for our carriages in case somebody would dare to escape. One of them, Theo Woortman, who had saved hundreds of Jewish children obtained permission for her, to go to a Children's Home to “feed her baby”. Their names were deleted from the Schouwburg lists, and Gompertz and her sister hid in the nursery, while the inmates of the Schouwburg were deported. After a short and dangerous stay at Woortman’s house, Gompertz moved to the resistance headquarters, where under the heroic leadership of Steef van Zuylekom, and Gerhard Badrian all kinds of forged papers were produced and distributed. In April 1944 the whole group was arrested and taken to the Huis von Bewaring. Attempts at rescue, during which Gerrit van der Veen was shot, failed, and Gompertz was sent to the punishment block in Westerbork which meant extermination. For the price of a geyser for camp commandant Gemmeke five Jews were released and Gompertz was one of them. She was reunited with her mother in the block for baptised. In September 1944 Gompertz and her mother were put on one of the dreaded transports and came to Theresienstadt. Most of the prisoners were ultimately sent to extermination camps, only those holding special stamps (for baptised Dutch Jews or barnevald) were spared. Fictitious cemeteries with fictitious tombstones were erected to account for the steadily decreasing numbers, just as shop, cafés and banks were established for show. When the camp became empty, it was filled with half-Jews, mixed marriages, Gypsies and nomad tribed. Gompertz had to work on building sites and in the Mica factory. After Theresienstadt was liberated, Gompertz was taken to a transit camp in Pilsen and eventually repatriated by the Americans. After consulting the Judenrat[1] how to fill in these pages, she followed their advice and only stated 2 grandparents as Jewish and she was regarded as Half-Jewish, so she was able to continue her training which she had begun as a nurse, which was not permitted for Jews. Her parents were considered to be Jews and had to leave their house and Naarden in 1942, as Jews were not allowed to live in this area. input_chunk: In addition, I was badly beaten for not fulfilling my work quota. This work quota was unachievable anyway because the material we were working with was always very bad and it was impossible to weave continuously with it. A friend of mine, Elizabeth Drilsma-Simon from The Hague in the Netherlands, was once beaten so badly for non-fulfilment of her work quota that she fell and, as she lay on the ground, was kicked in the face. I then became ill with erysipelas[1] and was taken in the evening with a temperature of 40 degrees to the infection block. After I was released from there, I went to Block 22a, the convalescence block. This was at a time when transports were constantly being assembled and - 3 - because of this our block was nearly always closed off. There were no washing facilities in the block. "Bathing" only took place once a week in the sauna, we were not allowed to undress during the day in the convalescence block, and because we were only able to wash once a week we became dreadfully dirty and infested with lice. Ostensibly due to 34 scratches I went to Block 2a and after 2 days went into the hospital block where, on the very first day, I got severe diarrhoea. I had a temperature of 40 degrees for 2 weeks. The relocation of the hospital to E-Camp took place in November 1944. Camp doctor Dr. Mengele entered our block just as we were about to eat to oversee the immediate removal of the sick from our block. The food had not yet been distributed. He simply had the pot containing the eagerly-awaited food thrown away. Mengele asked how many women there were. He was told that it would take at least two trips. Hearing this Mengele shouted: "What do you mean go twice? If I come with my list then everyone can go, I'm not making two trips". They carried me outside. Mengele stood outside by the truck with nurse Hanka, and then Mengele grabbed me by the shoulders, the nurse had to take my feet and they threw me, like you would throw a sack, into the truck. There were already so many women on the truck that I landed almost at the back of the truck. Mengele then used his feet to push me with great force further into the truck to make room for more women after me. More women then arrived and they were all thrown on top of those who were already in the truck. In this way layer upon layer piled up. When it looked as if the women lying at the back of the truck would slide out, the rear flap of the truck was closed and then they threw more women on top so that there were 3 and 4 layers on top of one another. While the sick were being loaded up, Nurse Hanka wept at Mengele's unbelievably sadistic behaviour. Mengele saw this, grabbed the woman's hand and turned this hand around so that the top of her fingers touched her arm. Then he sent the nurse back into the block, fetched the block elder and with her the loading ended. 2 fellow-sufferers lay on top of me and they threw a third on top. It was only because I lay to the side and had my head free that I did not die from suffocation. - 4 - We were dressed only in a shirt. This dreadful transport resulted in 2 dead on arrival at E-Camp. input_chunk: government to India, and in 1946 we embarked on our journey to Palestine, while the remaining prisoners were not released until September, among them my wife’s brother, who now lives in Ceylon. Regarding the Germans’ conduct in the camp I’d like to add that after the events of El Alamein and Stalingrad, tensions ran high amongst the prisoners, and fierce rows would erupt that often ended in violent clashes and punch-ups. They blamed each other, and some claimed amongst other things that the news in the camp’s own paper were made up and only printed for the benefit of the Germans, while in reality the Führer would surely be victorious. When the British felt one day that the rows and fights in the camp were getting too brutal, they summarily deported all the seamen who had communist leanings and were dreaded in the camp as they stopped at nothing, and sent them to Canada, since the British were keen on keeping the camp quiet. After my departure, a veritable riot broke out in the camp at Ajmer, in the process of which its commandant, a Czech Dr. Adler, was severely injured. The Germans interned in India were transported back to Germany in 1946, but I know that a large number of them are now back in India. The Indian government had no issues with the Germans. At our arrival in Palestine in 1946 we owned between us the total sum of - 6 - £30. We began looking for work immediately, and I started a job as a builder with Rassco. After a while I became head of department at the Foreign Trade Institute of the Jewish Agency in Tel Aviv for the export of goods to South East Asia. I took part in the Arab-Israeli War and fought as a Major in the Sinai War. Since 1949 I have been expanding my activities in the import and export business and have been working for Rassco as well as for the Manufacturers Association. I also have my own office in Helsinki, Finland. I have travelled widely to South East Asia, Africa, Scandinavia and Europe; my last journey was to French West Africa, South Africa and the recently independent Ghana with the aim of establishing trade relations between that young state and Israel. On the way home I stopped over in London, where I was asked by the Wiener Library to write down my experiences.

input_chunk: to inquire, you know, you have learned very fast not to ask for much and talk too much, this was not good, but I dared to ask, I said: "You know, in 1942 many of my friends I think they were brought here." And I mentioned my best friend's name, maybe you know her name was Helga Fayhee (ph)? So she points toward this chimney with the huge smoke, you could smell the flesh from that smoke, and said "That's were they all are, including your friend." I didn't know what she was talking about, then. And then everything "Schnell! Schnell!," so of course, everything was taken from us even little what we had, and "Schnell! Schnell!," we were chased into what they called "the sauna." It isn't a sauna that you picture, it was a huge place with showers, and they were real showers. We had to totally undress which was very unusual, in Europe in those days people just didn't undress in front of strangers, there were men there too who shaved us every place and they sprayed disinfectant on us and they, they handed us this soap that had initials. It said RJF. And RJF meant Rein Juedisch Fett, translated Clean Jewish Fat. In other words, the soap was made from the victims, everything was utilized there. And of course, we didn't know. So they turned on the showers and "Schnell! Schnell!" we had to soap ourselves, and we hardly rinsed ourselves, they didn't give you enough time, and "Schnell! Schnell!" you have to get your clothes. Now, you didn't get your clothes, you got what was thrown there on the floor. If it fit or didn't fit, made no difference, it's not, it's as soon as it's "Schnel!." Now you can imagine how I felt seeing my mother in this place, and probably she also felt seeing me, but I have to tell you that as soon as we got there, she was not my mother anymore in a practical way. She became the child and I was the mother. She just couldn't function in this place. And, so my allotment of clothes was a black dress with short sleeves, and no underclothes at all. The shoes were the most dire thing because they usually didn't fit, no one measured you, and if they were very bad, if the fitting was totally out, you were doomed because most of the time you were on your feet. There were no places where you could sit or anything. And many people died on account just not having the right shoes. Your feet swell or were so hurt that they couldn't continue, but my shoes were acceptable. And they were both the same size, both the same heel because it didn't have to be. You could have had the right foot in the wrong, you know, different size than the left foot, or different heel. So, then "Schnel! Schnel!" they painted a red stripe on our backs because they without this you could maybe escape, which was ridiculous. I don't know how they imagined that. But I didn™t realize, actually, that we were fishing in illegal waters. This man who was one of our drivers took us there, and he said, ﬁThis is where you can fish.ﬂ So, we fished until a policeman came up. And I was horrified. input_chunk: they were transported to Bergen-Belsen after a short stay in the Greek camp of Haidar. The Argentines were almost entirely of Eastern Jewish descent. Some were born in Argentina, nearly all of them had lived in Argentina and had later returned to Europe. They came to Bergen-Belsen from Lvov (Lemberg), Krakow, Antwerp, Vienna and Rotterdam. Those who had originated in Polish camps had been through a lot and were the first from whom we received - 4 - reports about the extent and nature of the German horrors committed against the Jews in Poland. The Turks came partly from Italy, mainly from Milan, partly from Holland, mainly from Amsterdam, some from Vienna and Berlin. Most of them spoke a Spanish dialect, many – with the exception of the German contingent- also Turkish, poor French, as well as the language of their country of residence. Some of them had been arrested in the street in Milan and had been taken to Bergen-Belsen after a short stay in an Italian camp. A French Conseiller d’Etat with his wife and a Hungarian Baron with his sister were accommodated in a separate room as “special cases” and enjoyed privileged treatment ( excused from roll call, extra food etc.) in the context of our camp. A Romanian family who declared that they originated from the Romanian part of Transylvania had been excluded from the Hungarian camp which originally contained 1600 people and was later reduced by half when a transport left for Switzerland, (destination Palestine). Two Swiss women, wife and daughter of an important tobacco industrialist, travelled back to Switzerland shortly after our arrival in the Neutrals camp. The Dutch contingent,who had only arrived in January in the final camp, consisted of two privileged diamond families and a group of privileged Jews from a firm in Rotterdam. B.2 - Social Composition of Camp Inmates The social divisions of the Neutrals camp were rather varied and differed considerably from those of the General Camp or the Hungarian Camp. Most striking was the almost total lack of intellectuals. There was no doctor at all, except for a vet. The camp elder Benadon was a dentist. Apart from me, there was one other lawyer; however, he had long since exchanged his law practice with business activity in his father-in-law’s cloth factory. A certain status was represented by Professor Joseph Nehama from Salonica, teacher, author, journalist, organiser, encyclopaedic scholar and banker. Amongst the Argentines were the Antwerp Yeshivah teacher Burak and a vet. Apart from these, the male contingent of the camp consisted almost entirely of business men. The Spaniards and Portuguese from Greece were, for the most part, wealthy wholesalers, some of them may have been rather rich. A few - 5 - of them were business employees. The most diverse lines of business were represented: trading in wood, shipping, banking, export and import etc. The Turks from Italy were generally small traders, surprisingly mostly in hosiery. Some of them will have been market traders. There was also one tailor amongst them. A few of them were wealthy. The Argentines did not present a homogenous picture; as most of them had already spent longer than the rest torn from their normal existence, their original occupations were more difficult to discern. There were business men, a vet, a construction engineer. Working women did not exist amongst the Spaniards, very few amongst the other groups. input_chunk: and indeed found a completely empty flat with two bedrooms, reception room, kitchen, and bathroom. We set ourselves up here in a homely fashion. The building from which we had moved that morning, was destroyed that same afternoon by a direct hit during a bombing raid. The incessant air raids prompted us to soon move in to the air-raid shelter of our new building, the stairwell of which was caused to collapse some days later by a bomb. Meanwhile, Gestapo and SS men went constantly through the streets of the Ghetto, shot with machine guns into the air-raid shelters, and killed many people. Jews had become completely fair game to them. When they came across a Jew on the street, who had something on him that appeared desirable to them, be it but a pair of gloves, they took them away from him and shot the owner. Piles of corpses lay all over the streets. The Arrow Cross Party were particularly active in these crimes. The Jewish congregation had set up kitchens in the Ghetto, where one could receive a daily meal, usually a soup of water with some vegetables. There was absolutely no bread. As the city was already in a state of siege, all foodstuffs were extraordinarily scarce. Meanwhile it had become highly dangerous to dare to go out on to the streets, as projectiles from the siege barricades constantly fell into the city. No one trusted themselves any longer to get the soup from the soup kitchen. The approximately 50 residents of our building agreed that whoever dared to go to the kitchen would have a double portion of soup. I, along with three others, put myself up for the journey, and we brought back for our building a great cauldron of soup. During further walks through the streets, we broke into Christian-owned flats in the Ghetto, whose owners had had to leave them, and we often found plenty of items there, with which we could improve our food intake. We also hauled pieces of furniture from them back to our building, took them apart and set them alight, in order to protect ourselves against the strong cold in this January of 1945. Finally, on the 16th of January 1945, the Russians marched into Budapest. Though we were initially afraid of a return by the Germans, we were still extraordinarily happy about our regained freedom. Together with the Russians, we immediately tore down the barricades erected around the Ghetto. Opposite us there was a large building with a vast courtyard. A great many loaded food wagons, left behind by the German, stood in the yard. The Russians gave us permission to take what we wanted from the foodstuff. I managed to take a horse-drawn cart there and loaded it with beans, margarine, and fresh meat. We received bread from the Russians. With the full cart we moved out of the Ghetto and took ourselves to the flat of a relative who was with the military. To begin with we stayed here. The city's streets, through which I was now able to wander free of danger, were barely recognisable. Many buildings were bombed out or gunned down. The shops were all shut and often looted. On one of my walks a Russian officer talked to me and relied on me to lead him to an address. This was a leather shop. As thanks for my leading him, this officer gave me a large roll of pig leather. In exchange for pieces of this leather I was later able to trade for a good amount of food, when it had once again become scarce. Upon one time coming across some Russians as they cleared out a fabric shop, I pleaded, pointing to my ragged clothes, for a piece of fabric. I then received a whole roll of fabric, which I was immediately able to use as goods for trade. After some time, the Jewish organisations also began to carry out their work again. Our transport comprised 3 groups of around 140 men, who, because lorries were no longer available, were to march the 60 to 70 kilometres to Ebensee in stages on the ‘A’ roads. The other Kapos and I were in the last group. As already mentioned, because we knew exactly what was going to happen to us upon our arrival, it seemed to be important for us to use every minute because the later we arrived at Ebensee the greater was the chance that the front would move closer and with it the possibility that we could save our lives. In our group, there were three of our comrades who were already over 60 years of age. We arranged with them that on the march at very strenuous places on the ‘A’ road, they should fall back and say that they could not go any further. Our guard team consisted of Werner and 3 SD people. When we had marched for a good while, one of the older comrades lay down. Werner threatened to shoot him immediately, but the prisoner did not let himself be intimidated and the Hauptscharführer was forced to have a break lasting half an hour. On the road, we noticed heavy traffic of army vehicles of all types and of the troops on the march, and saw the first signs of breaking up and disorder. During the break, the Spaniards from Redl-Zipp went past us also in the direction of Ebensee. After a half an hour, we, about 45 men, started moving again. After another 30 minutes, two comrades fell down. Werner again threatened to shoot them. However, because of the traffic, which constantly increased, drove around us and because of the general situation which he himself probably knew better than we did, it remained just a threat. He let us wait until the prisoners had rested. In the meantime, the Spaniards, who were before us on the same road, began to mutiny. We later learned that they marched towards the allies and their 4 man SS guard joined them and as a result saved their own lives. Through our delaying tactics, it became dark and Werner saw that it was necessary to look for overnight accommodation for us in the nearest place. He confiscated a barn from the Bürgermeister of the village and the guard had to watch over us the whole night. As a result there was no possibility of escape given to us, but it had won time. Several times on the way, civilians had attempted to give us bread, but they were always prevented from doing so by the SS guard. At daybreak on the 4th of May 1945, we marched again towards Ebensee. After about an hour’s march, another older comrade really could not go any further because of exhaustion, so again Werner had to have a break. We had come about 15 kilometres nearer to Ebensee. At that point, one of our comrades, a certain Dr. Kaufmann from Prague, had an idea and explained to me and the other Kapos that it would be better to mutiny here outside in a very public place and be shot than to be fiendishly murdered later in the Ebensee camp. We passed this suggestion on from man to man and everyone agreed. At first we went on a bit further and I waited until we came to a favourable spot. Then I asked Werner for a toilet break. The place where were stopped was very crowded and to the right of the country road was a lawn. We agreed that we all wanted to relieve ourselves and lie on the lawn and did this. The roof of the farm was already on fire. The pram had been a British flame- thrower. And already in the light of the flames they could see men in uniform slowly coming past in a semi-circle out of the dark forest, rifles at the ready. They called out something. Completely confused the teacher called back an answer in German. Fräulein Lakmaker however saw from the uniforms that they were allied soldiers and shouted an answer in English to them. They were British soldiers. They had come from Germany and had no idea that they were already in Holland. The war was over. Everyone started putting out the fire in the farmhouse, the soldiers came into the house. The farmer’s wife fetched some preserved produce from the cellar. However, the soldiers would only taste it after the Dutch people present had eaten, for fear of being poisoned. Then another British patrol arrived under the command of a British officer. Fräulein Lakmaker and the farmer’s wife asked whether they would be allowed to go to their female neighbour, who lived about a kilometre away, as she was expecting a baby. The British officer went off and returned with the news that during the last minutes of the battle a healthy child had been born: the first baby of the liberation. - 10 - The war was over – they were free. It was 1st April and Easter, and the Tommies had indeed brought them some Easter eggs. The next morning the men went to Winterswijk. This town had fallen without a single shot being fired. The farmer came home and said that he had suddenly seen all sorts of people again – all those who had gone underground. Then the teacher said, “And here with us is someone else who went underground. Stand up, Suze!” Then Fräulein Lakmaker stood up and said, “My name is Miep Lakmaker, I’m Jewish”. Of course then lots of them claimed to have known all along that she had gone underground and was Jewish. When a few days later the men were back in Winterswijk and Fräulein Lakmaker was alone looking after the baby, the farmer’s wife came into the room, made small cooing noises to the baby and said, “and they’ve left you all alone like this, with a Jew?…” The family found a couple of rooms in Winterswijk in a teacher’s house. However, they found out from people that they knew, that during the occupation not everything about this teacher had been quite right. Indeed, the next day a couple of men from the BS5 came to take him away. Then Fräulein Lakmaker heard the teacher say, “But I have a Jewish girl with me in the house…”. She ran downstairs and told the patrol, “I am indeed Jewish, I have been underground since 1943 with the so and so family. I have only known this gentleman for two days.” They took him with them, however it later turned out that he had been a member of a NS organisation, although only from personal cowardice, he had not been a henchman in the evil sense. input_chunk: though, but asked, what his plans were in Singen. My friend explained to him harshly that he kindly address himself to his adjutant, that was me. I told him that we had to inspect the aluminium factory in Singen. After the official had looked at my ID as well, he moved on. In Singen we wanted to leave the train station, but had to pass a city policeman first, who couldn’t engage with us right then, as he had stopped a small boy. We met the smuggler at the Bahnhofsplatz [square in front of the train station], who led us on detours through Gottmadingen into a forest. We had assumed that he himself would bring us to Switzerland. But he only told us the way we had to go in the night. We had to wait until complete darkness had descended and hid in the forest in the meantime. Unfortunately it was a moonlit night. We had to cross a road, which was checked by German guards on bicycles every half hour. We were lying in the ditch close underneath the road and heard the buzzing of the bicycle dynamo each time. When at about half one o’clock at night there were finally clouds covering the moon, we jumped out of our hiding place, crossed the road and ran as fast as we could into the opposite forest, in which the Swiss territory began. After a while we were caught by a shepherd dog, a man pointed his flashlight on us and to our anxious question, whether he was Swiss he gave a positive reply. He took us into his cabin, gave us milk to drink and handed us to the police inspector in Ramsen, who the next day, after drawing up a protocol, took us to Schaffhausen and into the prison. A few days later we were released from there into a reception camp and later taken to a work camp for three months. On 13 October 1943 I was released and began my studies at the University of Basle. The fund “Européen de Secours Aux Etudiants” (Geneva) had granted me a scholarship. Matriculation at the university and a certificate of the scholarship were the necessary preconditions to impel the police department in Bern to release me from the work camp. I was considered a refugee interned in Basle. In 1950 I completed my doctorate at the University of Basle. I have now lived 16 years in this city and I feel at home there. As he was the personnel manager of the big steel firm, Inden Söhne, Hohlweck took Frau Heidenheim on as an office worker in Cologne; as she possessed neither a work permit nor was registered at the labour office, she was dismissed by Herr Inden, who walked around wearing the party insignia. After the big air raid on Cologne in June 1943, when approximately 40,000 people were killed and among other things the electrical engineering factory which also belonged to the Indens was completely destroyed as well, Hohlweck went with Frau Heidenheim to the NSDAP and introduced her as one of his employees, every single one of whose papers had been burned, as she had been part of the anti-aircraft defence watch at the badly damaged factory. From then on Frau Heidenheim received food ration cards, 100 Reichsmarks compensation, as well as free tickets for the meals that were provided in field kitchens. After her registration with the police in accordance with the regulations was successful, because of the fact that in Cologne, where she had gone - 6 - to register her departure with the police, all the relevant documents had been destroyed in the bombing, she produced as “Fräulein Heuser”, the person dealing with the bomb damage, an account of the bomb damage for the Inden Company together with Hohlweck in his home. Because at that time – in September 1944 – even those Jews, who until now had been “privileged” through marriage to “Aryans”, were in danger of “work deployment”, the “Aryan” wife of Frau Heidenheim’s brother-in-law kept her husband hidden in their own home. Following the liberation of Düsseldorf on 16.4.1945, in May 1946 – a year later – Dr Meili, an investigating judge in Zürich, summoned Frau Heidenheim to Zürich to testify as a witness in a “clearing process” arranged by the British government about the Torre woman, who had been arrested after smuggled goods had been seized while she was passing through the city. The accused denied having betrayed Frau Mecklenburg, and although it could be proved that she had stolen a great many things, she was released again four months later. - 7 - Report of Walter Mecklenburg’s experiences (see above) based on statements made by Frau Heidenheim The 15-year-old nephew of Frau Heidenheim, Walter Mecklenburg, first of all went to Switzerland, to Lausanne to be educated, then to a school at a dye-works in Roubaix, Northern France to learn the trade. After the Germans had invaded in May 1940 he was interned as a German civilian prisoner in a camp situated between Calais and Dunkirk. As the French guards fled when the Germans took over, he himself escaped to a castle where, when the German troops arrived, he made himself known as a German civilian prisoner and from then on, as he did not look Jewish, was conscripted into the German army, whereupon because of his command of French, he was entrusted with the job of interpreter for a major for 6 weeks until the ceasefire in June 1940. At that time, he wrote to his mother in Berlin, “I am now a German soldier!” although when the major sent him to Stolp in Pomerania for officer training, he admitted to a junior officer, as required by the Aryan identity card, to being a Jew.
