input_chunk: But, one day, as we were standing, you could stand there for hours regardless of the weather, hours and hours until it didn't jive all the numbers in the camp. And the people who didn't stand in the front line had to have their arms up over their shoulders. There was a person who was in charge of each block, the block "Aelteste," the block elder, and she would tell you "Rensid Naramana," you know they spoke Polish, but knowing Slovak so it was sort of, you know, I could figure out what they meant. And you know, if you tried just for five minutes to keep your arms at that, in that position, you feel like you don't have arms. And if you have to do it five hours then you can imagine what it was. Q: What did that mean, what they were saying . . . ? A: "Arms on the shoulders." And, at that time they distributed your rations. Now the ration was bread, piece of bread, that was made mostly out of sawdust and some brown liquid. Now, I didn't have even my own cup, so I had to use from everyone, what everybody else used, you know? Lucky for my mother and me, the people found out that we got into camp and they knew who we were, some people yet from my home town and others, and they brought a sweater for my mother and they brought some bread for me when we arrived, which was very pleasant to be welcomed, even there to a place like this. And the thing was to adapt, which my father, that was his main teaching in my life as a child. To be flexible and to adapt. And I was able to do it, instead of like some, and they were very detested by the old prisoners, we called them "Alter Haeftling," means "old prisoner" and there were the new prisoners which, you know, they felt they still had a good life for a while, which was their right, you know. They came and started complaining to this "old heflinck" if they detested you. But if you adapted, they helped you. And I adapted. If I knew that I have to wash outside in a bucket so I washed outside in a bucket. And I offered to work. There was a job called "stubendienst", "Stube" means "room," "Dienst" means "service," so it's room service. In this place, they took great care to paint the tiles red, or whatever. They broke bricks to make the color with water. And I offered to help and I had an advantage with that, that they let my mother lie up after the bunks were fixed and she could lie there and rest, so that was my advantage. And we worked hard, and one time, we had to work outside, it was called "Aussenkommando" , meaning "working outside." So after we stood we'd file out there and got our ration, there were an orchestra playing for us. There was an orchestra at the gate of the camp that led outside with the vicious dogs on the other side playing a march for us to march out. And I remember seeing a rotten apple as I walked and I was dying to have that rotten apple and one of the guards just kicked it away before I could get it. And as 23 we walked, I saw a little hut, I guess some of the guards lived, seeing some steam coming out and shade, by biggest dream was to live in such a hut, to be away from everyone because you were never alone, you couldn't wash by yourself there are millions of things in the wash room. You couldn't run the toilet alone, there were latrines that you sat back to back with people.

input_chunk: into the factory with me. Had I not been able to do this, he would have been killed at that time. He was 63 years old; I said he was 55 and therefore he was allowed to come to work with me in the factory. Every morning, we always left the ghetto with a group of 35 Jews, in order to go to the factory. The groups, who went to work, were always led by a band of musicians composed of Jews, who had to play pleasing melodies. It was always the same torment for me each morning and I had the feeling that I was losing ever more nerves each morning. But, this was, of course, the intention of the Nazis. They were quite systematically driving us all mad! They wanted to ruin our nerves. From the groups of those going to work, there were, daily, hundreds brought out and murdered. You never knew, when leaving the ghetto, whether you would return alive. It was in this way that countless Jews disappeared into nothingness. In March 1943, they took my father from me at the entrance of the ghetto and I never saw him again. Every Saturday evening, I furtively joined a group of Jews who were working during the night. In the darkness of the street, I discreetly took off my armband and crept away through the whole town to Frau Wieth. Then, during the following Sunday, I altered her clothes, for it was only in this way that I could thank her for what she had done for my daughter. For some reason, Frau Wieth loved my needlework and, as her only interest was clothes, the work never came to an end. One of her rooms was full of cupboards filled with clothes. This is how I spent Sundays’ with her and every Monday, at 3.30am I crept from Frau Wieth’s, through the town and back into the ghetto in such a way that I joined a group of Jews unobserved returning from working through the night - 7 - In the ghetto, I turned around and went with another group who were going to work through the day in the factory, outside of the ghetto. The whole thing was, naturally, very dangerous and Frau Wieth said to me again and again that I would definitely be caught by the Gestapo one day. The streets were full of Germans, Ukrainians and Poles, who might recognise me. Even if I was inconspicuous, anyone could see that I looked very rough and hungry, as all Jews looked in comparison to other people on the streets. This is how I spent every weekend from December 1942 until the end of May 1943 without anything ever happening to me. On the 31st of May, it was proclaimed “The ghetto will be liquidated on the 1st of June. All Jews within it must voluntarily report to the concentration camp” The owner of our factory tried once more to help all of the Jews who had worked for him, so that we did not need to go into the camp. He negotiated with the Gestapo and explained that our 35 strong group of Jews could live in the factory. He promised the Gestapo that he would have a particularly good leather overcoat illegally finished for each one of them and the Gestapo agreed. However, after they had received their overcoats, they insisted that the Jews would have to leave the factory for the camp. As I left the ghetto, in order to resettle in the factory, I was not allowed to take my mother with me. She had had typhus and pneumonia and was very weak, but had survived both. I, thus, smuggled her out of the ghetto into the factory. And now we were supposed to go into the camp and the Director was ordered to hasten all of us into this camp. I did not know what to do! So she points toward this chimney with the huge smoke, you could smell the flesh from that smoke, and said "That's were they all are, including your friend." I didn't know what she was talking about, then. And then everything "Schnell! Schnell!," so of course, everything was taken from us even little what we had, and "Schnell! Schnell!," we were chased into what they called "the sauna." It isn't a sauna that you picture, it was a huge place with showers, and they were real showers. We had to totally undress which was very unusual, in Europe in those days people just didn't undress in front of strangers, there were men there too who shaved us every place and they sprayed disinfectant on us and they, they handed us this soap that had initials. It said RJF. And RJF meant Rein Juedisch Fett, translated Clean Jewish Fat. In other words, the soap was made from the victims, everything was utilized there. And of course, we didn't know. So they turned on the showers and "Schnell! Schnell!" we had to soap ourselves, and we hardly rinsed ourselves, they didn't give you enough time, and "Schnell! Schnell!" you have to get your clothes. Now, you didn't get your clothes, you got what was thrown there on the floor. If it fit or didn't fit, made no difference, it's not, it's as soon as it's "Schnel!." Now you can imagine how I felt seeing my mother in this place, and probably she also felt seeing me, but I have to tell you that as soon as we got there, she was not my mother anymore in a practical way. She became the child and I was the mother. She just couldn't function in this place. And, so my allotment of clothes was a black dress with short sleeves, and no underclothes at all. The shoes were the most dire thing because they usually didn't fit, no one measured you, and if they were very bad, if the fitting was totally out, you were doomed because most of the time you were on your feet. There were no places where you could sit or anything. And many people died on account just not having the right shoes. Your feet swell or were so hurt that they couldn't continue, but my shoes were acceptable. And they were both the same size, both the same heel because it didn't have to be. You could have had the right foot in the wrong, you know, different size than the left foot, or different heel. So, then "Schnel! Q: How long were you in Camp Kilmer, when you first arrived in the U.S., in New Jersey? A: I think it was no more than two weeks. It was just a screening process to just give a very superficial screening, so certain elements, undesirable elements would not sneak into the country. They were looking for members of the Communist Party and unfortunately, people who were sick, because with certain illnesses, you co uld not gain entrance to the United States. For example, if you had TB. And then, from there... and also, they were in charge of sending you somewhere. So, they were kind of dispatchers. Q: So it was then that you got sent to– 68 A: Saint Louis. Q: Saint Louis. A: Yeah, Saint Louis, Missouri. Q: Uh-huh, uh-huh, what did you do there? A: In Saint Louis... Saint Louis, Missouri, I was welcomed by the family, by that time, adopted, of course, just symbolically, my cousin, and we were united. They were a... you might say uppermiddle class American family with some problem s and they thought that getting two Hungarian refugees would probably mitigate their circumstan ces. And I was, within weeks, working for a wholesale jewelry company. I was just a stockboy. And, very simple work, and that was my job. And on weekends, as long as my cousin was with me, of course, we were walking around and going to a movie, even though we couldn™t understa nd much of it. There was not much more you could use for money, you know, for. And, but it really got very bad in 1942, that's when it started getting very bad and where we lived in the City Hall, the notary, which he was the head of the city government, lived in the same balcony as we did, on the same balcony, and he had a heart ailment and was very grateful for my father's closeness, he could help him a lot, and I taught his children English and small children, young children, and he came to my father one day, and he said, "You know, doctor, you would do right if you would send your daughter away. To my father, didn't sound right, he didn't trust the word "labor camp." He just, it was an unknown and he listened to this advice. input_chunk: My country - right or wrong” We were beaten through the ̍large gate̍. Beyond the gate SS men stood in a line. Heavy oak bludgeons beat down on us. SS men brought us down by "positioning their feet". I had my father before me, I held both of his hands tightly, he stumbled over a fallen man, I lifted him up, we ran together. Then we stood in rows of ten on the parade ground at Buchenwald concentration camp. Men lay on the gravel of the ground in front of us, being beaten by the SS with sticks. In front of us lay two seriously injured men, that couldn’t save themselves from the beating by the beasts: the war-disabled lawyer and an eighty year old with broken legs. I will never get rid of that image, how the old man pleadingly begged us to help him stand up as otherwise he would freeze to death on the cold ground. Blood ran down his face, our hearts bled: we weren’t allowed to help him. Two SS went past the eighty year old. Asked him if he was already dead. He raised his hands begging: "I am an old man, please help me. You can’t just leave me lying here." He could no longer grasp that he was no longer speaking to people. He was too old to know that they were creatures with human - 6 - faces, but without souls, understanding, without hearts, without anything that makes humans human. Both of them answered him: “You filthy Jew you have already lived far too long.” A kind fate released him from the torture of these animals. An hour later prisoners carried him as the first dead from the camp, many, many more would follow him. Next to us stood men with bloody heads, with scared, wandering eyes, which reflected all of the horror. Old Christian prisoners came to us, they were supposed to line us up in an orderly fashion. – These were the first humans that we met here. They tried to calm us down, they inspired us with courage, they warned us to remain brave; there was only space here for healthy people. – Healthy or dead: there was no space for ill people! Today an order had been given by the camp commandant: "a ban on medicine for all Jews" There were suffering and diabetic people among us, whose death sentence was signed with this order. In front of us stood a kind looking prisoner with sad eyes. He was strictly forbidden from speaking to Jewish prisoners. He spoke to us with courage. He helped us later as a good friend. – My father shook his hand welling up with huge thanks: "You are humans!" I would like to thank you, friend, again here: you helped us, brought us water, when we were dying of thirst, despite knowing the threat that placed upon you. And when I later heard how you were made to atone for this help it was as if I had been beaten, as if I had sat in the bunker! You are my chief witness: Germany isn’t called Hitler and National Socialism isn’t Germany! – We stood on the parade ground at Buchenwald concentration camp. Large watchtowers with huge spotlights and machine guns stared at us threateningly. – The huge roundabout of the camp was surrounded by a power cable, which later made it easier for some of us to die. In between our rows SS with sticks and whips: the protector of order in the Third Reich, the "racial elite germania". Through the huge gate the prisoners came into the camp from outdoor work: from the quarry, from the building sites of the SS estate, from road building. input_chunk: by the afternoon all of the ‘exchange’ was over. For example, I remember that the next day Carlebach fell in dressed as a bricklayer, that is, in the special work overalls of the building command. August Kohn also found a similar pretext. Some important people simply lay in the sick-bay as ‘sick’. Anyone who was not a builder or important was taken to some special block which were under the strict guard of the camp leadership. All of these Jewish prisoners were deported to Auschwitz from where some returned again to Buchenwald in 1944. At that time, only around 250 Jewish bricklayers remained in Buchenwald. The number increased again in the following months and years. After many months of apparent peace, apart from an air attack on the Gustloffwerk in 1943, approximately in the winter of 1943/44, a new action occurred and the first Jewish bricklayers were put on a report at work, that is, they received a notice as a result of allegedly bad work. The first cases went relatively well: withdrawal of food and later 3 days in the bunker accompanied by mistreatment by the SS. One day, some young bricklayers, actually from Vienna, were reported and we prepared in our community to give them bread and food. Instead, they were ordered at the morning assembly to gate 1 which was very suspicious. Gate 1 meant actually release and that was only for the Germans or other non-Jewish prisoners and never up till now for Jews. Of course, the Jewish bricklayers were not released, but taken to the sick-bay. Two days later they were murdered by an injection. Now panic spread amongst we Jews again. Nobody knew anymore how many days he had to live. There were other Jewish prisoners reported, Jewish bricklayers, and this was mainly by a new ethnic German SS man from Romania whose nickname was ‘ranger’. He would emerge suddenly somewhere and report some victims. When the Jewish bricklayer Max Umschweif, a communist who had fought in Spain, was reported, the prisoners’ leadership decided to save him. He was taken to the sick bay, received the name of an Aryan prisoner who had died and so was saved. When the communist bricklayer from Brünn, Max Galandauer, the nephew of the famous communist lawyer also from Brünn, Dr. Immanuel Stern, was reported he was not saved because apparently more than once would be too risky. When, one Saturday afternoon, I together with some other bricklayers was at work, the ranger appeared and reported me and two Jews from Vienna, Friedelhaar and Press. I attempted to hide in the sick-bay with the help of friends such as Dr. Kurt Sitte, now the director of the technical institute in Haifa, and others. That is, to be exchanged, but no one wanted to risk that. I and Friedelhaar and Press had two days to wait for death. When we appeared at the morning assembly on the 3rd day and expected to be commanded to gate 1, a number was called out which began like mine. I had the number 8603. This one was 86 followed by two other numbers of a German prisoner who actually was released. Then no one else was called out and the same day we 3 bricklayers were informed that we would have no food for 5 days. We were saved and later learned that prisoners’ leaders had begun to fear for themselves that after the Jewish bricklayers, they would be liquidated in the same way and persuaded the SS to stop the action. The last action which I had to survive was the evacuation from Buchenwald two days before the entry of the US army. I was evacuated at the beginning of April along with the majority of the prisoners. input_chunk: to be called your number, you were afraid to be called that was the biggest fear everyone because when they called your number it meant death most of the time. So, after we were tattooed, then "Schnell! Schnell!," they ran us through what was like a bunk, a wooden structure, and there were hundreds and thousands of them because the camp was divided into A-B-C-D-E-F. We were in 'A' camp, we were the . . . we just came and I think they waited for the visas for something, they kept you in sort of isolation for a short while and there 06:30:30 was space maybe for 100 people in this camp, we were 400 in this building. And where we slept were bunks, three-tier bunks. The way you have it in your museum there are no, we had no straw, we had no sheets, no pillows, no blankets and there was space for maybe three people in each bunk to stretch out, we were eight. If one person wanted to turn 22 sometime during the night all eight had to turn because there just was no way that it could be accomplished, there was no space whatsoever. And at 2:00 AM they would wake us up with their flashlight, again "Schnell! Schnell!," "Raus!" Raus!" And we would have to stand, everyone in front of the cottage and then we would look out into space, we saw these repeated, in front of each cottage, it was like black from the people, women, standing there, and the magic number was five, you stood five in width and five in length. The best place to stand, it depended how you ran out, you know, where you got your place, was in the middle. Number one, you were protected from being seen; number two, if it was cold and windy, the people somehow enclosed you. But, one day, as we were standing, you could stand there for hours regardless of the weather, hours and hours until it didn't jive all the numbers in the camp. And the people who didn't stand in the front line had to have their arms up over their shoulders. There was a person who was in charge of each block, the block "Aelteste," the block elder, and she would tell you "Rensid Naramana," you know they spoke Polish, but knowing Slovak so it was sort of, you know, I could figure out what they meant. And you know, if you tried just for five minutes to keep your arms at that, in that position, you feel like you don't have arms. And if you have to do it five hours then you can imagine what it was. Q: What did that mean, what they were saying . . . ? A: "Arms on the shoulders." And, at that time they distributed your rations. Now the ration was bread, piece of bread, that was made mostly out of sawdust and some brown liquid. Now, I didn't have even my own cup, so I had to use from everyone, what everybody else used, you know? Lucky for my mother and me, the people found out that we got into camp and they knew who we were, some people yet from my home town and others, and they brought a sweater for my mother and they brought some bread for me when we arrived, which was very pleasant to be welcomed, even there to a place like this. And the thing was to adapt, which my father, that was his main teaching in my life as a child. To be flexible and to adapt. The justifiably created slogan of the injustice of the peace agreements, which was constantly repeated to the population, brought about a national following. As -in 1938- the Austrians were still politically naïve, they never realised what National Socialism really represented and represents; an oversized deception of the population. To this can be added the feeling that the entire world left us alone in our political and economic needs, and the fact that Germany did everything to increase these needs. Meanwhile it approached from out there with flags and flowers, jubilation and music, so overwhelming and loud that it drowned out the progress of the Panzers (tanks) and the humming of the aeroplanes.250,000 people created the magic of the Anschluss (annexation). It is superfluous to speak of the April 1938 vote, it was the first massively staged act of terror in Austria. Since then, the number of Party members in Austria has risen to 210,000. The majority are officials and employees who entered the Party either under pressure or in order to further their career. The number of young people who were recruited from the Hitler Youth into the Party is 90,000 out of the 210,000. We leave it to you, Minister, to draw your conclusions from these figures. The Party badge alone, however, does not give an accurate view of the mood which prevails at present among the population. - 5 - There are many Party members who already bitterly rue having dedicated themselves to Hitler and that Hitler devoted himself to us. On the other hand, there are strata of the population who , out of the feeling “right or wrong – my country”, do their duty blindly and follow in a disciplined manner to the last. According to the documents and estimates by experts available to us, we believe to be justified in assuming that in the civil sector the industrial workforce, including employees of the railways, local transport, electricity and gas companies, whom we include although they are public employees, belong to the Communist Party and the Social Revolutionaries, allowing for fluctuations between companies of 60 – 90 %.The ideological differences between the two groups have largely blurred, and both groups are prepared to fight at a united front and to put back their old disagreements. The industrial workforce, including the above-named groups, constitutes around 40 – 42 % of the total population. the farmers, including agricultural workers; they have become opponents of National Socialism altogether. The circle of adherents encompasses barely more than Party officials, teachers, the local innkeeper where the meetings take place, their families and other direct or indirect beneficiaries of the system, all in all perhaps 10 – 15 % of farmers. A large section of the farming population is socially orientated and bound to Christianity. The remaining section rejects National Socialism and its war simply from their individual view of the economy. The agricultural workforce represents 39 – 40 % of the total population. - 6 - Enterprises in commerce, trade and industry comprise approximately 4 – 5 % of the population. As far as they are beneficiaries, i.e. about half of them, they are followers of National Socialism; where they are not, e.g. because of factory closures, lack of raw materials, high taxation, and other war-orientated economic sanctions, they are opponents without any particular designation. In this stratum, it is particularly the small tradesmen, feeling that their businesses are being systematically strangled, who are the main contingent of the dissatisfied. Employees, officials and free professions: the main component of the intellectual followership of National Socialism is recruited from this stratum of the population. So, after we were tattooed, then "Schnell! Schnell!," they ran us through what was like a bunk, a wooden structure, and there were hundreds and thousands of them because the camp was divided into A-B-C-D-E-F. We were in 'A' camp, we were the . . . we just came and I think they waited for the visas for something, they kept you in sort of isolation for a short while and there 06:30:30 was space maybe for 100 people in this camp, we were 400 in this building. And where we slept were bunks, three-tier bunks. The way you have it in your museum there are no, we had no straw, we had no sheets, no pillows, no blankets and there was space for maybe three people in each bunk to stretch out, we were eight. If one person wanted to turn 22 sometime during the night all eight had to turn because there just was no way that it could be accomplished, there was no space whatsoever. And at 2:00 AM they would wake us up with their flashlight, again "Schnell! Schnell!," "Raus!" Raus!" And we would have to stand, everyone in front of the cottage and then we would look out into space, we saw these repeated, in front of each cottage, it was like black from the people, women, standing there, and the magic number was five, you stood five in width and five in length. The best place to stand, it depended how you ran out, you know, where you got your place, was in the middle. Number one, you were protected from being seen; number two, if it was cold and windy, the people somehow enclosed you. But, one day, as we were standing, you could stand there for hours regardless of the weather, hours and hours until it didn't jive all the numbers in the camp. And the people who didn't stand in the front line had to have their arms up over their shoulders. There was a person who was in charge of each block, the block "Aelteste," the block elder, and she would tell you "Rensid Naramana," you know they spoke Polish, but knowing Slovak so it was sort of, you know, I could figure out what they meant. And you know, if you tried just for five minutes to keep your arms at that, in that position, you feel like you don't have arms. And if you have to do it five hours then you can imagine what it was. Q: What did that mean, what they were saying . . . ? A: "Arms on the shoulders." And, at that time they distributed your rations. Now the ration was bread, piece of bread, that was made mostly out of sawdust and some brown liquid. Now, I didn't have even my own cup, so I had to use from everyone, what everybody else used, you know? I just wanted to convince myself whether order prevailed where you are and whether you are nervous. Heil Hitler!” – We worked under such conditions and got used to it.) Both of the cases mentioned contain the "problematic" facts: a) criminal offence, which is also punishable in accordance with English law; b) communist activity. Both times a P.C.O of lesser human character wouldn’t have taken over the responsibility, but instead with reference to procedural requirements would have dismissed the application and let the applicant go to the concentration camp. Captain Foley took over responsibility. What impelled him was the noblesse of background, disposition and upbringing, who let a man in such a position feel that he has been given power, to help the powerless: noblesse oblige. People who don’t know Captain Foley or only know him fleetingly might think that I’m exaggerating or that I created a torchlit procession for him for whatever reasons. Far from it. The number of Jews that were rescued from Germany would have been smaller by the tens of thousands – yes: tens of thousands – if an "industrious official" had sat in Captain Foley’s position. There are no words of Jewish gratitude that could be exaggerated with respect to this man. After the 1938 November pogrom and the mass arrests there was a savage onslaught of all foreign agencies. Everyone hoped for a miracle and a visa. The B.P.C.O. was so overwhelmed for two days that the work became impossible. Then Captain Foley established order. He wasn’t just a man who – like all of his personal employees – worked a lot and worked thoroughly. (The English would say about his justification: - 8 - “Oh, don't mind that. He was educated in France”.) The three night watchmen from the embassy building in Wilhelmstraße were transferred to Tiergartenstraße. They arranged the visitors in rows of four which stretched from the street through the front garden and the stairwell through into the waiting room. input_chunk: guest house – to report a particularly grotesque case – made two S.A. officers living in her guest house spend the night in Jewish club located in the same house. She gave the rooms of the S.A. officers to “Jews on the run”. The Jews arrested in Berlin were probably selected according to the following criteria: 1. The basis was the register kept by the police of Jews who had assets of more than 5000 Reich marks, i.e. who were under obligation to declare their assets. 2. The Gestapo headquarters in Berlin ordered the arrest of all persons in leading positions within the Jewish organisations with the exception of the committee and Rabbi Dr. Baeck. 3. It is maintained but cannot be verified that the professional organisations of the medical and legal professions were used for the selection of the Jews to be arrested. Practically no Jews without financial means in Berlin were arrested. Almost every prisoner in the Sachsenhausen concentration camp had assets of more than 5000 RM. Just a few just happened to be “taken along” as well. In contrast to this – as we know – in the provinces all Jews with the exception of the very old were arrested; in Hamburg, Breslau and Baden-Baden Jews were sometimes arrested out of hotels, from the street, in the trains. In Hamburg, for example, a Jewish doctor who was confined to his bed seriously ill and could not be transported was left in his home. The officers asked the servant who took them into the room of his sick master whether he was a Jew. He answered that this was the case and was taken away. Thus relatives who were staying in a Jewish household, for example, but were not residents of the town in which the arrests were carried out were also “taken along”. Occasionally benevolent police doctors protected arrested Jews from being taken to the camps. In one Westphalian city the police doctor picked out his medical colleagues and insinuated that they had illnesses on the basis of which he declared them unfit for camp imprisonment. - 5 - In Berlin on 11th and 12th November arrestees with the Iron Cross, First Class, with serious war injuries and those visibly seriously ill were not taken to the Sachsenhausen concentration camp, whereas on the first day of the mass arrests no-one escaped being taken there. In the camp itself no heed was paid to visible illnesses, and no release from the camp suggested, so that cripples with severest disabilities had to suffer the camp for weeks. Amongst others, a schoolteacher was dragged along who as a result of polio was unable to walk on two legs without assistance and had to be carried to roll call suspended from the shoulders of two prisoners.

So, after we were tattooed, then "Schnell! Schnell!," they ran us through what was like a bunk, a wooden structure, and there were hundreds and thousands of them because the camp was divided into A-B-C-D-E-F. We were in 'A' camp, we were the . . . we just came and I think they waited for the visas for something, they kept you in sort of isolation for a short while and there 06:30:30 was space maybe for 100 people in this camp, we were 400 in this building. And where we slept were bunks, three-tier bunks. The way you have it in your museum there are no, we had no straw, we had no sheets, no pillows, no blankets and there was space for maybe three people in each bunk to stretch out, we were eight. If one person wanted to turn 22 sometime during the night all eight had to turn because there just was no way that it could be accomplished, there was no space whatsoever. And at 2:00 AM they would wake us up with their flashlight, again "Schnell! Schnell!," "Raus!" Raus!" And we would have to stand, everyone in front of the cottage and then we would look out into space, we saw these repeated, in front of each cottage, it was like black from the people, women, standing there, and the magic number was five, you stood five in width and five in length. The best place to stand, it depended how you ran out, you know, where you got your place, was in the middle. Number one, you were protected from being seen; number two, if it was cold and windy, the people somehow enclosed you. But, one day, as we were standing, you could stand there for hours regardless of the weather, hours and hours until it didn't jive all the numbers in the camp. And the people who didn't stand in the front line had to have their arms up over their shoulders. There was a person who was in charge of each block, the block "Aelteste," the block elder, and she would tell you "Rensid Naramana," you know they spoke Polish, but knowing Slovak so it was sort of, you know, I could figure out what they meant. And you know, if you tried just for five minutes to keep your arms at that, in that position, you feel like you don't have arms. And if you have to do it five hours then you can imagine what it was. Q: What did that mean, what they were saying . . . ? A: "Arms on the shoulders." And, at that time they distributed your rations. Now the ration was bread, piece of bread, that was made mostly out of sawdust and some brown liquid. Now, I didn't have even my own cup, so I had to use from everyone, what everybody else used, you know? We acquired a house, and Polish Jews took over the Committee, and after some time they told our German colleagues and founders that we were no longer needed. I was the only one they retained, a Christian Jewess, or maybe a Jewish Christian. I had to maintain the Polish books, run the German section, and concern myself with the kitchen; four German women helped me. The food for the Committee had to be cooked in the ‘kosher’ way (anyway, that was what they called it.) The chairman of the Committee, who went by the name of Bratman, and who was a very generous and decent man, was arrested shortly before I left, as he was a KAPO and had brought so many Jews to their end by machine guns. A colleague was re-allocated by the Russians from Lemberg to Kazakhstan, and now Silesia was meant to be re-populated by Jews originating from Galicia and who had since settled in Siberia and the Caucusus. The Committee members were paid as administration officials, and they received appropriate food cards, category 1, i.e. the highest class. The work of the Committee was varied and satisfying. We distributed ID cards for the German Jews and Christian non-Aryans (half-Jews), so that they were not subject to the same laws as the Germans (white arm bands, resettlement, confiscation of property). It was December 1945 when we first had news about father. We decided to remain in Hirschberg until we would have the possibility of travelling out to England. In March 1946 a large proportion of German Jews from Hirschberg returned to Berlin and West Germany. I myself had brought transport using UNRA vehicles to Kolfurth, where a British military mission was stationed, having already argued for a journey in February, because of the need to avoid the Polish customs post……. because otherwise Jews would only be allowed to take 200 Marks with them. I was not lucky, and can still see myself standing by the goods train which they were getting in to, and handing each one a packet of money from my brief-case. When I had made the last payment, I was caught by the railway police, and it was only thanks to an English major who pleaded my case energetically that I did not end up with the secret police. I was relieved to go back to Hirschberg. After some days we were approached by a Jewish member of the secret police who forced me to become a member, otherwise I would be arrested. I tried to use the excuse that I could not sign because the form was all written in Polish and I never sign anything that I don’t understand. But he translated it into Yiddish, and so there was nothing left for me to do but to sign. I was meant to name those Germans who possessed bicycles, radios or weapons. But he had no luck with me. I had too much to do and no longer had any contact with German ‘Aryans’. Meanwhile our plan to emigrate was progressing well and I travelled in a UNRA car with a female acquaintance to Warsaw to get an emigration affidavit for her, my mother, and for me. The wife had been the cook at the home of one of these families, and her husband was a simple worker at the gas works. Their daughter was in Holland with the English army. The first confession happened after he declared, “I am evil” during the hearing, and then requested a break. It was not until the recommencement of the hearing that he confessed to the murder of “about 14 Jews during operations”. The second confession concerning the Stern brothers did not come about until the fourth day of the hearing, on 19th July, after the interrogation of the witness, Wolf, and after Frau Stern had read the statement aloud. Then he did not have a choice, as Pöll had also accused him of the crime! Now we must examine his excuses; that all of these atrocities happened “upon command”. With regard to this, the first thing to highlight is that Para. 3 Section 1 of the War Criminals Act stipulates: “The fact that the crime was committed upon command does not excuse it.” Furthermore, we must differentiate between operations and individual shootings. As far as the operations are concerned, Mitas admits that he shot 14 people. In reality, he killed hundreds, for in Boryslav alone several thousands of Jews were shot – and ‘Mitas the weapon master’ is supposed to have only shot 14 of them? This is impossible. I now refer to the statement made by Nemec, who committed suicide, which declares that he himself saw Mitas murder twenty Jews by shooting them in the back of the neck. And even if it were true that Mitas had only shot fourteen Jews, then this is evidence that even at the mass-murders, during the “operations”, he did not exhibit any compelling signs of acting under coercion. If he had been able to resist the command without losing his own life, why would he only have shot fourteen? Not once during the entire Nazi regime has a policeman been shot on the spot. Where does this “coercion” come from, then? In the hearing held on 16 July, Pöll states, “The command to shoot was not required to be followed. You could have refused to shoot.” In the preliminary hearing Pöll says, “If someone did not want to, they did not have to. Viehtauer did not do it, and nothing happened to him.” Pöll also says in regard to O. 82, “The eliminations were carried out by Mitas. I got the impression that he enjoyed shooting Jews.” A witness, Plattner, says in the hearing held on 18 July 1956, “Mitas shot every last one in the back of the neck.” The dead talk too. input_chunk: woods, one that consisted of a more or less destroyed coal truck. Strewn all around it were all kinds of remains – ragged prisoners’ clothes, some items of uniform, steel SS helmets and caps - and everything was stained with blood. There were also broken rifles and indescribable cards, as were used in the work camps; all kinds of camp books, some new, some used, from which some sections had apparently been torn out. The carraiges were carefully checked over. In a goods carriage, which had apparently served as the sick quarters, we found hidden amongst the rubble of two beds two sobbing Jews wearing prisoners’ clothing. They were completely exhausted, they clearly had not eaten for days, and could hardly speak. The feet and legs of both were apparently frozen. Herr Quakernack surveyed the whole scene and then explained that this could only be - 2 - a prisoners’ transport that had been attacked and destroyed by partisans. He forbade anyone to follow the track of the items of clothing and weapons that was leading into the woods. We had to collect the books and cards and bring them into the canteen carriage. Both the Jews were taken and moved like corpses on wheelbarrows to our train; they were meant to be thrown to the carriage which was intended for the dead behind the sick carriage. Meanwhile the signal for our train to depart was given; it was difficult to quickly open the frozen door of the carriage for the dead; but the door of the sick carriage was open and so the two wretches were brought there. They recovered a little. It was possible to ascertain from their incoherent Yiddish that their transport of some 1,000 Jews had been killed by the accompanying SS. Some were killed in the carriages, and the rest, who had to drag the dead into the woods and make the scene appear as if they had been attacked, exactly as we had come across it, were then slaughtered in the woods. The SS then moved out after this had been done. The two that we had found were the only survivors. But they too died while being transported before we could establish their names or where they had come from. The train stopped for a while every morning. I had to run up and down the series of carriages and ask the elders of each car whether anyone had died. The doors of the affected cars were opened, one after the other, and the bodies were brought to the carriage for the dead. Every carriage had at least one person who had died. And every time there was the same terrible picture of the poor, starving, thirsty people, reduced to the state of animals, pressing to the doors to get some air. Four were allowed out to drag away the dead while another four were permitted to run to the kitchen carriage to get some bread for those in their carriage. I am incapable of saying more about this daily occurrence. After more than a year I still have an aversion of coming near to children; because I am still frightened that an image will form in my eyes of what I saw there. Our journey lasted six days together with six dark nights. We travelled via Mahrisch-Ostrau, Prerau – where we could exchange supplies of flour for bread -, Lundenburg to Vienna-Floridsdorf, where we saw the serious effects of the attacks launched from the overflying planes. We then travelled on via Stockerau, passing through regions where people were happily engaged with their winter sports, on to Mauthausen. It is worth mentioning the behaviour of our guards. The older marines were on guard whenever the train stopped for hours in the open country or at sidings. Stamping through deep snow, they patrolled both sides of the train. input_chunk: we thought we going to go into flames, so this old lady taught us how to say the last prayer before you die and we sat on the floor and said that prayer, that's all we could do. So you can't call it life, it was, you know, we talked and we, the poor two little children were there, you know, with their mothers. Q: Were you scared? A: Scared? We were more always scared of what's next somehow. The fear was always, you know I have to tell you when I was found out, when they took me away that Saturday morning and put me into that holding place, it was almost a relief. And then, I don't have to 18 anymore run from them. You know, because you were always afraid you'll be caught. You know, so after a while you just don't care, you want to be relieved of this fear, you know, we were constantly afraid. Fear of the unknown, really. Because we just knew it was horrible, but no one knew for sure exactly what it is. Q: During this period, did you ever try to pass yourself as a Catholic girl, or a . . . ? A: Yes, I did. In fact, I even had the, what do you call those . . . the beads? You know, in Sunday morning if I went out, that's what I carried with me and was holding it in my hands. And you know, I knew the prayers because, I knew it in Slovak because I learned it from our cook, I knew it very well, I knew all of it, so, I don't know how you . . . well, I knew it in Hungarian but I figured I could always say it in Slovak. Yeah, I did, you know . . . Q: Just on the streets, or . . . ? A: Yeah. Q: So, you got on this train . . . ? A: We got on the train, we were guarded, and the man's handcuffs stayed on, you know, they went to the toilet they had to go together. Q: There was a toilet on the train? A: Yeah, sure. It was a regular train. It was not the kind of train that most people that you have in your museum were taken. This train was a normal train because we were political prisoners, this was our advantage so to speak, you know, being labeled as such. You know, you never know what was your advantage. And we were just twenty some people, it wasn't hordes of people, it was just us. And there were no children among us. But the old lady was. And, there were even bombings on the train, we went through Vienna and they got us off the train into a holding place. And, you know, people looked at you, the other passengers, and you wondered: how do they look at you? Do they pity you, do they, are they happy to see you like this, do they hate you, you know? You didn't know what the expression _______ you saw on the walls of the train station against Jews, all kind of symbols and words against, so, and, the guards, they even fed us. They gave us bread and things and the guards told us we should give them our watches, our rings, because were we go, we won't need it. And I was very defiant as a young person and I just took my mothers and my things, I wished I could take everybody's, and went in the toilet and flushed it down with great satisfaction. input_chunk: Besides killing my father, I saw where the brush factory was situated, you could see truckloads of people brought up to the hill. Originally, we thought maybe these were workers or whatever, but a little while later we found where all the shooting was going on. And some were put on fire. They were burning them or whatever, there was a smell. And these were all young people, we saw them looking out. Some you could see in the open trucks. Some were closed, some were open. This was almost a daily -- if not a daily, several times a week, you know. And they were just slaughtering them like you wouldn't do it to an animal. This was going on, you felt there would be no end to it. You just, you know, but after a while somehow your mind becomes so dull, you don't want to think about it. It just -- it's hard to picture this even by myself what I saw. I can't accept that. It's like a bad nightmare, but it happened. Q: Does it surprise you when you think about it that you were able to take it? That you could see this every day, and still have the strength to go on? A: It does surprise me. But not in the beginning, at the end. It started with Mauthausen, it was hell on earth. Q: Well, why don't you describe the deportation out of Plaszów? A: How it was? Q: Yeah. A: On the -- when they made us go into the boxcars, after they pushed in as many as could fit in there, we didn't know where we're going. We went for, I can't remember how long we traveled. Not a long time. And we sat there for two days or three days. No food, nothing. People died in the cars, you know. It's tragic for me to explain, you know. People died, you actually sat on them because there's no room. You couldn't sit down, it was so in the beginning. There was no room. And what I found out not more than a year or two, maybe less than two years ago, that we were destined -- we stopped in Auschwitz. There was no room, so they sent us to Mauthausen. And some them, they did take off in Auschwitz. And some they didn't; they sent to Mauthausen. Q: And were you all men on these boxcars? A: Yes, yes. Q: And were you able to say goodbye to your mother and sisters? 37 A: No, they were taken away one day or one night in the middle -- or early morning. They didn't show up. All the women were gone. They didn't have an inkling, nothing. Q: So you and Maurice are in this cattle car? A: Yes. I even had a blade to cut, like a little saw that can cut steel. And I kept it, you know, under my pants, under my shoes. And I told my brother when I said, "Maybe we'll have a way of cutting out the window, the steel, or the floor when the train stops." We never used it, we didn't use it because there was no room. Plus I had an SS man on each side where the door was. Q: Outside the door? A: Outside. Maybe where the -- I don't know it they stayed there all the time or when the train slowed down and they came to a halt. You always had SS men, you heard them giving commands, you know. How he ma naged to talk to the Nazis, I don't know, but he trie d to do some kind of negotiation. We climbed in through the top into the tower and stuck mainly to bedlinen and valuables, which we could convert to money through our Christian friends. There was a constant heavily armed guard in front of the entrance, who occasionally came into the synagogue. We had to take the utmost care. Besides that, each time we risked our necks clambering in order to get in and out again via our unusual route. We tied the bundles of laundry to our backs, so that our hands stayed free for climbing. - 10 - My friend Julius, who very often made trips out, had meanwhile discovered that in a few of the buildings on the Schloßberg there were still Jews hiding. He visited them and took them money and food. The demand for food in general had risen greatly, and for that reason we had to undertake our 'robbing expeditions' three or four times a night. Since it meant each time a distance of around 300 metres, you can imagine in how much danger we used to find ourselves. What we achieved at the time seems to me today pretty heroic. But however bold my battle against the Nazis was, one day I got dreadful toothache and all at once became terribly cowardly. Anyone who has ever needed a dentist urgently will understand what I mean. My position was however far more difficult, as it was virtually impossible to go to a dentist. And my cheek grew more swollen by the day. What should I do? I cannot remember now who had the idea of going to the Barmherzige Brüder [= Merciful Brothers], who lived in a monastery. There teeth were drawn for everybody at no cost and – most importantly for me – the patient was not asked to give his name. Despite this opportunity I kept postponing my trip to the monastery. One day, when the pain could not be borne any longer, I waited for darkness and then went accompanied by Julius to the Barmherzige Brüder. After just a few minutes I was released from my pain. Without an injection, just with one hefty tug, a beanpole of a Friar had drawn the source of my pain. He had the tooth in his pliers and I had a hole in my jaw. My friend Julius always appeared much bolder, continuously helping wherever there was need. One day he was out and about again. When he did not return for a long time, we began to be fearful. The later it became, the greater our concern grew. Eventually I could bear it no longer and went to look for him. - 11 - Very cautiously I crept along the Judengasse in the dark as far as the Edelhof. There I was suddenly accosted by two harmless-looking men.'Gestapo! Your papers please.' I was so thunderstruck that I could not speak. I can remember only that after the initial shock I protested that I had forgotten my papers. Meanwhile the two Gestapo officers had become four, who told me to walk ahead of them. They took me to Edelgasse, where the Jewish community office used to be. Any attempt to escape was hopeless from the start, given four loaded pistols. When we arrived on the first floor of the aforementioned building, one of the thugs there beat me up straight away. Blows hailed down on my head randomly, while they yelled at me constantly to admit that I was a Jew and therefore a criminal. Moreover they wanted to know where the other Jews were hiding. Blood was already pouring from my mouth and nose when I thought of pretending to faint. They kicked me and hit me, finally also took my shoes off, ripped the belt from my waist and shoved me into a dark room. Vik{c}tor came, saw (with only one eye: he had forfeited the other in the First World War on the western front) and won. Within the first two weeks we had our first confrontation, which remained our only one. Loewenstein requested that the Berlin office, whose management I had just taken over remain closed on the Sabbath. “If you can persuade Hitler to stop the Risches (people of bad character)[7] from working due to the sabbath then I will close. Otherwise I consider it to be my Jewish duty to help out on the sabbath too.” As rude as this answer was Loewenstein took it in an equally friendly way – fifteen years older than me, but three hundred years older than me in wisdom. We came to an arrangement that was also acceptable from an Agudist point of view. And then a collaboration started that couldn’t have been more pleasant. There aren’t many people who I have been in awe of. Victor Loewenstein is one of them. This small man endlessly modest, but also endlessly powerful in his appearance was the bravest bloke I have ever come across. He had a deep and genuine faith and a clear, down-to-earth mind. He never shone with words, but always and everywhere thanks to his great, wise kindness and unwavering clever intentions. Only an intellectual fool could close themselves off to the impression left by this personality. Full of deep shame I remember my meeting, which took place one or two days after the November pogrom in the apartment of Dr Prinz. We had come together (Hilfsverein and Reichsvertretung), to discuss the possibility and the methods of continuing to work together. The only one who made objective suggestions rather than - 13 - losing himself in intellectual catchphrases was Loewenstein (Wilfrid was not in Berlin). A Zionist representatitve of the Reichsvertretung had nothing better to do than to announce that this was no standard for holding a debate and that the standards needed to be raised. input_chunk: would have hastened the same fate in Auschwitz as Gerda and little Peter. My magic placed me in dangerous positions in all the concentration camps, as I had to put on events for the SS rogues of an evening and had to teach each one of the peasants, so that they could do it all themselves, in order no longer to have need of the Jew. One day, I was attached to a group of workers under the protection of the Oberscharführer and it was the first time in the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp that 1,000 men left the camp alive. Naturally, I had to leave my wife and child behind, never again to receive a sign of life from them. I learned only later from the Jewish community in Prague in 1945, that they were gassed on the same day, 10 days after my departure, in another concentration camp with 800 children and the 1,000 wives of my companions. I, myself, was shoved from one concentration camp to another, until I was liberated by the Russians in Oranienburg Sachsenhausen on the 23rd April 1945. I was distressing and still wobbled with two sticks. I walked with sticks on the 10th May into a burning Berlin. The churned-up streets were empty of people. - 4 - I believed all the Nazis were dead, but, like vermin, they gradually crept out of their hovels and, 14 days later, they were all there again in full force. My first woe led me to Levetzow Strasse 19. The upper two stories were bombed out, but in our apartment a half-Jewish Doctor held a surgery. As I had no abode, the Mayor of Moabit gave me accommodation in the burnt-out Simcha room of the Levetzow synagogue and the Magistrate gave me food. I was really miserable and recovered slowly. I received approval from the Russian Command to cross the Czech border in prison clothes, which was naturally closed. I had to get to Prague to see Gerda and the boy, as I still hoped to see them alive. Besides, Gerda had stored my magic equipment with a craftsman of mine in Prague and this honest man handed everything out to me after 4 years untouched. Now, I stood lonely and alone in life, sick and mentally broken. I did not know left from right. Where should I now turn? To make matters worse, over the course of the years, I had forgotten Hettie’s address in New York. Of Fritz, I only knew that he had reached England with the last ship after 6 months’ imprisonment in Saarbrücken. As I really wanted to get to America, I rightly decided to get out of Germany and decided to travel back to Berlin. Still in stripy prison clothes, I entered Berlin and the Magistrate directed me to a furnished room, where I started up again as a magician. The other magicians lost their equipment as a result of bombings, while I still partly possessed it. I got appointments in abundance and newspaper interviews with my picture and in quite a short time I became very well-known there and, in the course of a year, acquired a rather large fortune. I converted it into rings etc. I contacted Hettie and Fritz via the resettlement organisation and the sky lightened for me after those hard, hard concentration camp years. I was in 4 concentration camps for four and a half years…, no kidding! With the help of the Joint, I got to America in 1947. I lived at Hettie’s and, here too, I got equally as big appointments on Broadway. Hettie assisted me, but as she could not stand Rudi, after a year, a change had to happen. I married again, a fellow sufferer, who arrived here a month before me, likewise, robbed of all relatives and spent three years in concentration camps. input_chunk: Schwalb, who was an assistant there and originally from Bratislava, and a Dr. Vilém Juikovič, who also had detailed knowledge of Clauberg‘s experiments. Dr. Clauberg had his own team of staff for these experiments, was in overall charge of all the procedures, issuing instructions and guidance as to how they were to be performed. The experimentation involved women having their reproductive organs injected, some were also given certain preparations to take, while others were operated on, causing serious damage to their health. I saw women who had been subjected to experimentation being removed from Block 10 and sent back to Birkenau. I saw how they had been weakened to such an extent that they were deemed unfit for work and consequently transferred to Block 25. This meant certain death in the gas chambers. The usual procedure was for them to be collected from Block 25 at night and taken off in trucks to the crematorium. In 1942, however, I also saw women just in their underclothes being loaded onto vehicles during the daytime, heading for the crematorium. The women cried out in desperation and many of them jumped from the trucks while they were moving. Physically weakened and mentally broken as a result of being experimented on by Clauberg, life for these female prisoners was completely devoid of hope. After just a few weeks in the camp, every prisoner in Auschwitz knew only too well that anyone who was physically weak ended up in the gas chambers. People outside the camp knew it too. As we were to find out after the war, the people of Auschwitz itself were fully aware of every detail of what went on inside the concentration camp. - 4 - Of course, Dr. Clauberg and all the members of the SS who served there were also well aware of this fact. He therefore also knew that the women, who had been completely healthy when he selected them for experimentation, were so weakened by what was done to them that they ended up being put to death in the gas chambers. During the whole time I witnessed these women being sent to the gas chambers, I would estimate the number of those going to their death as a result of Dr Clauberg’s experiments at several hundred. From what I observed, I would say there were a few dozen Czech women among them. It was while we were writing our book “Továrna na smrt”, (”Death Factory”) in 1945 that the full extent of the Nazis’ crimes became clear, including the experiments which Clauberg carried out in Auschwitz. I therefore asked former prisoner Frau Friedman to give us her testimony for use in “Továrna na smrt” which was published at the end of 1946. At that time we had no idea of Clauberg’s whereabouts. We thought he had been put on trial at Nürnberg (in the so-called “Doctors’ Trial”) and sentenced. We later learned that he had returned to West Germany sometime in 1955, and was once again attempting to cover up his actions. However, with the help of documentary evidence and the assistance of The International Auschwitz Committee, I was able to obtain detailed information. Approved and signed.

input_chunk: of Westerbork was put on “transport”. Just a small group stayed back. They had no idea where they went, nor did they know how long the journey would take. They were loaded into cattle wagons and had to stand with 70 people in one wagon without ventilation. Hot and without air, they stood pressed against each other, healthy and sick people. At times, they could sit on their backpacks. They left Westerbork at 6 am; at 10 pm the following evening they arrived at Theresienstadt. They once received food during the journey: a piece of bread with jam. - 8 - Upon their arrival, their clothes and a part of their belongings were taken from them. It appeared as if there was no rule about it. Her mother, for example, was allowed to keep the fountain pen of her father. They had to wait the whole night to be registered the next day and to be deloused. Then, they were put into barracks where they slept on straw. After three weeks, the transports to the extermination camps went off. Again, as explained before, families were not kept together; instead, men, women, and children were sent separately. Almost all the inmates who had arrived with them were sent away. Only the “stamps” of the “Dutch Baptized Jews” and those on the “Barneveld – list”[4] were kept back. The Barnevelds were a group of people who had shown cultural achievements. Some Czech and Danish people stayed back as well. When about 400 to 500 prisoners were left, new transports arrived. How remarkable was the saying that greeted the prisoners on entering the camp: “The Führer gives a city to the Jews.” The camp had a Jewish self-administration. Every now and then, a Red Cross Commission came. It consisted of a Portuguese, a Swiss and a Swede. Officially, no transports were allowed to go to the extermination camps. So, the Nazis had to think of a way of providing evidence where all the exterminated people had gone. They established fictitious cemeteries with fictitious tombstones. The stones were worked on, so that they looked old. The prisoners had to scrub and rewash the streets. There were so-called shops, but you could not buy anything in them. There were cafés, but you could not get anything to eat in them. There were so-called banks, and there was a concert hall where concerts really took place. At an earlier time, a film had been made about Theresienstadt in which the prisoners are shown e.g. sitting in the café, a glass of lemonade in front of them, but they were not permitted - 9 - to drink it. When the commissions came, the shops were full with food and their meat rations were four times as big as in ordinary times. Rita had to help building a barrack. Stones had to be lugged up a hill. She did not know that this barrack was to become a gas chamber. She also worked in the “Mica”, an industry essential for the war effort. Quite nearby was a concentration camp called “The little fortress”. That’s where you were sent when you had committed a specific “crime”; the punished never came out again of this camp. In February, March 1945, the number of people in Theresienstadt was very low. In order to show full occupancy to the Red Cross Commission, the camp was filled with Half-Jews, nomad tribes, gypsies, and mixed marriages from Czechoslovakia. At the end of the war, many transports from other camps arrived in Theresienstadt; the prisoners were delivered in cattle wagons; almost all were ill, many of them were dead. input_chunk: he was dead. Heart failure had shortened his suffering. I was then left with my younger son. I was very weak and hardly rose from my bunk. My boy, on the other hand, warned me not to let myself sink into this state of inertia. He insisted that as long as we possibly could we should get up and move about, since permanent lying had an even more weakening effect than some last attempts at bodily exercise. He may have been right, but by that time I had reached a stage of indifference in which the will to live proved a poor incentive. Removal. One day in February, 1945, we were ordered to move. Orders of this kind were dreaded, because they usually meant a severe worsening of living conditions, as removals were mainly carried out with a view to providing space for new-comers. They were thus tantamount to dispensing with even more of the precious space which so far had been available to us and which had been much too small up to then. This time it was to be a major removal. Even the Hospital had to change its hut, and the space allotted to our Camp was considerably smaller than before. Nothing was prepared in the new huts. For three nights we all, even the oldest people, had to sleep on the floor and a great number of people died of exposure. If up to February there had been some hope that we might one day be saved from our torture, this hope faded away during the following weeks. Now we were sure we were drifting towards certain death. Even in the ‘Home for Aged People’ each narrow bunk had now to be shared with another person. The food situation became - 3 - completely disastrous. Whilst so far we had received a warm soup fairly regularly at midday, we got it now in the morning at nine o'clock or at six o'clock at night. During the last fortnight, we did not obtain any bread at all, our only food being about a pint of thin turnip soup and one raw turnip a day. Up to this time we had sometimes received once or twice a week a little crust of dark bread, and even a tiny bit of margarine and sausage. With starvation progressing, people were usually first tormented by pains. Later on they became weak, and sometimes the feeling of hunger decreased with the increasing infirmity. Strangely enough, it was the tall and strong ones who first succumbed to the hunger. 75% of the men died, but perhaps only 25% of the women. We were at that time between 2000 and 3000 in our Camp, the “Albala-camp” which was only part of the big Bergen-Belsen compound. I was, of course, not able to assess properly the number of death; but I should think that there were one or two each day at the beginning, five or six when things became worse; and I am afraid a daily ratio of from 30 to 40 during those last few weeks will not be far off the mark. The sight of completely emaciated skeletons which later on appalled the world was at that time a continuous feature of our lives. What Occuppied our Minds. If you want me to deal with what was left of intellectual life in Belsen, I cannot limit myself strictly to these last weeks of abjection. Because if I did so, I would not have to touch upon this subject at all. These last weeks were characterised by an almost complete apathy. But before that time, we certainly had some matters in which we took interest. There was above all the question of exchange. We thought of Belsen as a camp of preference, from which people were to be sent on to neutral countries. Rarely enough such a transport of exchange came actually to pass, but the hope for it went a long way to keep us going. As to the military situation, we were by no means entirely uninformed. input_chunk: and vilification. In late 1939, I had to report to the Jewish employment agency on Fontanepromenade, like all able-bodied Jews. That employment agency had been created by the Nazis and “found positions” for all Jews, regardless of what occupations they had worked in before. I was assigned to work at the Lehrte railway station together with a senior teacher, a factory owner and an artist. We were told nothing else about the kind of work we would perform. The agency officer dismissed us with the words, “just go there, you’ll get a whiff of what you’ll have to do!” The chief inspector of Lehrte railway station, Bandmann, stood out because of his particularly nasty treatment of Jews. We had to clean the toilets of incoming long-distance trains. He put us to work equipped with nothing more than a rag and scouring sand. I meekly asked to be given a scrubbing brush, which made Mr Bandmann angry, - 2 - and he shouted, “You Jews are used to rummaging around in the filth, aren’t you? So get to the shit! Anybody who doesn’t like it will get to know me. You do know where I can have you sent to, don’t you?” I did this work, and after some time out of disgust I developed facial erysipelas. Bandmann didn’t want to discharge me. He enjoyed it if I did my disgusting work with my face reddened with fever. One day, he secretly followed me. I worked on a toilet that was badly soiled. A traveller had vomited there. I was just about to turn away in disgust, when I noticed him standing behind me. He brutally grabbed my hand and forcefully pushed it into the vomit. I cried with anger and shame. My feverish face and emotional pain caused me to collapse. The station doctor, Dr Schreiber, gave me a medical certificate and had me transferred to a hospital. I recovered and was discharged after eight weeks. I had to report to the Fontanepromenade office once again. My next job was at the Siemens Schuckert factory, where I worked with lead oxide all the time in the cable manufacturing department – a task that damages the internal organs and causes poisoning. The “Aryan” workers at the cable factory were given a litre of milk a day, but we Jews got nothing! I was quite content to stay there, though, despite the hazardous work. We Jews were not tormented, and it seemed like the head of the department, Baumeister, wanted to ingratiate himself with us just in case. He commiserated with the tough lot of the Jews in a slimy, insincere manner and never missed an opportunity to talk about his Jewish doctor, who had treated his family for years. But he only did this when he was by himself with a Jew. As soon as an Aryan colleague approached, he’d fling his arm up and voice a loud “Heil Hitler!” across the hall. He didn’t torment us, but out of personal cowardice he didn’t do anything either to make our life easier. In February 1943, I went to my work as always. On the 18th of the month, there were two men waiting for me at the gate to the factory hall. They were Gestapo officers who took me into custody [illegible] and took me to the former council offices in Rosenstrasse, where I spent eight days without - 3 - knowing why I had been detained. After that, I reported to the Jewish employment agency again. In Leitmeritz exercise in the prison yard was also on the agenda, but often, far too often, the cells were searched instead, and often daily for a whole week, so that we had to do without the necessary fresh air. Very often the exercise was anything but recreation: we were hounded as if we had to set a record. Then we returned to our cell, completely exhausted. We threw ourselves down onto the floor because sitting on the palliasses was forbidden. Often after such an event the cells were searched as well. Every guard was a law unto himself. One allowed paper cartons to put the washing in, another threw them out. A few allowed us to sit on the palliasses since there was only one stool and there was not enough room for so many prisoners to sit down. There were guards who were really inventive as far as torturing us during our exercise periods was concerned. When I said once to a guard that the treatment here was worse than in the KZ, he answered that it was in a KZ that he had learnt it. From then, whenever he was on duty I had to keep out of the way. As already mentioned I could have sent letters if I had had stamps or money. But how could I get money or stamps? That was sheer sadism. They had taken away my 450 Czech crowns. Now I wrote some letters and mentioned this money. Some months later the trusty showed me the letters – they had not been posted. The guard had not even tried. I tried to find another way to order a food parcel – we could not think of anything else. So I wanted to smuggle a letter out of the prison. I gave this letter secretly to a Czech fellow prisoner. A German fellow prisoner who had been the Managing Director of the Raiffeisenbank in Prague gave me away. The guard did slap me but he was fair and did not report me. I told him that I had been forced to write in order to get something to eat, since he had not posted my letters. Perhaps that was why he refrained from reporting me, and also because the letter was addressed to the Red Cross. In Leitmeritz it was not necessary to write letters secretly because the director was generous in allowing us to send letters; he even paid for my stamps. It was such a relief to meet this man – he treated all the prisoners as human beings. Unfortunately, every prisoner had to tell the head warder in advance what he wanted to speak to the director about, so complaints were hardly possible. I am sure the director would have stopped that at once. I know about one case when the prisoner invented something in order to be taken to the director. When at last he was received by the director he complained about being repeatedly maltreated. On the way back to his cell the guard led him to his office and mistreated the poor chap so much that he had to be carried back to his cell. If the prisoners had had the chance to do what they were allowed to do according to the prison rules or by the director there would have been fewer punishments. The guard was the power, the prisoner had no rights. I will always have fond memories of the director in Leitmeritz. It was to him that I owed contact with my sons. On 22 June 1946 I wrote to the examining magistrate in Leitmeritz in order to learn what I was accused of, so that I might be able to comment on it. I wanted to know the reason for my arrest. I received no reply. When I was released the examining magistrate told me that he had never had a letter from me, there had never been a file on me. input_chunk: Prague gave me away. The guard did slap me but he was fair and did not report me. I told him that I had been forced to write in order to get something to eat, since he had not posted my letters. Perhaps that was why he refrained from reporting me, and also because the letter was addressed to the Red Cross. In Leitmeritz it was not necessary to write letters secretly because the director was generous in allowing us to send letters; he even paid for my stamps. It was such a relief to meet this man – he treated all the prisoners as human beings. Unfortunately, every prisoner had to tell the head warder in advance what he wanted to speak to the director about, so complaints were hardly possible. I am sure the director would have stopped that at once. I know about one case when the prisoner invented something in order to be taken to the director. When at last he was received by the director he complained about being repeatedly maltreated. On the way back to his cell the guard led him to his office and mistreated the poor chap so much that he had to be carried back to his cell. If the prisoners had had the chance to do what they were allowed to do according to the prison rules or by the director there would have been fewer punishments. The guard was the power, the prisoner had no rights. I will always have fond memories of the director in Leitmeritz. It was to him that I owed contact with my sons. On 22 June 1946 I wrote to the examining magistrate in Leitmeritz in order to learn what I was accused of, so that I might be able to comment on it. I wanted to know the reason for my arrest. I received no reply. When I was released the examining magistrate told me that he had never had a letter from me, there had never been a file on me. On 2 October I had a longer discussion with the guard who was my boss. On the same day he brought me paper and ink, thus giving me the opportunity to submit a petition to the public prosecutor. He later handed it personally to the public prosecutor. Whenever he went off duty he took with him what I had written in order to give it back to me when he came to work. In this petition I described my fate in Theresienstadt and gave the names of about twenty Czechs who were in public life. The public prosecutor ordered these witnesses to be heard. Unfortunately they lived in different areas, all over Czechoslovakia, and of course I did not know their precise addresses. So the whole procedure took longer than expected. My file was sent to Prague, where the witness General Dr Pollak was heard, then they came back to Leitmeritz. After that they were sent to Brünn [Brno]. When four of the witnesses named by me had been heard the public prosecutor did not want to listen to any others and ordered my release. On 9 January 1947 I was taken before the examining magistrate who said to me: ‘There is nothing here held against you, you may go wherever you wish. If you want to stay in Czechoslovakia there is no reason why you should not. There are no restrictions.
