input_chunk: Dirlewanger division. Dirlewanger established a SS division which was constituted from prisoners who signed up voluntarily or were forced to. This division was deployed at particular hotspots, and there was little hope of surviving. The political prisoners did not forget the correct behaviour of the green Kapo. They ensured that Frau Klotzmann got the official certification and with it a pension (after the liberation). We also had to learn that in a concentration camp, it was not possible simply to generalize. There were pigs amongst the criminal Kapos, but there were also such types amongst those that wore the red triangle. There was more chance to find people with a heart with the politicals. We had to look for the humanity in everyone. That the majority of the political prisoners were decent, lay in the nature of the things. But the case of Klotzmann showed that also similar behaviour could occur with the criminals. Worst of all were the anti-socials. There was seldom a decent person amongst them. The struggle inside the groups for the roles lasted for some weeks. Then the SS gave in and assigned the politicals as Kapos again. Ernst Busse, German political prisoner became the camp senior. After the liberation, he became a minister in Thuringia. And now small episode which should epitomise what was possible in a German concentration camp: In 1938, there occurred in the „small camp“ in Buchenwald (see earlier) the so-called Jewish Action. That was those Jews who had been arrested after the murder of Rath. - 6 - There were very rich people amongst them. Gustl Herzog, who was the camp senior of the „small camp“, managed the jewellery and the gold that they brought with them. Some Jews could buy themselves free because of their wealth. Herzog then made their hoard available to them again on their exit. For that, he received the name: „Herzog with the diamond suitcase.“ Once, a criminal prisoner wanted to burgle him. He was scared away. Both met again many years later in Auschwitz. Although Herzog knew well enough that Osterloh, which was the name of the scared burglar, would have slaughtered him in cold blood if he had faced him alone, now they were both comrades again in sight of the smoking crematoriums. In this way, the fox and the hare do not add to each other’s misery in the time of need. There was always something happening. It was never monotonous, but it was a dangerous change. Each prisoner had his or her own account in the camp. This could be replenished from outside. A prisoner was only allowed to withdraw 10 RM per week. The rest remained in the account. Anyway, you were not allowed to have more than 15 RM in your pocket. Anyone who had more, was considered as a potential escapee and was punished. There were prisoners who received money. But there were also those who received nothing. The first resistance group in the camp was formed with the help of the accounts. And indeed, the 10 RM from the political prisoners were pooled together, in order to establish the so-called ‚mates fund‘. Additional food in the canteen was purchased for all political prisoners from this fund. Later it became no longer a purely charitable affair. Camp reports about the international situation at that time were passed on via this organisation. Prisoners, who worked in factories outside, brought material into the camp. As a result, we built a small transmitter and listened to foreign radio stations. The news was passed on. The Soviet Union was attacked on 22. June 1941, and in the camp there was great despondency because we expected drastic measures against the political prisoners. Now it was the task of this organisation to give the prisoners courage. So, we made our way, walking, to my father's address and the landlady hardly wanted to let us in the way we looked, you know, she couldn't believe who we were. And he then came out and, of course, we were together, which was incredible after all that time. His first job was to delouse me with all kinds of mixtures, then we went to eat. But I have to tell you, I never looked full, I ate and ate and I was continuously hungry, there was no end. And then after weeks of this, I finally upset my stomach and I knew this was it. I filled myself up. My father's birthday was in August and I had nothing else to give him, so I wrote down my entire experience for the year that I was away, totally, and I had total recall at that time, and I forgot all about it, but he didn't. He saved it and I found it after he died among his belongings, which was very helpful to me because I translated it then into English and added many things and now the Museum 08:09 41 has it among their archives. While we stayed in Budapest I finished the Gymnasium and then to the Jewish Gym they were very tolerate, you know, and I made in one year all six, seventh, eighth grades plus the diploma I got. Then, we wanted to go back and my father wanted to resume his practice. So we went back, but we couldn't find . . . we couldn't get back our apartment. Our furniture was being used by other people. Most houses in town were occupied by people who didn't belong to them. They just took them. And, someone who offered my father to put away things, put away so good, that when my father came to the door, he appeared in my father's suit, shocked that he had returned. And this was an old patient of his. The anti-semitism continued, it was not a very nice place to be, and it was like a ghost town. None of my friends were there, most of the Jews weren't there, it wasn't nice. All of a sudden, unnerving cries rang out through the night, awful screams: “Beat the Jew Lehmann till he is dead because he will not submit to the camp regulations!” The camp commander was there. “I want the regulations complied with!” And again, the stroke swished down upon him. And the dreadful yelling of a person badly tortured and in fear of his life echoed through the ice-cold night. The commandant had ordered 15 strokes. Later, it got about that it was an important professor, a mathematician from the University of Berlin … he had to stay in the “pit” for weeks. Then the SS started again: “The day after tomorrow, thousands of you have to die!” (Von Rath, the murdered ambassador, was to be buried the day after tomorrow, and because that act had to be balanced, sacrificial lambs were chosen). “A beautiful funeral celebration,” as we thought. However, we did not believe it. “I thought: “protective custody”, therefore protection against the “angry mob”. “Therefore the amusement will soon be over.” This … false optimism sustained me. However, it was noticeable: new clusters of faces came in continually through the gates of hell; a never ending train of Dante-like penitents. Then we suddenly saw in the brightness of the searchlights whole columns of prisoners in prison uniforms continually walking round in a circle. “Absolute reason expired at 11 o’clock last night!” Peer Gynt, Ch 10. How late was it? We looked at the illuminated clock on the tower above the SS post, where at a stroke he could strafe the entire place with his machine gun. We stood and stood. Gradually, it became brighter and gradually the knees began to hurt. However, no one was able to sit. - 12 - More and more cohorts arrived. Suddenly someone bellowed: “Move yourself. You are interrupting the shovelling! What is your job?” “Lawyer”. “It was”, answered the SS man. “Why have you not emigrated?” “Because I have an Aryan wife” answered the fool. “Oh, were your Saras too dirty?” It went on in this manner for hours. “Put your valuables in your hat!” I was in the front row. An SS man came up to me. “What have you got?” He searched my briefcase and found a tram ticket still with some valid journeys on it. They were valid for some time. “You won’t be needing that anymore” and he gave it to another prisoner who perhaps was being released earlier. A low ranking SS would not know if that was the case. He only wanted to rile me. Then we were dressed. First, we had to strip completely naked. All the scars on our bodies were noted exactly, so that we could not say later that we got them in the concentration camp. As a result, we became acquainted with the mentality of these pigs well-enough. They were the epitome of brutality, but they were ashamed to be responsible for it. Everything which they said was a lie. We received prison dress. I got army riding trousers which were too short for me and a striped cotton jacket. The underwear consisted of a shirt that did not have any buttons, a pair of socks and underpants. We did not have a coat, shoes or a vest. We only had a small cap … if we had it all. My family decided, as a form of insurance, so that in case one member was disco vered, one member of the family was discovered, at least the others would have a chance to survive, they decided we ought to split up. So the first ones to be placed were my two sisters. They were placed with a very devout Catholic family. The wife in that family had a vision of the virgin telling her to take Jewish children into hiding. So my two sisters were entrusted to that woman and her husband. input_chunk: the backbone so to speak, of the National Socialist system. In the beginning though the Gestapo was a very low-profile agency; as the National Socialist system was honed and radicalised, it came to ever-increasing prominence. At first, it was what its name suggested: a secret state police force, limited to specific areas and going about its business more or less under the radar. Later on, it became increasingly more visible, and the fear which it inspired largely silenced not only those in opposition to the National Socialist system but all moderate voices within National Socialism and the more or less independent section of the government. The following example illustrates this. The Reichsinnenministerium[2], in particular, the Reichswanderungsamt[3] in the Innenministerium, was responsible for Jewish emigration. At the beginning of the period covered in this report, i.e. the end of 1935 to the start of 1939, the Reichswanderungsamt was mostly staffed by officials who were previously members of the centre party or other political parties which were not the National Socialists. These officials had either been working in the ministry for a long time, or they had been shuffled off into this department, which was deemed to be unimportant, to get out of the political glare. The top officials, such as Undersecretary Mueller - a thoroughly decent and garrulous official who as far as I know belonged to the centre ground - or head of department Schmidt, who wore a swastika but whose attitude suggested he was probably a German National, were extremely obliging and did everything they could to make our work easier. They completely understood the Hilfsverein der Juden in Deutschland’s point of view that Jewish emigration, as long as it was not to Palestine - emigration to Palestine was managed by the Palästina-Amt[4], not the Hilfsverein - had to be to countries where the Jews’ capabilities would be an asset to the country into which they were immigrating. This brought with it a whole raft of implications: Jewish emigration had to take place after painstaking preparation, and consequently sufficient time had to be allowed for these preparations. Adequate preparation for Jewish emigration was one of the areas with which we were most involved: preparation in terms of - 2 - occupation, which was mainly professional retraining through the classes and institutions set up by the Reichsvertretung[5]. Further preparation in terms of language for which we in the Hilfsverein circulated not only extensive publicity but also established classes and whole teaching institutions. "Last not least" preparation by means of factual information about the conditions for immigration into the different target countries and individual guidance for emigration according to each person's abilities. To support this individual guidance the Hilfsverein distributed a range of materials, one guide in particular, ”Jewish Emigration”, sold tens of thousands of copies; alongside this, the Hilfsverein sent constant bulletins to its advice centres all over the Reich to keep them up-to-date about changes in the immigration rules, etc. All this happened in close collaboration with the Reichswanderungsamt, in fact, the gentlemen from the Reichswanderungsamt told us after the first guide was published that these guides should actually have been issued by the Reichswanderungsamt itself, but they would never have had time to do it, etc. To my knowledge, the co-operation between the Hilfsverein's advice centres and the official government emigration centres ran smoothly everywhere. With the exception of the requirements for individual guidance for emigration, the Reichswanderungsamt and its subsidiaries completely understood the need for Jewish emigration to follow the rule of law, this meant that all the emigrants' documents had to be in order and comply with the legal regulations of the country of immigration. input_chunk: I saw, out of 2,500 arrivals, only 200 walk into the camp. The others were sent straight to the gas chambers. This is also where belongings were left behind. We had to load everything into a storeroom. Needless to say, everything was “organised” here, and that also helped me keep up my strength. In June 1944 I became ill and got sent to Camp 8. There were 355 ill people in the block. I had typhus. On the third day, the notorious SS doctor, by the name of Mengele, came. We had to organise ourselves into columns of two, stark naked. I was in the fifth row. To everyone in front of me, Mengele was saying: “That way – that way – that way”. He then looked at me and asked: “Where did you come from? What are you?”, because I still weighed 80kg at the time. I told him I was from Vienna and I was working as a labourer. He let me step to the other side. Only one other 17-year-old Dutch boy stepped to my side. The others were destined for the gas – and they knew it, too. We had to go back to our beds. Next to me were two young Jews, who had come from Buna. Because I couldn’t eat due to illness, I had put my bread under my headrest. They both knew about it and said after the selection: “You can’t even eat, just give us the bread…”. They knew that they were going to die soon. On the evening of that same day, all 353 were gassed. Only the Dutch boy and I remained. We were put in another block. I spent four weeks in the camp hospital. In this time, I experienced three selections. The block elder always warned me beforehand and declared me the second block clerk. That saved my life. It was around this time that huge carriages arrived from Litzmannstadt. Four came every day, carrying around 10,000 people. Only fourteen per cent of them made it to the camp. I remember that once two carriages came from Mauthausen to Birkenau. The carriages stood on the ramp for five days. When we opened the doors, the prisoners were strewn across one another and could hardly move. Many were delirious. We had to carry them out to be loaded onto wagons and transported to the gas chambers, because they couldn’t walk any more. It was so horrible that even we, who were used to so much by now, couldn’t sleep for nights on end. A Viennese man helped me get a place in a work unit in Buna. I worked as a labourer in an electrical department. After a few months, I went back to Birkenau. Meanwhile, there hadn’t been any more gassing, because the Front was close at that point. In mid-December, five cremation commandos were formed. These commandos were tasked with destroying the crematories and erasing all traces of evidence. I, too, was in one of them. I was now able to see how the gassing process was carried out. Everything ran continuously, from the changing room to the gas chamber. The canisters that contained the poisonous gas emerged into the room through a shaft in the ceiling above. The dead were piled onto a small wagon and thrown into incinerators. I’ve worked out that from approximately January 1944 to October 1944 (the time of large transport carriages), around 3 million people were gassed. The people who worked in the gas chambers were eventually gassed themselves. There were to be no witnesses. I remember seeing a Kapo go out to work in the early morning with 99 men. input_chunk: and taken to the well-known Gestapo cellar in the Prinz-Albrechtstraβe. I franticly considered why I had been arrested. As I had shortly beforehand begun to prepare to flee to Hungary, I initially assumed it was because of that. The illegal passport station for this escape route had, in the meantime, been broken up. As I had still not paid any money, my name still did not appear in the records. I learned only too soon, what it was all about. The Gestapo had arrested my brother only the day before, in connection with the chest with the German Communist Party contents mentioned at the beginning and he had admitted that I was present at the burning of the papers. I was, thus, accused of aiding and abetting high treason. I was interrogated, which was not without beating and kicking. Then I was locked in isolation (3 steps long and 1.5 steps wide). I explained that I was not present at the burning of the papers, that my brother had only said to me that he had burnt them. Naturally, they did not believe me. My brother admitted that he had shown me an instruction manual on machine guns at the burning. Even my mother had mentioned my brother as a witness. She also explained that her son had told her he had burned the chest, but that she, too, was not there. She was held there from morning until evening, they did nothing to her, as she was already 71 years old. I was then put together with my brother a few days later, who looked really beaten up. He was also beaten in my presence, as he constantly contradicted himself. This meeting lasted around four hours. It was repeated a few times. During this whole time, I was in the small isolation cell. For one hour a day, you were allowed into the courtyard, hands on your back and two steps away from the man in front; you went ‘for a stroll’. Speaking with each other was strictly forbidden. About the other forms of treatment we need not talk about…., beatings and kickings were on the agenda. Abuse such as "Dirty shitty Jew!" was the colloquial speech. I was released on the 1st October 1938, as my involvement in the affair could not be proven. My brother received 3 years in prison, which he served, convicted and remained thereafter in Tegel under police supervision. On the 9th November 1942, he was deported to Poland. I’ve never heard anything from him since. Now, I attempted to find work again. At the Jewish-Polish Coordinators’ Office, I found employment. My earnings got ever worse and after Kristallnacht, there was no more work for us. Now, I decided to cross the border illegally with a Jew I knew and go to Holland. At the end of November we were there. My wife had worked with Dutch people and these bosses had promised us support. They resided in Amsterdam. This time, I wanted to go alone, because it was too demanding for a woman and child to run through the woods and fields and I wanted to make a request for her from Amsterdam. With my acquaintance, I travelled by train to Cologne. We acquired a good ticket from its environs and travelled with the narrow-gauge railway until we got close to the border. It was set up in such a way that we hoped to cross the border between 12 and 2 o’clock. As we travelled out of Berlin, it was around 2 degrees below zero. In Cologne it was minus 10 degrees with about half a metre of snow. However, it became colder and colder in the clear weather at night. input_chunk: a state of collapse. On the roads outside of the town soldiers and SS are going by car and on motorbikes via Leitmeritz to Germany. We are cut off from the outside world. Wild rumours, but unconfirmed. The commandant and two SS men are still here, but they keep very much in the background. Herr Dunant is here. It appears that he is not yet in a position to negotiate the repatriation transports as the governments of Poland, Hungary and Germany do not yet have any [diplomatic?] representation[13] here. – Arian partners from mixed marriages (Czechs from Prague) are appearing in the Ghetto, wearing the yellow star (so they are left well alone) and leave with their Jewish wives. The Czech police is turning a blind eye. – Everyone is so exited that not much work is getting done. Maintaining discipline is very difficult. At lunchtime the Czech blue-white-red flag was hoisted in front of the post office. Two red flags were hanging from a barrack. (All of this done by camp inmates). Lots of people out in the streets. It is being said that the Germans in the Protectorate have capitulated. We would be free. The Americans would be here in two hours. Three to four hours later disillusionment. The time has not yet come. There is still fighting going on. The commandant allegedly still here, awaiting the order to leave. 6 May 1945 It looks as if `a new world’ is now beginning after all. Yesterday Herr Dunant declared that he was now taking charge of Theresienstadt. Though there is as yet no written confirmation from Prague. The current Jewish Elder, Murmelstein (successor to Eppstein), has resigned from his office. The highest administrative body is the Ältestenrat[14]; Hofrat Klang, until now in charge of the law court, has been appointed as the representative of the Ältestenrat. For the time being the administration continues as before. Except that a 400-strong Czech-national vigilante group has been formed, allegedly on the orders of the police. Their equipment consisting of blue-white-red armbands and a wooden cudgel. Today a lot of aeroplanes. Apparently Americans. They were flying very high in the sky, but one could hear the humming of their propellers and see the fuselages brightly gleaming in the sun – it made me think of the hosts of heaven. – Rahm, the last commandant, is still here, together with a few SS men. It is cold and raining incessantly. Presumably that’s fortunate as it leaves restless souls are less inclined to be out in the street. 7 May 1945 Today at around 7.30pm Herr Dunant announced in French and German, in front of the Red Cross quarters on Paradeplatz[15], that the capitulation of Germany has been signed. Only in a few places was there still illegal fighting going on. He then requested that people remain calm and continue with their work. A magnificent spring evening. The chestnuts are in bloom. At night a nightingale sings in the trees near our window. The many lovely swallows from 1943 and 1944 have not returned. We can still hear gunfire: heavy artillery. Theresienstadt is now a strange legal entity: so to speak an extraterritorial territory of the Red Cross. 9 May 1945 The German capitulation came into force at midnight today. Last night towards 8 o’clock I was looking out of the window: suddenly a terrible bang – a house nearby had been hit by a bomb. Two people dead, one badly injured. The Russians were advancing towards German troops and the SS. Street fighting in Leitmeritz. Two smaller fires. Machine gun fire, heavy artillery and sub-machine guns. We could watch all of this from our window. Cosy it was

The physicians who were there, they have no wonder that he will die, he is so ill that he will die. Q: Your father was also ill? Did you know anything about --? A: I don™t know how. In my opinion, I told you my father was a humanist. He died because of illness, that™s my theory, but because that was such a great disappointment for him in mankind, that such a thing could happen, that people can treat pe ople like that, that this disappointment, because of this, he gave up. Q: You never saw your brother or your father after you entered Auschwitz? A: I told it at the beginning, I ha ve seen once my father. I told you that was this kommando, this garbage kommando that people, this cart was driven by people. It was at the place where they collected garbage. My father was not in this garbage kommando but somehow he arranged that he could go out from the lager with this garbage. The garbage of our lager was taken there. He told this kapo who was from our lager that she should bring me. What happened because the number. If you leave, not the person was importa nt, but the number. Te n people are driving the cart, they can go, eleven not, but ten can go. I was told go to the garbage kommando; they will take you out and you can meet your father. I met my father. Unfortunately, with the previous transport, my brother was there t oo, but then I was not there. I could see my father and I hardly recognized my father because he looked like, be fore Auschwitz like on this photo, he looked so young, not white hair or nothing. Then he was white and very, very old. Therefore, I tell you that was a disappointment in the whole mankind which took him away and not any of this. I met him in the garbage. Q: How long did you talk to him? A: Five minutes. You had to br ing the garbage and to take it. Q: You just exchanged news a bout your mother and brother? A: Yes, yes. Five minutes. This Auschwitz number is 8-13160. Q: Is there anything else that you want to tell about your experiences before the liberation? A: The story with my illness. I told you that I wa s one of the four most ill persons. This Russian military hospital was dissolved in ™45, Septembe r. In ™45 September, I was certified (??) tuberculosis already and they took me to Krakow because I couldn™t walk yet. They took me to Krakow, the university clinic. Ten more months, I had to stay there. I was there and I returned to Hungary ™46, the 1st of August. She slept with my little Peter in a bed and, as he grew, he did not leave her side. In September 1938, on the basis of an entitlement to an inheritance from the Freund family, Hettie had the chance to emigrate from the Czech Republic to America under the 'capital quota' without a Dollar in her pocket. We had, unfortunately, to remain behind, ever hoping, that Hettie would succeed at the eleventh hour in still bringing us over. Admittedly, the affidavits were lying with the consul in Prague, but the quota had already hit its limit, so that the thugs caught up to us in Prague. It was always clear to me what threatened us, but I was powerless, as our little mother was already almost 70 and our little child too small to jump onto a coal train, as thousands of people had done, in order to get to the port of Gdingen via Poland and, from there, via Sweden to England to save themselves. Even as Hitler entered Prague, it would still have been easy for individuals to intentionally jump onto the slow moving coal trains from the Czech coal region. We had to run towards disaster with our eyes open. At any rate, we had 5 good years until his entry into Prague in 1938. My businesses flourished and we could easier bear the evil deeds of this criminal from a greater distance, although the threatening danger was always known. After a night of pogroms in 1938, the sinister activity of the Gestapo and the Czech collaborators began underground too, until, one day, Heydrich was murdered and the death-knell of the Prague Jews had struck. The first transports of Jews left, consisting of rich Prague Jews, doctors, lawyers and industrialists. As we, luckily, did not fall into the first category, I was lucky enough, with 300 other strong people, to be ordered by the Gestapo to go to the formation of a ghetto in Theresienstadt on the 24th November 1941. We had to evacuate the garrison town and, as waves of hundreds of thousands of unlucky Jews from the whole of Europe flooded this small town, where the sanitary conditions mocked every description. Within a short time, vermin, disease, skin typhus, child paralysis and famine moved in and the people, robbed of all of their possessions, young and old, were stuffed in their hundreds into bulging wagons and transported like cattle to Auschwitz, where they never saw the light of day again. After train journeys lasting three days and three nights, people were beaten out of the wagons with sticks at the Auschwitz railway station, had soap and towels pressed into their hands on the pretext they went into the delousing station. In reality, gas bombs were thrown into the delousing station and the corpses were later burned in their thousands, so that the chimneys smoked day and night. If I had not later seen it for myself, I would neither believe it, nor be able to write it on paper. My family, Gerda, our child and our mother were naturally brought too to Theresienstadt and I was a member of the so-called ‘Aufbaukommados’ (Construction squad). Form and Contents : A letter dated 9 September 1945 reporting on the transports from Dresden to Riga, Theresienstadt and Auschwitz; the author’s personal good luck to get rescued from a selection through a doctor from Breslau, to get a job first in the camp orchestra at Auschwitz and finally in the camp office Ohrdruff in a leading position. No. 543 for further information (letter written by the same author) From Dresden to Auschwitz Paris, 09.09.1945 Dear Mr. Apt! Yesterday evening I received your 1b. letter. I will read it this morning, in order to reply to you in depth. Firstly, I do not want to miss out on wishing you and your family all the best for the New Year. I now wish for eternal peace for us all. Before I send you a description of the conditions in Dresden and answer your list, I wish to briefly report on my personal experiences in the last years. First, I must go back to 1941. During this time, I was in Berlin and had a very good position in the Jewish Cultural Federation as the 2nd concert master of the orchestra. Following the introduction of the stars for the Jews, the Cultural Federation was dissolved. My parents wanted me to go back to Dresden, as they had already begun to evacuate the Jews and my parents wanted the whole family to be together. On the 21.1.42, the first transportation from Dresden was dispatched. For the most part, it was middle-aged people. Only the young and elderly remained in Dresden. In other words, the workforce members of the Zeiss-Ikon factory were reclaimed. My parents were unfortunately not there and were transported alone. This transportation was sent to Riga. I indirectly received a message at the end of 1942 that my parents were still healthy and well. Throughout the year of 1942, the elderly were deported to Theresienstadt. Altogether, there were 7 transportations of around 50 people, plus one transport with wounded soldiers to Theresienstadt. I shall come back to this subject in detail later. On the 01.03.1943, this also came to an end, as the largest evacuation of German Jews took place on this date. The Jewish Community even had to pay for maintenance and repairs arising from the evacuation of Jewish apartments carried out by the Gestapo, with right of recourse against the Jewish residents who had been ejected! - 5 - Compulsory anti-intellectualism and forced labour. Of course, this material exploitation of the Jews must have a serious effect on their intellectual lives. The Jewish Cultural Association was banned, and their assets - including some private property - seized. Schools no longer had any status or influence. In fact, there were to be no more intellectuals. All teachers and academics were recorded in the official employment register as unskilled, and this was reflected in the low pay they received. Wages were set such that Jewish coalminers earned around 15% less than their “Aryan” counterparts. In Berlin, the forced labour programme extends to workers up to age 65; in Dessau, even people over 80 are liable for work! The work was hard, additional food rations were often refused, and Jews received no pay for holidays, breaks spent in the canteen or time lost during air raids. Arriving late for work or reporting sick were treated as acts of sabotage. Jewish doctors often received warnings from health insurers about being too ready to sign someone off sick. Those Jewish legal advisors who are still allowed to work have a hard time - endless warnings and being summoned to appear before the Gestapo, and always under threat of having their entitlement to practise removed. No telephones, no newspapers. It’s hard to imagine the amount of time taken up by having to queue to use public telephone boxes, given that Jews are no longer allowed to have their own telephone lines. In a few cities, such as Essen, Jews were actually forbidden from using public telephone boxes; there was no longer a postal service in the larger districts of occupied Warsaw, and Jews almost everywhere - including Berlin - were unable to get newspapers or bread delivered. In Magdeburg, the problem could be overcome by ordering newspapers by post. I don’t think there were any areas of everyday life where Jews did not suffer harassment of one form or another. Official hate propaganda. If at first the official hate propaganda - the wearing of the Star of David, for example - was considered “mis-judged”, before long more insidious techniques began to be used. In August 1941, Jews everywhere feared pogroms. However, the authorities explained to the police chiefs of the various towns and cities that this was not what they wanted; they were simply looking for guilty parties in anticipation of war with the USA, an event which the government had originally not expected. Apparently, there were disturbances in Frankfurt am Main and Breslau, and the military is said to have intervened with rapid success. - 6 - Party v. Military - New forms of harassment. Generally speaking, the Party reigned supreme over the military. Hence the introduction of new restrictions: wearing the Star of David became compulsory; a ban was imposed on the use of cars; and Jews were forbidden to travel second class on trains. On public transport, Jews had to stand if an “Aryan” had no seat; they were forbidden to go outside their local neighbourhood, or be out of the house after 8 or 9 o’clock in the evening; the wearing of medals was also banned. It goes without saying that Jews could not be admitted to hospital, even if their life was in danger. Any religious organisations objecting to these measures are viewed as suspect and immediately disbanded, for example the Christian Scientists and Catholic institutions such as Benedictine monasteries. Intolerable living conditions. With so many Jews living together in cramped accommodation, friction among them was inevitable. Jewish Community representatives acted as paid arbitrators, but were not particularly effective. It was not uncommon for the Gestapo to be called to disputes over certain privileges that one group felt they were owed. This is a post-Holocaust interview, and so I just wanted to give out some of your information first. You wer e born Hela Kirschner , April 8 th, 1925, in Lódz , Poland . You were in the Lódz ghetto from 1939 to August 1944. Then you were in Auschwitz from August 1944, and then to Stutthof , to Proust , and many other places. And when you were on the march, towards the end of the war, you were liberated March, 1945, near Gdansk . Answer: Yes. Q: Okay. So let™s talk now, what happened after that. The Russians supplied us with everything they could, but it didn™t take us long Œ w-we stayed in a group, maybe eight or 10 women Œ girls mostly, young women. And must be we ate too much food, or the dirt, because we were invaded by Œ by lice, and two days, three days after, everybody fell sick. And by being sick, the Russians were afraid to come near us, and we didn™t know what Interview with Helen Schwartz March 1, 2010 4 was wrong with us, because we probably had high temperature, and none of the girls was probably normal, and didn™t know what happening. But when the Russians didn™t come near us, we kept on asking, why don™t we get any help, or anything, to make us well? And we were told, either there were nurses, or they were Œ I Œ I s Œ to this day I don™t know who the people were who took care of us, that we have typhus fever. input_chunk: in Berlin and the General consul in Hamburg - father and son Rivas, if I'm not mistaken - were well disposed towards Jewish emigration for private financial reasons. They issued a large number of visas which unquestionably got hundreds of people out of Germany and into a very good immigration country. However, they made a lot of money for themselves from it because they actioned all requirements for character references needed by an immigrant and because they themselves travelled around Germany to check the authenticity of these references and were paid per diems for it. One day they were given notification by telegram from Uruguay not to issue any more visas, not even when the visa had been “promised". Since our emigrants were waiting, having given notice on their homes and packed their bags, the Hilfsverein was involved in this case and Herr Generalkonsul Rivas told me in these words: "What can I do if Uruguay tells me: You've earned enough, go away!". Among the South American consuls, there were even one or two idealists, in particular, the Brazilian consul in Berlin who was a liberal German merchant and issued hundreds of visas simply so he could save our people. He did not make any personal gain from it and unfortunately was put in an awkward situation for a time because of a Jewish scam. It hardly needs emphasising that English and North American agencies were not open to any National Socialist attempts to influence them and acted according to their own consciences. At the start of 1939, the immigration rules for all South American countries were becoming increasingly strict. Only Bolivia was until relatively late on still straightforward to get into. After the pogrom, there was in practice no longer any Jewish emigration policy - 11 - to speak of. Vanishingly few opportunities to immigrate were open to an enormous number of people, in many cases unsuitable, who had been forced into emigration. Anyone who was able to obtain the necessary affidavits went to the United States; South Africa was blocked, Australia only to be used in a few cases, even the whole of South America was barely accessible, even through illegal channels. The endpoint of the Jewish emigration policy was Shanghai because it was the only place for which no documents of any kind were necessary and no visa. The barriers placed in the way of all possibilities for immigration by the Gestapo through pressure and counter-pressure was the prelude to and prerequisite for the extermination of the Jews who remained in Germany. input_chunk: and was one of those which had been built in previous years at the cost of the Jewish community, in order to lighten the lot of the Jewish internees a little. In reality, they were two barracks in the backyard of a synagogue’s property. One was set aside for male and the other for female internees. The internees took the opportunity in good weather to walk freely throughout the day in the small courtyard at the rear of the synagogue. - 3 - It was a so-called reception camp, in which most of the time the internees only remained for a short period before their onward transport. Also, for that reason, when we arrived there were no more than 60 to 80 people there, the majority being men. They had been imprisoned together in the same manner without any choice, either in a raid or because of some sort of denunciations. Only a few of them were genuine ‘foreigners’. The majority had been hauled here under some arbitrary pretence. Amongst former acquaintances from Berlin, I met there the well-known theatre architect Oscar Kauffmann whose ‘case’ was similar to mine. The camp filled quickly in the days that followed. The KEOKH appear to have gone wild. They organised formal people hunts, did patrols in the streets and pubs, and dragged away anyone of Jewish appearance who could not at a moment’s notice prove themselves beyond any doubt to be a Hungarian citizen. Amongst those who were brought in, were people who had been born in Hungary and who had never set foot over the border, but whose parents had allegedly originated from abroad. Furthermore, in other cases, a foreign sounding name or a strange sounding accent in the pronunciation sufficed to get the person concerned brought into the camp. We remained three long days in the Rumbach-Gasse. Meanwhile, my lawyer had set all levers in motion and succeeded through personal contacts in having our case forwarded for review to the Inner Ministry which was the authority to which KEOKH reported. There, they either could not or would not compromise KEOKH and therefore stated that that the internment had proceeded legally. However, the person dealing with the case introduced so much humanity for my wife that he certified that she had lost her Hungarian citizenship “without any culpability and being unaware of the state of affairs”. On the basis of this decision and on the basis of an appeal to chivalry raised by my lawyer in which he pointed out that you cannot expose a recently married woman to the wretchedness of a camp just because she had married a man a few weeks before, who was now declared stateless, the provisional release of my wife was ordered. However, note well: she was not freed but merely “allowed out of the internment camp for three months” and at the same time placed under police supervision. The sword of Damocles of a new imprisonment remained hovering above her head. Even so, the release represented not only a great benefit for her, it was also of great importance because, as well as being able to work on the further progress of my own case, she could return to the apartment and secure it against confiscation. Meanwhile, I myself was taken from the Rumbach-Gasse to another camp in the Szabolcs-Gasse. Here, another totally different picture presented itself. This was also a camp - 4 - erected and supported at the cost of the community, but on a much larger scale. Two elongated barracks were built for men on a large piece of land lying on the edge of the city, and a one storey house for women and children was also erected. In the middle stood a large area meagrely covered with grass and furnished with some wooden benches available for the internees to sit on throughout the day. A high barbed wire fence surrounded the area with an entrance which was guarded by two policemen. Apart from that, the internees were completely left to themselves.

input_chunk: collect them from the police station. This was actually very dangerous for us. The other policeman then walked away. The one who stayed behind then looked at our papers again, which showed that we were Jews, returned them to us and said that we should find shelter somewhere. We later obtained false papers as so-called “Arians”. We were also not spared the raids that were constantly happening. When Dutch Gestapo officers once came to our flat, one of them asked my wife where she was from. My wife replied in Dutch: “From Maastricht”, in the particular dialect that was spoken in that area. The officer then stated that he also came from there, and was completely satisfied. Dutch Gestapo officers were often more harsh than - 4 - German ones. This became clear when we were stopped another time by two Dutch and one German Gestapo officers. They asked us for our passports and hesitated when we presented them. The Dutch wanted to take us away immediately. The German opposed this and said that he needed to double-check first. We were then asked to collect our identity papers the next day from the German Gestapo officer. When we got there the next day, the officer returned the papers to us and advised us to have a special stamp put on them so that we would not be bothered again in the future. We gratefully followed his advice. During this time, a friend of ours was taken away by the Dutch police and kept in custody. On the day of his arrest, someone rang the door bell to our flat at 11 o' clock at night. This frightened us, naturally. But we were reassured quickly again, when someone called: “Police here. Dutch police good people.” It turned out that Dutch police officers had made the effort to seek us out to reassure us about the fate of our friend. Finally, the time came when the Germans withdrew from Holland. Once we were finally able to move freely again, neighbours and lots of other people everywhere greeted and congratulated us warmly. We have since stayed in touch with our newly acquired friends in Holland and visit them frequently.

input_chunk: Ursel Finke had just barely managed to extricate herself from the situation. But now she needed somewhere else to live. The Daenes immediately offered to take Ursel Finke into their home. So Ursel Finke started working at one of the three branches of the Daenes’ lending library, - 3 - in Emdenerstrasse in Moabit, and went to Conradshöhe every evening. As the air raids became ever more frequent, Herr Daene urged me also to come to Conradshöhe in the evenings, as it was less dangerous out there. So after close of business I always met Ursel Finke at Gesundbrunnen station and we travelled together to Conradshöhe. Things went on like this for about a year after Ursel Finke had joined us – quite well under the circumstances. On 8 August 1944 I waited as usual, but I could not believe my eyes when, at the barrier, Ursel Finke walked past with a man who was holding her firmly by the arm. I knew at once what was happening. Ursel tried to throw her bag away from her, she wanted me to take it, but the fellow yelled at her to pick the bag up again right away. I was frozen to the spot. Later I learned that this was the informer whom Ursel had got away from that time at the Jacobsons. All the rest – how things went with her – she has recounted in her own report. It now fell to me, after the informer had gone off with Ursel Finke, to telephone the Daenes and explain to them what had happened. That same night I had to go and sleep somewhere else, because one had to reckon with the Daenes’ house being searched too. The other young girl had to go somewhere else as well. Of course this caused major problems for the Daenes – the two lending libraries being left without staff, and having to look for accommodation for me and for the other girl too. First I was able to stay for a few days with a customer whose attitude was very sympathetic, but the air raids were making everyone nervous about having a stranger sharing their cellar. People did not want me in their flat either, because if anything were to happen who would want to take on that responsibility? Herr Daene went to a lot of trouble, and through some customers whose political views were known to me I got a room in Weissensee; the owners were living out there in their summerhouse. I was able to stay there for about four weeks, and the story was that I had been bombed out and needed to spend my holiday there. Though my nerves were already in a bad state as a result of the first blows that fate had dealt me, they suffered even more during this period. Firstly having no occupation, and secondly the thought of what was happening to Ursel Finke. That uncertainty was terrible, and so was the question of how the other young girl was getting on. And then came the worst thing of all: A week after Ursel Finke had been caught, Herr Daene was arrested. In the factory where he worked the cover was blown on a group engaging in illegal political activity, which he was involved in too. This resistance group was put on trial and three death sentences were handed down. Herr Daene gave a speech in his own defence lasting an hour and a half, which ended with his acquittal. On 22 December 1944 he was released from custody. In the meantime I was always looking for somewhere to stay, as I was usually only taken in for a few days: everyone was afraid, which was completely understandable. I was in constant contact with Frau Daene; at this difficult time, with her husband in detention awaiting trial, she was always concerned about me and helped me. We had to totally undress which was very unusual, in Europe in those days people just didn't undress in front of strangers, there were men there too who shaved us every place and they sprayed disinfectant on us and they, they handed us this soap that had initials. It said RJF. And RJF meant Rein Juedisch Fett, translated Clean Jewish Fat. In other words, the soap was made from the victims, everything was utilized there. And of course, we didn't know. So they turned on the showers and "Schnell! Schnell!" we had to soap ourselves, and we hardly rinsed ourselves, they didn't give you enough time, and "Schnell! Schnell!" you have to get your clothes. Now, you didn't get your clothes, you got what was thrown there on the floor. If it fit or didn't fit, made no difference, it's not, it's as soon as it's "Schnel!." Now you can imagine how I felt seeing my mother in this place, and probably she also felt seeing me, but I have to tell you that as soon as we got there, she was not my mother anymore in a practical way. She became the child and I was the mother. She just couldn't function in this place. And, so my allotment of clothes was a black dress with short sleeves, and no underclothes at all. The shoes were the most dire thing because they usually didn't fit, no one measured you, and if they were very bad, if the fitting was totally out, you were doomed because most of the time you were on your feet. There were no places where you could sit or anything. And many people died on account just not having the right shoes. Your feet swell or were so hurt that they couldn't continue, but my shoes were acceptable. And they were both the same size, both the same heel because it didn't have to be. input_chunk: my employees, who were members of the SA or the SS respectively, suspected me to have made derogatory remarks about the new government. When I had to make a statement about this, the investigating office was very accommodating and rebuffed the allegations against me. Later, while I was away on travel, these employees called a meeting of the factory's workforce, which they were not authorised to do, and demanded my removal from my post. However, they did not succeed with this. I was then able to get permission from the regional councillor of the Labour Front to dismiss these two employees. During the period following, operation of the factory started to suffer, as it was regarded as being in Jewish hands due to my capacity as main shareholder. Our supply of required raw materials was curtailed or halted completely. Our travelling staff also had sales difficulties. This brought about my decision to sell the factory. The sale went through smoothly without any interference by the Nazi party in 1937. I myself spent the next few years travelling with my wife and daughter, which we were able to do due to our foreign nationality. When the risk of war became imminent in 1939, we moved our permanent residence to Amsterdam in the August of this year. At Whitsun 1940, Holland was occupied by the Germans. Raids were held immediately against the Jews having fled to this country, and also against Dutch Jews. Many of them were brought to the Mauthausen concentration camp. We remained undisturbed initially and had still taken the opportunity to send our daughter to Great Britain. As we were hoping to be better able to recover our assets that we left behind in Germany from Holland, my wife and I decided to stay in Amsterdam - 2 - for the time being. We expected our South American nationality to be respected still. We were proven wrong. When in 1942, we got back to our flat one evening around 10:30 pm, some Gestapo or police officers were already waiting there for us. They arrested us, but allowed each of us to pack a suitcase, and brought us to Westerbork camp that same night. Westerbork was really a transit camp. Most camp inmates were sent on from here. We ourselves, as foreign Jews, were brought to special barracks. Here, we were mostly met by Englishmen, [illegible] North Americans and also citizens of South American States, of whom many had obtained passports for themselves from these states only as a precaution. My wife and I were housed separately in the barrack. The furnishings of the bedrooms were extremely basic. Everyone just had a plank bed for themselves. We could not complain about our treatment. We were neither asked to do any kind of work nor were we exposed to any harassment. Three times a day, we had to report for our name being called. But the SS officers supervising the camp never stepped inside the barrack. The food was bad and not sufficient either. In time, we were allowed to have 3 more suitcases forwarded to us in Westerbork with our most essential things. We stayed in Westerbork for 4 weeks. We were then transferred to the camp Ammersfort. Again, we were brought to a special barrack that was intended for foreign Jews. The barrack was separated from the remaining camp by barbed wire and thus completely isolated. There was one bedroom for men and one for women, and a common room, in which some food and fruit was for sale. We were able to move freely in the fenced off area in front of the barrack. We also had to line up for roll call here three times a day, but were not harassed otherwise. The food was better than at Westerbork. After we were there for 2 weeks, the camp commander came to the barrack one day and told me and another husband to gather up our wives and take them home. input_chunk: The vom Rath Murder and the November Pogrom 1938 Frau Dr Spitzer makes the following statement concerning a conversation, which she had around the beginning of 1956 in London with the former Senior Cantor of the synagogue of Fasanenstraße in Berlin with Herr Magnus Davidsohn. There evidently only existed an indirect relationship between Davidsohn and the vom Rath family. Frau Davidsohn had ostensibly met Frau vom Rath through others and only then on some few occasions. One family lived at Prager Platz 1 and the other at Prager Platz 5. Herr Davidsohn had met the son of the vom Rath’s several times personally, inter alia, at Frau Műller’s. “He was a splendid young man, the example of a Prussian Civil Servant, with a wonderful, upright, open manner. A very natural and open young lad” It was in this way that Herr Davidsohn frequently asked him why “with such openness he would want to be a Diplomat” He intended to remain in the service of the state. As was usual in diplomatic service he was moved from one post to another. One day, he told Herr Davidsohn that he would be going to Paris. This was at the time when Hitler was already in power. Both father and son thought in a ‘good Prussian manner’. They did not agree with Hitler’s ideas and were anything but Nazis and for this reason the young vom Rath was presumably shipped off to Paris. At the time, he was 28 years of age. In the beginning of 1938, Frau Davidsohn told her husband in tears, as she returned home from visiting her friend, that an assassination attempt had been made on the young vom Rath in Paris and to the question as to by whom.., she answered “I fear it was by a Polish Jew!” A few days prior to this event, every Polish Jew had been deported or removed from Germany during the ‘Polish Operation’. Immediately upon learning this news, Herr and Frau Davidsohn went to see the parents of the young vom Rath. Both elderly and remorseful people sat there. Frau Műller, the friend, was Russian or Polish. Rath said “Dear Senior Cantor, neither you, nor any other Jew bears any guilt in this matter!” “I believe” said the father “that my son was murdered during the course of his duties. When we made this visit, news had already arrived that the young vom Rath had succumbed to his injuries. Approximately 2 days between this visit and the pogrom, word suddenly spread that at 1 in the morning ‘the synagogue was burning!’. input_chunk: some of the labourers that had stayed behind were engaged in loading all the machinery they had managed to save from the rubble onto waggons. Eventually, we were also loaded onto waggons and the train started moving. We were told that everything, the machines and all of us, were to be brought to Bavaria. Since the whole railway traffic was already in a complete chaos it was only possible to do so taking various detours. We arrived in Bodenbach but could not continue from there onwards. The train was standing still for a day, then tried to take a different route but without success. That is how we spent several days. We were under the impression that both, the SS soldiers as well as the civilian personnel accompanying us, were aware of the fact that it was impossible for the train to reach its designated destination but that they had still taken on the challenge in order to evade serving at the front; because everywhere we now went we saw boys and old men wandering around wearing uniforms or brassards. The rumble of gunfire was clinking all around us. All the regions we crossed and all the stations we entered depicted an image of pure chaos. After eight days of senseless driving to and fro, we returned to Siemensstadt on 20 April. Upon arrival, the carriages with all the machinery were left in the rain on the track whilst all of us were ordered by the SS to march back to Sachsenhausen. Even the roads were now all completely blocked; we had to wait for hours along the way and only reached Sachsenhausen after 24 hours. There, everybody was all over the place; detainees, forced labourers and refugees. After three of four days, all of us detainees were once again gathered and ordered to march in the direction of Mecklenburg. Again, we were accompanied by SS and, as before, they were utterly brutal and threatened to kill everyone who wanted to sit down or stray from the track. - 8 - The march led us from Neuruppin to Parchim where we finally arrived on 1 May after several interruptions and stop-overs along the way. Our journey of people had by then grown to several thousand since similar transport groups from everywhere had joined up with us along the way. Next to Parchim was a small village called Neuhof. There, about 7000 French forced labourers had converged. On our way there, we saw a motorcade of the Swiss Red Cross which was carrying American food parcels. They distributed a few parcels amongst us; the SS, who immediately treated us more humane at the sight of the Red Cross, divided us into groups of 5 and each group received a food parcel weighing between 4 to 5 kilograms. The parcels contained biscuits, tinned meat, sugar, honey, jam, and much more and for the first time in a very long time we were able to eat to our fill. On that same evening, the SS released the Capos from their duty who quickly dart off with filled backpacks. The Jews and the rest of the detainees, however, were driven on and some unlucky ones were still shot dead by the SS on the same day. On the outskirts of Neuhof we came across a half deserted camp that accommodated wounded and invalid members of the Wehrmacht. It was there that we made accommodation for the night. On the next day, all the SS soldiers that had accompanied us up to this point darted off in all directions. A few members of the Wehrmacht then took over control and wanted to take us to Luebeck via Schwerin but shortly after setting out we returned to Neuhof. During the following night, all the members of the Wehrmacht disappeared as well and we arranged ourselves in the camp. On the night of May 3rd, we heard wild gunfire sounding from the village; the day after, we saw that the Russians had occupied the whole region. But they did not worry much about us after their patrol had made sure that we were not carrying any weapons.

So, after we were tattooed, then "Schnell! Schnell!," they ran us through what was like a bunk, a wooden structure, and there were hundreds and thousands of them because the camp was divided into A-B-C-D-E-F. We were in 'A' camp, we were the . . . we just came and I think they waited for the visas for something, they kept you in sort of isolation for a short while and there 06:30:30 was space maybe for 100 people in this camp, we were 400 in this building. The way you have it in your museum there are no, we had no straw, we had no sheets, no pillows, no blankets and there was space for maybe three people in each bunk to stretch out, we were eight. If one person wanted to turn 22 sometime during the night all eight had to turn because there just was no way that it could be accomplished, there was no space whatsoever. And at 2:00 AM they would wake us up with their flashlight, again "Schnell! Schnell!," "Raus!" Raus!" And we would have to stand, everyone in front of the cottage and then we would look out into space, we saw these repeated, in front of each cottage, it was like black from the people, women, standing there, and the magic number was five, you stood five in width and five in length. The best place to stand, it depended how you ran out, you know, where you got your place, was in the middle. Number one, you were protected from being seen; number two, if it was cold and windy, the people somehow enclosed you. But, one day, as we were standing, you could stand there for hours regardless of the weather, hours and hours until it didn't jive all the numbers in the camp. And the people who didn't stand in the front line had to have their arms up over their shoulders. There was a person who was in charge of each block, the block "Aelteste," the block elder, and she would tell you "Rensid Naramana," you know they spoke Polish, but knowing Slovak so it was sort of, you know, I could figure out what they meant. And you know, if you tried just for five minutes to keep your arms at that, in that position, you feel like you don't have arms. And if you have to do it five hours then you can imagine what it was. input_chunk: We collected some timber in the near by woods and boiled them. It was a delicious meal, for we had never eaten any potatoes in the Camp. The farmers came to the train on their own initiative with a view to doing business of this kind. They kept saying that the war would be over in a couple of days. They seemed to be quite satisfied with the end in sight and their larders still well-stocked with all kinds of nourishing stuff. We had been told that the train was destined for Terezin, and we did not mind this at all. During our stay in Belsen, every now and then people had arrived from Terezin and told us that it was a great deal better there than in Belsen. We did not realise that from Terezin regular transports were being dispatched to the extermination camps in the East. But, generally speaking, we did not do much thinking ahead in those days at all. We hardly thought as far as the next day, we lived from hour to hour. Frequently while we stopped at a station, we had air raid alerts. Most people were too weak to feel even something like fear. But I recognise the revival of my spirits by the fact that I did. During an airraid at Wittenberge were allowed to hoist a white flag. We fastened a torn white shirt on a branch and showed it. Immediately the bombing stopped and did not start again until our train had left the station. I am wondering now whether this may not have been due to mere chance. But at that time we were firmly convinced that our sign of friendship had been acknowledged by the Allied bomber crew. Sometimes in the course of disorders caused by bombing, some of our people penetrated into military supply stores and brought home some booty. We also got from time to time a little food from Wehrmacht soldiers who were, on the whole, more helpful than the SS. Our train was guarded by ordinary soldiers who behaved decently, If it had not been for the two SS-men who were their superiors, we might have been thoroughly satisfied with our new ‘masters’. Nevertheless, we were - 10 - fully aware that we could not yet breathe freely. A very definite rumour would have it that the train was to be blown up by its own crew. It was only, so we were told, thanks to the efforts of our Jewish deputy leader that the driver had been dissuaded from obeying his orders. But who could assure us that this success was not only a temporary one? No doubt, more than one sword of Damocles was hanging over our heads even in those days of approaching relief. The Russians are coming. We no longer knew where we were. We only knew we were behind Berlin, for we had passed through Berlin, or rather we had by-passed it. Our train had been led round about Berlin by a number of suburbiar stations, where we had not been able to see much of the bomb damage. But where exactly we had got to we could not make out. We felt we were driven forwards and backwards or in circular routes, because what mattered was no longer to take us to Terezin but to prevent us from falling into the hands of their enemy - our Ally. We felt that the Russians were not far away. On Monday April 23rd one of our people was heard saying: “I think I have seen a Russian soldier”. The rumour spread with lightning speed. The guards got ready for making off, took as much of the remaining supplies as they could carry and distributed the rest to us. Then they cleared off, with the engine, and left the train to its destiny. Nothing much happened, however; there was some bombing, and suddenly the Germans re-appeared, brought also the engine along, and explained that it had been a false alarm. input_chunk: of culture. Later I became the film and theatre critic of several daily newspapers in Prague. In the year 1929 I was made the editor-in-chief of the Prague Monday Paper. Thanks to this position it was possible for me also to oppose the German Nazi regime abroad. After a journey to the Soviet Union in 1934 I tried again and again to point out how very close the inhumane methods of National Socialism and Communism were to each other. When National Socialism started to exercise its influence – via the Henlein Party – on the German Catholics in the Sudetenland, to whom I belonged from my religious and cultural background, I wrote the book Die Totengräber des Sudetendeutschen Katholizismus (The Gravediggers of German Catholicism in the Sudetenland) under the pseudonym ‘Christianus’. It had just appeared in print in that critical year of 1938 after the Anschluss of Austria. After the occupation of the Sudetenland it was no longer possible for me to publish in Czechoslovakia. I made efforts to emigrate together with my family, at the same time helping the St Raphaelsverein who mainly looked after Austrian refugees in Prague and got them out of the country, using the only route that did not lead through Nazi regions, namely by air from Prague to Amsterdam. Thus it happened that an Austrian whom I had been responsible for in the winter of 1935 soon after his arrival in The Netherlands sent some Dutch transit visas for me and my family. When Hitler marched into Czechoslovakia on 15 March 1939 I first hid for a few days at a friend’s to see whether I was on the list of those who were to be picked up by the Gestapo. As this was not the case I returned to Prague where my lawyer tried to get our emigration visas. These were refused three times. At that time my parents-in-law owned a delicatessen which was frequented by foreign diplomats. The wily chauffeur of the Peruvian embassy had soon established a private business with a Gestapo man to provide emigrants with such emigrant visas in return for an adequate sum of money. This chauffeur now contacted my father-in-law and in this way we had the visas within a few days. With nothing except ten Reichsmark in our pockets – our daughter was not yet eight years old – we travelled through Germany to the Dutch border. After a night in Oldenzaal we were taken by a Dutch police officer to the Rotterdam police headquarters in order to be officially registered and afterwards we were put into an improvised camp in the area of the Rotterdam harbour. To us the loss of our personal freedom and the bureaucracy of the Dutch police were very unpleasant A few days later we were taken from Rotterdam on a long journey southward to the refugee camp Sluis, an old monastery which at that time was the home for about two hundred people, mostly German Catholics of Jewish origin. input_chunk: of it! – I will continue writing tomorrow as we have to prepare for the night now; every evening washing yourself from head to toe with soap, except on those days when it’s possible to have a shower. Those facilities are good here: a large room with many showers that dispense warm water. Everything tiled and very hygienic. I can usually take two such showers a week. 22/09/1944 The things I conjure up in my imagination! Of course one is not supposed to do this, but the monotony and repetitiveness of the days here make this so tempting. – The strange thing here is that all the necessities of life, such as food, accommodation, clothing, laundry, medical care, washrooms etc. are provided free of charge. In return, one has to work for the community according to one’s strength and abilities. This could actually be an interesting experiment with Communism, but it isn’t because the Ghetto is not financed out of our own work and resources in a normal exchange with other groups; instead, the Ghetto’s maintenance is based on a fund created from confiscated Jewish wealth. – What puts human beings in a society to the test, that is to say a genuine sense of community and care for one another, as well as the readiness to submit one’s own interests to those of the wider community, is what many, though not all, here lack. There are many reasons for this. The main one is the lack of space, that one is never alone, never able to collect one’s thoughts, a life without silence, without any space to oneself. People are so close together the entire time that often they can no longer bear one another; and that’s when it comes to outbreaks of hatred, impatience, heartlessness and crass egotism. The atmosphere is not nice. The Jews have even lost almost entirely their ability to make jokes and to laugh about themselves. A good thing is the astonishing dedication to music. There are some very good musicians here: piano, violin, singing, true artists with a considerable reputation, who are a joy to listen to. In addition, a few good choirs (two secular, one religious). Especially some of the young Czech women have wonderful voices. Very beautiful performances of The Creation and Verdi’s Requiem (which was performed only once as more than half of the performers were put on a transport the following morning!!); also a few opera performances, though without costumes or acting, such as Die Zauberflöte, Die verkaufte Braut, Carmen etc. – There are also many talks and lectures, the particularly good ones by [Leo] Baeck, [Emil] Utitz and others. – I live in the house next to Baeck’s and talk to him and visit him a lot. He is one of the great personalities here. When I arrived, I was given a room in one of the large barracks, together with 22 of my travelling companions. The lack of space and with that lack of tidiness (no cupboards or wardrobes, the lack of cleanliness that it was impossible to get under control because space was so tight), were deeply depressing. It was in this way that I learnt that they had taken my husband and child. - 4 - I never heard from them again. When it was dark, I wanted to go onto the street to look for them. The Jewish shopkeeper was very friendly. The sister-in-law and niece fainted after the affair with the SS man at the door. They are now all dead. I spent 14 days wandering the streets at the time and tried to find out anything I could, but it was in vain. My parents were still alive. They were, along with 120 others, in hiding in an attic. At this time, the Germans had killed 40,000 Jews. Later, a ghetto was opened. All Jews had to go there ‘voluntarily’. It was a very small and cramped ghetto. We lived 8 people to a formerly very small commercial premises. I had my parents with me there, who only there learned of the disappearance of my husband and son. We all had to live inside the ghetto and work outside it. About six weeks after the ‘operation’ I found work as a tailor for two secretaries from the German Housing Office. The first secretary was called Irmgard Wieth. She was about 30 years old and came from Strasbourg where her father was a teacher at the grammar school. She was very enthusiastic to have found a good tailor and spoke to me often. She also enquired as to what had happened to my husband and child, whereupon she said “Why did you not hide the child?” At the time, I said to myself that she had to be a kind-hearted person, who sympathised and thought that I would possibly turn to her in an emergency. Like all German civil servants, Frau Wieth was very good at general management. She lived in a very nice one-bedroom apartment with a kitchen and bath. She was supplied with considerable quantities of food and clothes in particular. These were clothes which had been taken from Jews. It was these clothes which I had to alter for her. In November 1942, a second ‘operation’ began. In the very first night, I coincidentally did not find myself in the ghetto, but my parents and my daughter were there. I had spent the whole day working at a Polish lady’s. It was late and I said I wanted to go. She said that I had better stay the night there. Jews were not allowed on the streets at night, so I stayed. Very early, it was still dark, my daughter came. She had run away from the ghetto, so I took my daughter to work with me in the Housing Office. Whereas in normal life steady work for one’s livelihood provides fulfilment, regulates the need for nourishment and converts into social values, in the camp the minds of the inmates were focused primarily on obtaining the food which they had not worked for but were allocated. This concentration of mind and will escalated in the same measure as the distributed rations diverged from the minimum needed for life and the state of health of each individual deteriorated. The members of each family were occupied with queuing for the allocated provisions, considering and discussing how one could use them in the most rational manner and how one could increase their quantity. Food formed in every way the most important subject of discussions and disagreements. Memories of life in the past and dreams for the future circled largely around delicacies or special dishes. In this small social format of a community by coercion in the camp, the relationship between impulse and character revealed itself in its social significance. Large numbers of people who, in normal life, had been throughout useful members of society, increasingly lost the restraints on their character here and became antisocial elements. In this category one should count those who were involved in the distribution of provisions and who, to the detriment of the others, gleaned certain advantages for their clan, as well as those who, by shady means, achieved double and triple portions. Worse still was the theft of bread which was rare in the Neutrals camp, (however rife in the general camp), and also clothes and everyday objects disappeared regularly. There were fights for a cup of “diet” – a soup of better quality available in limited amounts mainly for the sick and for children – and the displacement of values was evident in the fact that even the utterly worthless coffee which, in any case, was readily available occasioned fierce arguments. In this context it should be noted that the Neutrals camp contained mainly Southern Europeans. The spirit of communal existence was therefore strongly determined by the mentality and temperament of these Sephardic Jews. Some members of the leading clique tended towards profiteering, others recognised this quickly. Then, one of the Greek Jews would rise, his coat draped artistically around his shoulders, and denounce the culprits in dramatic language. These would then loudly protest, - 13 - and soon the whole room was filled with fierce arguments between the parties. The men would scream at or hit each other, the women broke down crying. Eventually the hubbub would die down down and everything would return to the status quo. As hunger became stronger and the people weaker, they turned more and more apathetic and confined themselves to grabbing what they could. Courtesy towards the old and towards women had largely given way to a lack of consideration, and in place of a will to cooperate mutually and to observe self-discipline in the interests of the wider community which could have alleviated some of the difficulties resulting from coercion and deprivation, one could observe unashamed selfishness in many cases. These manifestations had little to do with genuine desire for freedom. Rather, they sprang from the depressing feeling of never being alone, never being free of the obtrusive noises or the desirable or undesirable curiosity of the other inhabitants of the hut, even concerning the most intimate matters of daily life. Any notion of freedom was further suppressed by the lack of space available for movement as well as the constant sight of the thick barbed wire and the watchtowers. Strongest, however, was the consciousness of being subject to a powerful force when exposed to members of the SS, at the daily roll call, during the checking of the huts, during the occasional supervision of the food distribution, on the march to the bath, during visits by the commander, en route to the dentist and during occasional particular incidents. And there was a little hut where you put them on or off and they served their hot chocolate or something and it was just fun. It was quite a distance, you walk through fields, but we were use to walking and we didn't mind that, and so there's summers and winters were spent that way except of course for going to school. And unfortunately, close to 1938 all this pleasantry disappeared. It happened quite, it didn't happen suddenly, but it came suddenly into our house, I would say. My mother loved music and she played very well the piano herself, and she spent her afternoons listening to music that was coming from Vienna, certain times in the afternoon. Once she listened to the music, expected to hear music, there came an angry voice through the radio. A man yelling and especially against the Jews. Of course, we then became to know that this was Hitler. And this was our first time that we heard his voice and what is behind that voice. And then, as he entered Austria, there were some refugees coming to us and they told us about how they had to disrupt their lives and run and come to us, they were guests many times at our house.
