input_chunk: joy. We did not always have it easy with him. He was a slow learner; I could not actually understand why. His mother was bright and I had not been a bad pupil. However, what Philipp had learnt once he held onto unshakeably. He grew up and became a master glass-maker like his grand-father. As a child, he already had a little girlfriend: Nelly, the daughter of the synagogue caretaker. He courted her for 7 years like Jakob and Rahel and for her love he converted to the Jewish faith because we had him brought up in the religion of his mother. Nelly was a good and gentle creature: I have to admit that I sometimes thought her a bit simple, but I saw that she made Philipp completely happy. It was as before. He held onto what he had once embraced. So, the years passed by. Nothing much changed with us. We all lived together and were often happy with each other. It sufficed for life and now and again it went beyond that. Nelly’s daughter came into the world. We called her Franziska after her grand-mother. The little, tender creation was so properly created to the joy of God and man. When the child became older, we often played music together. My son sat at the piano, I fetched my violin and little Franziska chipped in with her soft but clear voice. In short, we were a happy family. Franziska was 12 years old when the time came in which we felt for the first time the hostility of the people against us. First of all, I lost my job, then my son had to give up his business. It gradually became tighter for us. This did not bother Franziska. The child was always happy and satisfied. For her twelfth birthday we had given her a puppy. I still see her darling face, reddening in irresistible joy, and I hear the happy calls with which she greeted her new playmate. The most severe change occurred with Nelly. It had always been easy to frighten her. Now she became more retiring by the day and I noticed that she stood completely defenceless against the cruelty of people. She stopped going out; she did not want to see anyone; and she spoke only out of necessity. At this time, Franziska drew closer to her grand-mother. My wife had a very different nature to my son’s wife. She could not remain silent. - 5 – She reared up against every disparaging word which she encountered for the sake of her family. Only if she had the child around her was she peaceful and found her former happiness again. And the child felt that. The grandmother had more hold on her than the mother. Soon, it was as if one could not be without the other. It is now two years ago. It was a winter’s day and outside it was bitterly cold and foggy. I had travelled far out with my wife in order to fetch wood to burn. My son was in the factory where he now had to work. We came home and found the house empty. Nelly had been seized with her child and rounded up with many, who had been abducted, to meet a horrible fate. At first, I thought my wife would go mad when she could not find the child. The child’s shoes, out of which Franziska had slipped on that morning, still stood there; and the winter coat still hung in the cupboard. The January day was bitterly cold. However, the neighbours related that they had not allowed her to take it with her. My son came home and stood like us in the empty house. Then the search began in the corridors of power, of which there were many. There were no authorities to which Franziska and I did not go in the weeks and months that followed. This was a further branch of security duties in which much work unknown to the public was carried out In late September all the institutions mentioned here were merged to form the Sicherheitswesen (security) division. All need to be continually kept abreast of the changing requirements of ghetto living, updated and fine-tuned. Recently, for example, an Audit Office was instituted to continuously monitor the economic practices of the ghetto – that is, not confining itself to intervening only where an offence has been committed, but also wherever current business practices show deficiencies. - 4 - The extremely broad range of activities that had to be undertaken by the various subdivisions of the SW is best illustrated for us by a summary review of work done by our inmates in the first year: accommodation for massive numbers of people, kitchens, extension of water, electricity and sewage-disposal infrastructure, farm operations, hospitals, a crematorium, road-building, pastoral care for workers, children, invalids, the blind and the old: all these things were accomplished by the hands of men, women and children during this one year. 244 smaller and larger transports brought approx. 110,000 deported people into the ghetto; 31 transports carrying 44,000 people left for the east.- The 200-year-old fortress town of Theresienstadt, which previously had 8-9000 inhabitants, now accommodates 50,000 people packed closely together – people from all regions and all social classes, in wholly exceptional circumstances – wartime – which for the Jewish people in particular brought one of the most drastic political and social upheavals ever experienced. And individual human lives are the inevitable victims of this constricted fortress in which we are living. The young had to adapt; old people had to relinquish their accustomed way of life and submit to the community life. An immense task and an immense effort, the year’s achievements have only been possible by dint of self-discipline, sacrifice and self-denial. I have outlined the year’s main events for you. Now, as spokesman for the SW, I should like to make clear to you what is our attitude, the attitude of the SW, to the ghetto inmates. We are not a police state: we are the POLICE FORCE IN THE STATE, whose watchword is: “We are the ghetto inmates’ friends; we want not to punish but to help.” And the future? The strongly built defensive ramparts surrounding Fortress Theresienstadt have always impeded the development of this little garrison town. Previously, the will was not there, nor the tools, nor the money needed to demolish the rampart and enable a small town to expand freely. And Fate has ordained precisely the present soldiers of the fortress – the Jews – to undertake that work. Is it mere chance, or is it symbolic, that the initial breach in the walls, opened by the labour of Jews, is being made toward the south, the direction of warmth and sunshine? But why is the rampart being breached? Is it for a new railway route into the fortress, into the ghetto? However, it is our hope that the breach in the wall will become our new and happy exit route for our lives, out of the constricted fortress. input_chunk: My wife wanted to taker her life with me and our child. She only survived as a result of my survival. I promised her, in the event that we were not liberated by the 6th of the 5th, my birthday, we agreed to die together. And were I to get through this unending hard time unscathed? Had not dear God protected me often enough? In the beginning of April, there was a heavy night raid, during which our district had been pre-targeted in particular with ‘Christmas trees’. With the dropping of this many bombs, our living room wall also collapsed, which for me meant changing my accommodation as quickly as possible. In the morning, at 5 o’clock, I started to go to Schöneweide to Niesa. This accommodation I had already prepared, in the event the wall to our house collapsed, as through it our neighbour, the Nazi, had, of course, a clear view. Herr Niesa was politically disadvantaged, had also been imprisoned at the beginning of the Third Reich, but as he was ill, he was only under police supervision. Moreover, as a Mechanic, he was particularly necessary. My route to him was particularly dangerous, often enough there were checks and I had to hide. At 7 o’clock, I had arrived and time and again had to go into the wardrobe when anyone came. One morning, towards the end of April, the SA came to get Herr Niesa. Admittedly, it only concerned trenchwork, but how many had already been shot doing it? Initially, he wanted to flee, but his wife persuaded him well that he would put us all in danger, when they would search the apartment and find me in the wardrobe. With thanks to God, he came back in the evening. A camp was prepared for me now in the cellar, behind boxes and junk, where I spent a further 8 days. The Russians came ever nearer. One morning, we heard that the SA in Wuhlheide had hung members of the Landsturm, the Home Guard, who no longer wanted to fight. The next day, the shelling of Berlin began and Niesa no longer went trenchworking. When the SA came to get him, the women said that he had gone to work in the morning; hopefully nothing had happened to him in the shelling. It was a lucky thing, for in the night, the bridge was blown up, before which, however, they shot dead all political prisoners, who, beforehand, had to dig their own graves. On the 28th April 1945, the first Russians came and I could finally leave my hiding place. But, how did I look? Pale, scruffy with a beard! My weight…, 89 pounds! People moved aside aghast, as if confronted with a ghost, when they saw me coming. I, however, was so eternally happy and glad and thanked God for my wonderful salvation.

input_chunk: fell asleep. At day-break one of our Jews appeared and shouted: “The Russians are here! We are free!” I did not believe him. We had been disappointed too often. I only replied: “O, well, let me sleep a little longer”• But there was no more sleeping that morning. More people came and called: “It is true. The Russians are here.” - 11 - Everything belongs to you. The village, at which we had arrived was Tröbitz, in Lusatia. Although I could hardly move, my hunger oedema having become colossal during the journey, I dragged myself to the village. Some village children took our rucksacks on a cart. Of what followed then I have no proper recollections. It was so unexpected in spite of all, and we hardly could grasp the meaning of freedom. I only know that the Russians said: “Everything you find belongs to you. The Germans must give you what they have got”. Then I remember there was tasty bread and bottled fruit, and when my son and I had eaten, we felt satisfied for the first time for many years. My boy was looking round for accomodation, but Tröbitz being completely overcrowded he went on to a neighbouring village, Schilda, where he found us a place in the house of the former burgomaster, a Nazi, who had left. It had been ‘visited’ before and we did not find much foodstuff left. But we were glad to have a roof over our heads and real beds on which to stretch out our limbs. We took our clothes off, put them in the sun and wore what little was left in the wardrobes. After two days we were rid of the lice. Thypoid. Now when we might really have felt relieved, my son was taken ill with typhoid. Happily it was a light case and he recovered Last stages. At Schilda we stayed for eight weeks. We had no money, but the Russians saw to it that we received some additional rations without paying for them. The village people did not all behave alike; some were helpful and some were not. The baker's wife used to give the “people from the train”, as we were called, bread even when she had officially run out of it. People kept assuring us that they had not known what happened to us and that they were not responsible for it. From Schilda-Tröbitz we were taken to Leipzig, where we stayed in American barracks. There we were asked where we came from and where we wanted to go to. We stated that we wanted to return to Amsterdam. Our repatriation to Holland was carried out, but instead of to Amsterdam we were taken to an N.S.B.-Camp (a camp for the Dutch Nazis), which was a terrible experience. Happily we stayed there only - 12 - for a few hours, while another transport which had arrived before us had to suffer this hateful company for 10 days. From this camp we were moved to Manaelis, another camp where we were with German Jews and non-Jews. After another ten days there, we were conveyed to a quarantine camp, and from there eventually to Amsterdam where we were accommdated in emergency houses.

input_chunk: Then arrival, reception by the SS, luggage and body search (undressing in front of the SS down to one’s vest!), handing over all money and cigarettes, inoculation against typhoid fever. Then on to our accommodation. On the way there, I noticed the beautiful lighting and the colours of the houses and the trees. And with that began the first, terrible, seven weeks, in a large and rather dark barrack room, with colleagues, their wives and children, 22 people in total; on very hard beds, crawling with bugs and fleas that really went for us, making sleep impossible. We were accommodated in one of the large barracks, once built, like the entire fortress, by Emperor Joseph II. 20 September 1944. I was unable to get any further with this the other day, got distracted, was tired and lacked concentration, as so often here. The coffee you sent me was enough to make two wonderful cups full and had a tremendously stimulating effect, so that I felt a completely different person. But now the enjoyment and the coffee are long finished. The weather now is that famously good weather of Jewish religious festivals; we are between New Year and Yom Kippur. Cold, clear, thin air, but bright sunshine and at night gleaming stars. Most trees are still green, black-green, but the migratory birds seem to have left. Glorious scenery: in a semi-circle around the town, though quite in the distance, are beautiful mountains whose colours change every few minutes. Magnificent sunsets. But I cannot go to these mountains, walk on those tree-lined country roads into the fields and small towns and to the lovely river! We can see all of that from the walls, or rather the casemates, of our fortress that we cannot leave. These casemates are covered with a thick layer of soil in which trees and grass are growing – and one climbs up there as one would on to a hill and looks out towards the mountains, towards home, with thousandfold longing. One of these ramparts is right behind the barracks where our offices are. On it grow such charming small plum trees with round, smooth, silver-grey trunks and dark-green, laurel-shaped leaves, resembling the background of a medieval depiction of Paradise. During my lunch break I often go up those ramparts to sleep and to dream. Weirdly enough, one sleeps a lot here, though I never feel really bright and fully awake – perhaps because I am so used to having coffee, which I miss very much. Coffee is not allowed here and is removed from the parcels we get – if it hasn’t already been stolen beforehand anyway. The coffee the other day must have escaped the official’s attention. The food has improved since the spring, following visits from international committees from neutral countries.[1] In view of these visits, so-called `beautification projects’ were undertaken. For a start, the camp was `relieved’, that is to say, the overcrowded accommodation was dealt with by deporting 25,000 prisoners, so that only 45,000 were left. A number of houses were renovated. A music pavilion was ordered to be built, where an orchestra of prisoners had to give concerts. A children’s playground with carved wooden rocking horses was created; the most beautiful goods, which were unobtainable, were put in shop windows behind which there were no shops, but instead rooms with bunk beds; the menus displayed at the food distribution sites contained the most wonderful dishes that were not available, the menus disappearing immediately after the committees had left. This and various other deceits were executed by the Jews on the orders of the SS camp management. Once I had learned the ropes I ran it myself. Herr Daene issued me with a makeshift identity document so that I would have something on me if the need arose. Behind the shop there was a small room where I slept and could also make myself something to eat on a small stove. In the neighbourhood I passed for a war widow; I wore two fake gold wedding rings and was known as Frau Schneider, which was also the name on my identity document. Of course I was supposed to have been bombed out, and so I was able to live very comfortably in the back room. - 2 - Unfortunately there was not time to find somewhere for my sister, since she could not work in a public place because she would immediately have been recognized as Jewish. Luckily for me, people don’t immediately recognize me as being Jewish. And so 27 February arrived, when I learned that all the Jews in the factories had been taken away. I need hardly say what I went through when I heard this. I had suffered a nervous shock when we Jews were made to wear the star. At that time Herr Daene had managed to calm me down a good deal, saying that we should not feel ashamed – it was the Germans who should. When my mother died that was a second nervous shock, but when the round-ups at the factories took place I really didn’t want to go on living. The Daenes took me to their house in Conradshöhe and kept me there for several days. They were extraordinarily good to me, and so I did become somewhat calmer; the hope that perhaps my sister might survive after all lifted my spirits a little. The question of food was now rather a problem for me, as Herr Daene already had to provide for that one young girl and was also supporting other people who were in hiding. At the time of the factory round-ups he managed to hide three men and afterwards smuggled them out of the factory. Of course they had to be fed too. A Christian woman who was a forewoman in our Jewish section had a Jewish family of three living with her in her one-room flat; for them, too, Herr Daene provided some food, mainly bread and potatoes – he organised this through the factory canteen. He had good friends everywhere in the factory, and they all had to help. I usually went to have a ‘one-pot’ meal, because I had no coupons. Our old maid-of-all-work, who had worked for us for thirty years but had to leave our Jewish household because Jews were not allowed to employ Aryan domestics, cared for me in a most touching way. But of course she could not spare much of what she got with her single ration card. I thought that what she did was admirable, as she was by nature a very timid person. Then there was a married couple I was friends with who also sent me some coupons from time to time. On one evening a week I would go to visit some Jewish people I knew; they were Turkish Jews, to whom the laws regarding Jews did not yet apply. They also helped me a little. They too had several Jewish people living illegally with them, among them a Jewish girl whom I also knew, Ursula Finke. She worked as a dressmaker together with the daughter of the Jewish-Turkish couple. One dress she made was for Frau Daene. When Frau Daene met Ursel Finke she said to me, I would be happy to take that girl into my house too. When officials from the Hilfsverein and the Reichsvertretung appeared in person at the Reichswanderungsamt in December 1938 to effect a change of the terms under which the 30 000 arrested Jews should have been released just from the concentration camps, - namely emigration within a few weeks -, the following picture unfolded: the whole pogrom and the mass arrest of approximately 30 000 Jews was staged utterly without the knowledge and against the wishes of this agency. These gentlemen openly displayed their perturbation at what we were telling them. Personally, I remember a conversation with the head of the emigrant advice centre in Linkstrasse in which this official expressed his concerns and his sympathy for us. To these gentlemen, it was obvious that the condition imposed by the Gestapo on the Jews in the concentration camps, namely emigration within a few weeks, was unachievable or at least in a very short time would lead to complete chaos and subsequent collapse of Jewish emigration. One did not need to point out to these men that each individual case required time not just to prepare for emigration linguistically and professionally, etc. but also simply to get hold of the necessary documents. But the men also saw how the political situation had changed, and when we had convinced the Reichswanderungsamt to pass on to the Secret State Police a detailed memorandum by the Reichsvertretung and the Hilfsverein, endorsed by the Reichswanderungsamt, concerning the necessity of extending the period for emigration, the Reichswanderungsamt itself was in a state of anxiety and uncertainty, and asked us on the telephone what we, the named Jewish authorities, knew about the whereabouts of the memorandum, and whether we thought that the Reichswanderungsamt could ask the Gestapo about where the memorandum was. This exemplified the complete shift in the balance of power and the powerlessness of the agency that was once responsible for Jewish emigration. II. The Gestapo's position on Jewish emigration seemed to be conflicted and unclear to us at first. To us, the conflict appeared thus: on one hand the Gestapo was urging the Jewish authorities with increasing urgency to force through emigration. The Hilfsverein and Reichsvertretung were called to give reports with increasing frequency on how many Jews had been made to emigrate and how many could be made to emigrate over the coming years; alongside this Herr Krugmann and Herr Eichmann made it increasingly clear that the numbers achieved up to that point were insufficient and that more Jews would have to be sent away in a shorter time. On the other hand however the Gestapo did not see any need to remove the main obstacles in the way of Jewish emigration; on the contrary, while - 4 - they pressurised the Jewish authorities in every way to force through emigration, they regarded with a benevolent eye the propaganda emanating from Goebbel's Ministry of Propaganda which gave the impression throughout the world that Jews were total parasites and pests and which increased the resistance to immigration, as far as Jews were concerned, by foreign countries. The Auslandsorganisation[6] of Herr Bohle, which was particularly active and successful in South America, behaved in a very similar way because it could count on support from the large German colonies there. Without a doubt the relationship between the Auslandsorganisation and the Gestapo was very close. In the end, the Gestapo did not have the slightest inclination to engage with the Jews about their transfer arrangements in any way at all. At that time their idea seemed to be the expulsion of all Jews rather than an orderly emigration. There were a number of separate incidents arising from this which are noteworthy. A further attack had been directed against a merchant Paul Leven who was the owner of famous silk company nearby but he had never been very active in public. Leven had graze to his which wasn’t severe. Next to the Synagogue in Kiel all the Jewish shops including mine, which I had sold not long ago, were destroyed. Likewise, many houses were destroyed, and almost all the Jewish men were taken to concentration camps. The synagogues were burned down. I had to spend 6 weeks in the clinic drifting between life and death Later I received an instruction to leave Kiel for Berlin, which I did with my wife. In Berlin I had to present myself regularly at the police headquarters in Berlin, where I regularly heard screams, which had a rather depressing effect on my already weakened state of health. Later I was always required to register myself with the Gestapo, which was in a large building – I think in the Prinz Albrecht Strasse. The official there was friendly and approachable. - 2 - Kiel. Mr Hans Lask gives the following interview for the record: I was the owner of an art trade business, founded by my father and uncle in 1869 in Kiel. This was the official supplier of the court and incidentally was visited by the Kaiser Wilhelm II when he was in Kiel. There lived approximately 400 souls in the Jewish community, and I was the chair of the regional group of the Reichsbund jüdischer Frontsoldaten, and the regional representative of the local synagogue community. In my capacity as chair of the RJF I often came into contact with the late Admiral Raeder, who at that time was the Oberbefehlshaber of the Ostsee station of the Reich navy. This informal contact continued into the Nazi period. Admiral Raeder and many naval officers often attended the lectures organised by the RJF. Raeder occasionally mentioned that he had been advised particularly well by my uncle, at the time when he was becoming established as a young naval officer. No Nazi-sympathies were evident either coming from him or from the other naval officers, or from the unions. Even the university did not have a Nazi disposition. Up until the anti-Jewish Laws the legal scholar Kantorowicz and Opat taught there. The theologian Prof. Baumgarten was particularly sympathetic towards Jews. Even the student body were not especially Nazified. The press were restrained and there existed a good relationship between the press and the community and its rabbi Dr. Posner, which can also be said in relation to the general population.

On that evening the SA units were given free sausages, potato salad and beer at the Meiningen Schuetzenhaus. After they had got completely drunk they were let loose on the Jews. They smashed in all windows of Jewish homes and hauled out all young male Jews who they could find. They brought these to the police. The rabbi Fraenkel had a particularly hard time - he was both arrested and his home completely destroyed inside, when little destruction had happened elsewhere. The other exception was the synagogue, which was completely destroyed inside. During the following days the older Jewish men were also arrested. I was taken from my home at 9 o’clock in the evening and brought to the police station. Here we all stayed overnight. The policemen, who clearly condemned the actions of the SA, behaved well towards us. For some of the prisoners, who came without any bags to the police station, the policemen went to their homes to get the necessary things for them. - 3 - The next day they brought us in buses first to the Gestapo headquarters in Weimar. During the journey and on our arrival we had to suffer antisemitic comments. In the courtyard of the building all arrested people over 60 were separated out. They chased them up and down with blows and kicks to see how physically fit they were. In fact 6 of the elderly detainees were then sent back home. The rest of us were transported to Buchenwald concentration camp. As soon as we arrived at Buchenwald the SS people who were acting as guards behaved particularly roughly. Anyone clumsy or who didn’t follow orders immediately was shouted at and kicked. In the camp yard we were made to stand, counted and were mishandled, during the next days our personal details were recorded and we were made to join the Nazi party. Then all our hair was shaved off and finally we were placed in the barracks. There were 3 barracks in our section into which already Jews from all of Thuringia and Bavaria had been brought. Additional transports of Jewish detainees came continuously. Many of them were covered in blood and had large head wounds. As I heard it they were mishandled by SS people with rifle butts in the side streets of Weimar while on their way to the camp. Each of the 3 barracks had 2000 Jews in them fin the end. They were so full that at night time we couldn’t lie on our backs but only on our sides. Hygiene was particularly bad. There were no proper toilets only ditches over which you have to relieve yourself. Drinking and washing water was always lacking. A canteen was only built later, in which you could buy expensive clean water. You weren’t allowed to leave the barracks at night, even to relieve yourself. Their entrances were guarded by SS men with machine guns who often threatened to burn the barracks at night and so caused panic amongst everyone. The day’s schedule was such that each morning we would have to assemble in the camp yard at 7 o’clock. We were then counted and our names read out which often lasted hours. Before that we had received a small portion of synthetic coffee and some bread. For lunch we mainly received whale meat with vegetables and potatoes. In the evening bread and horse sausage was shared out, but often so little that it couldn’t feed everyone. On Sundays there was - 4 - nothing to eat. We weren’t expected to do any regular work. Separate from us in another part of the camp were about 5-6,000 political prisoners living in small barracks of about 25-30 men each. Rackers also constantly wanted medicines from me as clerk in the hospital. It was a dangerous situation. I did not want to put myself in his hands, so I always said that I did not have the key and so forth … Once, it happened badly here. There were about 100,000 prisoners here employed in the IG-Färben-Works. Amongst these, were approximately 10,000 French prisoners of war. We made contact with them. The French requested that we made written material available for them. We wrote this on the hospital’s typewriter. Rackers came behind it. He held an example and began to blackmail us with it. We bought from him the dangerous evidence by bringing him the food and medicines that he demanded. As a result, we actually possessed the leaflet again. If the directors of the IG-Works reported that the production ability of the prisoners had dropped, then the prisoners incapable of worked were weeded out. That was the feared selections. - 12 - The prisoners had to file passed the SS doctor naked. Every prisoners who could no longer close their buttocks were put on the list and gassed at the next opportunity. In this way, the productivity of the workers was raised to a peak through the constant threat of death. Lately, the gassings were disguised as „list F“. Allegedly, „F“ stood for „futtern / to feed“, only it was not bread that was fed, but the poison gas Cyklon B. The SS repeated their attempt at the selections to involve the doctors, who were prisoners, but they refused. Luk Wörl was transferred to the main camp and replaced by a certain man named Schuster. Later, he was succeeded as the number 1 camp senior by Dr. Budiaszek - a Pole. This was not a pleasant appearance. He was a Polish nationalist, who was the only doctor that stooped to carrying out selections for the SS. Here in the camp, Dr. Budiaszek educated himself as a surgeon. His victims were prisoners whom he laid on the operating table at night, which he had a preference for. This was very dangerous because there were often air raid alarms and the lights had to be put out. However, this did not deter Dr. Budiaszek from this method of operating, and as a result, he developed himself into a specialist at the expense of the lives of the prisoners. In addition, he was a profiteer and an ego-maniac. There was now a patronage economy in the infirmary for him and his friends. Dr. Budiaszek did not return to Poland after the liberation. He remained in Germany and wanted to go to the USA. Whether he succeeded or not escapes my memory. In any case, I have made a statement against this Dr. Budiaszek to the International Refugee Organisation (IRO) and reported about his disgraceful role in Monowitz. I remember the following incident about the methods of the SS doctors: A prisoner called Manfred Ascher was beaten to such an extent in the Buna-Werk that he was brought to the medical building completely lame and helpless. Yet with the yellow star -- I'm told on occasion I would have somebody follow me to school depending what the news was bringing. If there was a rash of people being whacked on the head, somebody would follow me to school. I didn't know this. Not necessarily my parents. So I did not experience any significant kinds of things but then I'm 6 years old. The realization of the star was not as much of a mark of the distinction. It happens later. But my life continues very much in the bubble that they created for me, in my apartment, some friends, that kind of stuff. I had some friends on the same floor. One floor below. And though it wasn't for the adults, it was for me. >> Bill Benson: Speaking of adults, your father was assigned to a labor battalion. What did that mean? >> Manny Mandel: Hungarian men were in the Army. They were in the Russian front. The work that had to be done by men who were not there was performed by these legions, battalions, of labor force of Jewish males who were not Army eligible. So they would be out -- my father would get a note or a phone call or a visit that said on Tuesday at 3:00, you'll be at the train station. You'll be gone for a day or a week or an indefinite amount of time. He was home and away with incredible frequency to the point I didn't realize when he would be home and not at home. I caught him with the bicycle discussion on one of his home stays. They did mining. They did agriculture. They did repair of roads, repair from bombings, heavy, physical work for which none of them were qualified but they learned. They were young enough to withstand that. input_chunk: near the top of the hierarchy a lot, those lower down the social scale a little less. WORK Work in Westerbork was voluntary. Soon after their arrival family B was working. Bobby was an orderly in the hospital. Mr. B was in the first aid squad. Mrs. B was working in the kitchen peeling potatoes. Mrs. B. only worked half a day and says that she liked the work and the companionship; a real Kaffeeklatsch. Some of the people in Westerbork held previleged positions which included their having privat rooms. The laundry chief and the chief of the kitchen shared one privat room and Mrs. B. got the job of cleaning it for them, Mrs. B. says that the main reason why she wanted that job was that it gave her the chance of being alone for a little while each day. Mrs. B got two little privileges: she was allowed to wash her laundry in their small basin - the camp laundry was accepted only once a fourtnight - and she got one extra ration. She asked the kitchen-chief if she might get a little broth from the kitchen. The chief, who, Mrs. B. says, was a thoroughly nasty man, said no. The chief of the laundry intervened on her behalf and fetched the broth himself to give to her. The laundry chief was a nice old man. He and his wife had emigrated to England. Just before the war he went to Holland on business. He did not return after the war. - 11 - Westerborg cont. The hospital in Westerbork was very good. It was staffed by a competent medical and nursing staff. They had a special hospital kitchen with a diatetic unit. The food reserved for the doctors was - unfortunately - every bit as good as their services; the cost was that some people had to go short. The hospital was considered a safe area and people who were hospitalised often avoided transports. Mr. B. was among those who pretended to be ill once to get into hospital and thus escaped one transport. He had a friend, it was the laundry chief who helped him in this escapade, which was quite comical if the implications had not been so serious. Later on a letter from an Ex-Westerborkian to a person still in Westerbork was intercepted in which the writer states that those people who were in hospital would not be sent East. The Gestapo was furious and just to prove their point sent all the patients from the hospital on the next transport. - 12 - Escapes. Some people attempted and were often successful in their attempts to escape from Westerbork. They were the people who held priviledged positions and had greater responsibility and thereby greater opportunities than the ordinary internees. German reprisals were very severe and these reprisals prevented many other people who might have escaped to do so. The sense of moral responsibility was as high as that! - 13 - Transport out of Westerbork. When the B. family was put up for the second transport Mr. B. was really ill in hospital, receiving treatment for his gastric ulcers. This treatment included his living on a milk-diet, a very effective cure in many cases, which yet leaves the patient very weak. The whole family had to go to Bergen-Belsen in spite of Mr. B’s serious condition. Mrs. B had collected bread in the Westerbork which they put into a wooden box and took this with them to Bergen-Belsen. Arriving at Bergen-Belsen they were met by the S.S. who had big Alsatians - vaguely reminiscent of Vught. The people coming off the train were told to put their belongings on a truck while they themselves had to walk ten miles into the camp. I occasionally met the detective who had interrogated me for so long at the time. He must have seen me with my friends, the English aviators, because, the next time I saw him, he said: “I am leaving Africa soon to go back to Paris. Could you get me some fat, cigarettes and other groceries, it must be easy for you as you are so friendly with the English?” …. I had sufficient presence of mind to assure him that I had nothing, but I begged him to help me to receive my repatriation quickly. At last it was my turn. In September 1945 I travelled, together with many French civilians, on an old German military plane to Lyon, from there by train to Paris. Friends took me in, as my flat had long since been rented out. My furniture and valuables had been saved, my friends had hidden them, and all the silver, linens, clothes, books were stored in boxes and suitcases. How lovely it was to be together again with all the people one loved, and who had proved themselves. It was impossible to find a flat. I found a furnished room and a position. I was employed by the “SER” (Service Europeen pour Recherches), and the useful, if sad work gave purpose to my life and helped me to get over the first, difficult months. We tried to find out who, amongst all the interned was still alive, we contacted offices, landlords etc., and reported to relatives and friends who wrote to us. I discovered many of my friends from the camp on the deportation lists, and it became clear to me - 10 - that, despite everything, I was one of the lucky ones. In Algiers, I had met an Englishman who appeared one day in Paris to take me to England as his wife. Thus, my story has a “Happy End”, and after all the disturbing years, my quiet suburban home near London seems to me a haven of peace.

input_chunk: where the windows were blacked out and nailed up with wood. The prisoners only wore thin cotton outfits and froze in cold weather. Sommer amused himself by having the prisoners bound together back to back with iron chains and facing in opposite directions. He made them stand to attention beside the concrete steps. Then he shouted ‘Go, go’, and they had to run at the double. Of course they couldn’t help stumbling. Others had to walk over them. They were kicked and bashed. I’m sure that this was Sommer’s own sadistic idea. I was in Buchenwald until 26 April 1939. Then I was released. I was not free for long, for in September on the outbreak of war I was arrested again. This time I went to Sachsenhausen, where I remained until the end of the war. There I was put to work on the brickworks which they were building. The foundations had not been laid properly and had to be re-done. The prisoners had to do everything at the double. If they dropped something or tipped it over, they were given additional punishments. There was a whole string of Dutch prisoners there too. One of them was Jan Telling, who now lives in Amsterdam on Populierenwg and with whom I am still friends. We correspond with each other, and he called his daughter after me. As the foreman of column 13, in which joiners, painters etc worked, I was in charge of up to 20 prisoners. I had to make sure that I always had work for these people, otherwise they would be sent somewhere else where they would have been in greater danger. There were prisoners from Greece, Belgium, Poland and France. In April 1945 there was an air raid. The target was a foundry on which building had begun in 1944. A whole series of machines had been brought in from Italy. Shells for mortars were manufactured in the foundry. On the machines they were shaped and rubbed down on a conveyor belt. The air raid was wonderfully accurate. At one o’clock midday I had been listening to the radio in the bath. The ‘alarm clock’, as we called it, was ticking. That meant an air raid warning. Soon I heard something in the air and off I went. Many large and smaller bombs fell on the site of the foundry. There were some 300 dead, all of them prisoners. There was no opportunity to take cover. The civilian workers had run away. Once the raid was over the whole workshop was smashed. Nothing more could be made there. Before the raid on Berlin another plane was shot down. One of its occupants had descended by parachute. He had got stuck in a tree and was brought into the camp. I think he was English. The camp commandant of the brickworks, Freesemann, a member of the SS, was going to interrogate him and slapped him because he said something he didn’t like. Then the airman asked ‘Are you an officer?’ Freesemann said yes with some pride, whereupon the allied airman gave him such an uppercut that he landed in a corner. Freesemnn jumped up and shot the man dead. His corpse was laid on the concrete floor beside the toilet and set alight. The intention was to create the impression that he had come down from the aircraft on fire. Freesemann was a really nasty bloke. It was said that he had found the body of Eicke, the notorious commander of the Totenkopf division, and had been promoted on that account. In April 1945 our camp was evacuated. Everybody was sent off. On foot, in the direction of Mecklenburg and Lübeck. We were supposed to be loaded on ships which would be sunk in the Baltic. The rapid advance of the allies prevented it. But the long march exhausted many prisoners and cost them their lives.

I can’t tell you much about it, as I did not get out of my cell, and nobody came to me. Just by way of knocking signals and other types of communication (telephone through WC etc.) I learnt about shootings and torture. Later I was taken to the hostage camp of Romainville; that was an old fortress to which a new section had been added. The entire fortress was divided; on one side were women, on the other men. The new section accommodated German soldiers (not prisoners). In this camp, one did not remain for more than 3 months. Either one was executed as a hostage or one was sent to another prison or on a transport. In Romainville, the prisoners were divided into political groups. I remember one incident. On one occasion, the men refused to do some work that had been required of them. Consequently, they were denied their soup. When we women heard about this, we declared our solidarity with the men. We stood in front of the entrance and prevented anybody -who might have wanted to- from fetching soup. Soon, a crush developed. The French guards fired shots into the air. As the entrance to the kitchen was inside the courtyard, the incident was observed by the German soldiers. We concluded from their calls that they were very impressed that we had not run away when the shooting started. They realized that there was a lot more to this. I remained in Romainville for 3 months, after which I got onto a transport to Auschwitz. We had been about 1,200 prisoners, women and men. After 3 months, only one young girl and I were alive. The transport was as usual. We arrived in Auschwitz more dead than alive. Until we eventually received our clothes and were sent to our block, -3 everyone had already been badly beaten up, had been standing naked outside for hours, had no hair left etc. etc. These matters are well known. The experiences in the camp were dreadful. They were only bearable because the camaraderie amongst the prisoners was very strong. I worked in several squads. For instance in the potato bunker. The easiest task there was peeling potatoes. However, each morning there was such a crush to get a knife, that I, being physically weak, only rarely had the good fortune to grab one. Having obtained it, I was deprived of it by a supervisor who gave it to someone else. Thus I always had to carry the heavy containers with the potatoes to the storage clamps. Each of these chests had to be carried by two women. It soon became clear to me that I would not survive such work for long, and so I decided, despite the danger of detection, to simply crawl under the table in the morning on which the potatoes were being peeled. This was possible as I was very frail. On another occasion I was in a squad that had to carry heavy stones. In return one received a weekly extra ration of sausage and margarine. Only those who gave their special ration to the supervisor received a shovel. My best squad was on a fruit plantation. Here, one could organize some food. We also smuggled some, especially tomatoes, into the camp. At first in our pants and on the chest. When this was discovered, we just carried them in the kitchen bowl. But this, too, was soon spotted. When there was a check-up, I just placed the bowl on the ground. When the sentry asked what I had done with the bowl, I replied in French, and as he did not understand, he let me go. Nursing Mental Patients in Theresienstadt Fräulein Marie Schnabel was born on 30 June 1897 in Reichenberg, Sudetenland, the daughter of a doctor. In 1917, she moved to Vienna where she was employed as a secretary in the Castiglioni-Bank until 1932. When her mother began to get ill, she returned to her parents and remained in Reichenberg until September 1938. Immediately before the Nazis marched in, the family moved to Prague where Dr. Schnabel died after a few weeks. They were expelled from their small, but extremely fashionably furnished apartment, by J. Rys, the leader of the Czech Nazis, who was later hanged by the Czechs. From then on, a time of constant upheaval and commotion began. On the day before the closing of the border, a brother of Fräulein Schnabel left the country and succeeded in going to Palestine with the last transport. Another brother was deported in June 1942 to Lodz and was murdered there. A card addressed to him came back with the note 'addressee moved away to an unknown destination'. In 1945, when papers and various other things left behind by those interned had been found in the camps and displayed in various cultural communities, Fräulein Schnabel found amongst them in Prague a shocking photograph which showed her well-built, energetic and mentally able brother, physically completely deteriorated and dulled with despair. Fräulein Schnabel, her mother and her sister had to change their accommodation eight times in Prague. Then they were notified one night that they would be deported. They were given 3 days to pack. They remained in the assembly camp under the Jewish administration at the Exhibition Hall in Prague for one night and two days. They were taken by train on the 20th of June 1942 to Bauschowitz and they had to march from there heavily laden to Theresienstadt. Those who were too weak for that were transported in lorries in which they had to stand. Fräulein Schnabel thought she would protect her family if she took a position as a nurse. She reported to the director of the psychiatric department because she thought that through her uncomplaining experience with her sister, who suffered from a nervous disorder, she possessed the necessary knowledge. However, her service as a psychiatric nurse and carer of the - 2 – female section under dreadful circumstances in the stalls of the cavalry barracks required a far greater sacrifice than she could have imagined. Also, in the 22 months that she worked there, 11 of her colleagues were deported. For one long year, she took on permanent night service so that she could look after her sick mother during the day who died in May 1944. During this time, a patient, who was in her care and who regularly stressed that she had been baptised and did not belong in Theresienstadt, died one night. She was Frau Neumann, who was a daughter of Theodor Herzl and who also did not conceal her anti-Semitic views. input_chunk: one or two hours in bed, on the third floor, when below us in the building all hell broke loose. Loud shouting, slamming of doors, smashing of china and glass could be heard. We quickly got dressed, but nobody came upstairs, and after about half an hour, things calmed down. The SA intruders had left, after smashing everything on the ground floor. We undressed again, but after we had eventually fallen asleep, perhaps around 4 or 5 in the morning, a renewed upheaval began, only this time much worse. I put on my trousers and jacket on top of my pyjamas, and before I had finished, our door was kicked open and two SA men ordered me to follow them. When I tried to take my coat which was hanging on the door, one of them threatened me with his pistol: “I’ll shoot you, you dog, if you take the coat!” All over the house, the same was happening. Most of the residents were families, ready to emigrate and waiting for their boat. On the ground floor, we had to stand facing the wall. My wife who had come down was thrown out with the following words: ”You Jewish sow, get the hell out of here!” After some time, it may have been around 6 o’clock, it was still dark, we were led into the street and marched off in rows of four. One man was barefoot. The streets were wet, it was raining. During the march, one man collapsed. The two men either side of him were told to drag him along. We arrived at the prison. There it was discovered that the man had died – heart attack. At the prison, we underwent the usual registration procedure by the prison staff: personal details, handing over of the contents of our pockets etc. I shared a single-bed cell with two other Karlsruhe men, a certain Dr. Fuchs, a well-known orthopaedic specialist, and a solicitor. We received one meal: soup and bread. Towards evening, we were led from the cell, received our belongings and, on leaving the prison, found large coaches waiting for us which brought us to the railway station in Karlsruhe. In the large underground passage connecting all the platforms, we were lined up; at least 1000 men from Karlsruhe and neighbouring towns and villages in Baden. While we were waiting, all the high-ranking SA and SS bosses paraded up and down in their uniforms, riding crops in hand, and amused themselves by insulting every known personality. Before leaving the prison, we had been presented to a higher-ranking SA man who was sitting behind a table and who asked us if we could put forward any reason for avoiding arrest. It is possible that one or two older men were released. - 2 - After waiting for several hours, we were hurried to a train that looked like an army transporter. Cattle trucks with backless benches. In each carriage sat a policeman in a blue uniform. No food! The train travelled through the night. At dawn, one could see through the slits in the door that we were heading towards Bavaria, Munich. That meant Dachau, an infamous and feared destination. It was daylight when we stopped at a goods station, probably Dachau. On all sides, SA men with rifles who hurried us out of the carriages and made us run to a siding where enclosed cattle trucks were standing into which we were driven amid constant threats, a problem for the older men as the access was about 1,20 metres above the rails. It was worst for a few rabbis, recognisable by their beards. They were made to feel the force of the rifle-butts. input_chunk: work, but there were Workmates amongst us, who literally collapsed as a result. When the first bombs fell, we had to turn down the heavy hit houses, whereupon many accidents occurred. With 6 other Jews, I was transferred to really heavy labour at Kronprinzenufer, the Crown-Prince Embankment on the river Spree. A ramp was constructed there and we had to load the barges anchoring below with rubble. It was very heavy and also very dangerous work, to which we were driven to in particular. Made nervous through haste, one of our co-workers opened the side wall of the barge too early, when I was on the ramp. I was buried in the falling rubble and fell into the barge 10 metres below. I was taken to the Charité Hospital nearby in an ambulance, with bruising, splinters and blood loss to both legs, broken ribs and a hernia on both sides, where both legs were put in plaster and I was told that I should remain at home for 6 weeks, as I needed to heal, as there was no room for Jews at the moment. The fracture wasn’t too bad, as I could have it operated upon later. With the fall, I had knocked out 4 teeth in my upper jaw…, but, despite it all, I was glad that I had come off easy. I certainly had that to thank to my trained body. After my legs had thoroughly healed, I had the fracture operated upon in the Jewish Hospital. In winter 1941, The Gestapo began to put my wife under pressure to divorce me. They explained to her that they would put me and our son into a concentration camp otherwise, as I had been seriously tainted by the trial of my brother and the accusation of high treason. In order to avoid all further measures, I consented and prepared for my illegal status, as I had got to know the Gestapo sufficiently well. My wife was required as a Handsewer First Class in the military haberdashery, but, as the wife of a Jew and a member of the Jewish community, she was not allowed to work for any Arians. She also had to leave the community and be re-baptised. On 14.01.1942, I was divorced and moved to a Jewish family at 12 Richthofenstraße, where I took an empty room. Nevertheless, with the help of an acquaintance, I continued to provide my wife with the necessaries. Mostly, we met at my mother’s in Gormannstraße in Altersheim. On the 7.4.1942, I was transferred by the labour exchange to the Klüssendorf Machine Factory in Spandau. There, I learnt to become a Moulder and Welder and was meant to work in armaments. We were around 200 Jews and mostly had to do the night shift. At first, the working day lasted 8 hours and later 10. It so often happened that Jews were collected from there during this time. As I was skilled and did good work, I was on a good footing with the Master and the Fitter. The man, admittedly, wore a party badge, but it so often happened that he put a few sandwiches in my pockets at his checkpoint. I was able to stop the Fitter being involved in a theft, which had the advantage for me that I was always aware about collection and whether I was there. He never named names. As a result of my work, I now came to the hardest and most complicated machine, but I now knew that I was indispensable on their list. I had now been working for 5 months on the machine, which dealt with the cooling of oil with acid. As a result of the affects of this substance, I got such heavily swollen feet, that I had to be registered sick. I spent approximately 3 weeks in the Jewish Hospital and was to return to work on 1.3.1943.

The family might not be interested, but an archive will be able to put history together, and without our history we have no future. Q: Well, Amy Gottlieb, it™s been a real pleasure talking to you. Your book, ﬁMen of Visionﬂ is something people should read if they want to know about what Britain did, and the stories that you tell is particularly poignant now when we have 50-80 million refugees in the world, and how difficult it is, and how much care it takes. And the care that you™ve given these people, I™m sure they all thank you, and we thank you for being here. A: Thank you. And I must say that there are volunteers today from many countries of the world helping refugees overseas. I only hope they get the kind of the care that the British gave to the refugees from Germany and Austria before the war and during the war, and after the war. Q: Yes, this history must be a repetition for you over and over again. A: Yes, you see the same kind of things happening that happened before. If I were younger, I would go out and help. Q: I™m sure. A: Thank you for inviting me. Q: Thank you. A: [Badge shown.] The badge that you see was given to all members of Jewish Relief Units who volunteered to go overseas during and after the war. This was the badge that the Central British Fund had set up for us so that we would be recognized as a Jewish team, so that survivors who saw the Shield of David would realize that we were Jews who had come to help them, and perhaps ease their burden somewhat.
